e: he had learned from his mother that he would die if he killed Hector, but if he did not do so would return home and end his days in old age, nevertheless dared, choosing rather to help and avenge his lover Patroclus, not only to die for him, but also to follow the dead man in death.”1) These are the καλαὶ ἐλπίδες of those ὅσοις τὸν βίον σωφρόνως διελθεῖν ὑπῆρξεν,2) these the conceptions which made Achilles and his circle of myth the center of a whole large class of funerary scenes. Through the virtue of the heroic life death is overcome and eternally blessed life is won. Immortality falls to the excellent. Blessedness is the reward of toil. To the ignoble it does not fall. Death indeed is the lot of all, and mournfully Homer laments that the idle man dies the same as he who has accomplished much; but virtue leads the noble to immortality in the realm of light. Γνῶθι μετ᾽ εὐσεβέεσσιν εὔφρονα Δωρίδα κεῖσθαι, Ἀντ᾽ ἀρετῆς ἱερὸν χῶρον ἀνευρομένην· Οὐ γὰρ ἁπᾶσιν ὁμῶς θάνατος βαρύς· ἀλλ᾽ ὅτις ἐσθλός, Οὗτος καὶ θανάτου κοῦφον ἀπέσχε τέλος.3) In these ideas we find the higher resolution of those sad reflections that attach to Harmonia’s bridal ornament. In the domain of material life only misery and lamentation follow it. Every wedding song turns into a dirge, and though all the immortals glorify the wedding feast of Peleus by their presence, as the gods also bring gifts to the weddings of Harmonia and Ariadne, yet unending sorrow is reserved for Thetis. The same lot is allotted to every mother; the laughing joy of the wedding night will one day reach her ears in gloom. Is she therefore to withdraw from the destiny of her sex? The commandment of Dionysus demands otherwise of her. The phallic god wishes her to wear the bridal ornament and thereby to prepare herself for union with himself. Two stages of life run side by side here, as in all mysteries: that of the lower world of becoming and that of the higher world of being. The closest union links the two. They pass constantly into one another: if at birth the soul descends into the realm of change, into which the genius leads it, so at death it returns to that of being. If at birth it takes on the garment of the body, so at death it lays aside its burden again. The constant transition from black to white has this higher relation in itself too. The two colors [PDF 89] — 75 — designate not only tellurian becoming and passing away, but also the ὁδὸς ἄνω καὶ κάτω, the entry into matter and the return from it. On this higher stage what appeared black on the lower stage of sensual life becomes white. In place of the black color of mourning, which corresponds to the tellurian conception, white is chosen, which represents the higher mystery idea. In Dionysus both stages are united. He lives at once in the dark tellurian sphere and in the higher sphere of light: there subject to change, here unchangeable. Those initiated into his rites share in the same double nature. Their corporeal existence stands in indissoluble connection with the incorporeal, and only through the fulfillment of the material destiny can the higher be won. For woman this connection of corporeal with extracorporeal existence has a twofold significance, on account of her preeminently material earthly nature. To the female sex the Dionysian cult offers the fulfillment of its highest hope. It is calculated above all for the nature of woman. It promises not only satisfaction to sensuality, but makes of this also the foundation of a better hope. In one idea both flow together, the satisfaction of the material and of the supersensible needs. Love becomes religious feeling, motherhood the fulfillment of the twofold, the corporeal and the psychic, destiny. To every stage of female nature Dionysus gives its due. He founds the spiritual life of woman not on suppression but on the regulated satisfaction of her material being, and so becomes in the fullest sense the god of initiation of the female sex. To every mother he offers Ariadne’s crown, and secures to her eternal duration in the region of the shining stars of heaven. Through the Dionysian consecration of marriage the curse that clings to the bridal ornament is removed. Through childbearing woman attains union with her god.1) Man is by nature the image of Dionysus; woman, however, requires for her exaltation man and sexual union with him.2) 7. It will be well at this point to recall the idea in the pursuit of which we have arrived at this development of the Dionysian religion in the ancient world of the tombs. o: brannten Erde in den Gräbern auf jenen thönernen Sarg zurückgeführt, in welchem Dionysos die ihm von Theseus überlassene Ariadne auf Naxos beisetzt, und im Anschluß hieran die Vereinigung aller jener physischen Momente, welche die stoffliche Grundlage der Bacchusidee bilden, in der Terracotte nachgewiesen. Auch darin erschien uns diese als vollkommener Ausdruck der Dionysos-Religion, daß sie in der Vereinigung des weiblichen Stoffes mit der männlichen Kraft jenem das Uebergewicht läßt. Das gleiche Verhältniß kehrt nun in dem Monde wieder, und Dionysos gehört auch der Mondregion an. Wir haben ihn bisher auf zwei Stufen des Kosmos gefunden, zuerst in seiner Vereinigung mit dem tellurischen Stoffe, den er als Träger der männlichen Kraft in Gestalt der chthonischen Gewässer und des chthonischen Feuers durchdringt, dann wieder als leuchtende Sonne, als himmlischen Phallus, apollinischer Lichtnatur verwandt, aber als stofflich zeugender Helios der metaphysisch reinen Apollonatur untergeordnet. Jetzt stellt er sich uns in einer dritten Gestalt dar. Er kehrt wieder als Lunus Deus, als νυκτοφαής und σύνδρομος μήνης, der den nächtlichen Reigen der leuchtenden Himmelsgestirne anführt, 1) und die ihm Geweihten gleich Ariadne's Krone unter die Sterne aufnimmt. In dieser Lunus-Natur führt er die tellurische und solarische Potenz zur Einheit zurück. Alle Bestandtheile seines physischen Wesens sind wie in der gebrannten Erde, so im Monde vereinigt. Nach der antiken, besonders der orphischen Auffassung nimmt der Mond eine Mittelstellung zwischen Erde und Sonne ein. Stofflich, wie die Erde, und darum als ἑτέρη γῆ οὐρανίη oder auch als olympische Erde bezeichnet, 2) heißt er der reinste der irdischen, der unreinste der himmlischen Körper. Er liegt auf der Grenze zweier Welten, der tellurischen, in welcher das Werden, und der solarischen, in welcher das Sein wohnt, und vereinigt in sich beider Natur. Von der Sonne borgt er sein Licht, mit der Erde theilt er die stoffliche Natur. Er ist wie diese eine wahre γῆ, Berge, Flüsse, Städte, sind auf ihm zu finden, 3) aber er ist nicht eine
e: clay in the tombs back to that earthen coffin in which Dionysus lays to rest on Naxos the Ariadne whom Theseus had yielded to him, and in connection with this we demonstrated in the terracotta the union of all those physical elements that form the material basis of the Bacchic idea. In this, too, it appeared to us as the perfect expression of the Dionysian religion: in uniting female matter with the male force it leaves the preponderance to the former. The same relation now recurs in the moon, and Dionysus belongs to the lunar region as well. Hitherto we have found him on two levels of the cosmos: first in his union with tellurian matter, which, as the bearer of the male force, he permeates in the form of the chthonian waters and the chthonian fire; then again as the shining sun, as the heavenly phallus, akin to the Apollonian luminous nature, yet, as the materially generating Helios, subordinate to the metaphysically pure nature of Apollo. Now he presents himself to us in a third form. He reappears as Lunus Deus, as νυκτοφαής and σύνδρομος μήνης, who leads the nocturnal round dance of the shining stars of heaven,1) and who, like Ariadne’s crown, takes up among the stars those initiated into his rites. In this Lunus nature he leads the tellurian and the solar potency back to unity. All the components of his physical being are united in the moon, as they are in burnt clay. According to the ancient, and especially the Orphic, view, the moon occupies a middle position between earth and sun. Material like the earth, and therefore designated as ἑτέρη γῆ οὐρανίη or as the Olympian earth,2) it is called the purest of the earthly bodies and the most impure of the heavenly ones. It lies on the boundary of two worlds, the tellurian, in which Becoming dwells, and the solar, in which Being dwells, and unites in itself the nature of both. From the sun it borrows its light; with the earth it shares its material nature. Like the earth, it is a true γῆ; mountains, rivers, and cities are to be found on it,3) but it is not an Διόνυσος, ἔχων ταυρώπιδα μορφήν. The bull’s head, which is here referred to the lunar nature (217. Ταυρῶπις Μήνη), is elsewhere a sign of the watery nature: 15, 31; 7, 321; 21, 214–218. 44, 203: Νυκτέλιος Διόνυσος. 227. Ὁ δ᾽ ἄρτι θάλλων σάρκα, διοπετὴς ὅπως Ἀστὴρ ἀπέσβη, πνεῦμ᾽ ἀφεὶς εἰς αἰθέρα, μικτὸν δὲ σῶμα καὶ μίμημα δαιμόνιον ὄντως τὴν σελήνην, τῷ τῇ τούτου τοῦ γένους συνᾴδειν περιφορᾷ, φθίσεις φαινομένας δεχομένην καὶ αὐξήσεις καὶ μεταβολάς, ὁρῶντες, οἱ μὲν ἄστρον γεῶδες, οἱ δ᾽ ὀλυμπίαν γῆν, οἱ δὲ χθονίας ὁμοῦ καὶ οὐρανίας κλῆρον Ἑκάτης προσεῖπον. κ. τ. λ.

o: tellurische, sondern eine uranische Erde, von reinerm Stoffe als jene, aber doch unreiner als die Sonne, der reinste der irdischen, der unreinste der himmlischen Körper. Darum bildet er auch die Grenze zwischen der seienden und der werdenden Welt. Unter dem Monde ist Alles vergänglich, in ewigem Wachsen und Abnehmen begriffen, wie der Mond selbst; über ihm alles unvergänglich, unkörperlich wie der Sonne Licht, und keinem Wechsel unterworfen. So scheidet die Mondregion den ὁδὸς ἄνω καὶ κάτω; in ihm nimmt das Unkörperliche Körper, das Körperliche Unkörperlichkeit an. Dort begegnen sich die absteigenden und die aufsteigenden Wesen; dort wohnt ψυχή, wie σῶμα der Erde, νοῦς dem reinen Lichte entspricht. Denn aus drei Bestandtheilen ist des Menschen Natur zusammengesetzt, wie der κόσμος. ψυχή ist die Mittelstufe, reiner als σῶμα, unreiner als νοῦς; durch eine erste Trennung wird σῶμα, durch eine zweite ψυχή abgestreift, und dann erst νοῦς seiner geistigen Lichtreinheit theilhaft. 1) In dieser Vereinigung zweier Naturen, der tellurischen und der solarischen, liegt der Ursprung der hermaphroditischen Mondnatur. Beide Geschlechter vereinigt in sich die himmlische Erde. Mann und Weib zugleich, ist sie jenes in ihrer Lichtnatur, dieses in ihrer Stofflichkeit: weiblich empfangend der Sonne gegenüber, das Empfangene in Strahlen befruchtenden Lichtes männlich nach der Erde entsendend. In dieser Vereinigung beider Geschlechter erscheint das männliche zwar, weil der Sonne entstammend, als das höhere, das weibliche aber durch die Stofflichkeit selbst als das überwiegende. Darum ist Luna häufiger als Lunus, und selbst Deus Luna 2) gebräuchlich; darum ψυχή weiblich, νοῦς männlich, σῶμα geschlechtslos; darum in den Thespischen Eros-Mysterien, in deren mimischen Darstellungen die Fabel von Psyche und Amor, wie Apuleius sie mittheilt, wurzelt, 3) Psyche immer in Weibesgestalt gedacht; darum auch in der Mysterienlehre von der Palingenesie des Menschen der Satz angenommen, daß die männliche Seele immer zuerst wieder in weiblichem Körper auferstehe. In dem Carurischen Heiligthum des θεὸς Μήν hat sich noch unter den römischen Kaisern die Lehre erhalten, wer den Mond als Lunus anrufe, in dessen Haus werde der Mann herrschen, umgekehrt sei mit Luna das Weiberregiment verbunden. 4) Wir entnehmen
e: earth that is tellurian, but a uranian earth, of purer matter than that, yet more impure than the sun, the purest of the earthly, the most impure of the heavenly bodies. For this reason it also forms the boundary between the world of being and the world of becoming. Beneath the moon everything is perishable, caught up in eternal waxing and waning, like the moon itself; above it everything is imperishable, incorporeal like the light of the sun, and subject to no change. Thus the lunar region divides the ὁδὸς ἄνω καὶ κάτω; in it the incorporeal assumes body, the corporeal incorporeality. There the descending and the ascending beings meet; there dwells ψυχή, as σῶμα corresponds to the earth, νοῦς to the pure light. For the nature of man is composed of three constituents, like the κόσμος. ψυχή is the middle stage, purer than σῶμα, more impure than νοῦς; through a first separation σῶμα, through a second ψυχή is stripped away, and only then does νοῦς partake of its spiritual purity of light.1) In this union of two natures, the tellurian and the solar, lies the origin of the hermaphroditic lunar nature. The heavenly earth unites both sexes in itself. Man and woman at once, it is the former in its luminous nature, the latter in its materiality: female receptive in relation to the sun, and sending forth what it has received, in rays of fecundating light, male toward the earth. In this union of both sexes the male appears indeed as the higher, because it springs from the sun, but the female, through materiality itself, as the preponderant. Therefore Luna is more frequent than Lunus, and even Deus Luna2) is in use; therefore ψυχή is female, νοῦς male, σῶμα without sex; therefore in the Thespian mysteries of Eros, in whose mimic representations the fable of Psyche and Amor, as Apuleius relates it, has its root,3) Psyche is always conceived in woman’s form; therefore also in the mystery doctrine of the palingenesis of man the proposition was adopted that the male soul always rises again first in a female body. In the Carrhaean sanctuary of the θεὸς Μήν the teaching was preserved even under the Roman emperors that in the house of him who invokes the moon as Lunus the man will rule, while conversely with Luna is bound up the rule of women.4) We derive id memoria traditum, atque ita nunc quoque a Carrenis præcipue haberi, ut qui Lunam fœmineo nomine ac sexu putaverit nuncupandam, is addictus mulieribus semper inserviat: at vero qui marem deum esse crediderit, is dominetur uxori, neque ullas muliebres patiatur insidias, unde quamvis Græci vel Aegyptii eo genere quo fœminam hominem, etiam Lunam Deam dicant, mystice tamen Deum dicunt. Cf. Horap. 1, 12. Ammonius in Aristotelem de interpret. p. 15.

o: daraus eine Bestätigung der Behauptung, daß die Bezeichnung Selene und Luna auch das Vorwiegen der weiblichen Stofflichkeit in dem Doppelgeschlecht der Lunarischen Welt darstellt. Diese Auffassung der Mondwelt greift leitend und erklärend in alle Theile der alten Mythologie ein. 1) Den physischen Grundlagen der Dionysos-Religion entspricht sie aber so vollkommen, daß wir diese selbst als den kultlichen Ausdruck der entwickelten Vorstellungen von der Mondwelt aufzufassen berechtigt sind. Die drei Bestandtheile des Dionysischen Wesens, Erde, Wasser, Licht kehren auch in dem Monde einheitlich verbunden wieder. Wie dieser zwischen Erde und Sonne eine beide verbindende Mittelstufe einnimmt, so hat auch Dionysos an tellurischer und solarischer Natur gleichen Antheil; reiner als die Erde, ist er doch unreiner als Apoll, ein stofflicher Helios. Der Mond vereinigt beide Geschlechter in sich, so auch Dionysos, der mit männlich phallischer Natur weibliche Weichheit der Körperformen verbindet. 2) In dem Monde herrscht die stoffliche Weiblichkeit über die männliche Natur, und so nehmen auch die Männer in den Dionysischen Mysterien und Oschophorien weibliche Kleidung an. 3) Verborgen ruht der Phallus unter dem Aeußern des Weibes. Worin aber der Mond die Dionysische Natur am klarsten darlegt, das ist in der innigen Verbindung beider Geschlechtspotenzen, deren Sehnsucht nach Vereinigung in der himmlischen Erde zu nie endender Erfüllung gelangt. Dio-
e: from this a confirmation of the assertion that the designation Selene and Luna also expresses the preponderance of female materiality in the double sex of the lunar world. This conception of the lunar world intervenes, guiding and explaining, in all parts of ancient mythology.1) But it corresponds so perfectly to the physical foundations of the Dionysian religion that we are entitled to grasp the latter itself as the cultic expression of the developed conceptions of the lunar world. The three constituents of the Dionysian being, earth, water, light, recur in the moon too, united into one. As the moon occupies between earth and sun a middle stage joining the two, so Dionysus also has an equal share in tellurian and solar nature; purer than the earth, he is yet more impure than Apollo, a material Helios. The moon unites both sexes in itself, and so does Dionysus, who joins to a male-phallic nature the female softness of bodily forms.2) In the moon female materiality rules over male nature, and so in the Dionysian mysteries and the Oschophoria the men also assume women’s clothing.3) Hidden, the phallus rests beneath the exterior of woman. But wherein the moon displays the Dionysian nature most clearly is the intimate union of both sexual potencies, whose longing for union attains in the heavenly earth a never-ending fulfillment. Dionysus’s and de Iside et Osiride, and by Macrob. in many passages of his two works. Its traces, however, reach into all domains of ancient literature. Of the moderns, Welcker in the first part of his Mythologie has most definitely emphasized the significance of that conception. What matters here, of course, is not its physical correctness, but only the question what views had found acceptance among the ancients. See, moreover, G. Leopardi, sopra gli errori popolari degli antichi, chapters 9–12: Del sole — Degli astri — Dell’ astrologia — Della terra. The connection with ebb and flood was well known to the ancients, De facie in orbe lunæ 25. Hutten 13, 81., as indeed they ascribed to the moon in general the effect of moisture and female softness, the growth of plants, the dissolution of flesh, the change of wines, the rotting of wood, and the easy birth of women. Clarac, musée de sculptures Pl. 666. F. no. 1554. D. It shows a hermaphroditic bodily form. The double ornamental chain crossing on the breast, the radiate crown on the head, the sphere in the left hand leave no doubt that we have here before us a conception belonging to the Bacchic mysteries. The hermaphroditic form has thereby likewise received its explanation. It rests on the Lunus-Aphroditos nature of the god to whom the initiate belongs, and to whom he looks up in an attitude of adoration and trust. “I am joined to the heavenly host; for the god was my leader.”

o: nysos Liebe zu dem Weibe, sein Verlangen nach Zeugung und Befruchtung, des Weibes Sehnsucht nach dem Gotte, von dessen Männlichkeit es die Erfüllung seiner Bestimmung erwartet, der Abscheu gegen vereinsamtes Leben, der sich in dem weiblichen Festgefolge und dem stets vereinten Auftreten zeugungslustiger Faune und Satyrn mit sinnetaumelnden Bacchen ausspricht: Alles dieß ist in dem Monde verwirklicht. In den Mond geht Osiris ein, 1) sehnsüchtig nach dem weiblichen Stoffe, zu welchem er herabsteigt, wie der Sonne Strahl auf den Mond niederfällt. Er entsagt, dem phallischen Zuge seiner Natur folgend, gerne der vereinsamten Herrlichkeit, in welcher Apoll wie die Sonne sich am besten gefällt. Er wird durch Luna zum Lunus. Nicht einsam will er in unnahbarer Höhe seiner eigenen Majestät genießen, und in unfruchtbarer Narcißartiger Selbstbetrachtung untergehn. Mene sucht er, zu ihr steigt er herab, versenkt sich in ihre stoffliche Natur, umkreist sie stets, ein unzertrennlicher Begleiter, σύνδρομος Μήνης. In dieser Natur offenbart sich am klarsten sein der apollinischen Reinheit untergeordnetes Wesen. Keine Zeugungsbegierde vermag diesen aus der solarischen Höhe herabzuziehen, in welcher er in metaphysischer Klarheit ewig thront. Apollo wird nie Lunus. Er gehört der seienden Welt, hat an der werdenden keinen Theil. Er tritt nicht in ihren Wechsel ein, sondern blickt aus unnahbarer Höhe auf die ewig sich hebenden, ewig sich senkenden Wogen der vom Naturfatum beherrschten Schöpfung, welcher Phaëton und Bellerophon nicht zu entrinnen vermögen. Der Dionysischen Stufe gehört auch Achill, gehört der Cretische Talos. Wie in seiner doppelten Feuer- und Wassernatur, so entspricht Achill der Dionysischen Gottheitsidee auch in seiner Erhebung zum Lunus und seiner Verwandtschaft mit Apoll, in dessen Heiligthum er, wie jener, in untergeordneter Stellung Aufnahme findet. Feind der Amazonen, gegen welche er auch auf Leuke den Kampf erneuert, durch unwiderstehliche Sehnsucht zu dem Weibe hingezogen, und gegen der Mutter Warnung auf Tenedos um Hemithea ringend, wird er erst auf der leuchtenden Mondinsel seiner Wünsche theilhaft. Dort führt, wie es Philostrat, heroica 19 schildert, der schönste der Männer, dem herrlichsten Weibe geeint, ein ewigseeliges Wonneleben, und befriedigt jene Liebe, die ihm auf Erden die sterbende Königin in einem Augenblick erregt, da ihm deren Erfüllung der Tod vereitelt. Als Lunus umkreist er nun die Geliebte, schnellfüßig am Himmel, wie auf Erden des nie ruhenden Wassers eilender Strom. So stellen ihn Vasenbilder dar. Als Lunus ist er den Feuererscheinungen des stofflichen Aethers verwandt, wie Dionysus. Als Lunus auch hermaphrodi-
e: love for woman, his desire for generation and fecundation, woman’s longing for the god, from whose masculinity she expects the fulfillment of her destiny, the aversion to solitary life that expresses itself in the female festal retinue and in the ever united appearance of generation-hungry fauns and satyrs with Bacchae reeling in their senses: all this is realized in the moon. Into the moon Osiris enters,1) longing for female matter, to which he descends as the ray of the sun falls down upon the moon. Following the phallic trait of his nature, he gladly renounces the solitary majesty in which Apollo, like the sun, is best pleased. Through Luna he becomes Lunus. He does not wish, alone on an unapproachable height, to enjoy his own majesty and to perish in barren, Narcissus-like self-contemplation. Mene he seeks, to her he descends, sinks into her material nature, circles about her constantly, an inseparable companion, σύνδρομος Μήνης. In this nature his being, subordinate to Apollonian purity, reveals itself most clearly. No desire for generation can draw the Apollonian god down from the solar height in which he sits enthroned forever in metaphysical clarity. Apollo never becomes Lunus. He belongs to the world of being and has no part in that of becoming. He does not enter into its change, but looks from an unapproachable height upon the ever-rising, ever-sinking waves of creation, ruled by the fate of nature, which Phaethon and Bellerophon are unable to escape. To the Dionysian stage belongs Achilles also, belongs the Cretan Talos. As in his double nature of fire and water, so Achilles corresponds to the Dionysian idea of the deity also in his elevation to Lunus and in his kinship with Apollo, in whose sanctuary he, like Dionysus, finds admission in a subordinate position. An enemy of the Amazons, against whom he renews the combat even on Leuke, drawn by irresistible longing toward woman, and, against his mother’s warning, wrestling for Hemithea on Tenedos, he first attains his wishes on the shining lunar island. There, as Philostratus, Heroica 19 describes it, the most beautiful of men, united with the most glorious woman, leads an eternally blessed life of rapture, and satisfies that love which on earth the dying queen aroused in him in a moment when death frustrated its fulfillment. As Lunus he now circles his beloved, swift-footed in the heavens, as on earth the hurrying stream of the never-resting water. So vase paintings represent him. As Lunus he is related to the fire phenomena of the material aether, like Dionysus. As Lunus he is also hermaphroditic [PDF 94] — 80 — as the statue on the Sigeum represented him.1) The Cretan Talos shows a similar nature. The guardian of the island, he circles it protectingly; every night he completes his course, and in moonlit nights one hears his splashing when he bathes his bronze limbs in the sea. His highest origin he has in the sun. As Lunus, Helios himself has entered into the moon; separated from it, he appears himself in his solar nature, like Achilles and Dionysus, yet in the phallic materiality of his being unable to press through to Apollonian purity of light. The Lunus nature of Dionysus finds confirmation and completion in the lunar relation of the women joined with him. They are all lunar women, Demeter-Ceres, Ariadne-Aridela, Aphrodite, Athena,2) Artemis. A higher elevation than that to lunar nature has not been granted to female materiality. If the incorporeal force of man appears in a threefold stage, and is completed only in the elevation to the sun, woman, on the contrary, remains standing at the lunar stage. Removed from the chthonian earth, she returns in the heavens as lunar woman, and even in this elevation she preserves that materiality of which receptive maternity can never divest itself. She is always the birth-giving earth, always γῆ, be it the tellurian, be it the heavenly- Olympian. Though Athena in her motherless birth from the head has pressed through to a higher stage of spiritual conception, her physical foundation is yet always the double earth, and in the material Dionysian religion this nature alone comes to the fore. The moon unites all the qualities of the Dionysian woman. As Penia, ever pursuing new fecundation, it follows the course of the sun eternally, and borrows from its golden light the silver sheen with which it shines. Erotic is the innermost core of its nature. It stands by lovers, and by lovers it is implored for help.3) Therefore, precisely, the Amazons so greatly misjudge the nature of the goddess whom they serve. Therefore Hippodamia’s girdle is loosed, in the light of the full moon, by the hero who leads her over to her maternal destiny,4) as indeed all generation of the earth thrives above. her statues, which are provided with horns to represent the changes of the moon. Her black garments, however, they interpret as the concealments and shadowings of the moon, in which it follows the sun with longing. Hence one also calls upon the moon for help in affairs of love, and Eudorus says that Isis is set over all such things as overseer.”

o: besten im Vollmond gedeiht, 1) wenn der himmlischen Königin udæ ignes 2) das Werk fördern. So nahe ist der Mond dem Weibe verwandt, daß es allein dem Weibe möglich wird, ihn auf die Erde herabzuziehen, 3) und schon in Josephs Traum ist die Erscheinung des Mondes auf die Mutter gedeutet. 4) Der Vater ist die Sonne. Seine unkörperlich weckende Kraft fällt von oben auf die weibliche χώρα γενέσεως, 5) wie (nach Plato) eine senkrechte Linie auf die wagrechte Basis. Des Mannes wie der Sonne Wirkung ist ein bloßes ἐγείρειν und von den Alten der Wirkung des Feuerstahls auf den Stein verglichen. Der Frau Mondnatur dagegen ist stofflicher Art. Darum trägt der Apisstier das Mondzeichen auf dem Leibe, 6) darum der Römische Patricier die lunula auf den Schuhen. 7) Nach seiner höhern väterlichen Natur ist er Sonnengeweihter, nach der stofflich mütterlichen des Mondes Kind. Dem Monde ist die biga, die weibliche Zwei, der Sonne das Viergespann, die männliche Tetractys, geweiht. Zu den Sümpfen hat der Mond genauere Beziehung. Aus den feuchten Ausdünstungen derselben zieht er seine Nahrung. Die Sümpfe aber zeigen das Bild der aus der innigen Durchdringung von Wasser und Erde hervorgehenden freiwilligen Erdzeugung. Daher tragen Sumpfinseln zumal die Mondnatur. Auf dem aus Schlammanhäufung, wie die Echinaden des Alcmäon, hervorgegangenen Eiland am Ausfluß des Liger führen die bacchisch begeisterten Samnitinnen ihr amazonisches Leben. Die leuchtende Pontusinsel, welche uns Philostrat als Schlammeiland darstellt, ist der Mondfrau Helena und der Amazonen Aufenthalt. 8) Wie der Mond am
e: best at the full moon,1) when the udæ ignes2) of the heavenly queen further the work. So near is the moon in kinship to woman that it becomes possible for woman alone to draw it down to the earth,3) and already in Joseph’s dream the appearance of the moon is interpreted as the mother.4) The father is the sun. His incorporeally awakening force falls from above on the female χώρα γενέσεως,5) as (according to Plato) a perpendicular line on the horizontal base. The action of man, like that of the sun, is a mere ἐγείρειν, and was compared by the ancients to the action of the steel on the flint. The lunar nature of woman, on the other hand, is of a material kind. Therefore the Apis bull bears the lunar sign on its body,6) therefore the Roman patrician the lunula on his shoes.7) According to his higher paternal nature he is one consecrated to the sun, according to the materially maternal nature a child of the moon. To the moon is consecrated the biga, the female two, to the sun the four-horse chariot, the male Tetractys. To the swamps the moon has a closer relation. From their moist exhalations it draws its nourishment. The swamps, however, show the image of the spontaneous generation from the earth that proceeds from the intimate interpenetration of water and earth. Hence swamp islands bear the lunar nature above all. On the island that arose from an accumulation of mud, like the Echinades of Alcmaeon, at the mouth of the Liger, the Samnite women, inspired in Bacchic fashion, lead their Amazonian life. The shining island of Pontus, which Philostratus describes to us as an island of mud, is the abode of the lunar woman Helen and of the Amazons.8) As the moon in the erari debet, ut luna crescente decima usque ad quintam decimam id fiat; nam et ipsa suppositio per hos fere dies est commodissima, et sic administrandum est, ut rursus cum excluduntur pulli, luna crescat. — Plut. Is. et Os. 41. triens læta semina, et Solis ambagibus dispensans incerta lumina etc. Thus Psyche invokes the queen of heaven, Aphrodite, who names herself rerum Natura parens, elementorum omnium domina, seculorum progenies initialis, summa numinum. p. 257. Similarly Plut. lib. amat. 13. Hutt. 12, 23. es existed, however, because the male was originally the offspring of the sun, and the female of the earth, but that which partakes of both, of the moon, which itself also partakes of both.” Heliodor. Aeth. 10, 4. 6. 7. after Zoëga, nummi Aegypt. imperat. tab. 2, 3. one, nevertheless deserve attention. 6

o: feuchten Nachthimmel, so thront Leuke einsam im Meere, dessen Wogen plätschernd sie umgürten. Die Kraft des Wassers und des Feuers umfangen sich in der Himmelskönigin nächtlich feuchtem Lichte, dessen Strahl, wenn er auf eine rindernde Kuh fällt, dem Gotte Apis seine Entstehung giebt. Die Idee weiblicher Fruchtbarkeit hat in der Eigeburt der Mondfrauen seinen höchsten Ausdruck gefunden, und diese Idee der σεληνίτιδες γυναῖκες ist für uns darum doppelt wichtig, weil wir der Dionysos-Frauen Mondnatur erkannt haben. Neocles der Crotoniate sagt, das Helena-Ei sei aus dem Monde gefallen; aus silbernem Ei, dem Bilde des Mondes, seien die Molioniden, λευκίππους κούρους, ἰσοκεφάλους, ἑνιγυίους hervorgegangen, schreibt Ibycus, und ganz allgemein fügt jener Neocles hinzu: τὰς γὰρ σεληνίτιδας γυναῖκας ᾠοτοκεῖν ἁπάσας. Athenæus 2, 50. Eustath. Od. 11, 298. Herodot von Heraclea fügt bei, fünfzehnmal größer seien die Mondmenschen, die aus jenen Eiern hervorgehen, eine Zahl, auf deren Bedeutung wir später zurückkommen. Plut. Pl. phil. 2, 30. In diesen Eiern offenbart der Mond seine stoffliche Mutternatur, in welcher er als ἑτέρη γῆ οὐρανίη erscheint. Er ist selbst Aphrodite's Mutterleib, selbst das Ei, das gleich Luna, hermaphroditisch beider Geschlechter Kraft in sich vereinigt, und aller sichtbaren Schöpfung Keim umschließt. Wenn der Mythus erzählt, das Ei, aus welchem Aphrodite-Syria-Semiramis hervorgeht, sei vom Himmel in den Euphrat gefallen, von Fischen ans Ufer gewälzt, von Tauben ausgebrütet worden, so ist auch hier zunächst an den Mond zu denken, und die Verbindung von Fischen und Tauben als eine Andeutung der zur Zeugung nothwendigen, in des Mondes udæ ignes vereinigten Doppelkraft der Feuchtigkeit und Wärme aufzufassen. 1) So ist der Löwe, den der Sonnenheld Heracles zu Nemea erlegte, wo auch die Eigebornen Molioniden, die nach der Mutter genannten Eliden, von denselben Pfeilen getroffen wurden, aus dem Monde in den Peloponnes gefallen, wie Aelian H. A. 12. 7, Plutarch de facie in orbe lunæ c. 23 berichten. Der Löwe aber vereinigt in sich dieselbe Doppelpotenz des Feuers und des Wassers, so daß er, wie so viele andere symbolische Thiere, wie namentlich das Pferd und das Rind, nicht nur der Sonne, sondern ebenfalls den tellurischen Gewässern und ihrer Zeugungskraft angehört, und den Phallus, mit dem ihn eine Florentiner Terracotta darstellt, 2) in dieser doppelten Beziehung trägt. Löwenköpfe ergießen aus dem Munde den befruchtenden Wasserstrahl,
e: moist night sky, so Leuke is enthroned alone in the sea, whose waves splashing gird it round. The force of water and of fire embrace each other in the nocturnally moist light of the queen of heaven, whose ray, when it falls on a cow in heat, gives the god Apis his origin. The idea of female fertility has found its highest expression in the egg-birth of the lunar women, and this idea of the σεληνίτιδες γυναῖκες is doubly important to us because we have recognized the lunar nature of the women of Dionysus. Neocles of Croton says that the Helen egg fell from the moon; from a silver egg, the image of the moon, the Molionidae, λευκίππους κούρους, ἰσοκεφάλους, ἐνιγυίους, came forth, writes Ibycus, and quite generally that Neocles adds: τὰς γὰρ σεληνίτιδας γυναῖκας ᾠοτοκεῖν ἁπάσας. Athenæus 2, 50. Eustath. Od. 11, 298. Herodotus of Heraclea adds that the moon-men who come forth from those eggs are fifteen times larger, a number whose significance we shall return to later. Plut. Pl. phil. 2, 30. In these eggs the moon reveals its material maternal nature, in which it appears as ἑτέρη γῆ οὐρανίη. It is itself Aphrodite’s womb, itself the egg, which like Luna, hermaphroditic, unites in itself the force of both sexes and encloses the germ of all visible creation. When the myth relates that the egg from which Aphrodite-Syria- Semiramis comes forth fell from heaven into the Euphrates, was rolled ashore by fishes, and hatched by doves, here too we must think first of the moon, and the connection of fishes and doves is to be taken as an indication of the double force of moisture and warmth, necessary for generation and united in the udæ ignes of the moon.1) So the lion that the solar hero Heracles slew at Nemea, where the egg-born Molionidae too, the Eleans named after their mother, were struck by the same arrows, fell from the moon into the Peloponnese, as Aelian H. A. 12. 7 and Plutarch de facie in orbe lunæ c. 23 report. The lion, however, unites in itself the same double potency of fire and water, so that, like so many other symbolic animals, notably the horse and the ox, it belongs not only to the sun but equally to the tellurian waters and their generative force, and bears the phallus, with which a Florentine terracotta represents it,2) in this double relation. Lions’ heads pour from their mouths the fecundating jet of water, the island of Kos, whose illustration Brönsted gives, is certainly also related to the island’s name Hydrussa, and is thus by no means a mere solar lion, but a representation of the whole force of nature.

o: und Charon bezeichnet den Wasserlöwen, der auf den Sümpfen der Unterwelt thront, und in der sutilis cymba wohnt, darum als Grabwächter namentlich in Etrurien viel vorkömmt, 1) und zu Sardes mit hetärischer Zeugung verbunden wird. 2) Des Peloponneses alter Name Apia stimmt mit dem Nemeischen Höhlenlöwen und seiner Beziehung zu dem tellurischen Naß überein. Denn daß er ebenso auf aqua zurückgeht, wie Eporedia, Epona, Epidius, Aper das Thier der feuchten Gründe, Apium die Quellpflanze ewig grünenden Gedeihens, wie Epus selbst, das mit Apa ebenso ein Wort bildet, wie es mit ihm eine Sache bezeichnet, das kann keinem Zweifel unterliegen. Der Fall des Mond-Ei's vom Himmel mag zu jenem Gebrauch geführt haben, den die Türken noch heute beibehalten, in Heiligthümern das Ei nicht auf der Erde niederzulegen, sondern aufzuhängen. Im Tempel der Leukippiden zu Sparta hängt vom Tholus, der oft die gleiche Bestimmung zeigt, durch Tänien gehalten, ein Ei herab; 3) daß es als das Urei gedacht wurde, aus welchem Hilaira und Phöbe selbst hervorgegangen, liegt auf der Hand. Wenn es daher auf das Leda-Ei bezogen wurde, dem die Mondfrau Helena ihren Ursprung verdankt, so war der Grundgedanke, bei aller Willkührlichkeit der Beziehung, doch ganz richtig wiedergegeben, und wie Helena, so trägt auch das Schwesternpaar Hilära und Phöbe in ihren Namen wie in ihrer Abstammung von Apoll den Mondcharakter, und in dem Silphium, das die heilige Trapeza bedeckt, die Beziehung zu der tellurischen Fruchtbarkeit deutlich zur Schau. In Tänien hängen die Eier des oben erwähnten Traumgesichts an dem Bettgestell, und die sechs Straußeneier der Grotta d'Iside zu Vulci zeigen Höhlungen, offenbar zum Aufhängen an durchgezogenen Bändern bestimmt. Darauf geht der Brauch, auch das bacchische Initiations-Ei mit Bändern zu schmücken. Sante Bartoli theilt in seinen Pitture auf Tafel 4 ein in den Thermen des Titus gefundenes Wandgemälde mit, dessen Mittelpunkt der jugendlich schöne Gott mit allen Zeichen, durch welche die Kunst traditionell die ruhende Stellung auszudrücken pflegt, mit dem Thyrsus in der Rechten und einem nach vorn völlig auseinander geworfenen Gewande bildet. Von der Rechten naht dem Gotte eine weibliche Gestalt, auf der Fläche der rechten Hand das mit Tänien reich umwundene große Ei darbringend. Zur Linken bläst abgewendet eine zweite die Doppelflöte. Die Beziehung der Tänien zu dem Gräberkulte ist bekannt. Sie hat ihren Grund in der Verbindung derselben mit der weiblichen Naturseite.
e: and Charon designates the water lion, who is enthroned in the swamps of the underworld and dwells in the sutilis cymba, and therefore, as a guardian of tombs, occurs often in Etruria especially,1) and at Sardis is connected with hetaeric generation.2) The old name of the Peloponnese, Apia, agrees with the Nemean cave lion and his relation to tellurian moisture. For that it goes back equally to aqua, like Eporedia, Epona, Epidius, Aper the animal of the moist grounds, Apium the spring plant of ever-green flourishing, like Epus itself, which forms one word with Apa just as it designates one thing with it, can be subject to no doubt. The fall of the moon egg from heaven may have led to that custom, which the Turks still keep today, of not laying the egg on the ground in sanctuaries, but of hanging it up. In the temple of the Leucippides at Sparta there hangs down from the tholus, which often shows the same purpose, held by taeniae, an egg;3) that it was thought of as the primal egg from which Hilaira and Phoebe themselves came forth, is obvious. If it was therefore referred to the Leda egg, to which the lunar woman Helen owes her origin, the fundamental idea, with all the arbitrariness of the reference, was yet quite correctly rendered, and as Helen, so also the pair of sisters Hilaira and Phoebe bear the lunar character in their names as in their descent from Apollo, and in the silphium that covers the sacred trapeza display clearly the relation to tellurian fertility. On taeniae hang the eggs of the dream vision mentioned above, from the bedstead, and the six ostrich eggs of the Grotta d’Iside at Vulci show hollows, evidently destined for hanging on threaded ribbons. On this rests the custom of adorning the Bacchic initiation egg too with ribbons. Santi Bartoli communicates in his Pitture, on plate 4, a wall painting found in the baths of Titus, whose center is formed by the youthfully beautiful god with all the signs by which art traditionally is accustomed to express the posture of repose, with the thyrsus in his right hand and a garment thrown wholly apart in front. From the right a female figure approaches the god, presenting on the palm of her right hand the large egg richly wound about with taeniae. On the left, turned away, a second blows the double flute. The relation of the taeniae to the tomb cult is well known. It has its ground in their connection with the female side of nature. tract special attention through their technique. They are formed of small wooden laths, over which the black clay is applied.

o: Zu Megalopolis steht neben dem Heiligthum der Muttergottheiten, in welchem die Weihen gefeiert werden, ein anderes der Demeter und Kora, in welches nur die Frauen das ganze Jahr über Zutritt haben. Die Basis, auf welcher die Götterbilder stehen, umfängt von allen Seiten der Tänien reicher Schmuck. Eine Tänie umschlingt der Io Hörnerpaar auf einer Grabterracotte aus Sicilien, die sich jetzt im Museum zu Carlsruhe befindet, und die ich nach neuer Zeichnung in den Beilagen zum Mutterrecht mittheile. Io's der Liebe geneigte Mondnatur, die den vieläugigen Sternenhimmel zum Hüter empfängt, spricht sich wie in dem Hörnerpaare so auch in ihrem argivisch das Licht bezeichnenden Namen, deutlich aus. So gewinnt die Verbindung der Tänia mit dem Ei eine tiefere Bedeutung. Sie begegnet uns auf Vasenbildern auch in folgender Gestalt. Ein Wiener Gefäß zeigt die auf einer Basis ruhende Grabsäule; das Wogenornament, τὰ κύματα, ziert jene, diese eine Doppeltänie, oben weiß, unten schwarz, die in einer Höhe von zwei Dritttheilen des Ganzen um die Stele geschlungen ist. Auf der Höhe der Säule liegen vier weiße, ovoïde Körper, in welchen mit mehr Bestimmtheit als auf ähnlichen Vasenvorstellungen, drei kleinere und ein doppelt großes Ei nicht zu verkennen sind. Der bacchische Charakter der ganzen Darstellung ist an den Attributen der zu beiden Seiten vertheilten Figuren, an der Strahlenkrone der Frau, der Sphära, dem leiterartig mit Sprossen versehenen Webegeräthe, dem Spiegel, der Patella bestimmt zu erkennen. Das Bild ist nicht veröffentlicht. Es trägt im Wiener Kabinete die Nummer 5,255. Welchen Gedanken wir in diesem Umwinden mit Bändern zu erkennen haben, ist nicht mit Bestimmtheit zu sagen. Am meisten empfiehlt sich der Anschluß an die Vorstellung vom Weben der großen Naturmutter. Wir haben oben das ägyptische χειρόμακτρον Demeters und die von Apulejus erwähnten laciniæ angeführt, und müssen auch in Juno Lacinia eine solche webende Hera erkennen. Gleiche Bedeutung hat der Schleier Helena's, als Webestück trägt er die tellurisch-aphroditische Natur in sich. Daran schließen sich die Binden, die eben als Produkte der Weberei den Muttergottheiten angehören, und durch ihre Verbindung des abwechselnden Erscheinens und Zurücktretens der Fäden einen besondern Bezug zu den Gräbern erhalten. Daher stammt ihnen auch ihre Mysterienbedeutung. Als Zeichen der Initiation erscheinen sie auf unzähligen Vorstellungen; unter den Mysterien-Symbolen nehmen sie einen hohen Rang ein, und schließen sich darin dem Ei und der Myrthe besonders an, daß sie wie diese in nächster Beziehung zu der weiblichen Naturseite stehen.
e: At Megalopolis, beside the sanctuary of the mother goddesses, in which the initiations are celebrated, stands another, of Demeter and Kore, which only the women may enter throughout the year. The base on which the images of the gods stand is surrounded on all sides by the rich adornment of taeniae. A taenia winds around the pair of horns of Io on a funerary terracotta from Sicily, now in the Karlsruhe Museum, which I publish from a new drawing in the appendices to my Mutterrecht. Io’s lunar nature, inclined to love, which receives the many-eyed starry heaven as its guardian, is expressed plainly in her horns and no less in her name, which in Argive signifies the light. Thus the connection of the taenia with the egg acquires a deeper meaning. It meets us on vase paintings in the following form as well. A Vienna vessel shows a funerary column resting on a base; the wave ornament, τὰ κύματα, adorns the base, the column a double taenia, white above and black below, which is wound around the stele at a height of two thirds of the whole. On the top of the column lie four white, ovoid bodies, in which, with more certainty than in similar vase scenes, three smaller eggs and one of double size are unmistakable. The Bacchic character of the whole representation is plainly recognizable in the attributes of the figures distributed on both sides: the radiate crown of the woman, the sphere, the weaving implement furnished with rungs like a ladder, the mirror, the patella. The picture is unpublished. It bears the number 5,255 in the Vienna Cabinet. What idea we are to recognize in this binding with ribbons cannot be said with certainty. Most to be recommended is the connection with the conception of the weaving of the great nature mother. Above we cited the Egyptian χειρόμακτρον of Demeter and the laciniæ mentioned by Apuleius, and in Juno Lacinia too we must recognize such a weaving Hera. The veil of Helen has the same significance; as a woven piece it bears within it the tellurian-Aphroditean nature. To these are joined the fillets, which, precisely as products of weaving, belong to the mother goddesses, and which, through their combination of the alternate appearing and receding of the threads, acquire a special relation to the tombs. Hence, too, their significance in the mysteries. As signs of initiation they appear in countless scenes; among the mystery symbols they occupy a high rank, and they are joined in this especially to the egg and the myrtle, that like these they stand in the closest relation to the female side of nature.

o: 8. Dies Verhältniß der lunarischen Welt zu der Dionysos-Religion erklärt uns einen Zug des Pamfilischen Grabgemäldes, der offenbar zu den wesentlichen Bestandtheilen desselben gehört. Es ist die brennende Lampe, die auf der Hand des Einen der Epheben erscheint. Sie verdient um so mehr Berücksichtigung, je seltner sie vorkömmt. Ihr Mysterienbezug wird durch die Vergleichung mit einem andern Monumente außer Zweifel gesetzt. Raoul Rochette, monuments inédits Taf. 78. p. 409 giebt die Abbildung und Beschreibung eines Vasenbildes, das auf seiner Hauptseite in doppelter Figurenreihe die Verbindung Apollinischen und Bacchischen Kultes, und die Aufnahme eines noch im Kindesalter stehenden Mysten 1) in die Dionysische Weihe darstellt. In dem obern Felde bildet Apoll selbst den Mittelpunkt. Zu seiner Linken erscheint Athene, zu seiner Rechten, der Unterhaltung der beiden Erstern aufmerksam zuhorchend, eine mit dem Arme auf die mystische Cista gestützte zweite weibliche Figur, in welcher wir Demeter oder Kora zu erkennen haben. Hinter ihr steht, das Gemälde schließend, eine viereckige Säule, die eine kleine brennende Lampe trägt. Auf der Rückseite des wahrscheinlich apulischen Gefäßes erscheint als Gegenbild eine auf breiter Basis ruhende mit schwarz-weißen Tänien umwundene Grabsäule, deren Höhe ein Kylix krönt. Von den beiden weiblichen Gestalten, die rechts und links in schwebender Haltung die Stele umgeben, trägt die Eine Spiegel und Traube, die Andere den Kranz und den oft erscheinenden eiförmigen Körper, dessen durchgängiger Auffassung als Tympanum bedeutende Schwierigkeiten im Wege stehen. Die bacchische Beziehung des Ganzen kann also nicht im mindesten zweifelhaft sein, und eben darum auch die brennende Lampe keinen andern Charakter tragen. Ihre bloß symbolische Bedeutung geht daraus hervor, daß sie auf dem Vasen-Gemälde keiner besondern Handlung zu dienen bestimmt ist. Sie hat ihren Zweck in sich und dasselbe gilt auch von dem Pamfilischen Grabbilde. Jahn weist ihr hier eine äußere Bestimmung an. Sie soll der ᾠοσκοπία, einer besondern Art der Divination, die aus den Erscheinungen des über das Feuer gehaltenen Eis wahrsagt, 2) dienen. Wäre dieses der Vorwurf des Künstlers gewesen, so hätte er seinen Gedanken auf sehr räthselhafte und unvollkommene Weise bildlich dargestellt. Warum sollte er es dann nicht vorgezogen haben, die Handlung selbst uns zu zeigen, und das Ei in der Hand des Einen der Jünglinge den Flammen zu nähern? Was aber den Gedanken an die ᾠοσκοπία völlig ausschließt, ist nicht nur die ebenfalls symbolische Dreizahl der Eier, sondern namentlich die Doppel- Manches, das an die alten Gebräuche und an die Mysterienlehre erinnert. Dem Jnitürten waren alle hier ausgesprohenen Gedanken vertraut. !) Plut. Qu. rom. 52. Livius 9, 30. -- Plut. e: 8. This relation of the lunar world to the Dionysian religion explains to us a feature of the Pamphili tomb painting that evidently belongs to its essential components. It is the burning lamp that appears on the hand of one of the ephebes. It deserves the more consideration the more rarely it occurs. Its relation to the mysteries is put beyond doubt by comparison with another monument. Raoul- Rochette, monuments inédits pl. 78, p. 409, gives the illustration and description of a vase painting that on its principal side, in a double row of figures, represents the union of Apollonian and Bacchic cult and the reception of a mystes1) still in childhood into the Dionysian initiation. In the upper field Apollo himself forms the center. On his left appears Athena; on his right, listening attentively to the conversation of the first two, a second female figure, leaning with her arm on the mystic cista, in whom we are to recognize Demeter or Kore. Behind her, closing the painting, stands a four-sided column bearing a small burning lamp. On the reverse of the vessel, probably Apulian, there appears as a counterpart a funerary column resting on a broad base and wound with black-and-white taeniae, its summit crowned by a kylix. Of the two female figures who, in hovering posture, surround the stele on the right and on the left, one carries a mirror and a bunch of grapes, the other the wreath and the egg-shaped body that so often appears, whose consistent interpretation as a tympanum is met by considerable difficulties. The Bacchic relation of the whole cannot therefore be in the least doubtful, and for that very reason the burning lamp too can bear no other character. Its purely symbolic significance follows from the fact that on the vase painting it is not meant to serve any particular action. It has its purpose in itself, and the same holds for the Pamphili tomb painting. Jahn assigns it here an external purpose. It is supposed to serve the ὠοσκοπία, a special kind of divination that foretells from the appearances of an egg held over the fire.2) Had this been the artist’s subject, he would have set forth his idea in a very enigmatic and imperfect manner. Why should he not then have preferred to show us the action itself, and to bring the egg in the hand of one of the youths near the flames? But what altogether excludes the idea of the ὠοσκοπία is not only the likewise symbolic number three of the eggs, but above all the double color [PDF 100] — 86 — which they show, and whose mystic significance appears incompatible with the performance of a particular action. Had this so essential a particularity not escaped the interpreter, he would scarcely have ventured his conjecture. I therefore hold fast to the purely symbolic significance of the double-colored eggs, and of the burning lamp as well, and I point out that the latter receives a new confirmation from the broad daylight that surrounds the scene of our tomb painting. Temple and colonnade, which appear in the distance on the right and on the left, are a hint, fully sufficient for the more suggestive than elaborative manner of ancient art, that we have before us a company of ephebes gathered under the open sky. The lamp, then, serves no more than the burning candles on the altars of our churches the purpose of lighting a dark space; it can therefore have only a purely symbolic significance, inwardly akin to Bacchic cult. The way to understanding it has been prepared by our discussion above. As Lunus, Bacchus is νυκτοφαής, νυκτέλιος, λαμπτήρ. In union with the moon he attains the fulfillment of the generative desire innate in his phallic nature, which always yearns for female matter and prefers entering into it to the majesty of the solitary, enthroned star of day. His festivals are therefore always and necessarily nocturnal celebrations. Thus in Livius 39, 13 the Italic Bacchanalia are described to us. The same is attested by the inscription in the Corpus inscript. no. 401, p. 449: ὃς τελετὰς ἀνέφηνε καὶ ὄργια πάννυχα μύσταις Εὐμόλπου. Nyctelia sacra Servius calls the Bacchic orgies in Aen. 4, 302. Virgil: ubi audito stimulant1) trieterica Bacho-Orgia, nocturnusque vocat clamore Cithæron. Georg. 4, 521. Inter sacra Deum, nocturnique orgia Bacchi. Justin 2, 15 speaks of noctes initiorum sacratæ, Apuleius of arcana sacratæ noctis. Plutarch, anima an corp. 4, 96: ἱεραῖς νυξὶν ὀργιάζοντες. Plutarch Is. et Os. 35, νὺξ τελεία. Charito 5, 4, 113: νύκτες Ἐλευσίνιαι. Aristid. Serm. Sacr. 3, 312: Νὺξ ἱερά, an expression that, like Νὺξ παννυχίς, Νὺξ μυστική, sank to the designation of all sexual license and libidinum momenta.2) Ovid Fast. 4, 536: Tempus Passeri, Nox Dionysiaca in Atlas Farnesianus, Florentiæ 1750. p. 183–190. The Hymnus ad incensum lucernæ of Prudentius (Cathemerinon 5.) will be compared with profit. The thoughts that the Christian poet reads into the burning oil receive their full weight only through the contrast with those that the old religion connected with it. In a poet of the time of Theodosius (born 348 A.D.) such retrospects cannot astonish. So the monile ecclesiæ (Passio Laurentii v. 305) too is surely to be thought of in antithetical connection with the Bacchic monile. In the Hymnus circa exsequias defuncti there is found [PDF 101] — 87 — habent mystæ sidera visa cibi. Thus the Bacchanalia are true Pervigilia Veneris, which begin with the first appearance of the stars and end with their setting, like all Aphroditean-Sacaean festivals, whose character is borne also by the festival of the flute players dressed as women, celebrated at Tibur.1) As the moon aids lovers in the fulfillment of their wishes, so the night in which it reigns is destined for the accomplishment of love’s business, and the light of the lamp is its companion.2) When Epicurus would withdraw the night from Venus, Menander objects that it befits her best of all the deities, which is why the deductio of the Roman bride too began with the rising of the stars. “Menander perhaps thought in this,” remarks Plutarch, Symp. 3, 6, where he takes his point of departure from Epicurus’s Symposium and the inquiry conducted in it, “that the pleasure of love must be enjoyed only behind the curtain of night, so as not to chase modesty from the eyes by embraces by day, or to make the inclination to voluptuousness bold and shameless through all-too-vivid and persistent recollections that kindle the desires ever anew.” The same ethical relation is attributed by Diodor 4, 15 to the nocturnal celebration of Sabazius, οὗ τὴν τε γένεσιν καὶ τὰς θυσίας νυκτερινὰς καὶ κρυφίους παρεισάγουσι διὰ τὴν αἰσχύνην ἐκ τῆς συνουσίας ἐπακολουθοῦσαν, and Athenaeus stresses as a special proof of Etruscan moral decay that they took Epicurus’s rule as their guide in this point too.3) But the nocturnal character of the Bacchic celebration has its ground in the first instance not in a moral precept but rather in the Lunus-Luna nature proper to Bacchus and Ariadne. Considerations of the former kind are in general little in keeping with that phallic religion. Not morality but immorality is the necessary result of a religion that chooses for its physical foundation the impulse of matter toward union and generation, and makes the material egg the center of its mysteries. The Roman Bacchanalia show how greatly the sensual meaning triumphed over the supersensible one, and the scenes of so many tomb paintings, much that recalls the ancient practices and the mystery doctrine. To the initiate all the thoughts expressed here were familiar. of Heracles among the Coans, among whom the bridegroom greets the bride in female dress. e: combined with the condemnations that the Church Fathers pronounce on the mysteries, form a strange contrast to that warning of the Eleusinia, ut nemo ingrediatur, nisi qui se innocentem novit.1) Xenophon relates at the end of his Symposium (c. 9) that the love of Bacchus and Ariadne, represented by skillful dancers, produced so powerful an impression on the guests of Callias that the unmarried swore to take wives before long, while the married straightway mounted their horses and hastened away to their wives. The processions themselves advanced, in ever greater departure from the old simplicity, as Plutarch describes it, to the pomp of an ever-growing sensuality, and so contributed not a little to excluding more and more the ennobling influence that might have been expected from the union of Apollonian with Dionysian religion.2) In place of the elevation above matter there set in an ever deeper sinking into it, and while men believed they were conquering the lust of matter, they succumbed to it beyond all rescue. The lamp is met with more often in authors than on monuments. According to Clement, Protrept. p. 11, Potter, in the nocturnal celebrations of Sabazius3) the kernos, a mixing vessel, is carried combined with a lamp, and by this combination the cooperation of the two basic forces indispensable to the flourishing of all physical life, water and warmth, is indicated. — Arnob. adv. gent. 5, 27 connects with his account of the Eleusinia the remark: A repugnantibus et invitis decus virginitatis eripitur? imminentes nesciuntur injuriæ? quidnam raptis acciderit, ignoratur? amissi quæruntur ut homines: et sub sole clarissimo cum lucernis et facibus orbis peragrant vastitatem? — According to Euseb. Plutarch gives his thoughts on this in the 75th Roman Question. “Is this done perhaps because the Romans honored light as related and akin to the eternal, inextinguishable fire? Or is this too a symbol that nothing animate, if it is not harmful, may be killed or destroyed? For fire is like an animal, since it needs nourishment, moves of itself, and in being extinguished, as if it were being killed, utters a voice. Or is this custom meant to teach us that we must destroy neither fire nor water nor other necessary things of which we have enough, but, when we have used them, must leave them also to others who need them for use?” — Isis joins the series of the great nature mothers who bear the lamp among their attributes. In her procession the lucerna ardens is carried in front. Apuleius met. 11, p. 261. Quorum (sc. antistitum sacrorum) primus lucernam præmicantem claro porrigebat lumine, non adeo nostris illis consimilem, quæ vespertinas illuminant epulas, sed aureum cymbium, medio sui patore flammulam suscitans largiorem. And further: Magnus præterea sexus utriusque numerus, lucernis, tædis, cereis, et alio genere ficti luminis siderum cœlestium stirpem propitiantes. It can therefore not be surprising that in the mythical narratives centered on the Egyptian king Mycerinus, the builder of the so-called pyramid of Rhodopis, the lamp plays a very prominent role. At Sais, where the great lamp festival was celebrated in honor of Athenaia, Herodot (I, 129–134) saw in the royal palace, in an ornamented chapel, the life-size image, made of wood, of a cow lying on its knees, whose body was covered with a purple cloth, while its neck and head were thickly gilded. Between the pair of horns rests the sun disk, likewise of gold. Every day perfumes of the most various kinds are offered to it, and throughout the night a παννύχος λύχνος is set before it. In an adjoining chamber there stood twenty female statues, likewise of wood, whose hands had fallen off from age. Herodotus saw them lying at the feet of the statues. Once a year the cow is led out of the sacred chamber into the light; this takes place at the festival when they mourn the death of Osiris. Works of art confirm the Herodotean description. A Venetian relief, whose illustration Gronovius and Wesseling add to their editions, shows the recumbent cow, the body cover, the image of the sun, the incense vessels, and, carried by two boys, the burning lamp, adorned at the end opposite the flame with the head of Isis covered by the ox-scalp. From the tombs of the Theban necropolis the authors of the description de l’Egypte, antiquités 2, p. 169, communicate a corresponding [PDF 105] — 91 — wall painting. We see here the burning lamp in connection with the cult of Isis. For that cow is the animal consecrated to Isis, omniparentis terræ fæcundum simulacrum, as its being led around, like the incense offering and the covering of the head with the ox-scalp, attests for her cult.1) The predominance of the maternal principle appears in the twenty naked female statues, and especially in the myths that attached themselves to them. They were said to have been the king’s concubines. Tellurian matter is thus conceived here in Aphroditean hetaerism, and this conception continues in the story of the king’s sexual mingling with his only daughter.2) If in all these features the luminous side of the life-giving female primal principle comes forward, others reveal the relation to death that Venus-Libitina too, the giver of life, bears within her.3) At the festival of Osiris’s disappearance the cow of Isis is led seven times around the temple. Mycerinus himself was said to have been buried in her body; according to another version he had buried in it his daughter, snatched from him by death. Both accounts show us the maternal womb of matter as the place of death,4) and thus confirm that double nature of the primal mother which Plutarch recognizes so rightly and emphasizes so definitely.5) To both sides of material maternity the lamp stands in relation. Like Isis herself it is an image of life and of death, a representation of the life-giving, eternally self-consuming and thereby eternally self-renewing natural force. In a second narrative the burning lychnos appears once more, and quite with the same meaning. Herodot 2, 133 relates: “After the death of his daughter another misfortune befell the same king. He received an oracle from Buto,6) that he had only six more years to live and would die in the seventh. Distressed at this, he sent to the goddess and reproached her that his father and his father’s brother, who had closed the temples and not troubled themselves about the gods, but had ruined the people, had for so long a time obducitur. — 2, 25: ut sinus et gremium quasi matris mortuo tribueretur. Then he received a second oracle: precisely on this account his life would be shortened, for he had not done what he should have done. For Egypt was to be unfortunate for 150 years, and the two who had been kings before him had noticed this, but he had not. When Mycerinus learned what was now once for all irrevocably decreed for him, he had a great number of lamps made, and when night came he lit them, and drank and was of good cheer, continued this day and night, and roamed about in the swamp lands and in the woods wherever he could find a place suited to pleasure and joy. This he did to give the oracle the lie, by making twelve years out of six, since the nights had become days.” The religious idea of this second Mycerinus myth lies plainly in the open. All its individual features are explained by the cult of a nature mother conceived as hetaeric, whether we call her Latona or Isis, and by the opposition of this cult to the religion of the shepherd kings, hated by the native Egyptian population. The service of the great material mother appears restored, who rules in the swamps around Buto, crosses the waters in the papyrus boat, is held sacred by the animals of the watery depth, out of innate generative desire seeks everywhere the vanished phallus of Osiris, is crowned by Horus with the ox-scalp on account of her wanton nature, and in the form of a swallow, on the swampy shore of Byblus, circles longingly the Osiris column in the palace of Malcander and Astarte.1) As priestly king of this goddess Mycerinus appears. In swamps and in moist forest thickets he roams about. There he has his pleasure and joy. Here the work of tellurian generation thrives most luxuriantly. But the most vigorous life consumes itself most quickly. Not a long existence, as he expected it as the reward of his εὐσέβεια, does Isis grant him; rather the goddess of swampy Buto announces to him a swifter destruction of it. In six years he will live through twelve; with the seventh a new generation begins. In this religious system the night side of nature comes especially to the fore. Swifter and more violent is the annihilation in hetaeric swamp generation, where the natural force continues its work of generation without interruption day and night. In the fate of Mycerinus death reigns all-powerful. Isis appears in it preeminently as the destroyer of life. As she did the daughter, so she consigns the father to swift destruction. Her cult image becomes a coffin. In hetaeric life both lie so close together, the highest enjoyment of material existence and its highest transience. The swiftly fading [PDF 107] — 93 — rose is the characteristic attribute of the hetaeric Aphrodite. At the highest intensification of sensual enjoyment Aphrodite-Rhodopis becomes the ever-threatening mother of the grave. The lamp, image of her life-giving maternity, becomes a grave light. As its glow invites to the enjoyment of love, so it now falls on the place of death. On funerary columns the lychnos is hung up,1) an image of self-consuming life, which expires the more swiftly the more violently the flame blazes. Especially instructive is the connection of the lamp with Psyche. In the myth of Amor and Psyche the burning lamp is assigned a role that enlightens us about its position and significance in the mysteries. For it cannot be doubted that neither Apuleius nor Aristophontes invented the fable, but that it was rather, as considerably older works of art irrefutably demonstrate, in existence long before their time. The fantastic garb in which it appears with them, and whose overloading in wordy elaboration of details Fulgentius Mythol. 3, 6 already censures, may well count as later, novelistic embellishment: the main elements surely rest not on arbitrary invention but on genuine tradition. Its root is itself to be sought in mystery practices and sacred representations.2) Psyche is led by the divine beauty of her body, more than by conscious decision, into the aberrations of sensuality and into the mire of matter. As Aphrodite’s slave she has to pass through a long series of penances and trials, and even to go through the terrors of the underworld. At last, seized by Stygian sleep, motionless, a soulless corpse, she receives, awakened by the touch of an arrowhead, the cup of immortality, and, in union with Eros, the tranquil enjoyment of all that blessed bliss which she had sought in vain in Aphrodite’s service. Two stages of female existence appear here, like the double row of figures on so many vase paintings, comparable to the two parts of Goethe’s Faust: the female soul first in the service of Aphrodite, dominated by matter, led by every step on the fateful path to ever new, unexpected sufferings, finally into the deepest abysses of the mire of matter — but then rising to a new, more vigorous existence, passing from Aphroditean to psychic life. That lower stage bears the tellurian, this higher the uranian character. From the chthonian earth contested, in my opinion without success, by O. Jahn in the Archäologische Beiträge, p. 121 f.

e: Psyche is raised to the heavenly one. We recognize that Helen who, yielding to Aphrodite’s natural law, finds no end of sufferings and wanderings until at last, on the luminous lunar island, the most glorious of women, united in eternal union with the most glorious of heroes, she finds the repose that not the tellurian but only the heavenly Eros is able to give. Down there all is unrest, suffering, deceptions as unexpected as solutions are inexplicable: here repose, eternity, and security of enjoyment, the magic of transfiguration, such as the stillness of the moonlit night pours over the dwellings of men, noisily astir by day. There the impurity of tellurian matter, the serpent and the reed, which find their origin in the mire of dark depths, the witnesses and symbols of the unregulated mating of water and earth; here the butterfly that has broken through from the chrysalis of matter to the light, seeking light and having become a partaker of the light; there the purely material, here the uranian Aphrodite; there hetaeric, here conjugal union; there σῶμα, here ψυχή; there the lightless matter of earth, here the purified heavenly earth, the moon, the purest of the tellurian bodies. In Psyche Aphrodite herself ascends to the lunar stage, the highest that the materiality of woman can attain. At her side appears Eros as Lunus. Amor and Psyche are united by the same bond that encircles Lunus and Luna, Achilles and Helen. The kiss that unites them is the basium, which the husband gives the wife, not the suavium, which the friend gives the hetaera.1) The purity and chastity of love that has attained its final fulfillment is expressed in the group of the figures embracing for the kiss with a perfection that no lyric depiction can attain. And yet it would be altogether contrary to the ancient artistic idea to think here of a depiction of purely spiritual love. We have before us not this but earthly love raised to the highest purity. As the moon is the purest of earthly, the most impure of heavenly bodies, so Psyche too takes the same middle position on the boundary of two worlds. She joins the materiality of the one with the purity and tranquil clarity of the other, compels the body to participation in the light, the light to connection with the body, and so holds herself equally far from the immateriality of the one as from the impurity of the other. σῶμα and νοῦς come in Psyche into indissoluble union, and so give origin to a being that raises matter to the farthest limit of ennoblement of which it is capable. To this stage the idea of sexual love is not foreign. But it has put off the Aphroditean-hetaeric character and taken on that [PDF 109] — 95 — of chaste conjugal union. Psyche’s sufferings and final redemption are themselves only a consecration of marriage, which leads the sexual life of woman out of the swamp depths of impure matter, in which it finds its destruction, over to that path of light by which it can become for her the starting point of a higher psychic existence. In this attainment of her highest and last vocation Psyche unites in herself those two concepts that seem to exclude each other, and yet in so many myths appear in the most intimate union, that of the highest motherhood and that of perfected virginity. And in this too she stands again on the same stage as the moon. Eternally fecundated, it is at the same time eternally virginal, as mother virgin, as virgin mother. With the moon the concept of marriage and sexual mingling is necessarily joined. It is by its nature the union of both potencies, by its nature hermaphroditic, by its nature Lunus and Luna, Eros and Psyche. It seeks the light, as the light never ceases to sink itself into it. The fulfillment of this highest longing has found its expression in the symplegma, in the kiss on the mouth, in the meeting glance. In this first kiss, sealing the marriage bond, “to which Cypria herself adds a fifth part of her own nectar,”1) the cosmic law that governs the uranian bodies seems to receive its fulfillment among men, and the harmony of the higher and the lower world to be restored. As the moon can do nothing through itself but, ever following the sun, borrows from it the light with which it shines in quiet glory, so woman can attain only in conjugal union with man to that higher beauty through which her materiality is able to bind to itself the more spiritual nature of man. We see what relation connects these Eros mysteries with the Dionysian religion, and to what stage of the Dionysian nature they correspond.2) Now the lamp too will acquire for us a deeper relation. By the light of the lamp filled to the uppermost rim with oil Psyche recognizes the divinely beautiful form of her nocturnal visitor, whom her sisters had represented to her as a hideous dragon. The sword that was to give the monster death sinks from her arm. Restlessly the flame flickers, while the girl with growing curiosity enjoys the forbidden sight of the glorious form, of the beautifully curled golden hair, of the many-colored pair of wings, lightly by Gerhard, Arch. Prodromus p. 246 f.) than to O. Jahn’s.

Die Entfernung des Modius, das Ergreifen der brennenden Lampe bezeichnet den Anbruch eines neuen Tages, den Uebergang zu einem neuen Zustand, den Beginn neuer, die endliche Erlösung herbeiführender Leiden. An die Stelle der tellurishen Feuchtigkeit tritt die höhere Stufe des Feuers, an die der Finsterniß und des Chaos jene des Lichts und der Ordnung, an die des ungeregelten Hetärismus die Sehnsucht nach Erhebung zu eheliche Verbindung. Auf die tellurische Stufe reiner Stofflichkeit folgt die lunarischt, auf welcher der Stoff selbst die Lihtnatur anzieht, und -dadurch zu höherer Läuterung durchdringt. Then from the lamp itself a drop of burning oil drips onto the right shoulder of the god, as though it itself were driven by longing to mingle with the lord of all fire. But Eros, awakening from deep sleep, avenges the girl’s disobedience by flight. Sinking exhausted to the ground, she sees the beloved torn from her at the very moment when she had recognized his glory. So the incident with the burning lamp forms the true turning point in the course of the trials which Aphrodite imposes on Psyche, who rivals her in beauty. In place of the sexual enjoyment covered with darkness there appears the longing for the possession of the god recognized in all his glory. To the bodily wound is joined the deeper suffering of psychic pain. For wounding is the principle of love, as Plutarch profoundly emphasizes. As the plowshare opens the earth, and the force of man opens woman’s maternal womb by wounding it, so too in the psychic domain the arrow of Eros pierces the girl’s heart by wounding it, and her whole being is flooded by the painful, ever-growing longing for union with the heavenly bridegroom once beheld and ever present before her eyes. In the restlessly flickering flame, in the glowing oil that strives to join itself with Eros, Psyche herself is prefigured. The nocturnally dark mingling with the dragon1) forms the content of a lower stage of sexual life. It is tellurian swamp mating, which rules in the moist depth of the earth. It is the mingling of Isis and Osiris in the lightless maternal womb of Rhea. Under the bushel stands the burning light, as the great courtesan Lamia reveals her purely tellurian hetaeric character by putting her eyes in a bag. The removal of the modius, the seizing of the burning lamp, denotes the break of a new day, the transition to a new state, the beginning of new sufferings that bring about the final redemption. Psyche seeks the light, as the moth, whose wings she bears, is drawn by an irresistible urge to the flame. In place of tellurian moisture there appears the higher stage of fire, in place of darkness and chaos that of light and order, in place of unregulated hetaerism the longing for elevation to conjugal union. The tellurian stage of pure materiality is followed by the lunar, on which matter itself takes on the nature of light and thereby penetrates to a higher purification. In the oil-filled burning lamp this lunar-psychic stage of the female being has come to symbolic representation.

e: It corresponds to it perfectly. As the moon is purer than the earth but less pure than the sun, so too the burning oil is a combination of materially tellurian matter with the light, and thereby a union of the purely tellurian and the purely solar principle into an intermediate stage of existence mixed of both potencies. As, further, in the moon the material nature of woman predominates over the immaterial force of the sun and draws this down to itself for entry into matter, so also the fire in combination with the oil takes on a preponderantly material nature. The oil itself, like the olive tree from which it comes, is brought into connection with the female natural principle. Thus Athena,1) thus Damia and Auxesia are recognized in the olive tree.2) Olive tree and palm make possible Latona’s delivery;3) petroleum is ascribed to Medea. When Codrus had died, and his sons Neleus and Codrus were contending for the rule, the oracle promised the rule to him who should first sacrifice ἔνθα ὁ σίαλος τὸν σίαλον τρίβει. Neleus recognized the fulfillment of the oracle when he saw two olive trees move and rub against one another. He brings the sacrifice and rules over Attica.4) The relation of the pig to Demeter and to material earth, however, belongs to the best-known remnants of the old animal symbolism, for which I cite only Ovid’s saying terræ plenæ victima plena datur. In Vesta’s sacred flame lies a similar connection of the oil with the female natural principle, and the preeminent purity of this liquid, which the ancients emphasize,5) as well as the calming influence to which even the wild waves of the sea submit, may well have seemed to many a special expression of the calmly chaste nature of that deity who unites in herself the concepts of motherhood and virginal chastity. In keeping with this significance of the oil, the living sensibility that Apuleius ascribes to it, as well as the prohibition against extinguishing the flame, seems wholly to correspond to the spirit of the old nature religion.6) The same desire for union with the beautiful Eros, the lord of all fire, whose sting drives Psyche, penetrates also the hot liquid. Psyche appears herein herself as a great nature mother, attesting her fertility in the gift of oil, no oil. ἀποστρέψαντας. 7
