Wie die Verwandtschaft mit dem Flußschilf die tiefste Stufe der tellurishen Zeugungslust ihr beilegt, so ersheint sie in jener Arbeit, die sie in Demeters Tempel verrichtet, in der Sichtung der Samenkörner, welche die Ameisen, omniparentis terrp agiles alumni, für fie übernehmen, endlich in der Herbeiholung der goldenen Schaafwolle als die allgebärende Ceres, als die Spenderin des höhern Aerbauseegens, und in dem Todesschlafe, aus dem Eros Berührung sie aufweckt, ist das Schicksal des Samenkorns und die durch den Tod desselben vermittelte Auferstehung zu neuem schönern Leben dargestellt. So wird Psyche's ganzes Wesen durch die Jdee stofflicher Fruchtbarkeit beherrscht. Sie theilt mit Aphrodite, mit Ceres, mit Juno die Mutternatur, die sih nach stets neuer Begattung mit dem aslerweckenden Gros sehnt. Aber fie erhebt sih über diese tellurishe Stufe, auf welcher sie nur den Gewächsen des Landes, der unbeweinten niedern Schöpfung Entstehung zu geben vermag, zu der höhern Mütterlichkeit, auf welche der Mensch , die Krone der irdischen Schöpfung, seinen Ursprung und seine Fortdauer zurüFführt. Gegenüber dieser höhern Vollendung der Weiblichkeit erscheint ihr Verhältniß zu den Sumpfpflanzen und den goldenen Früchten der Felder als tiefere Region der Stofflichkeit, als eine untergeordnete Funktion des weiblichen sporium, das erst in der menschlichen Che und in der Hervorbringung echter Kinder (daher confarreatis nuptiis mit Eros verbunden) seinen höchsten Beruf erfüllt. So ist Psyche zwar auf allen Stufen ihres Daseins die stoffliche Mutter, des materiellen Charakters nie entkleidet, immer tellurisch-lunarisch , nie über die Mondregion hivaus zu solarisch-geistigem Dasein durchgedrungen: aber doch über das rein tellurische Leben und den Shmerz des ewigen Wechsels von Werden und Vergehn, „der in jenem herrscht, [zu dem himmlischen emporgestiegen, ws sie nun auf der Grenze zweier Welten und beide in sich vereinigend, dem lichtbringenden Eros - ehelich vereint, in nie endender Wonne ein sinnlich übersinnliches Dasein führt. In dem brennenden Oele, das die bisher herrschende Finsterniß plößlich. erhellt, und durch die Enthüllung der nie angeschauten höhern menschlichen Schönheit in Mann und Frau die Sehnsucht nach ewigem Besiß erweckt, wird diese Gattung des Stoffes mit dem Lichte, der tellurischen mit der solarischen Potenz, der Feuchtigkeit mit der Wärme, mit einem Worte jene in dem Monde erkannte Verbindung zweier Welten, zu bildlicher Anschauung gebracht.
e: less than Athena, Auxesia, and Damia, the goddesses of marriage of tellurian-lunar nature, to whom the maidens dedicate hair, cloak clasps, and small earthen drinking bowls. Proofs of this relation to the fertility of the earth are laid down in individual, very essential features of the Psyche myth. As her kinship with the river reed assigns to her the lowest stage of tellurian generative desire, so she appears, in that labor which she performs in Demeter’s temple, in the sorting of the seeds which the ants, omniparentis terræ agiles alumni, undertake for her, finally in the fetching of the golden sheep’s wool, as the all-bearing Ceres, as the giver of the higher blessing of agriculture, and in the sleep of death from which the touch of Eros awakens her the fate of the seed grain is represented, and the resurrection, mediated by its death, to a new, fairer life. Thus Psyche’s whole being is dominated by the idea of material fertility. She shares with Aphrodite, with Ceres, with Juno the maternal nature that longs for ever new mating with the all-awakening Eros. But she rises above this tellurian stage, on which she is able to give origin only to the plants of the land, to the unwept lower creation, to the higher maternity to which man, the crown of earthly creation, traces back his origin and his continuance. In comparison with this higher perfection of femininity, her relation to the swamp plants and to the golden fruits of the fields appears as a lower region of materiality, as a subordinate function of the female sporium, which first in human marriage and in the begetting of true children (hence joined with Eros in confarreatis nuptiis) fulfills its highest vocation. Thus Psyche is indeed at all stages of her existence the material mother, never divested of the material character, always tellurian-lunar, never penetrated beyond the lunar region to solar-spiritual existence; but yet she has risen above purely tellurian life and the pain of the eternal alternation of becoming and passing away that rules in it, to the heavenly life, where she now, on the boundary of two worlds and uniting both in herself, wedded to the light-bringing Eros, leads in never-ending bliss a sensual-supersensible existence. In the burning oil, which suddenly lights up the darkness hitherto prevailing and, by the unveiling of the higher human beauty, never before beheld, in man and woman, awakens the longing for eternal possession, this pairing of matter with the light, of the tellurian with the solar potency, of moisture with warmth, in a word that union of two worlds recognized in the moon, is brought to pictorial presentation.

o: Die Anführung und Betrachtung der alten Zeugnisse über das Vorkommen der Lampe in dem Kult der großen Naturmütter, der Vesta-Hestia , der Pallas [PDF 113]  Athene, der Demeter, Themis, Jsis, Psyche-Aphrodite, seht uns in den Stand, die Gedanken zu würdigen, welche sich an ihr Erscheinen in den bachischen Mysterien anknüpfen, und die ihr Anblik auch den Epheben unseres Grabbildes nahe zu legen geignet war. Wie das Ei von den Wahrheiten physisch-stofflicher Art zu Betrachtungen höherer Natur, seine Doppelfarbe von den Geseßen der werdenden Welt zu den Hoffnungen einer seienden hinüberführt: so knüpft sich auch an die Mysterienlampe eine ganze Stufenfolge von Jdeen, die aus den tiefsten Regionen des Naturlebens zu den höchsten eines geläuterten psychischen Daseins emporsteigen. Das sinnlih Stoffliche bildet immer die Grundlage. Kann es auch keinem Zweifel unterliegen, daß die Mysterien und ihre Symbole einen höhern geistigen Inhalt hatten, der allein die Sehnsucht so vieler ausgezeichneter Menschen, ihrer bessern Hoffnungen durch Jnitiation theilhaftig zu werden, erklärt, so ist es dochß andererseits ebenso gewiß, daß diese vergeistigte Bedeutung nicht die tiefste, sondern die höchste Stufe der Lehre bildete , eine Stufe, zu welcher wohl nur die geringste Zahl der Eingeweihten sich zu erheben vermochte. Die Natur hat die Sprache, sie hat ebenso die Religion und ihre Symbolik auf den Shooß genommen. e: The citation and examination of the ancient testimonies on the occurrence of the lamp in the cult of the great nature mothers, of Vesta-Hestia, of Pallas [PDF 113] — 99 — Athena, of Demeter, Themis, Isis, Psyche-Aphrodite puts us in a position to appreciate the thoughts that attach to its appearance in the Bacchic mysteries, and which the sight of it was also capable of suggesting to the ephebes of our tomb painting. As the egg leads from truths of a physical-material kind to reflections of a higher nature, its double color from the laws of the world of becoming to the hopes of a world of being: so too to the mystery lamp attaches a whole sequence of stages of ideas which rise from the deepest regions of the life of nature to the highest of a purified psychic existence. The sensually material always forms the foundation. Though it can be subject to no doubt that the mysteries and their symbols had a higher spiritual content, which alone explains the longing of so many distinguished men to share in its better hopes through initiation, it is nevertheless equally certain, on the other hand, that this spiritualized meaning formed not the lowest but the highest stage of the doctrine, a stage to which probably only the smallest number of the initiated were able to rise. Nature has taken language upon her lap, and has likewise taken religion and its symbolism. As little as the history of a word begins with its figurative meaning, so little can the higher idea of the mysteries be chosen as the starting point of development. The spiritual has built itself up on the broad basis of matter, the spiritual truth on the physical one. In the latter the likeness of the former is recognized. He who, of deeper spirit, was able to discover it in the image has become the benefactor of the human race. In all human things the sensual forms the foundation; to this the spiritual attaches itself. First a material and then a psychic body;1) first the coarse garment of the body, which Aphrodite weaves, then a finer, more artful one, the work of Athena. First the tellurian, then the lunar, last the solar stage of pure νοῦς of eternally changeless being. That is the sequence of stages of the mystery idea, that the fundamental view of Orphic doctrine in general. Through a series of gradually progressing unfoldings all that is created, and with and in it at the same time the creative principle, has passed. From the formless to ever more perfect form, from darkness to light, from tellurism to cosmic order, from the somatic to the psychic and spiritual, from the motherhood of matter to the fatherhood ἔπειτα τὸ πνευματικόν. ὁ πρῶτος ἄνθρωπος ἐκ γῆς χοϊκός, ὁ δεύτερος ἄνθρωπος ἐξ οὐρανοῦ. 40: ἄλλη δόξα ἡλίου, καὶ ἄλλη δόξα σελήνης, καὶ ἄλλη δόξα ἀστέρων· ἀστὴρ γὰρ ἀστέρος διαφέρει ἐν δόξῃ. Conceptions whose connection with the Orphic mystery doctrine lies open to view.

Hidden under the bushel3) it shows us material warmth working invisibly in tellurian matter and, joined with the moisture of the depth, developing germ in the darkness of the maternal womb of the lower creation of earth. To this lowest stage corresponds the lightless mating with the dragon, to which female matter surrenders itself purely somatically. But the modius is lifted away, and illuminating, the rays of the lamp fall into the deep darkness that hitherto covered matter. With this man steps out of the harmony of creation in which he had lived before unconsciously. He has beheld the forbidden, and has carried away restless longing for the denied enjoyment instead of the former unconscious pairing. Without enjoyment, but also without suffering, is the sexual embrace with the dragon in the lightless spaces of the earth. Had woman never renounced this, never lifted away the lid that hid the lamp, she would never have lost the freedom from care of the lower creation. But Psyche is seduced to seeing; she wants light instead of darkness. The forbidden deed becomes the source of unspeakable sufferings, but also the beginning of a higher existence in which the lower creation has no share. To the first material awakening corresponds the burning lamp that emerges from the covering of the modius. At this stage it still has a purely material meaning. It shows us woman in her sensual-erotic excitement, given over to the pain of a not yet purified desire for satisfaction of bodily pleasure. It calls to mind the Aphroditean unregulated sexual love with all its aberrations. It is here the lamp of the wanton Latona, which Thereby the doctrine of the ancients concerning the female natural principle is rejected, and the male force, which in that doctrine occupies a derivative place, is set at the head of all things. nation corresponds to the implement used in the scenic representations of the mysteries to cover the light. From this the Gospel parable of the light under the bushel also receives its explanation.

e: conquest of sensual desire can woman press on to repose and to lasting happiness. Only when purified does Psyche attain eternal union with the god who had withdrawn himself from her purely sensual glow. In the place of the restless, eternally seeking, never fulfilled desire there now enters the blessedness of lasting possession, freed from every torment; in the place of Aphroditean unchastity, that of Cerealian chastity and maternity. Tellurism yields to uranian existence, the somatic to the psychic, the swiftly fleeting pleasure to the certainty of untroubled duration. In calm evenness burns the lamp that before, flickering restlessly, let the glowing drop of oil fall to the earth. At this height the oil flame is the image of Psyche raised to lunar nature, of womanhood that has pressed through to luminous nature. Material, like the moon, she has nevertheless attained the highest degree of purification of which matter is capable. As such a pure flame the eternally burning fire of Vesta-Hestia is conceived. Every unchastity destroys its higher nature and leads it back into the dark depths of impure matter. Marriage, on the other hand, does not violate it. Virginity and maternity stand in exact connection, while hetaerism negates both. Hence the guardians of the pure fire of Vesta are at the same time servants of the phallus, from which the chaste, virginal nature mother awaits her fecundation;1) hence the fire of the Greek prytaneia likewise becomes generative, and every hearth of the state is conceived as the center of material prosperity on the foundation of the chaste, Cerealian-conjugal life. To a still higher stage of purity woman cannot raise the flame. It is not granted to the materiality of her nature to rise above the lunar stage of existence and to press through into the realm of immaterial light. Every further elevation proceeds from man. The light of the sun has entered into the moon and descended to female matter. Thereby it has itself taken on corporeal nature. Above the moon, on the other hand, it stands alone; at its highest source it enjoys exclusive masculinity, full purity, and unmixed clarity. There it is a monad, while in the moon it becomes a Trias; there it is unmixed being, here it has entered into the change of the world of becoming, which moves in threeness. The moon points, by its luminous nature, to the highest stage of the purely solar region. The derived silver gleam leads the idea back to the primal source that lies in the sun. This highest stage the Dionysian religion has ascended only by the hand of the Apollonian and within it. Dionysus is always of material, phallic nature, a material Helios, and for that reason [PDF 117] — 103 — is conceived as Sol in infero id est nocturno hemisphærio. Apollo, on the other hand, has pressed through to the monad, finally removed from union with matter, the source of light in its unmixed originality, and is therefore opposed, as Sol in supero, id est in diurno hemisphærio, to the nocturnal Dionysus.1) Thus separated from Apollo, Bacchus nevertheless enters into union with him, and whither he could not rise through himself, thither he lifts himself through Apollo. The latter draws him up to himself, and transfigures and purifies in his own nature the impure luminous nature of Dionysus. The lamp follows the same elevation. Its material fire points back to Apollo as its pure primal source. Through Apollo himself it becomes the image of the purest immaterial sunlight. This last elevation is the consummation of the mystery idea, and the greatest spiritualization of which the impure material fire of the earth was capable. Now the lamp steps forth from its connection with nocturnal festivals and takes its place beside the Apollonian-Bacchic light of day. So we see it on the funerary vase mentioned above, which unites Apollonian and Bacchic religion, so on our Pamphili painting, where sub sole clarissimo the Bacchic initiates gather to contemplate the three mystery eggs. If here the eggs are images of the material life that is destined for reawakening in the uranian world, and so belong wholly to the lunar stage of the cosmos,2) then at the sight of the burning lamp the spirit presses on yet one stage higher, and by the flame that eternally strives upward arrives at the primal source of light, at the region of Apollonian-metaphysical being, of the pure νοῦς stripped of all material admixture. If in the eggs the female natural principle prevails over the male, then, on the other hand, fire at the highest stage of purity is essentially of male nature. Still subordinate to matter in the moon, and therefore at the lunar stage an attribute of the female deities, it becomes in the solar sphere an expression of masculinity, and shows us force in its elevation above matter. Motherhood, which rests in matter, yields to fatherhood, which has its seat in the force of the sun. Apollo purifies the matricide, and annihilates the primeval law of the female-material powers. Into his Delphic sanctuary no woman has entry, any more than into that of the light-hero Heracles, combatant and enemy of women.3) Harmonia’s necklace is offered to him, and thus from the curse with the words: in sacris enim hæc religiosi arcani observatio tenetur. e: of matter that clings to him, he is freed. At this solar fire, the purest flame, the dying lamp of Vesta must be kindled anew. At Delphi, at the Apollonian hearth, the Greek cities fetched it after the defeat of the Persians. From Delos it comes every year to the island of Lemnos, as Philostratus, Her. 19, attests. For in contact with matter it has lost the purity that it always preserves at the primal source of light. The three stages of the cosmos, earth, moon, sun, are repeated in fire as well. Materially impure as the Vulcanian-chthonian flame, purer in the moon, but even here still perishing in matter, it attains in the sun its greatest clarity and complete incorporeality.1) If Prometheus stole the spark in the fennel stalk from the Vulcanian flame of Mosychlus, Sappho on the contrary has him kindle the torch at the wheels of the sun’s chariot, and thus designates the highest elevation to which it is man’s task to press through.2) The material flame is to be purified; through a second death the pure νοῦς, which dwells in the solar region, is to emerge from Psyche’s mixed nature.3) Of the three means of purification of the Dionysian cult, water, fire, air,4) fire, if conceived materially, is the middle one; lower is water, which belongs to the dark tellurian region, higher the air, which belongs to the ethereal region, the dwelling place of Bellerophon, Phaethon, and Achilles. But when raised to immaterial nature and the highest purity, fire is the most effective of all means of purgation.5) We can therefore no longer be in doubt prohibent gressus, ac limine curant sætigeros arcere sues: nec discolor ulli ante aras cultus. — Pes nudus, tonsæque comæ, castumque cubile, Irrestincta facis servant altaria flammis. Fire in its highest purity excludes the approach of women, every unchastity, and the swine consecrated to the earth, which are admitted at a lower stage of force (Sext. Empir. Pyrrhi Hyp. p. 155, Phædrus 5, 4.). Discolor cultus designates the change of color between white and black, which is incompatible with the fire nature of Heracles. His priests wear white linen. Pes nudus shows what significance of light the bare feet of our Pamphili painting have. Silius speaks of the cult of the Gaditane Heracles, whom Arrian, Exped. Alex. 2, 16, calls the Tyrian. Cf. Paus. 7, 5, 3. El. 6. Plutarch, Qu. gr. 24. reliquit — Aetherium sensum, atque auraï simplicis ignem, to which Servius remarks simplicis, non urentis, i.e. not a material fire, qui constat de ligno et aëre, but the πῦρ νοερόν, ignis sensualis, where sensus is explained by νοῦς. Likewise Plato in the Timaeus distinguishes the burning and the non-burning fire. phure Liv. 39, 13. Aristoph. Ranæ 447.

o: welcher lezte und höhste Gedanke sich an die Mysterienlampe anschließt. Es ist derselbe, der in der Lösung der Prometheis, in der schon die Alten die Offenbarung der Mysterienlehre erkennen wollten, vorliegt. Hier und dort der gleiche Fortschritt von Stofflichkeit zu Unstofflichkeit , von Unreinheit zu dem Zustand höchster Läuterung. Hier und dort Uebertritt aus dem Mutterthum in das Vaterrecht des Lichts. Hier und dort die Unruhe des erwachenden Bewußtseins als Beginn eines Kampfes, der durch die schwersten Prüfungen hindurch zum Siege des geistigen Sonnenprinzips über die Macht der Materie hindurchführt, und den dem Mutterprinzip des Stoffs in schwerem Kampfe entrissenen Menschen zu der Gemeinschaft mit den Göttern erhebt. Die Aufnahme dieses Kampfes und seine Durchführung ist das Ziel des menschlichen Daseins. Dem Mysten, der zu den höchsten Graden der Weihe gelangt, wird sie als höchste Vergeistigung des Jnitiationsgedankens nahe gelegt. Durch die Finsterniß zum Licht , durch die Materie zum Geist, von der Erde zum Himmel, durch das Mutterthum des Stoffs zum Vaterthum der Sonne , das ist die Vollenduug der dionysischen Religion, zu welcher sie in ihrer Verbindung mit dem apollinischen Kult durchdringt. Die männliche Sonnennatur ergreift nun auch das weiblich stoffliche Ei. J< habe oben bemerkt, daß es der mütterlichen Materie nicht gegeben sei, über die lunarische Natur hinaus in die unstofflich-solarische hindurchzudringen. Des Stoffes sich ganz zu entkleiden, vermag sie niht. Sie bleibt, wie Helena, wie Psyche, wie alle großen Naturmütter, auf der Mondstufe zurück, und kehrt als nächtlich leuchtende Luna, als uranische Erde, am Himmel wieder. Um so beachtenswerther ist e8 nun, daß in einigen Vorstellungen der alten Religionen auch das mütterliche Prinzip die Sonnennatur anzieht, und jener Stofflichkeit entkleidet erscheint, auf der es seinem innersten Wesen naH ruht. Athene , das mütterliche Prinzip , das als <thonishe und als uranische Erde des stofflichen Lebens materielle Grundlage bildet, das beim Scheine der nächtlichen Lampe der tellurischen Körper gröberes, der uranischen feineres Gewand mit vollendeter Künstlerhand wirkt, sie geht in geistiger Natur aus Zeus Haupt hervor, vollendet welche Stellen in ihrem ganzen Zusammenhange nachzulesen sind. Diese , erst ganz stofflich gedachte Lustration wird zum Bilde der geistigen erhoben. Prudentioribus tamen aliud placet , qui dicunt 8acra Liberi patris ad purgationem anime pertinere : omnis autem purgatio aut per aquam fit, aut per ignem, aut per aörein etc. Als höchste Lustration erscheint das Feuer in den Isismysterien. e: as to what last and highest idea attaches to the mystery lamp. It is the same that lies before us in the resolution of the Prometheis, in which the ancients themselves wished to recognize the revelation of the mystery doctrine. Here and there the same progress from materiality to immateriality, from impurity to the state of highest purification. Here and there the transition from motherhood into the father right of light. Here and there the unrest of the awakening consciousness as the beginning of a struggle that leads, through the severest trials, to the victory of the spiritual solar principle over the power of matter, and raises to communion with the gods the man wrested, in hard struggle, from the maternal principle of matter. The undertaking of this struggle and its carrying through is the goal of human existence. To the mystes who attains the highest degrees of initiation, it is brought near as the highest spiritualization of the idea of initiation. Through darkness to light, through matter to spirit, from earth to heaven, through the motherhood of matter to the fatherhood of the sun: that is the consummation of the Dionysian religion, to which it presses through in its union with the Apollonian cult. The male solar nature now seizes the female-material egg as well. I remarked above that it is not granted to maternal matter to press through beyond lunar nature into the immaterial-solar. To divest herself wholly of matter she cannot. She remains, like Helen, like Psyche, like all the great nature mothers, behind on the lunar stage, and returns as the nocturnally shining Luna, as the uranian earth, in the heavens. All the more noteworthy is it, then, that in some conceptions of the ancient religions the maternal principle too draws to itself the solar nature and appears divested of that materiality on which, in its innermost being, it rests. Athena, the maternal principle, which as chthonian and as uranian earth forms the material foundation of material life, which by the light of the nocturnal lamp weaves with consummate artist’s hand the coarser garment of tellurian bodies and the finer one of uranian bodies, she comes forth in spiritual nature from the head of Zeus, complete which passages are to be read in their whole context. In sacris Liberi omnibus tres sunt istæ purgationes: nam aut tæda purgantur, aut sulphure, aut aqua abluuntur, aut aëre ventilantur: quod erat in sacris Liberi. This lustration, at first conceived wholly materially, is raised to the image of the spiritual one. Prudentioribus tamen aliud placet, qui dicunt sacra Liberi patris ad purgationem animæ pertinere: omnis autem purgatio aut per aquam fit, aut per ignem, aut per aërem etc. As the highest lustration fire appears in the Isis mysteries. Apulej. 11. p. 260. (Isidis navem) summus sacerdos tæda lucida et ovo et sulphure, solemnissimas preces de casto præfatus ore, quam purissime purificatam, Deæ nuncupavit, dedicavitque. On the lustration of the nest before the brooding of eggs, Columella, R. R. 8, 5. p. 332. Bip. Sulfure atque bitumine atque ardente tæda perlustrant.

o: wie das Wort aus dem Munde. Nicht aus des höchsten Gottes Senkel ist sie geboren, wie Dionysos, nicht Zuyrop wie dieser, sondern mutterlos, ausschließlich auf dem geistigen Vaterthum ruhend. Eine gleiche Verklärung zeigt das weiblihe Prinzip in dem delphischen Kult. Themis-Gäa, die stoffliche Urmutter, hat das Orakel zuerst inne. Apollo selbst ist der Mutter Sohn, und wird bei Aeshylus von den Erinyen dieses stofflichen Ursprungs gemahnt, da er zum Umsturz ihres alten Mutterrechts siH erhebt. Aber er ersteigt die höchste Stufe des metaphysisch solarischen Seins, und bekleidet so das in seinem Ursprunge stofflich mütterliche Ur-Ei mit der reinen Lichtnatur. Jn Eiform erscheint der delphishe Omphalos auf einem Vasenbilde bei R. Rocheite, mon. incedits. planche 35, das gerade dadurch so besondere Bedeutung gewinnt, daß es die wahre Gestalt des so vielbestrittenen Tempelsteins über allen Zweifel erhebt, und den Ursprung der übrigen, bald aus der Halbirung des Eis hervorgehenden, bald der Pyramidalform sich nähernden Bildungen erklärt. ') Auf einer Basis von zwei Stufen steht der in vollkommener Eiform dargestellte Omphalos, auf dem breitern oder weiblichen Ende aufgerichtet. Bei ihm sucht Orest Schuß gegen den Angriff der Erinyen, welche der auf dem Dreifuß sißende, mit dem Lorbeerzweig versehene delphische Gott zurüdweist.2) Nach Strabo's Bericht war der Omphalos rings mit Tänien umwunden,2) wie wir ihn auf den übrigen genannten Monumenten, z. B. auf dem Vasenbild bei R. Rochette Tafel 37, erblicken. Die Binden zeigen hier den Wechsel der schwarzen und weißen Farbe, dessen Bedeutung und dessen Beziehung zu der Ei-Idee nach den früher gemachten Bemerkungen nicht zweifelhaft sein können. Der Wechsel von Leben und Tod in der tellurishen Schöpfung, welher eben dadurch ewige Jugend erhalten wird, wiederholt sih in dem Mythus von den beiden Raben oder Adlern, die von Aufgang und Untergang her in entgegengesehter Richtung fliegend, zu Delphi fich begegnen, und auf dem Omphalos selbst dargestellt waren. Sie entsprechen den beiden ewig sich entgegenfließenden Strömen des Werdens und Vergehens,
e: like the word from the mouth. Not from the thigh of the highest god is she born, like Dionysus, not διμήτωρ like him, but motherless, resting exclusively on spiritual fatherhood. A like transfiguration is shown by the female principle in the Delphic cult. Themis-Gaea, the material primal mother, first holds the oracle. Apollo himself is the mother’s son, and in Aeschylus is reminded by the Erinyes of this material origin when he rises to overthrow their ancient mother right. But he ascends to the highest stage of metaphysical-solar being, and so clothes the primal egg, maternal-material in its origin, with pure luminous nature. In egg form the Delphic omphalos appears on a vase painting in R. Rochette, mon. inédits. planche 35, which gains such particular significance precisely in that it raises beyond all doubt the true shape of the much-disputed temple stone, and explains the origin of the other formations, which now arise from the halving of the egg, now approach the pyramidal form.1) On a base of two steps stands the omphalos, represented in perfect egg form, set upright on the broader or female end. By it Orestes seeks protection against the attack of the Erinyes, whom the Delphic god, seated on the tripod and provided with the laurel branch, repels.2) According to Strabo’s report the omphalos was bound round about with fillets,3) as we see it on the other monuments named, e.g. on the vase painting in R. Rochette, plate 37. The bands show here the alternation of the black and white color, whose meaning and whose relation to the egg idea cannot, after the remarks made earlier, be doubtful. The alternation of life and death in tellurian creation, by which it is precisely preserved in eternal youth, repeats itself in the myth of the two ravens or eagles which, flying in opposite directions from the rising and the setting of the sun, meet at Delphi, and were represented on the omphalos itself. They correspond to the two ever counterflowing streams of becoming and passing away, the Berlin Museum. On the omphalos cf. Brönsted, Reisen und Forschungen in Griechenland 1, 113. R. Rochette, p. 188, n. 3; p. 193, n. 3. Forms of the same: vignette to p. 155. Millin, gal. mythol. 16, 55. Gerhard, auserlesene Vasenbilder 3, 323. Metroon. Es bezeichnet ursprünglich den eiförmig gestalteten Kultstein der Mutter Erde, und erhält erst später unter der Herrschaft der apollinischen Religion jene Ausgung geographischer Natur, wonach Delphi als der Mittelpunkt nicht nur von
e: and recall those two combating birds of the sacred island of the Liger, likewise the Corvus, whose plumage Apollo changes from white into black. Thereby the omphalos itself receives the significance of the two-colored egg of our Pamphili tomb painting. The light side and the night side of nature, death and life, are contained in it. Both sexes, too, it encloses in itself. Undivided there rest in it Omphalos and Omphale, the natural potencies which, by constant change of sex, pass reciprocally into one another. From this is explained the number five of the likewise egg-shaped black bodies that cover the surface of the omphalos on the Ruvo vase. For the relation of the five to the union of the two sexes, to marriage and material mingling, can, according to the testimonies cited above, be subject to no doubt.1) Thus everything combines to restore the female-material idea of the primal egg for the Delphic omphalos as well, and to raise its egg-shaped form, as an expression of its religious significance, above all doubt. In this nature it attaches itself to the cult of Themis-Gaea, and traces its origin back to the time when the Delphic oracle was still in the possession of the material, maternal earth, and belonged to that Themis in whose mysteries the female κτεὶς found its veneration to the last. Ὀμφαλὸς Γῆς gains from this point of view a significance that differs essentially from the one later connected with it. It designates originally the egg-shaped cult stone of Mother Earth, and receives only later, under the dominion of the Apollonian religion, that interpretation of a geographical nature according to which Delphi, as the center not only of relation to Apollo through the fact that it denotes the number five. This number Apollo, who is otherwise Hebdomagetes and joined with the seven, bears on his still less pure, Dionysian stage of nature. Read on this c. 9, from which I give here a passage that throws clear light on the relation of the two gods indicated. “The wise call the transformation into fire Apollo, on account of the aloneness (ἀ-πολύς, an etymology whose incorrectness does no harm to the idea that is to be supported by it), and Phoebus on account of purity and unspottedness. The transformation into winds, water, earth, stars, into the races of animals and plants, on the other hand, as well as the arrangement and ordering of all this, they represent under a rending asunder and dismemberment, call it Dionysus-Zagreus, Nyctelius, Isodaetes, and clothe destruction, annihilation, death, rebirth, in such fables and riddles as correspond to the transformations named. Hence one sings to Dionysus dithyrambic songs full of emotion and change, full of events and digressions, — ‘for, as Aeschylus says, the loud-resounding dithyramb must follow the communal Dionysus,’ — to Apollo, on the other hand, one sings the paean, a chaste and well-ordered Muse. The latter one represents on statues and paintings always young and unaging, the former, however, under many and manifold forms; and in general one ascribes to Apollo equality, order, and unmixed gravity, to Bacchus, on the other hand, all sorts of jest, wantonness, frenzy, and inequality, and invokes him as Evius, who stirs the women to frenzy, or as Dionysus glorified by frenzied honors.”

Von Themi8-Gäa geht das Ei mit dem Orakel auf Apoll über, und ersteigt die gleiche Höhe der Bedeutung, zu welcher der männliche Lichtgott durchdringt. Die höchste apollinishe Entwicklung der Bachus-Jdee tritt in der Darstellung des den Omphalos fassenden, von dem Gotte des Lorbeers gegen der Erinyen Strafe in Schuß genommenen Muttermörders, mit besonderer Bedeutsamkeit hervor. Jn diesem hat das Ei seine stofflich weibliche Natur ganz abgelegt, und die männliche des solarischen Lichtes angezogen. Aus Myrrhen bildet der Vogel ein Ei, so groß er es zu tragen im Stande ist. Dann hölt er es aus, legt seines Vaters Leiche hinein, und füllt die Oeffnung wieder mit Myrrhen an. Das Gewicht wird durch die hineingelegte Bürde nicht schwerer. Dieses. Ei nun trägt er nach Aegypten, legt es zu Heliopolis auf dem Altar der Sonne nieder, und Übergiebt es den Flammen.) In allen diesen Zügen, so wie in des Vogels Farbenshmuck, seiner Lichtkrone, die er auf Münzen führt, seiner Verbindung mit der apollinisch männlichen Palme, ist das männliche Lichtprinzip nicht zu verkennen. Gewichtlos ist das Sonnenlicht, und gänzlich unstofflich, körperlich dagegen und schwer das, was es erzeugt, die Myrrhe als Sonnenprodukt. Mutterlos, aus !) So Herod. 2, 73. e: Hellas, but of the whole οἰκουμένη, the omphalos was in this sense to be the navel of the earth. From Themis-Gaea the egg passes with the oracle to Apollo, and ascends to the same height of significance to which the male god of light presses through. With Apollo himself it is more and more removed from the material nature of which it was originally the expression. In the image of the primal mother Earth, Orestes finds his protection, although he himself had violated the law of the earth, like Alcmaeon, whose foot Gaea could no longer endure upon herself. In union with Apollo the egg takes on Apollonian nature and significance. It becomes the representative of the paternal principle that rests in the sun, and the expression of that highest lustration by which Apollo purifies the soul of the dross of bodily existence and leads it back to the quiet clarity of his own highest luminous nature. In this transfiguration the Delphic omphalos-egg appears on the Ruvo vase painting. All the components of the painting emphasize quite deliberately its relation to initiation. The highest Apollonian development of the Bacchus idea emerges with particular significance in the representation of the matricide who grasps the omphalos, taken under protection by the god of the laurel against the punishment of the Erinyes. To this egg, raised to Apollonian solar nature, the Indian-Egyptian myth of the phoenix attaches itself as an elucidation. In this the egg has wholly laid aside its materially female nature, and put on the male nature of solar light. Of myrrh the bird forms an egg, as large as it is able to carry. Then it hollows it out, lays its father’s corpse inside, and fills the opening again with myrrh. The weight is not made heavier by the burden laid in. This egg it now carries to Egypt, lays it down at Heliopolis on the altar of the sun, and gives it over to the flames.1) In all these traits, as in the bird’s adornment of colors, its crown of light, which it bears on coins, its connection with the Apollonian male palm, the male principle of light is not to be mistaken. The incorporeality of light is brought out still more by the contrast of the burden of myrrh. Weightless is the light of the sun, and wholly immaterial, corporeal on the other hand and heavy is that which it generates, myrrh as a product of the sun. Motherless, from Taciti annal. 6, 28; Solinus c. 33; Philostr. vita Apollon. 3, 49; Tzetzes, Chil. 5, 6; Schol. Aristid. Tom. 2, p. 107. e: the father alone, the phoenix has come forth.1) The egg is not its birthplace, but rather the shroud of death which, consumed by fire, returns to the light to which the father belongs. The egg thus appears here not as the foundation of bodily birth, in which significance both the Indian and the Egyptian mythology knew it, hence also not as a representation of the material maternal womb; it is rather destined to be consumed by fire and itself united with the primal principle of all light. Material and perishable is what the maternal-tellurian egg brings forth out of itself, immaterial and partaking of immortality what proceeds from the myrrh egg. With matter the mother shares the property of heaviness, with light the father that of weightlessness. The material egg leads the life born from it to death, the sun egg conversely death to life. There white is changed into black, here black into white. Thereby the idea of rebirth from death links itself with the phoenix egg, and it is shown how near the Christian conception of the phoenix myth, as a prototype of the doctrine of the resurrection of the flesh, lay to the pagan idea itself.2) The interpreters of the Egyptian-Indian legend hitherto have confined themselves to emphasizing its astronomical-chronological relation to the idea of a great world year, and of time returning eternally, in fixed periods, to self-rejuvenation. Now if this is entirely incontestable on the express testimony of the ancients, it nevertheless shows only a particular development of the general solar fundamental idea that dominates the phoenix myth. On its connection with the conceptions of the ancients concerning the primal egg, on the other hand, it throws no light. This question has never yet been answered, and yet it was so obvious to raise it. From the female primal egg all creation has proceeded; it is ascribed to the great material nature mothers, it belongs to all the lunar women; from the two halves of the egg heaven and earth, from its content has eique vim genitalem adfundere, ex qua fetum oriri. p. 320). That even non-Christians connected the same meaning with the phoenix is shown by the many coins which indicate the apotheosis of the emperors by that bird, often with the inscription Aeternitas, Aeternitati Aug. Claudian in Phœnice 63 calls it æterna avis, and to this belief the Christian poet refers when he sings: Ἑλληνικοῖς Ἕλληνες εἴξαντες λόγοις Πείθητε, λοιπὸν τὴν ἀνάστασιν σέβειν. The phoenix on the cenotaphs of the holy martyrs, which is also mentioned in the actis passionis St. Cæciliæ, is therefore, like the majority of the oldest Christian symbols, borrowed from pagan art and the pagan conception.

As a representation of the maternal natural principle it stands at the head of the development of the material world. In the phoenix myth, on the other hand, we see it in a wholly different nature: not female but male, not tellurian and not lunar but solar, not material but incorporeal, not as beginning but as end, not entering into the change and movement of the world of becoming, but removed from it, and through fire given back to the primal source of pure light and to the harmony of the Apollonian world of being, into which the deified bird ascends amid the sound of the death songs that it sings to itself. The egg appears here in its highest elevation. But this is at the same time its dissolution. In union with the solar potency it loses its egg nature. The consummation is at the same time a passage into a new form. The transformation into fire the mystics call, according to Plutarch’s passage communicated above, Apollo, on account of aloneness, whereby fire is conceived as simplicis auraï ignis.1) Consumed by fire on the altar of Helios, the myrrh egg lets the incorporeal force of fatherhood enclosed in it, purified of every burden of matter, ascend to heaven and return to the primal seat of the purest light. In the sun egg of Helios the Aphroditean-material primal egg attains its consummation. If the primal egg falls from the moon to the earth, the sun egg returns as pure flame to the sun. If the primal egg enters downward into the lower world of becoming and passing away, the sun egg, after the great generation year is completed, takes the upward direction, in order, leaving behind every material covering, to exchange the boundaries of the lunar world of becoming for the eternity of the solar world of being. In connection with matter, which moves between two poles, the egg becomes a representation of time; for Chronos is the necessary form of all becoming, of all material development; he is creation itself in motion. In this sense Heracles-Chronos, whom the Orphics call Χρόνος ἀγήρατος, carries the material world egg, which here too is traced back to the πατρικὴ δύναμις; he is winged, like all movement of the world of becoming, hastening swiftly along, like all life in time.2) With becoming its form, time, also ceases. Above the lunar region of transience and of material origination there is no time any more. There is no matter, hence also no origination and no swiftly along; on others he holds it quietly in his arms. The more exact later.

e: passing away, hence no time. The Chronos egg can therefore find no admission there. Into the solar world the force enters, divested of the egg’s covering. Laid aside is the tellurian materiality of the maternal egg, consumed the myrrh ball of the phoenix; freed of every material nature, as pure fire the paternal principle returns to the realm of light, completed time to the timeless world of solar being. Thus, progressing from below upward, the egg has by stages divested itself of its corporeality, and has found its dissolution at last in the highest principle of light. With the successive development of what is created, the creative principle itself too has arrived at an ever purer representation. At last every materiality appears overcome, the female egg nature wholly laid aside. The light ascends from the chrysalis of matter, and presents the divine force, the νοῦς, the νοητόν of the creating potency, in full purity. What was first comes last to representation and to human consciousness. There takes place what Aristotle states in On the Parts of Animals 2, 1 thus: “What follows in becoming is first by nature, and what is last in origination is first. — — Accordingly, in the order of time matter and origination must be first, but in the order of concept the essence and form of each thing.” — What is materially first is no longer the principial; as in the second Orphic cosmogony, purely intellectual ἀρχαί take precedence over the materially comprehensible. 9.

o: Die lunarische Stufe der Dionysos-Natur, welche uns zu der solarischapollinischen und zu der richtigen Würdigung des in der brennenden Oellampe enthaltenen Mysteriengedankens führte, bietet noch eine Seite dar, die mit der Gräberwelt in der innigsten Beziehung steht. Dieselbe Verbindung des Werdens und Vergehens, der Licht- und der Schattenseite des Lebens, des schaffenden und . des zerstörenden Prinzips, welche die unterste Stufe des reinen Tellurismus beherrscht, und die es allein vermag, der stofflichen Schöpfung ewige Verjüngung zu sichern , dieselbe kehrt auf der Mondstufe wieder. Ja, je entschiedener die Zeugungsidee fich mit dem Monde und dessen nothwendig hermaphroditischer Natur verbindet, um so klarer muß an ihm auch die negative, zerstörende Naturseite, der Todes8gedanke hervorgetreten. Jede Naturkraft umschließt nothwendig beide Potenzen, und zwar nothwendig in demselben Grade der Entwicklung. Nur wo zwischen beiden das volle Gleichgewicht herrscht, und die zwei einander entgegenfließenden Ströme des Entstehens und Vergehens mit gleicher Kraft fich treffen, kann das Leben seine ewige FrishHe und Jugendlichkeit bewahren. Jsis sieht es ein, daß sie den gefangenen Typhon wieder frei geben, und dadurch den  [PDF 126]  Kampf mit dem bösen Prinzip selbst wieder hervorrufen muß. Typhons zerstörende Thätigkeit ist der sichtbaren Schöpfung so unentbehrlich als die schaffende des Horus. Nur was jener verzehrt, kann dieser durch neue Zeugung ersegend verjüngen, nur so auch Isis zu stets neuer Erfüllung ihrer Mutterbestimmung gelangen. In Typhons Freigebung offenbart die große Mutter ihre Mondnatur. Der Mythus hat dieß dadurch angedeutet, daß er ihr Haupt zur Strafe jener That mit einem Ochsenscheitel shmückt, den Mercur auf des erzürnten Horus Rath der Mutter statt des Kranzes, den sie trug, aufseßt.') In diesem Shmude erscheint sie als gehörnte Jo, die von der Sonne ihre Befruchtung erhält, und von ihrem Lichte erleuchtet den nächtlichen Himmel beherrscht. Durch gleiche Verbindung des Gedankens sind auch alle dionysischen Mondfrauen Repräsentanten der negativen Naturseite, Herrinnen des Todes nicht weniger als des Lebens, und als Grabgottheiten die Mütterlichkeit ihrer stofflichen Natur nicht weniger offenbarend, als dieß durch ihre Leben und Gedeihen leihende Bedeutung geschieht. In Ariadne's Verbindung mit dem Labyrinthe, in Aphrodite's Verehrung alt Venus Libitina 2?) in Artemis schnell treffenden Geschossen, in Demeter's und Kora's Verhältniß zu Aidoneus tritt die finstere Grabeöseite der mütterlichen Mondnatur deutlich hervor, und darum erscheinen die Bilder der großen Grabesmütter oft, wie z. e: The lunar stage of the Dionysian nature, which led us to the solar- Apollonian and to the correct appreciation of the mystery idea contained in the burning oil lamp, presents yet another side that stands in the most intimate relation to the world of the tombs. The same combination of becoming and passing away, of the light side and the shadow side of life, of the creative and the destructive principle, which dominates the lowest stage of pure tellurism, and which alone is able to secure eternal rejuvenation for material creation, the same recurs on the lunar stage. Indeed, the more decisively the idea of generation joins itself with the moon and its necessarily hermaphroditic nature, the more clearly must the negative, destructive side of nature, the thought of death, have emerged in it. Every natural force necessarily encloses both potencies, and indeed necessarily in the same degree of development. Only where full equilibrium prevails between the two, and the two streams of origination and passing away, flowing against each other, meet with equal force, can life preserve its eternal freshness and youthfulness. Isis perceives that she must set the captive Typhon free again, and thereby [PDF 126] — 112 — summon again the struggle with the evil principle itself. Typhon’s destructive activity is as indispensable to visible creation as the creative activity of Horus. Only what the former consumes can the latter replace and rejuvenate by new generation; only so, too, can Isis attain ever new fulfillment of her maternal destiny. In the release of Typhon the great mother reveals her lunar nature. The myth has indicated this by adorning her head, in punishment for that deed, with an ox-scalp, which Mercury, on the counsel of the angered Horus, sets upon the mother in place of the crown that she wore.1) In this adornment she appears as the horned Io, who receives her fecundation from the sun, and, illumined by its light, rules the nocturnal heaven. By the same connection of thought all the Dionysian lunar women, too, are representatives of the negative side of nature, mistresses of death no less than of life, and, as tomb goddesses, reveal the maternity of their material nature no less than this happens through their significance of bestowing life and prosperity. In Ariadne’s connection with the labyrinth, in the veneration of Aphrodite as Venus Libitina,2) in the swift-striking shafts of Artemis, in the relation of Demeter and Kore to Aidoneus, the darker tomb side of the maternal lunar nature comes clearly forth, and therefore the images of the great tomb mothers often appear, as e.g. on a beautiful terracotta relief from Tarsus in the Louvre, combined with the sign of the moon. The same combination of life and death shows itself also in individual attributes. I single out especially the dog. We have already come to know the dog above as a representation of matter that is ever anew fecundated, conceiving within itself, κύων and κύειν, and have mentioned the temple image of the κυνοειδὴς γυνή pursued by a man of phallic formation. In this significance it enters also into the closest connection with the moon. It is Diana’s animal, consecrated to her service and inwardly akin to her nature.3) It is the idea of generation that it shares with the nature mother; in this significance it appears connected with Aphrodite and Isis,4) and in this significance, according to Nonnus’s account,5) it ever accompanies Dionysus on his nocturnal ἄγαλμα φωσφόρου κύων ἔσῃ. Callimach. in Dian. 90 ff. blandientis. Isis herself is described as follows: Isis iuncta religione celebratur (cum Sarapide), quæ est vel terra, vel natura rerum subiaciens Soli. Hinc est quod continuatis uberibus corpus Deæ omne densetur, quia terræ vel rerum naturæ altu nutritur universitas. On her Roman temple Isis was represented riding on a dog.

e: the boundary of two worlds, whose lower and higher nature it unites in its existence mixed of both. As the moon imitates the sun, so the ape imitates man, and as in the former the material character retains the upper hand, so too in the ape, which, as the story of the ape soldiers of King Ptolemy, applied by Alciato to Italian students, vividly shows, is unable to resist the allure of nuts. I do not doubt that Horapollo’s statement, that the urinating ape designates a man concealing his missteps, because it is accustomed to cover its excrement, originally rests on the animal’s relation to the night that buries everything in its darkness. — Its relation to death and destruction is shown by the moon, which otherwise is represented preeminently as the life-giving, growth-promoting mother Aphrodite, in its designation as the region of Proserpina;1) in its identification with Kore, who is now in heaven and light, now in darkness and night;2) in its division into two halves, of which the one turned toward heaven is called the Elysian plain, the one directed toward the earth the plain of Persephone, or Antichthon;3) in the sojourn of the demons on the moon;4) in the belief that moonlight promotes putrefaction and spoiling in trees, flesh, and grain;5) in the significance that the Egyptians give to the crescent at the burial festival of Osiris;6) in the designation of Luna as Τύχη, who leads the life of men around in constant change;7) in the representation of the moon as the beginning of the corruptible world, subject to constant destruction; in the myth that Typhon found the corpse of Osiris at the full moon. The same thought has received the following expression in Hesiod and Virgil, Georg. 1, 276: Of the five days that Luna grants, the first four are fortunate and favorable to every undertaking. The fifth is an unlucky day; on it Orcus, the Eumenides, and the Giants were born. The number five belongs to the moon in its conjugal union of is to be distinguished from the friend, sets, as an object of laughter, against the gravity of the working animals, correspond wholly to the character of the Bacchic festivals, as Servius Georg. 2, 389 describes these on the occasion of the oscillatio and the jests practiced in connection with it, ad risum populo movendum. 3, 10.

e: of sisters only Medusa, the youngest, is mortal. Only One eye, only One tooth have the Graeae-Gorgons, who are also listed in the singular,1) just so the Amazons only One descent, the maternal, after which alone they are named.2) Persephone is called Mounogeneia, the only-begotten.3) In all these phenomena the same idea expresses itself. Material creation knows only one origin, the maternal. The children are all unilateres, not διφυεῖς, as, according to Athenaeus and Justin, the Athenians were only since Cecrops. They have only a mother, no father. This system rules also on the lunar stage, on which woman has so much the upper hand over man that the invocation of Luna joins of itself with gynecocracy, and Plutarch, de facie in orbe lunæ, ascribes to the moon quite generally the effecting of moisture and femininity. But if the predominance of the one-sidedly maternal nature is proper to the life side and the light side of creation, it stands in still closer relation to the night side and the death side. Here matter emerges completely in its exclusive dominion. To the matter from which it sprang the soulless corpse returns. The same maternal womb that bore it into the light takes it back again into its darkness. If already in generation the activity of the father is one that loses itself in the darkness of matter, withdrawn from sight, the father therefore never natura certus et verus, but only fictione iuris pro vero habitus: so in death too this his cooperation falls away. Here the mother alone stands at the side of the corpse, whether it be Mother Earth or the earthly woman who takes the other’s place, and in all respects, in birth and in death, appears as true γῆ (γυνή from γῆ). Therefore the dead are called not Plutonii but Demetrians, and from Mana-Geneta, Manes; therefore in the Ocnus fable it is a θήλεια ὄνος that unravels the rope; therefore the mother follows the corpse,4) the mother stands at the pyre, women, the φιλοθρῆνοι γυναῖκες, take over the lament for the dead; therefore the Lycians, when they take part in mourning, dress in women’s clothing, on which I have compiled a good deal in my Mutterrecht. This Lycian custom is doubly noteworthy because it is joined with the Lycian gynecocracy, the χρηματίζειν ἀπὸ μητέρων, and with the Lycian winged egg mothers who take the dead into their keeping, as the monument of Xanthus represents them. For here we see [PDF 131] — 117 — the predominance of maternal materiality in three different, most remarkable expressions. The same ideas of the one-sidedly female-material nature are expressed in like manner by the Amazons, the Amazonian Gorgons, and the Gorgonian Persephone, and to all of them lunar nature is common, which here again preeminently reveals its shadow side and death side. Shall I add to all this Hecate’s threefold nature, and the double relation to life and death of the water so closely bound to the moon? For Hecate unites in her female nature the double pole of all life, the nascendi et vivendi and the moriendi potestas, both in her tellurian and in her lunar stage.1) Water, moreover, this life-generating element, which rolls the phallus of Osiris in its waves, hides Aphrodite’s egg, stamps Dionysus as Poseidon γενέσιος, and so often expresses the concept of male generative force in its name, as in Peneus, the Elean and Thessalian πέος (penis, πηλός),2) in Larisus, Larius, in Arsen, in mare, πέλαγος, θάλασσα (related to τάλος, τύλος), κῦμα (related to κύων, κύω), is on the other hand connected again with tomb and death, now as the subterranean Acheron, Anio, Eridanus,3) now as favorite place of the dead, whose tombs are erected preferably on the banks of waters. In the swamps around Babylon Alexander sees the royal tombs of the native rulers. At the Gygaean swamp lake those of the Lydian kings are erected. In the marshes of the Velabrum Acca Larentia has her tomb. On the forest stream Oceanus Lycians show Pausanias (1, 35, 6) the tomb of Geryon. Why should I heap up further examples, when the necropolis of Castel d’Asso shows the same arrangement, Strabo designates the Campus Martius on the Tiber as a place of tombs, and Plutarch, de mul. virtut., at the end, himself cites an example of how one sought, just as by the Euripus of the circus, to replace by artificial means the lack of water at tombs. The life-generating element4) becomes the stream of death, and the eternally mourning, as his myth represents him, from ἀνία; hence Anio, like Acheron, the stream of suffering, although the etymology ὁ ἄχεα ῥέων is in itself incorrect, and is to be subordinated to the other, according to which Acheron attaches itself to Ach just like Achilleus, Achelous, Achaïa, Acharnæ, Acis, Acca, and other formations. ta, sed ex Aegyptiis tracta sunt sacris: nam certis diebus in sacris Nili pueri, de sacris parentibus nati, a sacerdotibus Nymphis dabantur: qui cum adolevissent, redditi narabant, lucos esse sub terris, et immensam aquam omnia continentem, ex qua cuncta procreantur. Unde est illud secundum Thaletem: Oceanumque, patrem rerum. Hence [PDF 132] — 118 — monotonous lament of its waves is the Nereids’ song of mourning for the untimely death of Achilles. So sings the chorus in Aeschylus’s Prometheus: And plaintively roars the wave-beat of the wide sea, the deep sighs, Far echoes the gloomy abyss of Hades, The trickling springs of the sacred streams bewail your affliction. Everywhere the same fundamental idea shows itself: life is at the same time death; Venus also Libitina; Aphrodite also the slayer of men; the moon at once source of becoming and of passing away, lovely and white in the former, hideous, terrifying, and black in the latter function; in both akin to water, in which it finds its nourishment, which it causes to well forth from the earth,1) with which, in the nocturnal dew, it refreshes the thirsting fields,2) and in which, as the ancients already knew,3) it also calls forth ebb and flood, the image of change, by its influence so mightily acting on everything tellurian. This night side expresses itself also very definitely in the outward appearance of the moon. Corresponding to its double dominion over life and death, it appears ever changing, ever leading fullness back into nothing, so that, as an ancient remarks, no garment would ever fit it. Ever it wages the struggle against darkness, as Horus against Typhon, now succumbing, now victorious. As the double color in the egg, so white and black divide in its disk. Black spots disfigure its bright surface. The same variegation is shown by the hide of the stag, which thereby confirms its kinship with Diana.4) For its relation to the lunar woman does not rest in this similarity alone. In its tree-like antlers and in its custom of shedding them5) and hiding them in the earth, it appears as an image of maternal earth, which lets the trees of the forest grow forth from her womb: a relation that is embedded even in the designation Dama. For Dama is related to Damia, Damium, Damiatrix,6) Pythagoras, who adhered to that doctrine, is greeted by the river Cosa: Salve, Pythagora. Aelian. V. H. 2, 26; 4, 17. the starry heaven. By the one relation the other is not refuted. Enough that the symbolic conception is established. As attribute of Artemis ἐλαφηβόλος and Laphria: Paus. 7, 18, 7. As the moon cries out for water, so the stag cries out for the spring, a property that even in Christian antiquity lends it a relation to baptisteries.1) As an accompaniment of the earth it appears on a cameo of the Museum Florentinum, which Stark in his de tellure Dea chose as the central point of his account.2) By its connection with night the moon is, moreover, the star of death. It brings sleep and repose and that stillness which is attributed to primal chaos, as to the grave that leads back to it, and to the mysteries; which makes the solemn still more solemn and the terrible still more terrible, lets the very face of the lunar disk appear as a grinning mask that threatens destruction, corresponds to the Manes and the silentia regna, and has found a moving expression in the tombs through the many representations of those scenes designated in art as still lifes. As the sun each morning awakens life and movement, and thus with its rays draws from Memnon’s column its first sound, so conversely the moon leads all things back to rest and silence.3) It is the star of ruins, by the same property also that of tombs, and is often depicted on funerary lamps, as e.g. also on a Tarsian one. At night the lemuria are celebrated, at night the funera are held.4) The moon yields to the sun, as night to day. The ancients conceive this phenomenon as a birth of light out of darkness,5) and recognize in it the daily repetition of a great act of cosmogony. Here too the female-material principle maintains its primacy in creation. It is the first, the originally given. Helios stands to Nox in the relation of a son; he is the mystery of the male solar force revealed through birth, he is the Dionysus-Enorches who breaks through from the egg to the light, the visible creation that steps into day from the dark maternal womb. Accordingly night shows an inner kinship with the dark egg. Like it, it is the female natural principle, like it the ἀρχὴ γενέσεως. So it appears in the first Orphic cosmogony, which Damascius, principia pp. 380–384 Kopp, designates as the common doctrine, shrouded by a Ovid. F. 2, 607.

cloud, and Aristophanes follows it in the Birds, lines 693–704, in that he lets an egg come forth out of Night in Erebus, from which then the birds, those winged creatures surpassing gods and men in age and nobility, arise. In the cosmogony of Acusilaus Nox is joined, as the female principle, with Erebus, the male; in that of Epimenides, with Aer. Here too one recognizes the foundation of Orphic doctrine, which forms the chief content of the Bacchic mysteries, and of that gradual succession of becoming, already emphasized above, which takes as its basis an unfolding of creation and of the creator out of the formless into form, out of chaos into definite configuration, out of darkness into light, out of matter into the νοητόν, out of materiality into a being comprehensible only to the spirit, thus in everything a progress from below upward, in contrast to emanation in descending embodiment. On this female-material fundamental principle rests the reckoning of time by a twenty-four-hour period beginning at midnight, in which the male day appears enclosed by two female nights. On it rests also the lunar year, which expresses in the reckoning of time the lunar-material stage of religion. From it, too, the idea of the Roman Mater Matuta receives its explanation. She is at once the great nature mother and the goddess of the early light, at once Leucothea, the shining moon, and Ino, who seeks her death in the waves of the sea. All this by virtue of her significance as the female-material natural principle, which has its physical basis in the earth and its waters, but also in the moon, and which as such comprehends within itself life and death, light and darkness, and, as Aurora, gives birth to the day out of itself. In the abduction of Cephalus the significance of death in maternal nature emerges again. In the same moment origination and destruction unite. Minerva carries both attributes at once, the golden lamp and the cock. In the former she shows her kinship with the night and the nocturnal moon; in the latter she stands before us as Matuta, who gives birth to the early light. In both relations she is the material mother who, as Gorgon-bearer, as Amazon hostile to marriage, as barren Pempta, represents the side of night and death in the maternal nature of matter.

Auf diesem weiblich stofflichen Grundprinzip ruht die Zeitrehnung nach einem mit Mitternacht beginnenden 24stündigen Abschnitt, in welchem der männliche Tag von zwei weiblihen Nächten eingeschlossen erscheint. Auf ihm das Mondjahr, das die lunarisch-stoffliche Religionsstufe in der Zeitrehnung ausdrückt. Aus ihm erhält auch die Jdee der römischen Mater-Matuta ihre Erklärung. Sie ist zugleich die große Naturmutter und die Göttin des Frühlichts, zugleich Leucothea, der leuchtende Mond, und Jno, die in des Meeres Wogen ihren Tod sucht. Alles dieß kraft ihrer Bedeutung als weiblich-stoffliches Naturprinzip, das in der Erde und ihren Gewässern, aber auch im Monde seine physische Unterlage hat, als solhes Leben und Tod, Licht und Finsterniß in sich begreift, und als Aurora den Tag aus sich gebiert. In Cephalus Raub tritt wieder die Todeöbedeutung der Mutternatur hervor. In dem gleichen Augenblick vereinigen sich Entstehen und Untergang. Minerva führt zugleich beide Attribute, die goldene Lampe und den Hahn. Jn jener zeigt sie ihre Verwandtschaft mit der Nacht und dem nächtlichen Monde, in diesem steht sie als Matuta, die das Frühlicht gebiert, vor uns. Jn beiden Beziehungen ist sie die stoffliche Mutter, die als Gorgoträgerin, als ehefeindliche Amazone, als unfruchtbare Pempta die Nacht- und Todeösseite der Mutternatur des Stoffes darstellt. ' So vereinigt sich Alles, dieselbe Verbindung von Weiß und Shwarz, welche das Wesen der dionysischen Natur bildet, auch für die Mondstufe der stofflichen Weiblichkeit herzustellen. Luna trägt die Mutternatur in ihrer zwiefachen, ihrer wohlthätigen und ihrer verderblichen Seite, in sih. Die Mischung von Furcht und Freude knüpft sich vorzugsweise an den Mond. Hoff [PDF 135]  nung verbunden.) Den Sclechten zeigt das himmlische Gestirn das furchtbare Antlitz, das ihnen Strafe verkündet, die Frommen dagegen werden die volle Schönheit desselben erkennen. Die physische Jdee kehrt in vergeistigter Bedeutung wieder. Die finstere und die helle Seite des nächtlichen Gestirns wird das Bild des Looses, das die Seelen der Verstorbenen erwartet. e: Thus everything unites to produce, for the lunar stage of material femininity as well, the same combination of white and black that forms the essence of the Dionysian nature. Luna bears maternal nature within herself in its twofold aspect, its beneficent and its destructive side. The mixture of fear and joy attaches itself preeminently to the moon. Precisely thereby it acquires special significance for the mysteries. For the mood that one feels at initiation is that of fear and anxiety, with joyful hope [PDF 135] — 121 — united.1) To the wicked the heavenly star shows the terrible countenance that proclaims their punishment; the pious, on the other hand, will recognize its full beauty. The physical idea returns in spiritualized significance. The dark and the bright side of the nocturnal star become the image of the lot that awaits the souls of the departed. For after separation from the body the souls wander about in the space between earth and moon. Here the unjust and the vicious atone for their transgressions; the pious, on the other hand, after all the stains that stem from the body, the author of evil, have been effaced, will pass through and gain firm footing on the moon. Here, crowned with wreaths and like a ray of the sun, they hear the cry of lament and wailing, rising from below, of those who are being punished. But they also recognize the mixed nature of the star itself into which they have been received. The light and the heavy, the tellurian and the uranian component, hold each other in perfect balance in it. To the plain of Persephone corresponds the Elysian. The former is turned toward the earth, πατρίδα, γεύονται χαρᾶς, οἵαν οἱ τελούμενοι μάλιστα θορύβῳ καὶ πτοήσει συγκεκραμένῃ μετ᾽ ἐλπίδος ἰδίας ἔχουσι. Instead of ἰδίας, read ἡδείας. Thus Cicero and Apuleius have used the expression melior spes of the Initia, and this agreement seems to point to an entirely technical expression. Apuleius explains its meaning through the novæ salutis curricula, which he emphasizes at 11, p. 270. I seize this occasion to cite the saying of Sophocles in Plutarch de audiend. poetis, Hutten 7, 81: Πολλὰς γὰρ ἀνθρώπων μυριάδας ἐμπέπληκεν (ὁ Σοφοκλῆς) ἀθυμίας περὶ τῶν μυστηρίων ταῦτα γράψας ὡς τρισόλβιοι Κεῖνοι βροτῶν, οἱ ταῦτα δερχθέντες τέλη, Μόλωσ᾽ ἐς Ἅδου. Τοῖσδε γὰρ μόνοις ἐκεῖ Ζῆν ἐστι, τοῖς δ᾽ ἄλλοισι πάντ᾽ ἐκεῖ κακά. Among the scholars of today there may now be many who ask mockingly, with the Cynic Diogenes (in Plut. l. c.), whether the thief Pataecion, because he had been initiated, has a better lot than Epaminondas? Others may see everything in the light of priestly fraud. To the latter we answer what Gorgias (in Plut. l. c. p. 59) said of tragedy: that it is a deception in which the deceiver is more just, and the deceived wiser, than he who does not deceive and is not deceived. To the former, however, we give this to consider, that the highest purpose of the mysteries was none other than sanctification and purification, and the strengthening of the conviction that between the state of the soul in that life and the morality demonstrated on this side there prevails a necessarily corresponding relation. Those who emulate the gods will return to them after death, but the vicious will be excluded from the community of the gods. Cicero, Tusc. 1, 30. The ancients combined with a religion material in its foundation the most earnest striving for ethical and moral sanctification, whereas the moderns leave nothing undone to subordinate their religion, purely spiritual in origin and content, once more to matter and to impure matter. For them no excuse is at hand. Timæus p. 90 a.

e: this one to the sun. From the former a second death leads the pure νοῦς into the realm of light of the sun; from the Elysian they descend again, and sink anew into the abyss of matter. This conception, which for the most part follows word for word the statements of Plutarch on the face that appears in the lunar disk, c. 28–29, gives the moon, for the world of spirits, the same significance that it has for the corporeal-material world and for the cosmos in general. It is the connection of two worlds, a higher and a lower, the point of passage where the two currents, the ὁδὸς ἄνω καὶ κάτω, meet; thus it maintains the connection of the tellurian with the solar, of the corporeal with the incorporeal sphere, whose constant passage into one another constitutes the highest harmony of the cosmos, and at the same time the joyful hope of the initiate.1) 10. We have now become so familiar with the egg, with its Bacchic relation, its relation to the world of the tombs, and with the mystery idea contained in it, that it becomes of ever greater interest to add still more new ones to the number of monuments that represent the egg symbol. What puts difficulty in the way of this endeavor, and makes great care doubly necessary, is the slight exactness that ancient art devotes to the representation of smaller objects, often of little importance for the main picture. Since the merely suggestive manner, especially in accompanying attributes, prevails over naturalistic execution, the question often arises whether what the eye, predisposed in favor of its task, is inclined to take for an egg may not perhaps be assignable to other objects, especially apples, whose erotic significance is, after all, beyond all doubt. The egg seems to me certain on the following monuments. A vase painting of the Louvre collection shows a square pillar resting on a broader base, on whose upper surface a white egg stands upright. A nude, wreathed female figure shows Virgil, from which lines 221–227 may find a place here: Deum namque ire per omnis Terrasque, tractusque maris, cælumque profundum. Hinc pecudes, armenta, viros, genus omne ferarum, Quemque sibi tenuis nascentem arcessere vitas. Scilicet huc reddi deinde ac resoluta referri Omnia: nec morti esse locum, sed viva volare Sideris in numerum, atque alto succedere cœlo. Cf. Manilius, Astron. 2, 60 ff. Aen. 6, 726.

The sphere leaves no doubt about the Bacchic relation. — On a vessel of the Vienna collection, designated there IV, 167, a pillar appears, surrounded by a goose and a laurel branch. On the top of the stone lie two eggs. The ephebe approaching, adorned with a radiate crown, carries on his outstretched right hand the patella, on which likewise three white egg-shaped objects lie. MVTILI | MARVLII | VIX. ANN. | XVII. This monument can shed light on the egg-crowned grave stelae discovered in the Praenestine tombs, which Braun describes in the Bulletino 1855. The great number of them shows how generally current the egg symbol was. Similar monuments are known from the Museo Guarnacci. On a square base rises the egg, whose form reproduces the truth of nature. Great kinship with it is shown by the stone monuments of the united collections at Munich, which are said to come from Salzburg. From these may have proceeded those variously modified representations on other funerary monuments of Etruria. See Inghirami, mon. Etrusci ser. 1. tav. 100. Canina, Etruria maritima 2, 31. In this use the egg alternates with other equivalent symbols, with the pomegranate, with the pyramid, the palmette, but especially with the ball and the flat disk-like circular section, as these not infrequently occur on the tops of funerary pillars. On monuments of unambiguous significance the circle appears as the sign of apotheosis.1) The circle derives this symbolic use from the property of the circular line, which, like all life of the tellurian creation, returns ever again to itself and, in its progress, to its point of departure. Like the egg, therefore, it encloses both poles between which creation moves eternally to and fro, and which, like white and black, constantly pass over into one another. It thereby becomes itself a sign of the natural force that encloses life and death within itself. This significance recurs intensified in those concentric circles that are so frequent on funerary monuments. They correspond to the plurality of eggs, the three circles of Praenestine discs to the 3 eggs of our tomb painting. On this also rests the significance of the discus. The swiftness with which it flies along the course is equal to that of the two-horse team, a representation of the swiftness with which the united forces of death and of life bring about the revolution of visible creation and that eternal alternation of generations. Thereby ball, discus, and circle gain a definite relation to the physical bearers of natural force, to the tellurian water as well as to the heavenly sunlight. Likewise the racotta.) Cf. o: Symbol hat, wie die Kraft, tiefere und höhere Stufen, deren Mehrheit es in fich verbindet. Als Bezeihnung der Wasserkraft erscheint die Sphära in der Hand der Nymphen, ') als Sonnenmacht wird die Erfindung des Discus auf Perseus zurückgeführt.?) Daraus erklärt sich die Verbindung des Discus mit dem Lotus, welche in dem pränestinischen Grabe zuerst zum Vorschein kam. Es ist die Verbindung der Sonnen- und der Wasserkraft, deren Zusammenwirken zu jeder tellurischen Zeugung erforderlich ist, so daß Plutarchs Untersuchung, was nüßlicher sei, Wasser oder Feuer, den Jdeen der alten Religion nicht sonderlich entspricht. Nun scheint das Discusrund selbst der Sonnen- und Mondscheibe zu entsprechen, und die Kugel eine Darstellung des Erd- und Himmelsgewölbes. Alle diese Beziehungen des Kreises und seiner verschiedenen Darfiellungen haben neben einander Wahrheit und Berechtigung. Die ursprüngliche Beziehung aber, an welche sich die übrigen und zulegt die Mysterienbedeutung anschließen, ist keine andere, als jenes in der Kreislinie zur Anschauung kommende ewige Zurückkehren der Schöpfung auf sich selbst, jenes ineinander Ruhen von Ende und Anfang, das auch dem doppelgefärbten Ei seine Bedeutung leiht. DadurHh wird der Kreis zum Ausdruck des Fatums, oder des höchsten alles Leben beherrschenden Naturgeseßes, vor welhem auch die Götter sich beugen z2) dadurh ebenso zur Darstellung der Unsterblichkeit, welhe aus der ewigen Verjüngung des Lebens mit Hilfe des Todes hervorgeht. (Es macht somit für die Idee selbst wenig Unterschied, ob ein eiförmiger oder ein kreisrunder Körper, oder andere aus beiden Formen zusammengeseßte Figuren die Grabsäulen und Meten krönen. Der Künstler folgte der alten Sepulcral-Tradition , und konyte, da er sich weniger durch den Jnhalt des Gedankens, als durch das Gefühl für Harmonie der Form leiten ließ, zu den verschiedensten Modifikationen und Verschönerungen der reinen Ei- und der vollendeten Kreisform seine Zuflucht nehmen. So sind diese beiden Symbole gleich den zruara und den vielen Gattungen von Schlinggewächsen zuleßt die Grundbestandtheile einer äußerst reichen Ornamentik geworden, die, wie auch einzelne Architekturstüke, wie namentlich die Jonische Säule, aus den Gräbern in die Wohnungen der Menschen herausgetreten sind. Bilder tiefsinniger Jdeen, welche den Grundinhalt der Religion selbst bildeten, und die ganze Fülle der mit Tod und Grab verbundenen höhern Ahnungen
e: symbol has, like the force, lower and higher stages, the plurality of which it unites in itself. As a designation of the force of water the sphere appears in the hand of the nymphs;1) as solar power the invention of the discus is traced back to Perseus.2) From this is explained the combination of the discus with the lotus, which first came to light in the Praenestine tomb. It is the combination of the solar and the aquatic force, whose cooperation is required for every tellurian generation, so that Plutarch’s inquiry as to which is more useful, water or fire, does not particularly correspond to the ideas of the ancient religion. Now the round of the discus itself seems to correspond to the disk of the sun and the moon, and the ball to be a representation of the vault of earth and heaven. All these relations of the circle and of its various representations have truth and legitimacy side by side. The original relation, however, to which the others and finally the significance for the mysteries attach, is none other than that eternal return of creation upon itself that comes to view in the circular line, that resting of end and beginning in one another, which also lends the two-colored egg its significance. Thereby the circle becomes the expression of Fate, or of the highest law of nature governing all life, before which even the gods bow;3) thereby likewise the representation of immortality, which issues from the eternal rejuvenation of life by the aid of death. It makes, therefore, little difference for the idea itself whether an egg-shaped or a perfectly round body, or other figures composed of both forms, crown the funerary pillars and the metae. The artist followed the old sepulchral tradition, and, since he let himself be guided less by the content of the idea than by a feeling for harmony of form, could take refuge in the most various modifications and embellishments of the pure egg form and the perfected circular form. Thus these two symbols, like the κύματα and the many kinds of climbing plants, have finally become the basic components of an extremely rich ornamentation, which, like individual architectural pieces, such as especially the Ionic column, has passed out of the tombs into the dwellings of men. Images of profound ideas that formed the fundamental content of religion itself, and in which the whole fullness of the higher intimations connected with death and the tomb φέρουσα, ἡ δὲ κλεῖδα. Connect with this the speaking name Sphaerus, which Pelops’s charioteer bore. Paus. 2, 23, 1; 5, 10, 2. The other name Κίλλας can be explained from Servius Georg. 2, 389.
