To the funerary monuments communicated I append some that are exposed to greater doubts, and which must therefore be reserved for further verification. On a Cornetan tomb painting, whose copy is preserved in the Philosophical Transactions, and which is communicated after it by Inghirami, Monumenti Etrusci ser. 4. t. 24. p. 124. 128, we see the egg in the left hand of a male figure who extends his right hand in farewell to another, a female figure. The gate seems to await the impending entry of the egg-bearer, and to be one of those gates of purification through which the departed pass before they attain the highest stage of blessedness.1) — On an Etruscan mirror in the museum of the collegio romano, in Lanzi, saggio 2, t. 8. f. 6. Gerhard, etruskische Spiegel, plate 171, the two Dioscuri, Poloces and Amuces,2) surround Losna, who is made recognizable by the crescent moon. The scene is closed by a funerary pillar that bears an egg on its top. The enigmatic object at the right edge of the picture, to which a similar one on the opposite side corresponds, I take for a female sporium, the κτείς, which we also see depicted on Etruscan tombs, particularly on the doorpost of a tomb at Fallari, of which the drawing is to be found in the appendices to my Mutterrecht, and which appears on Asiatic monuments as an object of religious cult.3) The inner connection of all these symbols, of the egg, of the moon, of the female locus genitalis, cannot be doubtful after what has been said above. Thereby it also gains significance that this mirror was found in the cista of Novius Plautius, which is preserved in the Kircherianum, and which, in its lid figures, as well as in their number, three, and that of the vessel feet, declares a decided relation to Bacchic initiation.4) The cista belongs to the female nature deities, and under this designation are to be understood both the plaited baskets that occur with the serpent on many monuments, and the cylindrical bronze receptacles of the tombs, and the square, now taller, now flatter de Vénus, pl. 1, nr. 1, 2, 8. and Recherches sur le culte de Vénus, second mémoire p. 52– 55. The testimony of Euseb. Pr. Ev. 2, 3 in f. on the significance of the κτείς and its veneration in the mysteries of Themis, as well as Augustin. C. D. 6, 9. Cf. 711 has escaped this scholar.

e: little chests that we often see represented on vases and terracottas. The cista is attributed especially to Demeter;1) the surviving bronze vessels come for the most part from Praeneste and stand, beyond doubt, in the closest connection with the cult of the Fortuna preeminently venerated there, of Bacchic- Cerealian nature, a representation of the female-material natural principle. On a terracotta of the Vogelberg collection at Munich the cista appears on the arm of one of those earnest tomb mothers whom we may with equal right call Ceres, Aphrodite, Fortuna, Pherephatta. In connection with initiation the same little chest appears very often on vase paintings, always as an accompaniment of female beings. The meaning, therefore, cannot be doubtful. The cista is the representation of the maternal womb, of the locality in which all life is conceived and developed to birth, of the χώρα καὶ δεξαμένη γενέσεως, as Plato calls femininity in contrast to masculinity conceived as the vertical line, of the Varronian locus genitalis, in quo vitæ primordia consistunt, of the female chamber, which German usage has retained, and which many a myth, such as the one mentioned above of the Dioscuri’s penetration into the maidens’ chamber in Phormio’s house, has in part made the subject of its representation. To male force every idea of locality and spatiality is alien and opposed; in the materiality of woman, on the other hand, it is necessarily contained, woman by her nature χώρα καὶ δεξαμένη, a locus, a chamber, a spatiality,2) which only matter, not force, admits. Thus the cista corresponds perfectly to the female nature. It is the attribute, or better the representation, of maternity in its natural determination, of fecundation, of the seminis immissio in monetam, of the conception, cherishing, and sheltering of the seed and of every young life. Dark is its space, like that of the gloomy maternal womb. In it, shut off from the light, the male phallus develops its work. It is therefore also enclosed in the mystic cista, as it penetrates, invisible as generative force, the maternal matter of the earth and of the moon. When in so many myths the newborn child is shut up in a chest and entrusted with it to the sea, the idea of the sheltering maternal womb is repeated therein, whose image the ancients also recognized in the shells,3) 25, 4; 8, 37. Here the discussion is of Despoina-Ceres, whose initiation ceremonies Pausanias saw depicted on a relief of the temple. Tibull Ecl. 1, 8, 21. Buonarroti, M. A. p. 448. γένεσιν εἶναι. Ovid. F. 1, 673. Hon dem Kasten hat Kypselos seinen Namen erhalten, das heißt, er ist na; der Mutter genannt. Unechter Geburt, hat er keinen Vater, sondern nur eine Mutter. Er heißt von dem weiblichen locus genitalis Kypselos , wie spurius von dem weiblichen 5porium der in demselben von unbekanntem Sämann Gesäte. Wir erkennen also nun die innere Verwandtschaft des Ei's mit der Cista und beider Beziehung zu Luna und dem aus dem Mond-Ei gebornen Dioscurenpaare , die wie Tod und Leben, einen Tag um den andern das Licht und die Finsterniß am Himmel emporführen. Wir erkennen aber zugleich auch den Zusammenhang der verschiedenen Bedeutungen von Mundus. Der geöffnete Mundus, in welchen die Städtegründer Erstlinge aller Früchte und aller Reihthümer hineinwerfen, ist der mütterliche locus genitalis , aus dem aller Seegen hervorgeht. Seine Oeffnung steht mit dem cerealen Ei und der Funerär-Bedeutung der Circusspiele in nächster Beziehung. Wie aber das Ei zum Bilde des Weltalls, so wird der tellurischt Mundus die Darstellung dessen, was die Pythagoreer zuerst xoöuos nannten. Wie endlich in der Psychefabel Proserpina's Pyris alle zu Aphroditens Schmut erforderlichen Schönheitsmittel birgt, so verändert sih auch der Mundus zur Toilette und zum Behälter alles dessen, was aphroditischen Liebreiz zu geben vermag. Durch dieselbe Begriffsverbindung wird die Cista zum Shmukkästchen der Frau, und völlig verständlich, warum die meisten der erhaltenen weiblict Toilettenstücke, auch wohl mit männlichen gemischt, in sich bargen. Sie mögen Lebenden zu wirklihem Gebrauch gedient haben, und also den Namen der Schmudkästhen rechtfertigen. Jhre religiöse Bedeutung aber, die der Natur der pränestinischen Mutter entspricht, ist von der Frage der praktischen Bestimmung durchaus unabhängig. I< wende mich zu andern Monumenten, die über das Vorkommen des Ei? noh einige Zweifel übrig lassen. e: the nuts, the legumes, such as peas and beans, which owe their tellurian significance precisely to this property. From the chest Cypselus received his name, that is, he is named after the mother. Of illegitimate birth, he has no father, but only a mother. He is called Cypselus from the female locus genitalis, as spurius is named from the female sporium the one sown in it by an unknown sower. We now recognize, then, the inner kinship of the egg with the cista, and the relation of both to Luna and to the pair of Dioscuri born from the moon egg, who, like death and life, bring up light and darkness in the sky, one day after the other. But at the same time we recognize also the connection of the various meanings of Mundus. The opened Mundus, into which the founders of cities throw the first fruits of all produce and of all riches, is the maternal locus genitalis from which all blessing proceeds. Its opening stands in the nearest relation to the Cerealian egg and to the funerary significance of the circus games. But as the egg becomes the image of the universe, so the tellurian Mundus becomes the representation of that which the Pythagoreans first called κόσμος. As finally in the fable of Psyche Proserpina’s pyxis holds all the means of beauty required for Aphrodite’s adornment, so too the Mundus changes into the toilette and the container of everything that can give Aphroditean charm. By the same combination of concepts the cista becomes the jewel box of woman, and it is entirely understandable why most of the surviving ones held within them female toilet articles, perhaps also mixed with male ones. They may have served the living for actual use, and thus justify the name of jewel boxes. Their religious significance, however, which corresponds to the nature of the Praenestine mother, is entirely independent of the question of practical purpose. I turn to other monuments that still leave some doubts as to the occurrence of the egg. On the Xanthian tomb, which in the British Museum, in the hall of Lycian antiquities, under the gloomy clouded sky of England proclaims the laughing splendor of Asia, the egg that forms the womb of the Harpies is beyond doubt; but less certain is it on the scenes that adorn its west and south sides. I unfortunately neglected, on my last visit to London, to give that detail the proper attention, and must therefore leave it to others to make good what I represents the winged phallus penetrating an opened shell. On the west side the egg appears twice, namely in the left hand of the female seated figure, in whom an Aphroditean earth mother is unmistakable, and likewise in that of the last figure, which closes the procession of women. The position that the cow suckling the calf occupies precisely in this picture seems not only to explain the thought of the offering of the egg, but even to require it. For the egg is, like that cow symbol so generally diffused in the ancient world, omniparentis terræ fœcundum simulacrum, and by this significance a symbol that expresses the whole Aphroditean nature in its twofold aspect. In the representation of the south side the egg enters into a similar combination with the dove, whose connection with the Aphroditean nature and with Aphrodite’s egg is already clear from the above. Such a predominance of the egg symbol cannot in the least surprise on a funerary monument of Lycia, which was devoted to gynecocracy. The predominance of maternity emerges clearly enough also in the fables of Bellerophon’s reverence before the sight of the female κτείς, of the meaning of Leda in the Lycian language, and in the myth of the Lycian frog lake of Latona-Leda, the great primal mother. All this has in a certain measure found its total expression in the egg. On the tomb especially, where maternity always emerges as alone ruling, the egg symbol is doubly justified in its twofold significance, embracing life and death equally.1) 11. Having so far found the egg preferentially on funerary monuments, we shall now demonstrate it on monuments of other purpose as well. I begin with the one that offers the most doubt and difficulty. On various coins the Minotaur holds in his right hand a round object, which has been taken now for an apple, now for a ball. The one is a silver coin of Knossus, depicted in Pellerin, recueil, T. 3. tab. 89, 24, and Böttiger, Ideen zur Kunstmythologie 1, pl. 5, 1. On its reverse the labyrinth is represented in square form. The other Mercury’s hand. I ascribe it to the slight attention that representations of the egg have hitherto found when the interpreter here thinks of an apple, and thus puts himself in obvious contradiction with the representation of his own picture. Here too we cannot mistake the Bacchic relation, as indeed the significance for the mysteries of the ἔσοπτρον in the service of Dionysus is established according to Euseb. Pr. The form that this coin gives the object excludes the thought of an apple, and there remains only the question whether we have before us a circle or an egg. Both assumptions would in the end yield the same idea, and agree with the total significance of the Minotaur. For the egg, several reasons seem to me to speak. First, the special prominence of the female natural principle in the Cretan religion. In Ariadne, Pasiphaëssa, Artemis, Dictynna, Britomartis it appears with the physical foundation of the tellurian and the heavenly earth, the male generative potency standing over against it preeminently still as Poseidonian force of water, conceived in a chthonian manner. As Ariadne’s labyrinth represents the inextricable passages of the maternal womb of earth, so too the Minotaur shows force on the lowest stage of the Dionysian nature, as chthonian potency of water, with the bull’s head, διὰ τὸ γόνιμον τοῦ ὕδατος, and therefore with special emphasis on the dark, destroying side of life, in which significance he recommended himself especially to the usage of the legions as a victory-bringing standard.1) On this tellurian-lunar stage of religion female materiality has the preponderance over male potency. Therefore Ariadne appears as ruler of Crete. Therefore the Cretans say even later, as Plato and Plutarch testify, not “fatherland” but “dear motherland,”2) and therefore the egg also would be quite eminently suited as a symbol of this Aphroditean-female religious principle, which encloses earth and moon, death and life. Given the close kinship that connects Crete with Lycia, the community of the symbol too cannot surprise, and when we recall the inner relation that connects the Minotaur with the bull-bodied Bacchus-Hebon, the Cretan egg of the Minotaur leads back in the end to the Bacchic one of the Dionysian-Orphic mysteries. By just this kinship with Dionysus the occurrence of the Minotaur in Magna Graecia is explained, where he enters into the closest relation with the bull-shaped Bacchus. His defeat by Theseus stands on a line with the destruction of the Amazons. Both deeds prepare the transition from a lower, more material stage of religion to a higher one, more akin to the Apollonian luminous nature; it is the progress from the stage of earth and moon to the solar region, which in Dionysus is still more phallic and directed to fecundation, in Theseus, on the other hand, ever since [PDF 145] — 131 — he left Ariadne on Athena’s counsel, comes to be represented in higher Apollonian purity. I turn to a second doubtful work of sculpture, but one that is probably to be counted among the egg monuments. Winckelmann, Monumenti inediti, communicates to us at the end of the trattato preliminare the illustration of a relief in rosso antico preserved in the Capitoline Museum at Rome,1) whose content admits of no doubt. We see here the representation of a sacrifice that a newly wed woman offers to the goddess Hygieia. If the significance of the whole is thus unmistakable, yet precisely the determination of the offered object presents difficulties. In the left hand of the girl an egg-shaped object appears, which, however, according to Winckelmann’s assurance, shows a flat surface, whereby it remains undecided what share time may have had in the form now visible. Winckelmann guesses at the oblation of the Πέμματα, which, mentioned by Pausanias 7, p. 600, 10, p. 817, are explained by Pollux 1, 29 and Hesych. Even in her connection with the maternal Athena, Hygieia presents herself as a material nature mother who bestows prosperity.1) The same principle that gives life bestows also health and the adornment of bodily beauty. All this is Hygieia’s gift, and herein she shows the general maternal nature of matter developed on a particular side and in a particular direction. The egg too has gone through the same transition from the more general to the more specific significance. By its foundation the beginning of all life, the ἀρχὴ γενέσεως for the whole and for each individual thing, it now becomes the bearer and symbol of every kind of salvation, especially of bodily well-being. Lustration with the egg protects against the harmful influence of the fever-laden September, and against the enervating sirocco, which Horace 2, 6, 18 calls plumbeus. Metuique jubet septembris et austri adventum, nisi se centum lustraverit ovis, the castrated mendicant priest of the Great Mother proclaims in Juvenal 6, 518 to the superstitiously listening people. The same purpose of averting misfortune is served by that egg lustration of which Ovid A. a. 2, 329 expresses himself thus: Et veniat, quæ purget anus lectumque locumque, Præferat et tremula sulfur et ova manu. Thereby blessing is brought into the house, especially into the marriage bed. The eggs that serve for lustration are offered to Hecate, the great material mother, the mistress over life and death, at the crossroads. This ᾠὸν ἐκ καθαρσίου Lucian mentions, Dialog. mort. 1, 1. ed Bipont. 8, p. 129, on which one must read Hemsterhuys’s exposition, more collecting than explanatory, ibid. pp. 397–401. Plutarch, Symp. 7, 6 places Hecate together with the gods who avert misfortune, and sees in the δεῖπνα set out for her at the crossroads, which are called καθάρματα and Ἑκάταια, Sueton August. 80.) rests the egg to which the serpent draws near. On this summis digitis Deos colere, which emerges on so many monuments of sacral purpose, speak Lactant. 1, 20; 5, 19; Ovid. F. 2, 573. The combination with the tripod and other Apollonian attributes cannot be surprising for Hygieia any more than for Aesculapius; and Eros, who stands as a little boy at the right of the goddess, enters into connection with her as with Fortuna and other mother goddesses, as he is indeed called her father by Proclus on Plato, Timæus 3, 158. On the present monument he may moreover have a still more specific relation to love, marriage, and fertility, and thus stand close to the idea of the egg. — On a Pompeian wall painting in Zahn, second series, pl. 52, Müller, pl. 61, 782, Hygieia stands wreathed with laurel, holding a laurel branch in her left hand. The serpent entwines the whole figure in great coils, and brings its head near a patella that the goddess holds out to it on her right hand. On it lie, intended for feeding, fruits and eggs. On the bronze coin of Hierapolis in Phrygia illustrated in Wieseler 791 I do not wish to decide. Nevertheless here too I think first of all of egg feeding, which would be especially fitting for Phrygia.

e: a means of averting misfortune and harm from one’s house. The egg thus appears here too as a means bestowing salvation and prosperity, as a true fundamentum salutis. The superstition of the time grasped the process quite externally. It was believed that the misfortune threatening the person was now diverted into the egg, as Juvenal 6, 520 puts the purpose of another purification ceremony in the words ut quicquid subiti et magni discriminis instet, in tunicas eat. Clement of Alexandria, Strom. 7, p. 844 Potter, follows this conception in order to bring the nonsense of egg lustration fully to light. People are said to believe that the egg takes upon itself all the evils of the one purified with it; but this is already refuted, he says, by the fact that one can see how those lustration eggs, supposedly afflicted with misfortune, when hatched, bring living chicks into the world.1) Here one sees quite clearly how the purifying force of the egg itself is only an expression of its nature, which bears life and salvation within it, and hence attaches itself to the fundamental significance of the ἀρχὴ γενέσεως. The same connection holds also for the other καθάρματα, torch and sulfur, which emphasize the generative element of fire, and water, which bears within it the generative force of tellurian moisture. As they give life, so they are able also to rejuvenate it, and to take from it every blemish and sickness. Therefore it is preeminently woman who performs the purification ceremonies. As Ovid speaks of an old woman who carries sulfur and eggs before her with trembling hand, so Clement, op. cit., quite generally entrusts women with the lustration, and by the same thought the ἐγχυτρίστριαι appear at Athens, of whom Plato, Minos p. 315 D speaks. Female is the natural principle that rules over life and death; a woman must therefore perform the ceremonies that are to check destruction and promote welfare. Only the primal mother Earth is able to banish misfortune, because from her proceed all blessing and all plague.2) Thus the lustration egg must appear in the hand of woman. If, therefore, a trembling old woman is preeminently chosen, this corresponds to the same conception of the maternal principle of earth that reappears in the representation of the friendly, beneficent nymph of the Numicius, Anna Perenna, who nourished the hungry people with warm loaves even during the leanest months of the year, as a busy, trembling anus, canens sæclis innumerabilibus.3) Countless centuries have turned her hair τοῦτο ἐγίνετο, εἰ ἀνελάμβανεν τὰ τοῦ περικαθαρθέντος κακά. meis pedibus). In a trembling hand the ᾠὸν ἐκ καθαρσίου has a double significance. In connection with the anus it appears quite properly as a leading back of life to that primal ground from which, aeons ago, the development of the κόσμος and of every individual life took its departure.1) As in the lustration significance of the egg the idea of the salus lying in it emerges, so also its application as a means of divination leads back to the same. On ᾠοσκοπία Hermagoras of Amphipolis wrote in his book περὶ σοφιστείας πρὸς τοὺς Ἀκαδημικούς, according to the report of Suidas. On Persius Sat. 5, 180: Tunc nigri lemures, ovoque pericula rupto, the scholia give the following explanation: Sacerdotes, qui explorandis periculis sacra faciebant, observare solebant, ovum igni impositum utrum in capite an in latere insudaret. Si autem ruptum effluxerat, periculum ei portendebat, pro quo factum fuerat, vel rei familiari eius. Here the egg appears as a true augurium salutis, and indeed in its twofold direction toward bodily prosperity and toward the extension of the personality in property. Periculum has accordingly here, like the egg itself, a wholly material meaning. It denotes diminution or total destruction of substance, as salus denotes not so much health as the existence of life and of goods in general. In this meaning periculum is found often, e.g. Macrob. Sat. 1, 7, p. 242 Zeune, quite generally in the usage of the ancient jurists. It is, however, the corporeal substance of earthly things that has its origin in the egg, so that the ᾠοσκοπία remains entirely faithful to the fundamental significance of the egg, which embraces prosperity and ruin alike. A further proof of the close relation of eggs to the idea of material salus is found in a remarkable account of Pliny 29, 3, 12. That the ovum anguinum, to which the Gauls ascribe such lofty powers, had no physical existence but owes its origin to a mythological combination of egg and serpent, such as we find also among Greeks and Romans, I need not remark. But whatever may have given occasion to the assumption of such a serpent’s egg, formed from the coiled body of a serpent and covered with a mushroom-like priest. Apul. M. 11, p. 266. Ibidem, simulacris rite dispositis, navem faberrime factam, picturis miris Aegyptiorum circumcirca variegatam, summus sacerdos, tæda lucida et ovo et sulphure, solemnissimas preces de casto præfatus ore, quam purissime purificatam, Deæ nuncupavit dedicavitque.

Ad victorias litium ac regum aditus mire laudatur, tantæ vanitatis, ut habentem id in lite in sinu equitem Romanum e Vocontiis a divo Claudio principe interemptum non ob aliud sciam. The agreement of this Gallic conception with that of the classical peoples is completed by the fact that here as there the salus bound up with the egg has an entirely material content, and is conceived as the preservation of personal and material well-being.1) If we now hold this significance of the egg together with that of Hygieia, there results for both so perfect an inner agreement that the connection of the symbol with the goddess establishes itself of itself. What offering could be more agreeable to Hygieia than the egg? what could correspond more to her connection with Dionysus and Telesphorus than the egg of Bacchic initiation? what could also more clearly reveal the thoughts of the sacrificing girl herself? That she prays for fertility of her maternal womb, for prosperity for house and marriage bed, for preservation of life and health for herself, for her beloved, and perhaps also for the egg’s little chick, is clear enough. Should she perhaps go still further in her thoughts, and implore a male offspring from the goddess? Pliny 10, 55 relates what use Julia Augusta, daughter of Drusus Livius, made of the egg in her pregnancy. Julia Augusta prima sua iuventa Tiberio Cæsare ex Nerone gravida, cum parere virilem sexum admodum cuperet, hoc usa est puellari augurio ovum in sinu fovendo atque cum deponendum haberet nutrici per sinum tradendo, ne intermitteretur tepor; nec falso augurata proditur. For, as Sueton in Tiberio 14 adds in explanation: pullus insigniter cristatus exclusus est. Scribonius prophesied, etiam regnaturum quandoque, sed sine regio insigni. Here the egg is not only the image of the fruitful maternal womb: a significance in which the hen itself also occurs, as the augurium that befell Livia Augusta hand depicted in Pignorius, magnæ Deum matris Idææ et Attidis initia, p. 4., which holds an egg between thumb and forefinger, while the serpent winding around the forearm approaches it with open mouth. Pignorius gives the following notice: Octavius Rossius monuit in operoso illo et erudito volumine, quod appellavit antiqua Brixiæ monumenta, in summa hasta simulacri Tillini, indigenæ numinis, stetisse manum æream. On this Tillinus and the hand in question I have been unable to obtain any further information.

Sie steht dem männlichen Gott als Darstellung der weiblichen Naturpotenz zur Seite, und beißt darum auch ganz allgemein uäres und avasga.?) Dieser generellen Bedeutung gegenüber, ist die Art der Verbindung unerheblih, von dem Mythus in einer Zeit fixirt, als die allgemeinen Naturideen von einer doppeltgestalteten stofflichen Kraft in die Formen menschlicher Erscheinung und menschlicher Familien- und Verwandtschafts8gliederung eingekleidet wurden, und daher in diesem, wie in vielen andern Fällen, auf die scheinbar unvereinbarste Weise dargestellt. So ist auch das Urweib bald aus dem Ei geboren, bald seinerseits das Ei gebärend, bald das Ei selbst, aus dem sie in Zweiheit oder Dreiheit doppeltgeschlechtig wieder hervortritt. So selbst Aesculap bald Coronis Tochter, bald ihr Gemahl.s) Also Mutter, Tochter, Gemahlin und Shwester sind nur vier Benennungen derselben Weiblichkeit, untergeordnet der allgemeinen Bedeutung des mütterlih empfangenden Naturprinzips, dem in gleicher Allgemeinheit das männlich-aktive bald als Vater , bald als Gemahl ergänzend zur Seite tritt. Daß Hygiea und Aes&culap in diesem Verhältniß, also wie das tenedische Doppelhaupt, neben einander zu denken sind, und von den Alten wirklich gedaht wurden, beweist ihre mehr« fache Vereinigung zu Einem Kulte, wobei es an jeder Bestimmung des verwandtschaftlichen Bandes fehlt. In solchem Zusammenhang finden wir sie zu Corinths) und zu Argos7), und dieselbe kehrt auf Bildwerken wieder , so in der schönen, aus Palestrina stammenden Gruppe des Pio-Clementino, abgebildet bei Visconti 2, 3, Clarac, muste de sculptures 4, 546, n. 1141 B., so auch auf zwei Reliefs im Louvre, deren Abbildung und Beschreibung man bei Clarac Atlas 2, pl. 177,
e: demonstrates:1) but, in connection with the cock that comes forth from it, a perfect repetition of that Orphic-Bacchic primal egg from which the phallic god, as revelation of the male force hitherto concealed in maternal matter, steps forth into the light in the form of Enorches, Phanes, Metis, Ericapaeus. This leads us to the discovery of a still further relation of the egg to Hygieia. We know what close kinship connects Hygieia with Aesculapius. She is called now his daughter,2) now his consort.3) She stands at the side of the male god as the representation of female natural potency, and is therefore called quite generally also μᾶτερ and ἄνασσα.4) In the face of this general significance the manner of the connection is of no importance, fixed by the myth at a time when the general ideas of nature, of a doubly shaped material force, were clothed in the forms of human appearance and of human family and kinship articulation, and therefore in this, as in many other cases, represented in the seemingly most irreconcilable way. Thus the primal woman too is now born of the egg, now herself in turn giving birth to the egg, now the egg itself, out of which she emerges again in duality or triplicity, double-sexed. So Aesculapius himself is now Coronis’s son, now her consort.5) Thus mother, daughter, consort, and sister are only four designations of the same femininity, subordinate to the general significance of the maternally receptive natural principle, at whose side, in equal generality, the male-active principle steps, complementing it, now as father, now as consort. That Hygieia and Aesculapius are to be thought of side by side in this relation, thus like the Tenedian double head, and were really so thought of by the ancients, is proved by their repeated union in a single cult, in which any determination of the kindred bond is lacking. In such a connection we find them at Corinth6) and at Argos,7) and the same recurs in works of art, so in the beautiful group from Palestrina in the Pio-Clementino, illustrated in Visconti 2, 3, Clarac, musée de sculptures 4, 546, n. 1141 B., so also on two reliefs in the Louvre, whose illustration and description may be found in Clarac Atlas 2, pl. 177, in Aelian. V. H. 13, 33.

e: text 2, pp. 312–315.1) From this connection of Hygieia with Aesculapius it follows that the egg-birth of the latter corresponds to the nature of Hygieia as well. That Aesculapius, the life-giving god who calls back from death to existence, was conceived, no differently from Dionysus-Enorches, as the son of the materially maternal primal egg as well, is shown by Lucian’s account in the Pseudomant. 12–16 of the frauds of the charlatan Alexander. For in order to secure success for his arts, this man was obliged to take as his starting point religious ideas that were familiar, and in particular related to the mystery cult. How closely he adhered to them is shown by the circumstance that he fetched out of the muddy waters of the earth, with the phiale, the egg from which the new Aesculapius was to emerge as a mighty dragon: a connection of water with the egg such as recurs in the story of the egg of the Euphrates, in the egg-bearing moon women, who stand in such close relation to swamp waters that Helen-Aphrodite herself is called after ἕλος, and in the general conceptions of the primal generative force of tellurian moisture. In the egg-born Asclepian dragon Glycon2) female materiality appears once again as the natural principle at the head of things, the male force in the relation of son as the revealed mystery, the former as egg, the latter as the egg-born dragon. Accordingly it could not contradict the ancient manner of viewing things to conceive Hygieia as well in the same way. The dragon belongs to her no less than to Aesculapius. On the numerous works of art of antiquity, of which a rich selection is to be found in Clarac, nos. 1145–1182 B, it is her constant companion, and for the most part, as on the Capitoline relief, it is represented in connection with the water bowl, whose related contents it thirstily longs for. It is therefore Hygieia herself, and sank from the independently venerated fetish to a mere attribute only with the progress of anthropomorphic formation of the gods. Hygieia and Aesculapius are accordingly originally to be thought of as a pair of serpents, the egg as ἀρχὴ γενέσεως, from which they, in their duality representing the duality of the sexual potencies, have issued. It would therefore correspond perfectly to the spirit of the ancient nature religion were we to represent the said divine pair itself by the image of two dragons in connection with an egg set upright in their midst. This group is in fact to be found. On a cameo of the Museum Florentinum, depicted batis aliisve (vol. 1, pp. 211–224, London 1717), the coin types relating to Lucian’s account.

e: in Gori 2, 23. 4 and again by Passeri, thesaurus gemmarum astriferarum vol. 3, pl. 123, vol. 2, pp. 158–159, there appears between two upright dragons an egg, which both seem to hold with their opened jaws. Above it is the sign of the crescent moon, and on both sides, corresponding to the two serpents, two stars. Below the egg, set upright between the dragons’ bodies, is the winged staff, which a third serpent encircles in three coils. Distributed equally to the right and left in the field are four letters, which form the word ΥΓΙΑ. The same representation is repeated on gems of the Berlin collection. Tölken, Verzeichniß der antiken, vertieft geschnittenen Steine, Berlin 1835, p. 217, gives the following descriptions: 1210. Carnelian. Two upright serpents, between them an egg. 1211. Brown antique paste. Two similar upright serpents, which hold an egg between them; above them the moon and two stars; below the egg the staff of Aesculapius, entwined by the serpent; around it the inscription ΥΓΙΑ. 1214. Carnelian. A mystical monogram composed of two Υ fitted into one another, which form the letters ΥΓΙΑ, instead of ΥΓΕΙΑ or ΥΓΙΕΙΑ.

e: These three pieces come from the Stosch collection, and are also described by Winckelmann in the Description des pierres gravées du feu Baron de Stosch, Florence 1760, where, however, instead of the word ΥΓΙΑ the form ΥΙΓΑ is given through an incorrect arrangement of the letters (Cl. 3, no. 1427). Against this Passeri remarks: Vox ΥΓΙΑ vel nihili est, vel nihil cum typo commune habet. Puto ex initialibus conflatam esse, vel potius, ut monet Gorius, in ea scriptum ΥΓΙΑ, Hygia, hoc est Salus. It seems incredible that anyone could ever have been in doubt about the word ΥΓΙΑ. It is perfectly certain. Whether we take it as a designation of the goddess, or, more indefinitely, as an expression of well-being in general, it remains perfectly indisputable that the symbolic representation of the cameo must agree with the content of the inscription. The concept ΥΓΙΑ and the egg coincide. The latter expresses symbolically what the former word renders in language, and the two dragons as guardians of the egg join themselves, in perfect accord, to the divine union of Asclepius and Hygieia. The inscription of the picture on the Florentine cameo and on the cut stones of the Stosch collection throws light on the representation of a funerary monument which Fabretti, Inscriptiones domesticæ p. 28, no. 17, communicates. As its founder one A. Herennuleius Hermes is named. Fabretti describes the pictorial representation in the following words: vir libamen ex patera effundens et gemini ad utrumque latus serpentes cristati et erecti, ovum ore apprehendentes. On the sense of the picture the same scholar expresses himself as follows. Suspicor, [PDF 153] — 139 — postquam sibi et uxori adhuc in humanis agenti Hermes hanc memoriam constituit, vel longævitatem hac expressione in votis habitam: serpens quippe, ut ait Sanchuniathon apud Eusebium de Præpar. Evangel. 1, 7 longævum animal est, nec solum senectam cum pelle deponens reiuvenescit; sed crescit etiam in adolescentiam redactum; vel ut ex concordia illa quasi maritali serpentum, coniuges improles adhuc sobolem sibi augurarentur ex ovo prodeuntem, tamquam principio et originario fonte generationis, ut illud vocat Plutarchus Quæstion. Conviv. 7, 3. Passeri, gemmæ astriferæ ad tabulam 123, Genii symbola, t. 2, p. 159 adds: In Aegyptiorum hieroglyphicis, immo fere in omnium obeliscorum apice, observari ovum hoc, unde serpens exsiliit. Fabretti’s twofold explanation has little probability; to express on the funerary monument the wish for a long life, or to implore the blessing of children for a hitherto barren maternal womb, corresponds too little to the purpose of a funerary stone and to the usage of the ancients for us to be able to presuppose such a thought. The salus that can alone be thought of here is that higher one which lies beyond the limits of bodily existence and of tellurian being. These are the nova salutis curricula which Apuleius presents as the higher content of the mysteries. The egg, in its physical significance the inexhaustible primal source of tellurian life, becomes on that higher stage the symbol of the existence that presses through material death to a rejuvenated, higher being, in which Psyche, freed from the coarse husk of matter, like the chick breaking forth from the dark egg, rejoices in a purer existence in the realms of heavenly light. The serpents too are raised to the same significance. They, too, designate here not the natural force, conceived as material, of the generative phallus, but rather rebirth, which renews life by rejuvenating it. It is not the dragon of the dark depths, but the pair of serpents of light, the spiritus qui per universum orbem permeat,1) that holds and guards the egg of the higher rebirth. The connection of the egg with the mouths of the serpents stands in a special relation to this idea. The Egyptian world egg proceeds from the mouth of the demiurge Kneph,2) a formation of the divine breath, not generation by the phallic force of matter. Thus we see on the Fabretti tombstone the pair of serpents guarding the egg as the expression of a higher idea, such as best befits a tombstone, as the symbol of a higher salus that grasps death itself as the point of departure of a rejuvenated existence. Here too Hygieia is the [PDF 154] — 140 — guiding fundamental idea, but this Hygieia is no longer the material one, who secures the well-being of the body and bestows fertility on the maternal womb, but a spiritualized potency leading matter itself through to a higher blessedness, in which that physical-sensual one continues and is fulfilled.1) Through the representation of the Florentine cameo the egg sacrifice of the Capitoline relief seems to me removed from all challenge, and a secure basis of explanation is given for several other monuments as well. Gorlaeus communicates, on pl. 233, fig. 492 of his pierres antiques gravées, a gem picture that shows serpent and egg once more in connection. A male figure kneels before the altar and brings the egg near to the blazing flame, in a posture which permits us to think of the ᾠοσκοπία. A standing female figure directs her attention to the result of the divination undertaken, the relation of which to the augurium salutis is emphasized by the attribute of the serpent coiling in the girl’s left hand. On another gem picture in the same work, pl. 256, fig. 579, a young female figure hands to Aesculapius, recognizable by his serpent staff, an object in which we may recognize first of all an egg. On other monuments the feeding of a dragon seems rather to be represented. To this belong Gorlaeus pl. 43, no. 86, and the relief from the collection of the Louvre, already mentioned earlier, in Clarac, pl. 177, no. 268. Hygie ne tient ici, says the French commentator 2, 315, ni sa patère, ni son serpent; c’est à celui de son père, qu’elle présente, à ce qu’il pârait, un gâteau, et elle est en aussi bonne intelligence avec cet animal favori, qu’avec celui, qui l’accompagne ordinairement. The setting out of cakes for sacred serpents is often mentioned, for which the story in Herodotus 8, 41, Propert. 4, 8, 3– 16, and Museo Capitol. t. 4, t. 42 furnish decisive examples.2) A vase painting in Caylus, recueil d’antiquités vol. 4, t. 40, 1, is to be joined to the egg monuments. On an altar lie three eggs; a bird, whose identification is difficult, seizes in its beak a serpent, which seems to defend them. The whole representation recalls the myth of the raven, the serpent, and the Crater, as Hygin. Poetic. astr. 2, 40; 3, 39 and Ovid Fast. 2, 243–266 relate it. The connection of the serpent with the egg is found also in the ovum anguinum of the Gauls, about which we at Leiden. The male figure reclining on the couch holds it in his hand. Opened at the top, it serves him as a drinking cup, as water is presented to the Persian king in a golden egg. holy table and the altars of the god. ll. 677 f., 710 f.

Bei der großen Syrtis steht am Meeresufer, von den Wogen bespült, ein Grabmal, auf breiter Basis eine Säule. Auf dieser findet sich folgendes Bild: im Sumpfe steht, Tantalus vergleichbar, ein Mann, Wasser schöpfend, als wollte er trinken. Um seinen Fuß windet sich eine Schlange, die giftige Dipsas. Weiber tragen in Gefäßen Wasser herbei, und übergießen damit den Durstenden. In der Nähe liegen einige Straußcn-Eier. By the great Syrtis there stands on the seashore, washed by the waves, a tomb, a column on a broad base. On this is found the following picture: in the swamp stands, comparable to Tantalus, a man, drawing water as if he wished to drink. Around his foot a serpent coils, the poisonous dipsas. Women carry water in vessels and pour it over the thirsting man. Nearby lie some ostrich eggs. An epigram, which we must imagine engraved on the base, compares the sufferings of the man with the never-quenched thirst of Tantalus, the water carriers with the eternally vain labor of the Danaids. Four other verses, which Lucian does not communicate, mentioned the eggs and told how the poor man, while he was occupied in gathering them, was bitten by the dangerous serpent.1)— The connection of egg and serpent is met with further in the second Orphic theogony, which Damascius, principia p. 581, Kopp, traces back to Hieronymus and Hellanicus. Threefold in form is the dragon. Between the head of the lion and that of the bull, in the middle, appears the divine countenance of Heracles, who is called Χρόνος ἀγήρατος, and is joined with Ananke-Adrasteia, who spreads herself through the All. From the force of the dragon-shaped Heracles an egg proceeds, and from this Protogonus Zeus, who shows wings on his shoulders, bulls’ heads in his flanks, and a serpent on his head, and assumes manifold animal shape. From the Orphic conception certain Sicilian and Cilician coin types become intelligible. The bearded double head on a coin of Camarina points to that Heracles-Chronos of the Orphic Müll. Here an Etruscan work of art deserves mention, which seems to receive its explanation from Lucian’s account. Micali, antichi monumenti to the Storia degli antich. popoli, pl. 40, 3, p. 53, communicates the picture of a bronze candelabrum found in the tombs of Vulci, from the collection of the Prince of Canino. As its pedestal serves a nude satyr, recognizable by the formation of his ears, who with his staff presses down a huge serpent striving upward, while the raised right hand seems ready to hurl a stone. Expression and bearing of the figure show fear and horror, which find their explanation only in the appearance of that dangerous inhabitant of the swamps. This thought finds its confirmation in a small, inconspicuous attribute that the startled companion of Bacchus holds in his left hand. It is a plucked mushroom, represented with perfect distinctness. Could we not connect with this a story very similar to Lucian’s? As he gathers mushrooms the serpent appears; frightened, the satyr seeks to defend himself against it. With the staff he holds it down, with the right hand he wants to throw the stone at it. We recognize here the same fundamental idea as in the Syrtis stone. For comparison let there serve further the story in Plutarch de Is. et Os., according to which Dictys, the ward of Isis, reached for an onion and thereby lost his life in the river. The onion, which brings forth tears, is abhorred by the priests. As the image of every swift, unexpected death the serpent’s bite appears in Plin. 7, 7.

e: sun, surround the divine countenance of the light hero Heracles. Immortality is his attribute; the principle of transience and of death lies wholly on the side of the femininity assigned to him, Ananke-Adrasteia, who pervades all matter. As a power of the sun, Heracles bears the principle of time within himself. But in him it never ages; he is not Chronos, who always and necessarily belongs to the world of becoming as its temporal form; he is rather Χρόνος ἀγήρατος, the never-aging principle of time itself. From this solar nature is explained the connection of the egg-generating Heracles with Dionysus-Hebon, as it appears on the Camarinian coin. As the highest power of light, even if still conceived as material, Bacchus himself becomes Heracles-Chronos, the son of the maternal egg becomes its solar father. The same meaning belongs to the egg encircled three times by the dragon on a coin of Antoninus Heliogabalus, the representation of which Felix Lajard communicates in the recherches sur le culte de Vénus Pl. 14. H. no. 11. The original, of bronze, lies in the collection of the Bibliothèque nationale at Paris. Beside the egg stands a fruit-bearing palm. The inscription shows the Phoenician Tyre as the place of minting.1) The relation to the sun cult cannot be doubtful here. The egg is subordinated to the highest male force of light, and is itself represented as its creation. So there appeared to us above the Delphic omphalos-egg, so the myrrh egg of the Egyptian phoenix, itself represented as a generation of light, so the great egg that on a vase from Panticapaeum the Bacchante offers to the initiate riding on the sun-griffin.2) With this conception is connected the report of Porphyry in Eusebius Præp. Evang. 3, 11. According to Egyptian doctrine Kneph causes an egg to proceed from his mouth. It is the world egg; the father is the demiurge, who lets it go forth complete from his mouth, like the word, as the highest λόγος. The creative act is here conceived as νοητὴ ἀρχή, as that first unspeakable causality which the Orphic cosmogonies passed over as ἄρρητον. Passeri gives in his Atlas Farnesianus etc. p. 180 the representation of a bronze serpent which in his time was in the museo Gori. In the opened mouth rests an egg. Here the dragon appears, as Kneph does among the Egyptians, as demiurge. And that the Egyptians thought of and represented Kneph, the father of the egg, as a serpent god is definitely attested by Euseb. Pr. Ev. 1, 10. In this elevation the serpent appears at the highest stage of spiritualization. In its lowest materiality a representation of tellurian waters and of their generative force working in the dark [PDF 158] — 144 — depths of the earth, as we find this in the myth of Psyche, and again in the cult of the cave dragon of Lanuvium,1) the serpent now presents itself as the animal of light, and is therefore provided with the cock’s comb, and often too, like the phoenix, with a head radiating light,2) and finally, in the last spiritualization, becomes the symbol of the causal νοῦς of all things, uncreated, eternal, never aging. Through this relation it becomes an expression of the highest mystery ideas, and as the διὰ κόλπου δράκων a sign of participation in the best hopes of initiation.3) Now it gains a new relation to the egg. It becomes, like the egg, a speaking sign of the initiation received, and of that confidence in immortality and in passage to a higher, more divine stage of existence which the ancients emphasize as the consoling content of the doctrine of the mysteries. This idea of initiation is not to be mistaken in the description of that tombstone erected at the Syrtes. Serpent, eggs, and purification by water combine into a totality 59. Cf. Philostrat. The story that Lucian has connected with it appears only as an attempt to lay a historical event at the foundation of the symbolic representation, and to transform the mystical content into the death story of the one buried. But even in this dress the religious idea is still clearly enough present. Egg and serpent lead through to life only by way of death. Only out of destruction does a higher existence bloom. Passing away as the precondition of new becoming, darkness as the passage to light, the terrors of the underworld as the ground of a more vigorous revival, through suffering and affliction to joy: this is the mystery idea that governs the fable of Psyche, which is also the innermost kernel of Lucian’s story and of the Vulcian candelabrum. The search for the egg, the plucking of the mushroom, becomes the occasion of death, the serpent brings destruction. But both prepare the fulfillment of the higher hopes of the mysteries. The harmful animal of the swamps is not only the destroyer but also the redeemer of the initiate, the egg not only the bearer of death but, through death, the giver of salvation, of the renatio ad nova salutis curricula.1) On the candelabrum this is indicated by the female figure issuing from the opened flower calyx at the upper end of the candelabrum’s shaft. A pair of serpents serves her instead of feet. Here the life-giving side of the Bacchic animal comes forth, as at the lower part of the candelabrum its life-destroying side.2) We see anew the union of the light side and the shadow side in the same force. What wounds heals at the same time; what brings death bears within itself also the force of life. From the serpent’s bite the serpent heals. So the Mosaic story represents it, of the serpent set up at Jehovah’s command.3) The dragon is to curricula. assumption seems to me by no means certain. On these funerary implements everything down to the smallest detail has symbolic meaning and relation to the Bacchic mysteries. What meaning, then, can the stone contain? More fitting is the assumption of an egg, which Micali’s drawing brings out clearly enough. It appears here as a saving Bacchic attribute. Thereby everything gains a far more satisfying sense. Against the threatening serpent’s bite stands the saving symbol of the Bacchic mysteries. This rescues from the destruction that the plucking of the mushroom prepares. The assumption of the egg, moreover, does not exclude the idea of defense with it. So the wheel too appears on well-known funerary monuments of Etruria as a weapon of defense and at the same time in a symbolic-hieratic significance. Its consecrated force is joined with the use that the threatened man makes of it. Raoul-Rochette, mon. inéd. t. 39. The same representation is found also on a cinerary chest of the Leiden Museum. 10

e: heal the dragon’s bite. ὁ τρώσας καὶ ἰάσεται. Among the manifold applications that antiquity already made of this natural proposition, the healing lance of Achilles deserves special emphasis. It not only wounds, it also brings healing. The same force necessarily embraces both potencies. The serpent is at one and the same time ἀγαθοδαίμων and κακοδαίμων, as the water, to which it belongs in its lowest stage, is at one and the same time the origin of life and the seat of death. On a coin of the elder Faustina in Spanheim de usu et præstant. numism. 1, p. 415 it bears side by side an ear of grain and a poppy, the symbols of the life-bringing and of the death-bringing power, just as two dragons are assigned to Demeter, and the two serpents that hold the Hygieia egg are represented, by the stars set above their heads, in the nature of the Dioscuri, who bring up life and death, day and night.1) Egyptian mythology clothes not only the good but equally the evil principle in the form of a serpent. So appear Serapis, so Python, so the great serpent Ahriman, who girds and combats the realm of light. This identity of both forces, by virtue of which Marsyas first blows the double flute with a single breath, holds first of all for the domain of physical life; through the mysteries, however, it is transferred to a higher domain; here the serpent, like the egg, appears not only as the preserver of life in material creation, but as the image of the higher existence of the individual that issues from death. It is the idea of the palingenesis of the individual life that attaches itself equally to the egg and the serpent. It is this spiritualized meaning that we must recognize above all on so many funerary monuments: in the serpent of the sarcophagus of Bomarzo, now in the British Museum, in a gravestone of the Louvre that shows nothing but an upright dragon, in the bronze serpents, some of which are preserved in the museum of the Collegio romano at Rome, in the remarkable amber fragment from a tomb at Ruvo in the Pourtalès-Gorgier collection,2) in the serpent of the rock sarcophagus of Thera,3) and on many similar funerary monuments. Not the physical significance of material generation, but the mystical one resting upon it, that of the higher existence mediated through death, is what was to be expressed pictorially by the serpent symbol on the tombs of the initiates, and has also found its representation in Lucian’s account of the gravestone at the Syrtes.4) [PDF 161] — 147 — 12. To the egg monuments considered thus far is joined a group of three Pompeian wall paintings, all of which go back to the same type. We see the serpent once more in the closest connection with the egg. On the first of the monuments belonging here, the representation of which is also to be found in Gargiulo’s Raccolta, two mighty dragons approach an altar in powerful coils from the right and from the left, in opposite directions; on its top, surrounded by smaller fruits, lie two eggs. The head is adorned by the cock’s comb. From the opened jaws the tongue springs forth, formed as a fine line, its double curled tips touching the two eggs. The plants shooting high up indicate the luxuriantly fertile meadow ground which the serpents traverse before they halt their mighty movement all at once before the egg altar. This whole representation forms the lower part of a picture whose upper half, separated from it by a dark line, sets before the eyes the preparation for a sacrifice of a pig to be performed at a rustic altar. The same division appears on two other Pompeian wall paintings, of which one was found in the so-called casa di Castore e Poluce, the other in the casa del Labirinto. The former is reproduced in the Museo Borbonico vol. 8. t. 24, the second in the same work vol. 11. t. 38, both together in the monumenti dell’ Instituto. 1839. vol. 3, t. 6. On these two paintings a strip is set apart at the lowest place, on which the same altar with two eggs and the dragon is represented. The only difference of the last two pictures from the first consists in this, that here we find only one serpent in each, which on the one picture approaches the altar from the right, on the other from the left. I do not rate this deviation highly, and see in the singular number of the serpent not so much a conscious intention as rather merely one of those abbreviations which ancient art often permitted itself, especially in the execution of such accessories. The dual number of the eggs shows that we are to add in thought to the one dragon a second, approaching the altar from the opposite side: a supplement which presents itself to the eye of the modern, but especially of the ancient beholder, from the composition of the whole and from familiarity with other more fully executed recognized, since hardly any of the ancient animal symbols, from crude fetish worship to the highest spiritualization, has passed through so many stages of development, and appropriated so manifold interpretations, physical and mystical relations, as the serpent.

On this one she carries in her raised right hand an olive branch,1) while the left rests on a rudder and holds a scepter staff. For Aphrodite, Leda-Nemesis, Demeter, Hygieia, Fortuna would not only agree with both representations in respect of the general fundamental idea, but would also meet with no significant difficulties in the particulars. Most closely, perhaps, to the native Italic cult will correspond Fortuna Primigenia, who in a wholly Cerealian conception formed the center of religion at Praeneste, but was also venerated in all Latium, at Rome, at Antium, and under various names in Etruria, as a representation of the great female principle of nature, as giver of all blessing of the earth, of all wealth, as mistress over the light and shadow side of life,2) as bearer and announcer of all good and evil fortune. e: the power over both. She shows us, then, in human form what the egg on the lower picture represents symbolically. A complete correspondence governs the two. We found the egg earlier in connection with Leda-Nemesis, with Hygieia, with Demeter, with Isis, with Aphrodite-Syria. We see it here united in the same way with Fortuna-Tyche. In all these combinations it appears constantly in the same character: as ἀρχὴ γενέσεως τῶν πάντων, as the content of all material life, in general as a representation of the great female principle of nature, which has received its human form in all those primal mothers. But it is older than all anthropomorphization, and has no part in the individual developments which the common idea of material primal motherhood has taken among the single peoples of antiquity under the combined influences of national disposition, occupation, political fortunes, and the character of the land, and the result of which appears deposited in the differing individual coloring of those mother goddesses. Whether Demeter, whether Aphrodite, whether Leda-Nemesis, and Hygieia with all those lunar women to whom egg-birth is ascribed, each have developed in a different direction, and so the common fundamental idea finally appears in a plurality of different local nuances: the physical foundation on which they rest is the same in all, and only this foundation comes to representation in the mother egg.1) For this reason the egg can also appear by itself alone, and without the accompaniment of a personally formed mother goddess. So we find it in the Orphic-Bacchic doctrine. So it is represented on the Pamphili tomb painting, so on the Fabretti stone. If, then, for the Pompeian wall paintings the connection of the upper and lower halves is established in relation nomine multijugo totus veneratur orbis. All these combinations contain a definite recognition of the original and inner identity of those mother goddesses, whose fusion was made possible only thereby.

e: to Fortuna and the egg, then the same correspondence continues for Eros- Sosipolis and the serpent. When I designate the genius who stands on the column in boyish form on both pictures as Eros-Sosipolis, I claim for this individualization no other value than that of a designation correctly rendering the general idea. A more far-reaching determination will hardly be possible, and every attempt to establish the ancient name under which Pompeii may have venerated the dwarf demon or genius of those pictures is met at once by doubts and misgivings. The general idea, on the other hand, is quite clear. Beside the mother stands a son: beside the Cretan Adrastea, Zeus; beside Proserpina πρωτογενής, Dionysus; beside Demeter, Jacchus; beside Pallas, Erichthonius or Plutus.1) From the dark womb of matter there issues a Protogonus, in whom the mystery of the male force attains corporeal representation. What hitherto worked invisibly hidden in female matter, that now comes forth into the light. Originally given is only the female birth-giving principle: the male-active comes to visible representation with the first birth of a son.2) In the child the mother herself now recognizes the fecundating phallus, to which her materiality owes the awakening of the life resting within it. With delight her gaze rests on the revealed mystery. With tender love she embraces the fruit of her womb. The son now becomes her own fecundator, her beloved, for whose embrace, like Penia, she longs eternally. He is the most beautiful of all gods, he now becomes himself the great father of all generated, perishable creation. As Adonis he is called Papas. He is also called Eros, the god of generative force, the principle of sexual union. So too Jacchus, whom the nymphs tend, whom the faun rocks in his arms and regards with a gaze of delighted inquiry, as if he now beheld for the first time the salvation of the world, the mystery of generation, in bodily form. He is for the Orphics Phanes, Ericapaeus, Metis, beside Hygieia Telesphorus, Acesius, Euamerion-Eros, for the Etruscans Tages, who is plowed up out of the furrow of the tellurian maternal body, child and bald-headed old man at once, the former according to his appearance in the light, the latter according to the aeons he has spent in the dark maternal body, unbeheld by mortals. He is Telephus and Ascus, whom the hind, image of the earth, suckles; he is Plutus, who through his fecundation becomes the founder of all tellurian wealth; he is the virile Hippolytus-Virbius; he is Endymion, whom Ops-Diana loves; he returns again in [PDF 166] — 152 — the veiled dwarf god who is represented in Fortuna’s temple seated beside Aphrodite-Tanaquil; he can be called by the general name Δαίμων, from δᾶ, γᾶ, Eros, Arsaphes-Ombrimos, Jupiter-Arcanus,1) just as Jacchus too is called in Pausanias ὁ τοῦ Δήμητρος δαίμων. No less fitting for him is the designation Genius, for like Eros, Virbius, Palaemon, Arsaphes, this name contains from the outset nothing other than the meaning of male generative force, of the Juventas formed as a phallus on the well-known Etruscan mirror,2) who comes to light in the form of an Eros-Protogonus, whom Jupiter Arcanus reveals, and who in the highest elevation is conceived as Jovial Genius, as the material generative potency emanating from the highest divine force.3) In another form this revealed male god returns again in the cock-dragon, which recognizes its own origin in the maternal egg. It attaches itself to the egg as Eros-Protogonus, the phallic boy, to the mother goddess, as Jacchus to Demeter, Adonis-Papas to Aphrodite, Euamerion to Hygieia; what the egg encloses within itself has come to light in the dragon. The correspondence is so complete that the demons themselves also assume the form of serpents. As a serpent appears the Elean Sosipolis, as a serpent we found the Orphic Chronos-Heracles, as a dragon Glycon-Asclepius, the Bonus Deus favorable to all mortals. In the serpent appears Bacchus, that διὰ κόλπον θεός, whom the initiates let glide through their bosom, whom the women wind around their bodies at the nocturnal orgies. As Genius, finally, every serpent is conceived, so that the concepts of the generating Genius and of the generating serpent coincide completely. — With the appearance of the male force the movement of life begins. With the action of the phallus on maternal matter the stream of creation takes its beginning. Whereas earlier all was at rest, now that cycle begins in which every advance becomes a return to the starting point. From the opened carceres the two-horse team storms forth, in order to run through again and again, with unattainable speed, the course assigned to it. This movement brings the first generative act of the revealed phallus ὀνόματος. darum?) Aufustius: Genius, inquit, est Deorum filius et parens hominum, ex quo homines gignuntur. Et propterea Genius meus nominatur, quia me genuit. August. C. D. 7, 13. Nigidius in Arnob. 3, 34. Festus v. Tages, Genii filius, nepos Iovis. Plin. 36 in fine.

Stillness and rest prevail in the egg; but when, driven by the desire of becoming, the male god breaks through the shell and begins his work as Enorches, then all becomes movement, all restless haste, all impelling force, all a never-ending cycle. The male generative principle appears, then, itself as the representative and bearer of movement in visible earthly creation. As it gives the impulse thereto by the first act, so it renews it without cease through constant repetition of the same. The natural principle of action appears at the same time as the moving one. It is necessarily joined with the law of swiftness, and therefore winged, like Eros, like the phallus itself,1) like Pegasus, the horse of the tellurian waters, like Heracles-Chronos, like Mercury, distinguished by agility of running, like water,2) like Achilles’ δρόμοι,3) like Scythius-Scyphius, the first horse that the earth bore from its womb.4) Storming, it bursts forth from the maternal body, marking the first moment of its existence by unrest and hasty speed, like the spring that wells forth with inborn mobility and acknowledges restlessness itself as its highest law. Stare loco nequit, micat auribus et tremit artus Ingentemque vomens volvit sub naribus ignem. Thus the male potency enters into a new opposition to the female, the serpent to the egg. Winged is the phallus, resting the woman; the principle of movement is man, the principle of rest woman; the cause of eternal change is force, the image of eternal rest woman, which is why the earth mothers are mostly represented seated. For this reason woman’s nature is so closely akin to the rest of death, while the funeral games always attach themselves to the cult of a male hero. For the movement that is furthered by death proceeds from the activity of man, while the rest of the tomb is akin to the female principle. We can now conceive the connection of the serpent with the egg also as a union of the two, of the resting and of the moving principle of things. On the altar the egg rests immovably. e: on the other hand shows by the coils of its body that movement pervades it. The former is the ἕδος ἀσφαλὲς ἀεί, the ἀκίνητον or sanctum, which no one may move from its place, which the earth itself holds fast, like the immovable terminus, the funerary column set on a level with it, the meta, and the walls, which, like the tree, are rooted in the maternal womb of the earth and, like them, have come forth into visible existence from the slumber in which they lay. The dragon, on the other hand, is visible creation that has attained the development of life. It can itself be regarded as the egg set in motion. In this significance, however, it must always be thought of as two, as the first of the Pompeian pictures represents it, as it is repeated in the pair of the Fortuna and Nemesis at Antium and Smyrna, and emerges in the pair of the genii.1) For movement is the result of two streams rolling against one another with equal force. In order that it may continue always with equal swiftness, the destroying force must perform its work as well as the life-generating one. Two horses, therefore, tear the chariot along with united power. Two brothers guide the team, like Actor’s sons, the egg-born Molionids: “Both now drove together: the one held and guided the reins, Guided the reins with might, and the other plied the whip.”2) If what the egg contains within itself is to attain complete outward representation, two serpents must surround it in opposite directions of movement. Like the two Molionids, the mighty victors in the chariot race, like the two Dioscuri, whose swiftness no one surpasses, so too two dragons glide swiftly toward the egg from which they themselves have sprung, and in which they recognize the resting primal ground of that creation which they keep in constant movement and freshness by their united but opposed onset.3) Thus in the pair of dragons the egg itself attains its outward unfolding. Both belong wholly to the region of material, ever-decaying life. But the egg shows us this in the unopened fetal state, the pair of dragons in the movement of life that has come to light. The former is the as it was also fastened to the triumphal chariot of the Roman dictator. In this significance it passes to the mother goddesses, as indeed Isis carries it on countless monuments. Here the goddess herself is represented as mother of the creation caught up in constant swift course, thus as having entered into the movement of becoming and passing away. mæ astriferæ 3, 90 f., with which the two of Ceres agree.

Die Drachen bringen zur äußern Darstellung, was das Ei in sich verschließt. Sie entwickeln aus ihm immer neues Leben, rufen aus ihm immer frishen Seegen hervor. Sie find eben dadurch die Geber alles Reihthums, aller nährenden - Frucht, alles leiblichen Wohlergehens. Seine stoffliche Grundlage hat das Gedeihn in dem Ei, hervorgerufen und zu stets neuer Entwicklung gebracht wird es durch die Schlangen. Wir sehen jeht ganz deutlich, wie sich die cerealische Beziehung der obern Hälfte unserer beiden Pompeianishen Bilder in dem untern Streifen, seinen Eiern und Sclangen .fortseßt. Wird oben das Opfer dargebracht, das von Fortuna den Seegen der Erde, des Ehebettes, und jegliches Gedeihn des Hauses an Gut und Körper erflehen soll: so sehen wir unten in dem Ei und dem Drachen die Naturpotenzen, durch deren Kraft alles Lebens Keim gelegt, und stets erneuert „wird, dargestellt. Aus der Verbindung beider Bilder geht die Jdee des häuslihen Wohlergehns und der über alle Theile des Familienlebens verbreiteten salus mit doppelter Stärke hervor. Darum ist es auch bezeihnend, daß wenigstens das eine jener Bilder, nämlich das der casa del Labirinto, über dem Hausaltare angebracht war. Hier am häuslichen Heerde, im Mittelpunkt der Wohnung, hat Fortuna ihren Siß. Hier erscheint sie als interna'), als shüßende Mutter des ganzen Hauses, das ihrem Wohlwollen Alles zu danken hat, die vollen Sheunen, den Kinderseegen, das leibliche Gedeihn, Schuß gegen Feinde, kurz Alles, was wir als irdische Wohlfahrt zu bezeichnen pflegen. Hat fie hierin die Bedeutung einer Schirmherrin im umfassendsten Einn, so gewinnt auch der Drache die Natur eines schüßenden Genius, dessen Wachsamkeit das Wohl der Stätte, in welcher er seine Wohnung genommen hat, anvertraut ist, Er theilt mit der großen Mutter die Bedeutung eines numen tutelare, dessen Wachsamkeit das Gi als Symbol der Fülle und des Reichthums, übergeben ist. Er erscheint auH hier als Vertreter des aktiven, thatkräftigen Prinzips, dem die Weiblichkeit, sei es in Gestalt Fortuna's, sei es in Gestalt des Ei's, als das ruhende, der Hegung, der Pflege und des Shußes bedürftige, Prinzip entgegentritt. Durch seine Beweglichkeit selbst eignet sih der Drache zur Vertheidigung des ihm geweihten Ortes. Den Einheimischen freundlich gesinnt, zeigt er sich nach Aristoteles den Fremdlingen furchtbar. Er trägt, wohin - jene ihm folgen, Furcht und Entseßen, und bringt als Feldzeichen vorangetragen, Verderben unter die Feinde.2) Er begründet also auh äußere Macht, !) Stobwus, Ecl. e: resting primal ground, the latter the continued development of all tellurian creation; the former is matter, the latter the moving force in its double pole. The dragons bring to outward representation what the egg encloses within itself. They develop from it ever new life, call forth from it ever fresh blessing. By this very fact they are the givers of all wealth, of all nourishing fruit, of all bodily well-being. The material foundation of prosperity lies in the egg; it is called forth and brought to ever new development by the serpents. We now see quite clearly how the Cerealian relation of the upper half of our two Pompeian paintings is continued in the lower strip, with its eggs and serpents. If above the sacrifice is offered which is to implore from Fortuna the blessing of the earth, of the marriage bed, and every prosperity of the house in goods and in body, then below, in the egg and the dragon, we see represented the natural potencies by whose force the seed of all life is laid and ever renewed. From the connection of the two pictures the idea of domestic well-being and of the salus spread over all parts of family life emerges with doubled strength. It is therefore also significant that at least one of those pictures, namely that of the casa del Labirinto, was set above the household altar. Here at the domestic hearth, in the center of the dwelling, Fortuna has her seat. Here she appears as interna,1) as the protecting mother of the whole house, which has everything to thank her good will for: the full granaries, the blessing of children, bodily prosperity, protection against enemies, in short everything that we are accustomed to designate as earthly welfare. If she has in this the significance of a protectress in the most comprehensive sense, then the dragon too takes on the nature of a protecting genius, to whose vigilance the welfare of the place in which he has taken up his dwelling is entrusted. He shares with the great mother the significance of a numen tutelare, to whose vigilance the egg, as the symbol of plenty and wealth, is committed. Here too he appears as the representative of the active, energetic principle, to which femininity, whether in the form of Fortuna or in the form of the egg, stands opposed as the resting principle, in need of tending, care, and protection. By his very mobility the dragon is suited to the defense of the place consecrated to him. Friendly toward the natives, he shows himself, according to Aristotle, terrible to strangers. Wherever the former follow him, he carries fear and terror, and borne ahead as a standard he brings destruction among the enemy.2) Thus he also establishes external power, olog. gent. 9, 29.

e: as he circles protectively around the home hearth. But all the fruits of his activity he brings to the household altar, as Mercury lays the purse of the gold he has won in Fortuna’s lap.1) The relation of the two potencies is always the same. From primal matter the force of the man calls forth every blessing; at its feet he lays down again what he has gathered. If Fortuna has her immovable seat at the hearth, the task of the man is activity and movement without rest or respite, defense today, attack tomorrow. By this quality the dragon becomes the holder of power. The source of kingship and of all dominion lies in the material primal mother, but the crown is worn by the man. We find the serpent as a symbol of dominion. So the Egyptian king carries it,2) and to this significance the cock-dragon owes its name βασιλίσκος.3) One might ask why the crown does not rest on the head of the primal mother, since she stands at the head of all material creation, while the male principle stands to her in the subordinate relation of a son? The answer, after what has been said above, cannot be doubtful. The visible creation, to which alone all earthly dominion can extend, is the work of the male force that has stepped into the light, before whose appearance there exists as yet no creature at all, but only the material primal egg that holds within itself the seeds of all things. As life on earth therefore begins with the activity of the man, and through it first that which is to be ruled is called into existence, so he alone can wield dominion. This belongs to the son, not to the mother, to the pair of serpents, not to the egg. Thus Horus rightly tears the diadem from the head of his mother Isis, in order to set it upon himself, the vigorous lord of the generated creation.4) Thus Aphrodite too gives dominion to the man. So we see her, on a bas-relief from Basili-Kaia published by Texier, investing the king with the insignia of power; so Tydo raises her favorite Gyges to the throne; as Fortuna brevis she was in one night the consort of two kings. So Croesus is born ἐν ἑορτῇ Ἀφροδίτης; Fortuna-Tanaquil, in a wholly Lydian manner of conception, raises Tarquin and Servius in succession to the throne. o: Grunde als regium augurium von den Alten betrachtet. ') Quelle der Macht ist die weibliche Urmutter, wie aus ihrer Stofflihkeit auch alle tellurische Zeugung hervorgeht. Aber die Herrschaft führt nicht sie selbst, sondern der Mann, dessen Kraft in dem Stoff das Leben erweckt, und der durch seine That das zu Beherrschende ins Dasein ruft. Wir finden diesen Gedanken wieder in dem Mythus von Tarutius und Larentia.?) Tarutius ist reich, ein wahrer Plutos, Larentia arm, die stoffliche Penia, in der erst der Mann der Schöpfung Keim erwet. Aber Taxutius legt Alles in Larentia's Schooß, wie Hermes den gefüllten Beutel in den Fortuna's. Sie hinwieder seßt das römische Volk zum Erben ein. Die gleiche Jdee liegt in dem Güterreht der Gynaikokratischen Völker. Der Mann erwirbt. Aber Alles wird dem Weibe gegeben und ausschließlih auf die Töchter vererbt, so daß auch "die Alimentationspfliht bei den Aegyptern ausschließlich auf diesen, nicht auf den Söhnen ruht. Dennoch, ja kraft desselben Prinzips , herrscht der Mann mit dem Scepter der Macht, nicht die Frau. Jhm steht das Recht zu über Leben und Tod, wie er dur seine Wirkung auf den Stoff, und nicht die empfangende Frau, die Bewegung von Leden und Tod in die Welt eingeführt hat. Darum haben wir au keine Andeutung, daß das Ei je Symbol der Herrschaft geworden wäre. Zeichen der Gewalt ist die Schlange, Zeichen der stofflichen Fülle das Eil. But dominion is wielded not by her but by the man, whose force awakens life in matter, and who by his deed calls into being what is to be ruled. We find this idea again in the myth of Tarutius and Larentia.2) Tarutius is rich, a true Plutus; Larentia is poor, the material Penia, in whom first the man awakens the seed of creation. But Tarutius lays everything in Larentia’s lap, as Hermes lays the filled purse in Fortuna’s. She in turn appoints the Roman people her heir. The same idea lies in the property law of the gynecocratic peoples. The man acquires. But everything is given to the woman and inherited exclusively by the daughters, so that even the duty of maintenance among the Egyptians rests exclusively on these, not on the sons. Yet, indeed by virtue of the same principle, it is the man who rules with the scepter of power, not the woman. To him belongs the right over life and death, since it is he, through his action upon matter, and not the receptive woman, who has introduced into the world the movement of life and death. Therefore we also have no indication that the egg ever became a symbol of dominion. The sign of force is the serpent, the sign of material plenty the egg. So too in that dream in Chrysippus, wealth and hidden treasure are foretold from the egg, not power and dominion, and Scribonius promises the latter to Julia Augusta only when a pullus insigniter cristatus came to light. So the Persian king drinks from a gilded eggcup the generative, salutary water, but as a symbol of dominion no king, no ruler on earth bears it. The relation of egg and serpent is always the same: there the woman, here the man; there the material primal ground, here developed life; there the concept of material plenty, here that of energy and dominion; there that of rest and preserving, here that of acquiring, struggling, increasing, of fighting in attack and defense; there Fortuna at the hearth, here the serpent genius, wholly given over to life, generating, sustaining, and ruling it. On this is founded the duality of kingship, as it reveals itself at Rome in Romulus and Remus,3) then again in the consulate and in the duumvirate of so many magistracies, and as it appears at Sparta.
