For primal matter is in itself necessarily a unity; only the life that has proceeded from it is twofold, a life that a twofold male force, that of becoming and that of passing away, keeps in motion and ever rejuvenates anew.1) In Romulus and Remus this nature of duality emerges with particular clarity. For that Remus represents the dark side of life, Romulus the luminous half of force, is evident from all the features of their myth. The twin pair of Rhea is comparable to that of the Molionidae and the Dioscuri, and the hetaeric swamp as mother could, without in the least doing violence to the idea of the ancient conception, quite properly be conceived as an egg. But it can also be set beside the two Lares and Mania, the mother of the Lares, and likewise beside the genius-dragons and the mother egg. The fundamental idea of all these mythological formations is the same: woman stands as material primal principle and as a unity, whereas developed life is the result of a double male force, which appears as generating and sustaining, and therefore also as ruling. Only in the union of two holders of power lies the guarantee of welfare. Therefore the death of one is a particular misfortune, and for the censors the dissolution of the rule of both. Therefore they are to be chosen iisdem auspiciis and bound by a relation of colleagues in which each bears the whole right in himself, and in which, as in the case of the partes pro indiviso, the restriction of each individual comes into play only concursu.2) The duality of the male force passes likewise to the insigne imperii. It is the double ax, the Albanæ secures,3) of Asiatic origin, as we find it in the hands of the Zeus of Labranda, in those of the Lydian rulers,4) and, above all, surrounded by very significant myths, on Tenedos.5) The bipennis too shows the duality of force, the power over life and death. It corresponds to the double dragon, which rules all mortal life, and as with the latter the significance of dominion rests on the significance of physical generation, so too with the former. Proof of this the 24 good and 24 evil gods enclosed in the egg, the latter are the first to pierce the shell. That is to say: with the piercing of the egg begins the cycle of life, in which death rules. The beginning of generation is therefore an act of the evil principle. Similar is the idea of that myth in which Cronus gives Hera two eggs, which he has smeared with his seed, and from which, in the Cilician Arimaia, where they were laid in the earth, Typhon now proceeds. The opposition of egg and serpents, of the female-material primal principle and the male force of movement, recurs in two designations that play a great part in the ancient sacral law, in the concepts of the sanctum and the sacrum. The former has its root in a quality of tellurian matter, the latter corresponds to the realm of light. The sanctum stands under the protection of the chthonian powers, the sacrum is consecrated to the gods above:4) a distinction that is repeated in ἱερόν and ὅσιον.5) Among the res sanctæ the walls in particular are singled out.6) In this example where it is reported that at the Oschophoria not the herald but his scepter is wreathed. — — quod eum plebes — — discedentes Jovi consecraverunt. In a more general sense sacrum means everything given over to the gods as their property, in which case the nature of the deity no longer matters. Thus Trebatius libro 1 de religionibus in Macrob. Sat. 3, 3 says: Sacrum est, quicquid est quod Deorum habetur. The idea of property is wholly foreign to the sanctum. What founds sanctitas is the connection of a thing with the maternal womb of the earth. The sacral quality rests on a legal act of men, sanctity on a quality belonging to the thing from the outset. rom. 27. Διὰ τὶ πᾶν τεῖχος ἀβέβηλον καὶ ἱερὸν νομίζουσι, τὰς δὲ πύλας οὐ νομίζουσιν; here the gates are distinguished from the walls. The elaboration of Plutarch’s question shows that such a distinction certainly exists, but that it does not touch the quality of sanctitas itself. Moreover, the ancients nowhere state definitely the true content of the sanctum and its nature. The quodammodo divini juris of Gaius is very indefinite. No better is the following definition of Trebatius libro religionum in Macrob. 3, 3: Sanctum est interdum idem quod sacrum idemque quod religiosum; interdum aliud, hoc est, nec sacrum nec religiosum. — Gallus Aelius in Festus, p. 278 Müll. Inter sacrum autem, et sanctum, et religiosum differentias bellissime refert: sacrum ædificium, consecratum Deo; sanctum murum, qui sit circum oppidum: religiosum sepulcrum [PDF 174] — 160 — the fundamental idea of sanctitas can be most clearly recognized. Plato’s Laws say of Sparta that the lawgiver who forbade encircling the city with walls had done well to let them sleep in the earth.1) Longinus censures this comparison as too bold and tasteless, since walls neither sleep nor wake. But the Latin expression excitare muros rests on the same fundamental view, and proves that Plato’s representation, even if he borrowed it from a poet, followed a traditional conception. This conception evidently saw in the walls rising from the depths of the earth a birth proceeding from the maternal womb, which slept in the dark depths until the working of the male force roused it from slumber and drew it forth into the light. For the sexual act of the man too is called ἐγείρειν, which corresponds completely to excitare. Thus walls, like trees, are a birth of Mother Earth, and through their foundations, as trees through their roots, remain in lasting firm connection with the maternal womb even after birth. In the wall as in the tree the male potency comes to the light of day. The phallus, which until now had mated with matter unseen in the depths of the earth, now for the first time comes to visible representation in the product that appears. Therefore the tree becomes the tree of life, as already in the Mosaic account, and as, proceeding from the same idea, according to Philostratus’s report, men in Lydia held the belief that the trees are older than the earth that bears them; therefore the wall becomes the male murus, which the ancients very often clothed with the image of the phallus, not only, as one might later indeed chiefly have thought, to protect it by the fascinus from hostile attacks and influences, but because it had given the wall itself its origination, as the phallic Poseidon Genesios, united with Apollo, laid the foundation deep in the earth for the walls of Troy.2) The same conception underlies yet another ubi mortuus sepultus aut humatus sit, satis constare ait. e: that of the sacrum. Joined firmly to the maternal womb of the earth, it is immovable, and this ἀκίνητον forms the real fundamental meaning of sanctum.1) Projecting above the earth, it is the phallus-birth that has come into the light, and, now consecrated to the gods of light, is in this relation sacer. Sacrum means everything consecrated to the gods above. It refers, then, just as much to the luminous nature of masculinity as the sanctum does to the relation to the earth. As sancta res the wall is inseparable from the matter with which it stands firmly joined, as sacra it is committed to the protection of the higher force of light, into whose realm it was born. If the ἀκίνητον rests in the former quality, the latter carries within it the assurance of divine protection. In the former the wall has the quality of the earth itself, immovable rest and innate divinity; in the latter it is protected and defended against every hostile attack, as by the phallus, so by the serpents. Persius, Sat. 1, 112, gives an example. Hic, inquis, veto quisquam faxit oletum? Pinge duos angues; pueri, sacer est locus, extra meiite! discedo. No one is to relieve himself at the wall. Against this the image of the serpent protects. By it one makes the place sacer; it is now consecrated to the gods of light and under their protection; given over to them, it is defended by them. So there stands on the gate of Mycenae the sun pillar held by the sun lions, the sign of the highest shelter through the highest potency of divine force. The heavenly ones watch over what man transfers to them as property. Sanctitas expresses only a quality, even if one grounded in the religious views of tellurism; the concept of protection and defense it does not carry in itself. This lies in the consecration and the duty of protection that arises from it for the deity. As sancta res the walls share in the holiness of earth matter, in whose realm they rest; they are not so much divini iuris as themselves bearers of a deeper stage of divine force; as sacræ, on the other hand, they enter objectively into the right of the powers of light, who now undertake their defense. So the sacrum stands to the sanctum as the guarding dragon to the egg. The former designates the sacrum and the protection it enjoys; the latter the object which, as res sancta, carries within itself the divinity of tellurian matter itself, but has need of a ipso solo est, quod nulla vi moveri neque deleri potest, atque ut cetera extinguuntur, sic sepulcra fiunt sanctiora vetustate. Cf. Elvers, Romanorum de reb. religios. doctrina. p. 23. The hymn in Isim 4 names στάλαν ἀσάλευτον, σᾶμα τεᾶς μοναρχίας.

e: higher protection. The true concept of the sanctum as ἀκίνητον μὴ κινεῖν emerges clearly in the importance of the pomœrii prolatio,1) in the holiness of the terminus, in the myth of the immovable Terminus of the Capitol,2) in the immovability of funerary columns and boundary markers, likewise in the sanctio legis, the penal clause contained in the last chapter of the law, which carries with it the idea of firmness and unalterable validity, as well as in many applications at whose foundation lies always the sense of immovable steadfastness, unshakable firmness.3) Again, the concept of the sanctum finds application to the holiness of the treasure hidden in the earth. Plato speaks of the belief of the ancients that the raising of a discovered treasure brings misfortune into the marriage bed. Whoever, then, raises such a hoard is punished by the barrenness of his wife. Here we see once more the ἀκίνητον in its connection with the female-material natural principle. Whoever lays hands on this calls down upon himself the vengeance of Mother Earth. From him woman withholds her fertility; for him no blessing will any longer bloom forth from the egg. After his fashion Plato has spiritualized the old belief into a proposition of truly Christian sublimity. “If you leave the treasure lying, you will gain more in your soul than in your goods if you raise it.” Wholly material in nature is the old popular conception, wholly ideal-spiritual Plato’s Capitoli immobile saxum. Liv. 5, 54. irrogatione pœnæ ab injuria defendere, sic et leges sanctæ, et muri sancti esse dicuntur. — Macrob. Sat. 3, 3. Sancta ad vos anima atque istius inscia culpæ descendam. Non enim sacro aut religioso ejus anima tenebatur, quam sanctam, hoc est incorruptam, voluit ostendere, ut in illo quoque: Tuque o sanctissima conjux, felix morte tua. In quo castitatis honorem incorruptæ uxoris amplexus est, unde et sanctæ leges, quæ non debeant pœnæ sanctione corrumpi. Sanctæ leges are therefore those which contain no clausula de sanctione, i.e. no penal clause, whose unbreakable validity rests in themselves, for which one must compare, with the commentators, the beginning of Ulpian’s Fragments. — Macrob. continues thus about the sanctum: If Virgil calls the fire on Iulus’s head sancti ignes, that is inexact; for the fire is sacer, quia divinitus contigit. Here we see the distinction of the tellurian and the heavenly confirmed. Festus p. 278 places the sanctum in this, ut violari sine pœna non possit, whereby the idea of inviolability, unassailability again emerges as the chief thought. Therefore Remus’s deed appears in Plut. Qu. rom. 37 as an infringement of the ἄβατον. Through this development of the concept sanctum is brought very close to augustum, which likewise includes the inviolability of what is consecrated by the augustum augurium. On this Bachofen, Röm. e: interpretation.1) The example becomes all the more instructive since we know from Chrysippus’s interpretation of dreams what inner affinity binds the treasure to the egg. By this very fact we are entitled to place the sanctum in closer relation to the material primal egg, as the sacrum to the cock-dragons akin to light, and to recognize in those Pompeian paintings an allusion to the character, doubly consecrated by sanctum and sacrum, of the space surrounding the household altar. 14. This exposition may form the transition to another, in which the connection of the material primal egg with the material goods of man emerges in a new and very noteworthy form. As from the here in full. “Let us first cite a treasure that someone has carefully laid away for himself and his descendants, among whom I do not belong. Far be it from me ever to ask the gods that they let me find such a one, and if I found it by chance, to raise it, or even to turn to so-called soothsayers who might know how to advise me in this or that way how I could lift the property entrusted to the earth. For the increase of my wealth, if I raised such a treasure, would be far less important to me than the increase in the virtue of my soul if I leave it lying. I shall obtain a better possession for my nobler part if I esteem justice in my soul a higher possession than wealth. That saying of manifold validity finds application here too: one should not move the immovable. The legend, too, deserves all credence that such goods bring misfortune into the marriage bed. (Πείθεσθαι δὲ χρὴ τοῖς περὶ τοῦτο λεγομένοις μύθοις, ὡς εἰς παίδων γενεὰν οὐ ξύμφορα τὰ τοιαῦτα.) Suppose now that someone, heedless of the blessing of children and without regard for the lawgiver, took away something that neither he himself nor any of his forefathers laid in keeping, without the permission of him who laid it down, and thereby violated the simplest and fairest of all laws, and at the same time the ordinance of a most distinguished man who gave us the rule: what you have not laid down, you shall not raise — such a despiser of these two lawgivers, who has embezzled not merely a trifle that he had not himself put aside, but perhaps a tremendously great treasure, how shall he be punished? How the gods will punish him, that is known to the god. — — Another law, which concerns small things as well as great, may next follow upon this one, running thus: If anyone has left something of his own anywhere, with or without intent, he who comes upon it shall let it lie, and follow the principle that such things are watched over by the goddess of the roads and are consecrated to her by the law. e: female natural principle all material life and all material wealth proceed, in respect of their material ground, so too the idea and the origin of law attach to it. Law orders the relations of economic life on earth. It belongs wholly to matter, refers exclusively to matter. It is therefore itself wholly material in nature, and for that reason in its innermost essence female. In this quality it meets us in the ancient world of myth. The founders and bearers of law are the same nature mothers who also let the goods to which it refers proceed from their womb. The idea of maternity thereby receives a new addition. The disposition favorable to mortals lies now no longer merely in this, that she sends all good gifts to men, and, like the primal mother Anna Perenna, feeds the hungry people with warm loaves even in the poorest months of the year; it lies notably also in this, that with truly maternal love she apportions equally to all her children and gives each his own. Aphrodite thereby becomes Nemesis, she who distributes justly. For herein lies, as in Ἰσοδαίτης, the idea of just νέμειν, the idea of giving joined with that of equal distribution, hence the idea of a true Justitia. As such she is the judge over every dispute, causarum et arbitra regum, as Ammianus Marcellinus 14, 11 calls her.1) The same nature is shown by Aphrodite Syria, the virgo cœlestis. Especially noteworthy is an inscription found in England in Orelli-Henzen vol. 3, no. 5863. Imminet. Leoni. virgo. cœlesti. situ | spicifera. iusti inventrix. urbium. conditrix | ex quis muneribus. nosse contigit deos | ergo eadem mater divum pax virtus. Ceres | dea Syria lance vitam et iura et pensitans | in cœlo visum syria sidus edidit | Lybiæ etc.2) We see here the two tendencies of maternity, the one that bestows wealth and the one that devises, administers, and apportions law, joined and derived from the same fundamental idea. Caesar therefore attached himself to a view rooted equally deep in the Aphroditean religion and in the nature of law when he built his forum, destined for the administration of justice, around the temple of Aphrodite.3) The goddess who gave origin to the Julian lineage, whose name Ἰουλώ, as it gave its name to the Coan-Aphroditean city Ἰουλίς, so also gave to the Trojan lineage of Anchises the maternal name Julia memor fuerit. — Pervigilium Veneris l. 7. e: in the renewal of legislation rejuvenation again and again, as the serpent puts off its henceforth useless skin and returns from age to youth. At the birth all nature is in joyful movement. Peace reigns in creation, and joins the wild animals with the tame in harmonious union. Astraea, the nurse of men versed in law (line 334), nourishes the child with Attic honey; law and eloquence are its first utterances. So Beroë thrives to the beauty of Aphrodite, which stirs even the desire of the Olympian. The mother, delighted by the splendor of her daughter, wishes to found in her memory a city that would surpass Athens itself in the fame of its laws. For Zeus had once, when Aphrodite united him with Hera, given the goddess the promise that to one of her cities the statutes of justice (θεσμὰ Δίκης) should be granted. To learn to which such fame is allotted, she hastens to Harmonia, whom she finds at the loom, busy adorning the garment with the artful images of the earth, the starry heaven, the ocean, and the river-bull with human countenance. Now, at the appearance of the troubled mother, the mistress, nurse of mortals and immortals, lays the weaving implements aside, and shows Aphrodite, on the seven tablets of destiny that bear the names of the seven planets, Beroë’s name as the first, to whom the promise applies. Highly delighted, the fortunate Cypris hastens to her son Eros, and persuades him to fill Dionysus, who happens to be staying on Lebanon, and Poseidon with love for the beautiful Beroë. Chance brings the two gods together. They are inflamed with a common love. Combat is to decide the possession of the bride. In fearful strife the powers of water and of fire wrestle with each other. In five hosts the army of Dionysus is drawn up. All the gods look on at the combat. But at Psamathe’s entreaties Zeus decides for Poseidon. To him the child of the sea-born Aphrodite is wedded in solemn marriage; Dionysus is consoled by the promise of Ariadne, Aura, and Pallene. In keeping with the promise he gave before the battle, he too is well disposed to the newly founded city. These are the main features of the younger myth, whose elaboration extends to the end of the 43rd book. However much of this we may now regard as Nonnus’s own invention, the myth is nonetheless what the poet himself gives it out to be, a native Berytian legend. On coins the city appears now joined with Poseidon, now with Dionysus, and Sanchuniathon too relates that Cronus gave to Poseidon (so closely related to him) the dominion over Berytus.1) The praise of the law school, which has little connection with the combat of the [PDF 183] — 169 — two gods, is evidently Nonnus’s own work, and perhaps grounded in personal circumstances of the poet. Indeed, in one single feature there emerges a very clear allusion to the marriage laws of Augustus and to the compulsion to marry, which does not please Aphrodite.1) But it is another question whether the idea of bringing the praise of the school of Berytus into such a connection with the myth of Beroë’s birth likewise rests on free poetic invention, or rather has its deeper ground in the divine nature of Aphrodite-Beroë. The latter seems to me so irrefutable that I regard even the main features of the myth itself as given in the native Berytian temple legend, and as laid by Nonnus at the foundation of his account, which he has, to be sure, very carefully embellished. Aphrodite was thus conceived and venerated at Berytus itself as Justitia. She is not only the mother of the moist deep, not only as Beroë the nymph of the nearby fecundating spring, not only as Astraea-Astarte the queen of the moist night sky, not only as Harmonia with the seven tablets of destiny the primal mother who maintains the harmony of the cosmos: she is also the content of all law, thereby the founder of peace among the creatures of the earth, and the bearer of a highest world order that embraces all parts of material creation, the perishable and the imperishable. She is at once matter and the law of matter, the latter conceived on the one hand as cosmic order, on the other as the law of material creation, hence the great peace of the All, which joins heaven and its bodies, the earth and the sea, men and animals into one harmonious whole. Therefore it cannot be doubted that the first care and administration of law was bound up with the cult of Aphrodite- Beroë and connected with the priesthood of her temple. Ulpian, whose parents were citizens of Tyre in Cilicia,2) calls the jurists entrusted with the jus respondendi Justitiæ sacerdotes,3) an expression that is more than a mere image, and, in right connection with the primeval union of religion with law, presents the administration of law itself as a priestly function. If Merillius, Observationes 1, 11, recognizes in this the Stoic conception, then Stoicism appears on this point, as on many others, only as a revival of primeval views. The expression of Ulpian recurs in Symmachus, who in Epist. Ambros. 30 calls the emperors justitiæ sacerdotes. Correspondingly [PDF 184] — 170 — we find δικαιοσύνης ἱερεύς in the Declamat. Liban. T. 1, 459, λήρων ἱερεύς in Dionys. de compos. verb.1) The expression τὰ σεμνὰ Θέμιδος μυστήρια points to the fact that the doctrine of law itself was treated as a priestly secret doctrine, as, in the case of medicine, which was likewise tied to temple care—think of Tricca and Epidaurus—cannot in any event be doubted. Then we also have a point of connection for that patrician principle which conceives knowledge as well as administration of law in general as a function of priestly character, and surrounds it with the same secrecy that protects the mysteries too from every profanation by communication to the uninitiated. The Aphroditean Syria bears the character of a Justitia in Hyginus’s account too, fab. 197. For the egg of the Euphrates, hatched by doves, lets a goddess issue from it, of whom it is said: et justitia et probitate ceteros exsuperat. Compare with this Ovid. Fast. 4, 86 f., where it is said of the all-mother Venus: Juraque dat cœlo, terræ, natalibus undis. Hence the primal mare2) too is called Δίκαια, as I have shown, following Aristotle, in the Mutterrecht. The same conception recurs with particular definiteness for the Egyptian mother Isis. Of her Diodor. 1, 14 emphasizes the following: θεῖναι δέ φασι καὶ νόμους τὴν Ἶσιν, καθ᾽ οὓς ἀλλήλοις διδόναι τοὺς ἀνθρώπους τὸ δίκαιον καὶ τῆς ἀθέσμου βίας καὶ ὕβρεως παύσασθαι διὰ τὸν ἀπὸ τῆς τιμωρίας φόβον. διὸ καὶ τοὺς παλαιοὺς Ἕλληνας τὴν Δήμητραν θεσμοφόρον ὀνομάζειν, ὡς τῶν νόμων πρῶτον ὑπ᾽ αὐτῆς τεθειμένων. According to 1, 27 there stood on the Isis pillar: Ἐγὼ Ἶσίς εἰμι ἡ βασίλισσα πάσης χώρας, ἡ παιδευθεῖσα ὑπὸ Ἑρμοῦ, καὶ ὅσα ἐγὼ ἐνομοθέτησα, οὐδεὶς αὐτὰ δύναται λῦσαι. Since Demeter will be discussed further below, it suffices here to call attention to the Orphic hymn 40. In this Deo,3) the divine mother of the All, the nurse of youth, the giver of fortune, the goddess equally rich in offspring and in fruits of the harvest, blessed with children, is invoked: Bring back peace, and the pleasing ordinance of law, Overflowing fullness and royal health. In the hymn to Isis found in 1841 on the island of Andros by Ross, published by Sauppe, Zürich 1842, which in its main content agrees with the inscription of the Isis pillar mentioned by Diodorus, the δῆμος, dama, Jodama, and others. e: goddess’s relation to law and legislation is likewise emphasized: l. 19: αἰπυνόῳ βασιλῆϊ δ᾽ ὅσον μένος ἐν φρεσὶ[ν ἔγνω] θεσμοθέτις μερόπων . . . οὐδ᾽ ἀπαμαυρώσει . . . i.e. “what the mind of the high-minded king perceives in his spirit, that comes from me, the lawgiver of mortals, and no length of time will be able to obscure it.” l. 34: ἀδὲ θαλάσσας πρᾶτον ἐν ἀνθρώποισι περάσιμον ἦνεσα μόχθον, ἀδὲ δικασπολίᾳ ῥώμαν πόρον, ἀδὲ — γενέθλας ἀρχάν, — ἀνδρὶ γυναῖκα συνάγαγον ἔν τε σελάνας ἐς δεκάταν ἀψίδα τεθαλότος ἄρτιον ἔργου φέγγος ἐπ᾽ ἀρτίγονον βρέφος ἄγαγον, ἀδὲ γονήων ἀζομένως τιμὰν ἔτι νηπιάχως ὑπὸ μαζῷ δωρησμοῖς ἐδίδαξα μελίφροσι. etc. That is: To men I first recommended the venture of sailing over the sea, and gave force to the administration of justice, and as the beginning of generation gave woman to man, in the tenfold revolution of the moon led the work to perfection, gave the young offspring to the light, and through sweet gifts impressed upon the infant reverence for its parents. l. 53: ὑπάταν βασιλήϊδ᾽ ἀτε[ιρῆ] πτήσσονθ᾽ ἀμετέραν, δεσμῶν δ᾽ ἀέκουσαν ἀ[νάγκην] ἀλλύω. That is: Before our highest royal power they tremble, but the constraint of fetters not agreeable to me I loose. l. 69: Ἶσις ἐγὼ πολέμῳ κρυερὸν νέφος ἕρκεσι μόχθων ἀμφέβαλον, κλήζοισα πολυκτέανον βασιλείαν θεσμοφόρον. That is: the sufferings and distress of war I have banished, and the royal power, the enriching, law-founding, I have raised to fame. From this conception a cult practice in the service of the great Egyptian primal mother now receives its explanation and its deeper meaning. According to Apuleius, Metam. 11, T. 1. p. 262 ed. Bipont., the fourth priest in the Isis procession carries the cast of a left hand, which was called the Aequitatis manus. Quartus Aequitatis ostendebat indicium, deformatam manum sinistram, porrecta palmula: quæ genuina pigritia, nulla calliditate, nulla sollertia prædita videbatur æquitati magis aptior quam dextera. Idem gerebat et aureum vasculum in modum pupillæ rotundatum, de quo lacte libabat.1) The explanation by which Apuleius here seeks to justify the choice of the left hand may correctly reproduce the view of his time. Nor can correctness and inner justification be denied to the conception which sees in the left hand the image of an equity remote from all cleverness and art, in the right, on the other hand, the seat of active, enterprising, self-interested cunning. Yet I believe that this meaning is itself only a derived one. The left hand shows us the passive, sustaining, the right the active, acquiring principle.2) ἕπεται, ἔχων τὸν τε τῆς δικαιοσύνης πῆχυν καὶ τὸ σπονδεῖον. o: Die linke ist also die weibliche, die rechte die männliche Naturseite. Das mütterliche Naturprinzip steht demnach mit der linken Seite des Menschen in einer natürlichen Verbindung. Diese tritt in jenem von Theseus auf Delos errichteten Keraton, das aus lauter linken Hörnern aufgebaut ist, hervor. Um den Hornaltar tanzen die Jünglinge den nach DicäarH sogenannten Kranichtanz, der im Kreise herum, und immer wieder zurügetanzt wird. ') Tritt hierin wie in dem Umdrehen der Römer auf dem Grabe ihrer Eltern, die Jdee der Kreisbewegung und des in sich Zurücfkehrens alles Lebens hervor, so zeigt die Verbindung mit Ariadne's Venussäule, daß die weiblich-stoffliche Naturauffassung zu der Wahl der linken Hörner führte. Jn der Vertauschung der linken mit rechten Hörnern, welche derselbe Plutarch an einer andern Stelle, nämlich in der Schrift über die Land- und Wasserthiere meldet, tritt der Uebergang aus der weiblichen zur männlichen Naturauffassung , aus dem aphroditishen zum apollinishen Prinzip hervor. Eine weitere Anerkennung der Verbindung der linken Seite mit dem weiblichen Naturprinzip liegt in folgender Nahricht des Plinius 7, 7: Supra Nassmonas confinisque illis Machlyas Androgynos esse utriusque naturg inter se vicibus coeuntis , Calliphanes tradit. Aristoteles adiicit dextram mammam üs virilem, Ievam muliebrem esse. Plut. Symp. 8, 8. besonders 5, 7. (Die Knaben aus dem rechten, die Mädchen aus dem linken Hoden). Also wurde die Weiblichkeit auf die linke Seite verlegt. Sehr merkwürdig ist ferner die von dem Soliasten zu Pindar Ol. 1,37 Boeckh. p. 30 angeführte Sage. Die Pelopiden sollen auf der rehten Schulter den neptunischen Dreizack, auf dem linken Oberarm das Gorgonenhaupt gezeigt haben. In jenem wird ihre männliche Abstammung von Poseidon genesios , mit dessen Hilfe Pelops die Hippodamia gewann, in diesem die weibliche hervorgehoben. Aus der Jdee der Weiblichkeit leitet die linke Seite die ihr in der Augurienlehre beigelegte Bedeutung ab. e: The left is therefore the female, the right the male side of nature. The maternal natural principle accordingly stands in a natural connection with the left side of man. This emerges in that Keraton erected by Theseus on Delos, which is built entirely of left horns. Around the horn altar the youths dance the so-called crane dance, as Dicaearchus calls it, which is danced round in a circle and back again, over and over.1) If in this, as in the turning about of the Romans at the grave of their parents, the idea of the circular movement and of the returning into itself of all life emerges, then the connection with Ariadne’s Venus pillar shows that the female-material view of nature led to the choice of the left horns. In the exchange of left horns for right, which the same Plutarch reports in another passage, namely in the treatise on land and water animals, the transition from the female to the male view of nature, from the Aphroditean to the Apollonian principle, emerges. A further recognition of the connection of the left side with the female natural principle lies in the following report of Pliny 7, 7: Supra Nasamonas confinisque illis Machlyas Androgynos esse utriusque naturæ inter se vicibus coeuntis, Calliphanes tradit. Aristoteles adiicit dextram mammam iis virilem, lævam muliebrem esse. Plut. Symp. 8, 8, especially 5, 7. (The boys from the right, the girls from the left testicle.) Thus femininity was assigned to the left side. Very remarkable, further, is the legend cited by the scholiast on Pindar Ol. 1, 37 Boeckh. p. 30. The Pelopidae are said to have shown on the right shoulder the Neptunian trident, on the left upper arm the Gorgon’s head. In the former their male descent from Poseidon genesios, with whose help Pelops won Hippodamia, is emphasized, in the latter the female. From the idea of femininity the left side derives the significance attributed to it in the doctrine of augury. passage on the religious significance of wearing rings; in this it is said: Hinc factum est, ut usus anulorum exemtus dexteræ, quæ multum negotiorum gerit, in lævam relegaretur, quæ otiosior est: ne crebro motu et officio manus dextræ pretiosi lapides frangerentur. — The Bacchantes carry the thyrsus in the left hand, Pentheus in the right, Euripid. in Bacchis 937. On this Marmora Taurinensia 1, p. 58. According to Philostrat. Her. 19, p. 322 Asteropaeus has two right hands: δεξιὸς ἄμφω τὼ χεῖρε, an emphatic highlighting of his male-active nature. — On right and left compare also Grimm, Geschichte der deutschen Sprache, p. 981. On the connection of Hecate and of the soul with the left side of man, Selden, de Diis Syriis Synt. 2, 2. Finally I recall that the hot drop of oil from the Psyche lamp falls on the right shoulder of Eros (above, p. 95), that Jason wears the sandal that alone remained to him on the right foot (Pindar, Pyth. 4, 133. 165, with the scholia), that, on the other hand, Charicleia has on the left arm the black mark, the sign of her birth from the Ethiopian queen Persina. Heliodor, Aethiop. 10, 15.

o: Denn hier ist die linke Seite die glückbringende, sowohl in Beziehung auf die Erscheinung der Vögel als auf die des Blißes. ') In varruos und äpwreges drüt sic die Anschauung der Alten auchH sprachlih aus. Das Weib ist der Grund alles Seegens, daher die linke oder weibliche Seite die gute. Wenn bei den Griechen Links Unheil verkündet, wie bei Homer. Od. 20, 242 f., so ruht dieß auf einer andern Eigenschaft der Weiblichkeit. Das Weib verzehrt alles Leben, so daß Gorgo als Quelle des Todes aufgefaßt, Ocnus Seil von einer 94ua ovos benagt, und dem Monde die orbandi potestas und die Eigenschaft der Sterilität beigelegt wird. So sind die beiden einander widerstreitenden Auslegungen doH nur zwei Seiten desselben: Grundbegriffs, von denen bald die eine, bald die andere in den Vordergrund tritt. J< halte die glübringende für die ältere, die unheilbringende für die neuere Bedeutung, und führe die letztere auf den Sieg des väterlichen über das mütterliche Naturprinzip zurück. 2) -- Die Römer sagen sinister avis, und der von den Alten behauptete Zusammenhang dieses Wortes mit sinere scheint mir unzweifelhaft. Darin zeigt die linke Seitewieder ihre Passivität, wie die Rechte das aktive Princip ausdrükt. Das Zulassen ist ein passives, das Hindern ein aktives Verhalten. Denn da in ihnen die Trägheit der Kälte herrscht, so sind fie die shwächern weiblichen, wie die zeugungsfkräftigen Südgegenden die stärkeren männlichen Theile der Erde. e: For here the left side is the auspicious one, both with regard to the appearance of birds and to that of lightning.1) In εὐώνυμος and ἀριστερός the view of the ancients expresses itself linguistically as well. Woman is the ground of all blessing, and therefore the left or female side is the good one. When among the Greeks the left announces misfortune, as in Homer, Od. 20, 242 f., this rests on another property of femininity. Woman consumes all life, so that the Gorgon is conceived as the source of death, Ocnus’s rope is gnawed by a θήλεια ὄνος, and the moon is credited with the orbandi potestas and the quality of sterility. Thus the two conflicting interpretations are nevertheless only two sides of the same fundamental concept, of which now the one, now the other comes to the fore. I hold the auspicious one to be the older meaning, the inauspicious one the newer, and I trace the latter back to the victory of the paternal over the maternal natural principle.2) — The Romans say sinister avis, and the connection of this word with sinere, asserted by the ancients, seems to me beyond doubt. Here the left side shows its passivity once more, just as the right hand expresses the active principle. To permit is a passive, to hinder an active mode of conduct. The former is therefore associated with the left or female side, which Plutarch too calls the naturally weaker. The same idea recurs in the identification of the sinistræ partes with the septentrionales, which is cited as a fixed tenet of augural doctrine. For since in these the sluggishness of cold prevails, they are the weaker, female parts of the earth, just as the generatively powerful southern regions are its stronger, male parts. If in this way the left side appears as an expression of the female divine nature in general, the hand in itself is no less a symbol of the maternal the second rank, and the parts of the left side shall be offered to the gods of the earth, and sacrifices of odd number, of the first rank, and the parts of the right side to the Olympian gods. Odd number and left side are also joined by Pythagoras in Plin. 28, 3. The tellurian is femininity, the Olympian the masculinity of the realm of light. In Plut. Is. et Os. 45 it is said that of the two opposed forces, the one (that is, the creative) leads toward the right hand, while the other (that is, the destructive) turns back again and leads backward. Agreeing with this is the fact that in Homer Hephaestus hands the cup toward the right, (Eurip. Rh. 352) the herald carries the lots toward the right, Odysseus begs his way toward the right among the suitors, the suitors too rise toward the right for the shot, and toward the right, according to Theogn. 922, the suppliant turned. According to Plut. qu. rom. 97 the victorious right-hand horse, the October Equus, is sacrificed to Mars. This again probably has its ground in the connection of the right side with the male principle, a relation that has practical significance also in the differing task of the two animals of a two-horse team. At the founding of cities the bull goes outward, the cow inward.

e: natural side of matter. We find all the great nature mothers conceived as weaving deities. I recall Harmonia, who finds Aphrodite at the loom, and add Penelope, the dædala Circe, the tres anus textrices of the Eros mysteries, the spinning Parcae, the spindle of Athena and of Tanaquil,1) the acus as one of the septem pignora imperii, the golden χειρόμακτρον of Rhampsinitus, which Demeter gives him, and the many examples in which priestly matrons, in imitation of the goddesses, weave a peplos. Here the hand appears as the seat of all skill. Deep in the depths of matter the artful web is plaited with which the earth adorns itself as with a beautiful carpet, and which earns for the creative mother herself the epithet dædala or Πλαστήνη (from Πλάσσειν).2) It is the hand by which this work is performed, the hand therefore is the symbol of all work of nature; hence Hermes the shaper is called Εὐπάλαμος,3) and Εὔχειρ is the name of the companion of Demaratus, but also of the artist of a Vulcian vessel, and in Egyptian hieroglyphics, according to Horapollo, one fond of building is indicated by a hand.4) Insofar, then, as the shaping work of nature proceeds from the female-material principle, the hand becomes the image of maternity, which bestows upon all things in the depths of the earth the artful development with which they come forth. For this reason the Palici appear on well-known vase paintings as a birth from fingers; for this reason Persephone herself is called Χειρογονία, the finger-born, and accordingly also, in turn, she who gives birth from her fingers. For this reason Hera-Aphrodite, whom mothers invoke at the betrothal of their daughters, is Ὑπερχειρία.5) For this reason the Sirens are depicted on Hera’s hand.6) For this reason the mother of the Lares is a Mania; for this reason the concepts of Mana and Geneta are joined. For this reason the dead who reunite themselves with Mana are called Manes, as from Demeter Demetrii. Now the connection, too, of manus equal to bonus and manus equal to χείρ, and of both with Mania and Mana geneta, from which they differ only by the difference in the quantity of the vowel, as populus and populus do, is explained. The hand of the mother who forms all life is that through which she becomes Bona Dea, and the same concept of maternal goodness lies in Mania and Mana geneta. With all these various but inwardly unified relations the hand appears on tomb stelae, so on one depicted in Raoul-Rochette, mon.

e: inéd. pl. 47, 2. This example is all the more instructive because the Greek inscription forbids us to think of mere word symbolism, manus as Manes. Among the recent Praenestine tomb finds, of which E. Braun reports some in the Bulletino dell’ Instit. 1845, p. 46, hands too are mentioned.1) They are not, as on the tomb stelae, cut off at the wrist, but joined with a piece of the forearm. This shows several rows of bas-reliefs on which appear the representations of centaurs and various fantastic animals so familiar from archaic, especially Chiusine, vases. Since these gain their upright position only when the hand itself is turned downward, I do not doubt that all those pieces, like the others, were meant to be hung up. A single one of these hands came to light undamaged. Others were found only in shards. The place of discovery, Praeneste, permits us to connect them with the cult of Fortuna and the Praenestine Digitii, whereby the relation of the symbol to the Cerealian, all-birth-giving maternal nature is confirmed anew. Now the votive hands too, still preserved in considerable number, with which O. Jahn in the Reports of the Leipzig Society, H. Meyer in the Communications of the Zurich Antiquarian Society, and Pignorius in his work de manu ænea deal, have found their explanation. The one that comes from the ruins of Aventicum and belongs to Herr von Bonstetten shows on its lower edge the picture of a woman in childbed, which raises beyond all doubt the relation of the hand itself to motherhood and birth. We have to recognize in it the vow for fertility and happy delivery, and see therefore how the choice of the hand for this purpose is wholly grounded in the general views about its relation to the artfully shaping activity of Mother Earth. The many attributes placed on the hand itself, which vividly present the religious syncretism of later times, all show a very definite relation to generation, fertility, and the flourishing of all life on earth, and thus attach themselves to the fundamental idea of the hand itself. Oberflacht. Beside them were found shoes and a violin-like instrument. Remarkable, and noteworthy for the Phoenician home of the symbol, are the gravestones preserved in the museums at Leyden and Copenhagen, which are adorned now with one hand, now with two. See Leemans, asiatische Monumenten te Leiden 1842, p. 56. 57. The relation to a vow, which Gesenius and Lindberg find probable, is merely an inadmissible makeshift. In the Leyden museum there is among the Egyptian antiquities a left hand whose palmula porrecta rests with its outer side on a circular disk, all of burnt clay.

e: If in the examples of the hand symbol enumerated so far its connection with the female side of natural force emerges especially, in other cases the male active generative principle too is traced back to it. It is the hand that gave its name to the artful, wise centaur Chiron, the teacher of Aesculapius and of Achilles.1) In the Ocnus pictures we see the man plaiting, an activity that rests on the same fundamental view as the weaving and spinning of the nature mothers. The activity that creates is the artful work of the hands; the destructive one, on the other hand, is artless, and is therefore performed without their aid, by animal gnawing. The hand appears, further, as an expression of male natural force in the name of those hundred springs that gush forth from the burial mound of Briareus-Aegaeon, and which Eustath. Il. p. 123, 35. Eudocia. p. 144. Aen. 10. 566. calls Βριαρέω παλάμας. So too in the practice of the Greeks of honoring the rising sun by kissing the hand, as Lucian de saltat. 17 reports. By this, then, the meaning of the hand is established. It designates the creative activity of natural force, and in doing so brings out more the idea of skill, of beautiful shaping and forming, than that of crude force,2) and therefore more the maternal πλάσσειν than the paternal ἐγείρειν. The meaning of the hand continues in that of the fingers, as indeed the skill for all artistic work rests precisely in the articulation of the fingers. The ancient view of nature therefore lends to the fingers entirely the same meaning that belongs to the hand as a whole. Already in the designation δάκτυλος the idea of natural generation emerges. For this word is composed of the two roots δακ and τύλος. But τύλος designates the male fecundating force which makes itself known in the swelling of the sappy growths of the earth. I refrain from any further elaboration of this, because I have attempted it in the most comprehensive manner at a suitable place in my work on mother right. Dac is one word with lac, as the same interchange is found in many examples, dacrimæ-lacrimæ, dautia-lautia, and others.3) Thus by Dactylos that force of natural generation is designated which gives origination to the most nourishing has also been found as a proper name on vases (Annali 1834, p. 47), in Εὔμαρος from μάρη, Laconian for hand (Schol. Ven. Il. 15, 37), Ἀμφίμαρος, Εὐπάλαμος. Apollod. 3, 15, 5. Welcker, Prometh. p. 265. slew the cupbearer boy Cyathus with a single finger. Paus. 2, 13, 18.

Wir verstehen jeht den Sinn jenes Mythus, nac welchem Jsis zu Byblos den ihr anvertrauten Säugling, Astarte's und Malcander's Kind, dadurch nährte , daß sie ihm statt der Brust den Finger in den Mund legte. ?) Die Fingergeburt der Paliken, die Genienfrucht auf den mittlern Fingern der oben genannten Votivhände, und Apuleius Ausdruck per frugiseram tuam dextram gewinnen jeht erst ihre volle edeutung. Verständlich wird nun auch die ägyptishe Kultübung, von welcher uns Macrob. Sat. 7, 13 unterrihtet. Den Götterbildern wird der dem kleinen nächste Finger (der sog. digitus medicinalis) der linken Hand mit künstlich zubereiteten Wohlgerüchen bestrihen. Daher konnte nach ägyptischer Lehre auc nur dieser Finger den Ring tragen, während nah Ateius Capito jus pontificium es den Römern der ältern Zeit freistand, quacunque manu, quolibet digito den annulus anzuziehen. 3) Als Grund des besondern Kult8s jenes Fingers wurden, wie Macrobius andeutet, gewisse anatomische und Zahleneigenthümlichkeiten geltend gemacht. Wie es sich nun auch damit verhalten mag, so viel zeigt sich bestimmt, daß die linke oder weibliche Naturseite besondere Bedeutung hatte, und vor der rechten höhere Ehre genoß, was mit der Nilreligion und der Voranstellung des mütterlichen Prinzips in derselben, im engsten Zusammenhang steht. Haben wir so den Finger in seiner allgemeinen Bedeutung als Träger der zunächst weiblich gedachten Naturkraft gefunden, so tritt uns in Griechenland ein Beispiel entgegen, das ihn mit Tod und Untergang in Verbindung seht. Pausan. 8, 34, 2 erwähnt das 4a»rc)ov ur7ua bei Megalopolis in Arkadien. Ein konischer Erdschutt trug auf seiner Höhe einen aus Stein gehauenen Finger. In der Nähe lag das Heiligthum der Raria« Heal. Die Mythen von Orestes Wahnsinn, von dem Erscheinen der Erinyen, von dem Wesel ihrer schwarzen Farbe in weiße, nachdem der Muttermörder sich den Finger der einen Hand selbst abgenagt, lassen den Zusammenhang des daxrvlog mit dem mütterlihen Naturprinzip, und die in ihm liegende Verbindung der beiden Seiten des Lebens, der schwarzen und der weißen, mit hinlänglicher Klarheit erkennen. Der Finger erscht auf der Höhe des Grabmals den Phallus, !) Plut. de fac. in orbe lunw hebt hervor, daß sie eben teßhalb keine spiegelartigen Bilder von sich gebe, an einer andern Stelle, daß sie, weil zu nahrhaft, nicht zum Getränke gebraucht werden dürfe.
e: and richest of all primal foods,1) to that one in which the earth displays most clearly its birth-giving and sustaining maternal nature. We now understand the meaning of that myth according to which Isis at Byblos nourished the infant entrusted to her, the child of Astarte and Malcander, by laying her finger in its mouth instead of the breast.2) The finger-birth of the Palici, the fruit of the genii on the middle fingers of the votive hands named above, and Apuleius’s expression per frugiferam tuam dextram now first gain their full significance. Intelligible now, too, becomes the Egyptian cult practice of which Macrob. Sat. 7, 13 informs us. The finger next to the smallest (the so-called digitus medicinalis) of the left hand of the images of the gods is anointed with artfully prepared perfumes. Hence, according to Egyptian doctrine, only this finger could wear the ring, whereas according to Ateius Capito the jus pontificium left the Romans of the earlier period free to put on the annulus quacunque manu, quolibet digito.3) As the ground of the special cult of that finger, certain anatomical and numerical peculiarities were adduced, as Macrobius intimates. However that may be, so much is certain, that the left or female side of nature had special significance and enjoyed higher honor than the right, which stands in the closest connection with the Nile religion and the precedence of the maternal principle in it. Having thus found the finger in its general meaning as the bearer of the natural force conceived in the first instance as female, we meet in Greece an example that connects it with death and destruction. Pausan. 8, 34, 2 mentions the Δακτύλου μνῆμα near Megalopolis in Arcadia. A conical mound of earth bore on its summit a finger hewn from stone. Nearby lay the sanctuary of the Μανίαι θεαί. The myths of Orestes’s madness, of the appearance of the Erinyes, of the change of their black color into white after the matricide had gnawed off the finger of one of his hands, allow the connection of the δάκτυλος with the maternal natural principle, and the connection lying in it of the two sides of life, the black and the white, to be recognized with sufficient clarity. The finger replaces on the summit of the tomb monument the phallus, like images, and at another place, that, being too nourishing, it may not be used as a drink. παιδίου διδοῦσαν. o: der so oft in Gräbern gefunden wird -- man denke an die oben zusammenge stellten Beispiele --- und der auch die Spie des Alyatte8smals krönte, wie wn dieß bei Herodot dargestellt, und von neuern Reisenden, den Herrn v. Prokesh, Welker, Hamilton bestätigt wissen. Für die Verbindung der Lebens- und Todesbedeutung in demselben Symbol, welche wir oben sHon als Ausfluß einer alle Theile der alten Götterwelt beherrshenden Grundanschauung hervorgehoben haben, liefert auc die Hand eine sehr belehrende Analogie. Symbol des Lebens, wird sie Symbol des Todes. Mit dieser Funerärbedeutung spielt sie eine merkwürdige Rolle in dem Rhampsinites-Mythus, den uns Herodot 2, 121. 122 erzählt. Denn von dem Leichnam des Bruders lös8t der Dieb den Arm, birgt ihn unter dem Gewande, und tritt so zu der Königstochter ein, welche auf des Vaters Befehl dem Hetärismus sich ergeben hatte. Da nun diese ihn festzuhalten suchte, reiht er ihr statt seiner eigenen die Hand des Todten hin, und weiß so unter dem Schuß der Dunkelheit den Anschlägen des Weibes zu entrinnen. Der Wechsel der lebenden und todten Hand entspricht den beiden Seiten des Natulebens, die in allen Theilen jenes ägyptischen Mythus in ihrer Wechselwirkung und innern Identität hervortreten. I< brauche darauf jeht nicht näher einzugehen, da meine Abhandlung in den Annali dell Instituto 1858 über die Bedeutung der Würfel in den Gräbern der Alten, sih genauer darüber verbreitet. Nur eines Zuges mag noch Erwähnung geschehen. Den betrunkenen Hütern wird von dem schlauen Betrüger die rehte Wange zum Schimpf kahl geschoren. Hier erscheint die rechte Seite wiederum in Verbindung mit der Idee der Thätigkeit und Kraft, die linke als die weibliche Passivität. Die bisher entwickelte Naturbedeutung der Finger kehrt wieder in den Jdäischen Dactylen und Pränestinischen Digitiern. ') Auch sie sind nicht bloß Erzarbeiter, und nicht deßhalb Dactyli oder Digitii genannt, weil zum Schmiedehandwerk Hand und Finger besonders erforderlich sind; vielmehr hat in jenem Namen ihre allgemeine Gottheitönatur, welche die Zeugungskraft des Stoffs in sich schließt, ihren Ausdruck gefunden. Die Dactyli bilden in ihrem Vereine die Gotteshand, welche alle Organismen der Erde erschafft und bildet. Wie Xeipoy, werden sie als Kenner der geheimen Kräfte der Pflanzen, daher als Zauberer wie Medea-Circe dargestellt. 2) Auch in dieser Eigenschaft schließt der Chironzögling Achilleus, der auf Creta den Namen Pemptus trägt, sich ihnen an. e: which is so often found in tombs — recall the examples assembled above — and which also crowned the summit of the tomb of Alyattes, as we see it described in Herodotus and have it confirmed by more recent travelers, Herr von Prokesch, Welcker, and Hamilton. For the connection of the meaning of life and the meaning of death in the same symbol, which we have already emphasized above as an outflow of a fundamental view governing all parts of the ancient world of the gods, the hand too supplies a very instructive analogy. A symbol of life, it becomes a symbol of death. With this funerary meaning it plays a remarkable role in the Rhampsinitus myth that Herodotus tells us in 2, 121. 122. For the thief severs the arm from the corpse of his brother, hides it under his garment, and so enters the presence of the king’s daughter, who at her father’s command had given herself over to hetaerism. When she now sought to hold him fast, he extends to her the hand of the dead man instead of his own, and so, under the protection of darkness, contrives to escape the woman’s designs. The alternation of the living and the dead hand corresponds to the two sides of the life of nature, which emerge in all parts of that Egyptian myth in their interaction and inner identity. I need not go into this more closely now, since my treatise in the Annali dell’ Instituto 1858 on the meaning of the dice in the tombs of the ancients deals with it more precisely. Only one feature may still be mentioned. The drunken guards have the right cheek shaved bald by the cunning deceiver, as an insult. Here the right side appears once more in connection with the idea of activity and force, the left as female passivity. The natural meaning of the fingers developed so far recurs in the Idaean Dactyls and the Praenestine Digitii.1) These too are not merely bronzeworkers, and are not called Dactyli or Digitii for the reason that hand and fingers are especially required for the smith’s craft; rather, in that name their general divine nature, which encloses within itself the generative force of matter, has found its expression. The Dactyli in their union form the divine hand, which creates and forms all the organisms of the earth. Like Χείρων, they are represented as knowers of the secret forces of plants, and therefore as sorcerers like Medea-Circe.2) In this quality too Achilles, the pupil of Chiron, who bears the name Pemptus on Crete, joins them. Beside the five male ones are set five female ones, as a complement to their sexual imperfection. These are distributed in such a way that the [PDF 193] — 179 — male ones are assigned to the right hand, the female ones to the left.1) The idea of birth from the fingers finds its expression once more in Hellanicus’s statement that the name of the Dactyls derives from the fact that these demons had held fast to Rhea’s fingers in the Idaean cave. According to Diomed. 3, 474, Ops lays her hands on the rock and so gives birth to the Cretan Zeus. From the impression of the fingers, however, the Corybantes arise, who have been called a qualitate facti Dactyli-Digiti.2) In all these turns we have always the same idea. In the five fingers of the hand rests the forming and shaping force of nature: uti homo per digitos, ita Rhea per illos ministeria sua exsequitur.3) Hence they are at first connected with the female birth-giving principle, but then they become the representation of the male generative force, which proceeds from the primal matter in the relation of a son, and so take their place beside the primal mothers as beneficent earth demons. In this significance five female fingers are added to them. Thus the human pair of hands appears as the perfected representation of the whole force of nature in its double potentiation. The left is the passive, the right the active principle. In the left sits the spell, in the right the power to dissolve it. What is thus distributed between the two hands is, however, already contained in the number five of the fingers. For we have shown above that this number signifies marriage, which proceeds from the union of the male 3 with the female 2. Herein lies the explanation why the number five of the Dactyls also alternates with the number three. Kelmis, Damnameneus, and Acmon are named in the Phoronis. In Strabo 10, 473 the Dactyls beget 9 Curetes, each of whom in turn brings forth 10 fingers.4) Here the number three and the number five appear in the closest connection: the three as the representation of the male, the five as the union of the male and the female potency. In both conceptions the idea of material generative desire prevails, which forms the fundamental nature of the Dactyls. It is the destiny of these dwarf demons, by their male action upon matter, to awaken the hidden treasures resting in it and to bring them forth into the light. They are no less fathers of all earthly generation than extractors and workers of metals. Indeed it is precisely in their fiery nature that they possess the power for both activities, and Schol. e: just as Achilles-Pemptus too, the bearer of the united force of water and fire,1) stands in the closest relation to metalwork, to the power of the two elements mating in it, and to Euboean Chalcis. Hence they are also the fathers of the Eteocretans dwelling on Ida,2) whose name indicates legitimate birth in the sense that, like the Athenians since Cecrops, they possess not only a mother but also a definite father given by marriage, and so from unilateres become διφυεῖς. It is precisely this male descent that is brought out by the number three, the διφυές by the number five, more perfectly by ten, and most developed by the hundred that prevails on Crete. Marriage, which the number five represents, is conceived wholly in material terms, and therefore in the union of the two sexes femininity has the preponderance. As Luna encloses Lunus, so here the mother encloses the father. Thereby the five again receives a predominantly material-female significance. In this sense the ten and the five stand opposed to the male solar number twelve. Wherever in the Roman state the five comes into use, the material plebeian standpoint lies at its base. In his account of the progress of the Twelve Tables Livy uses a turn of phrase that deserves full attention. Instead of the expression postquam animadverterunt, duas deesse tabulas, one would rather expect quasdam deesse leges. But the sense would thereby receive a different nuance. It is the number ten that appears questionable to the decemvirs, and that they wish to replace by twelve. This alone corresponds to the consecration to the sun, whose bearers are the patricians, and to the paternal principle on which they rest. Ten is the material plebeian number, as at first it seemed to correspond better to the material-female principle of law, and to the no less material principle of the plebeians (τὸ πλῆθος). — As a lunar number we have already found the five earlier. The ten-month lunar year shows it to us in contrast to the twelve-month year of the sun. As a woman of the moon Minerva-Athena receives a special relation to the five. We found her above as Pempta, and Achilles- Lunus as Pemptus. Now, however, the five fingers of the hand are also consecrated to Minerva, as we are informed by Servius Ecl. 6, 3, and with this a still further relation of the fingers is connected. e: Endymion reckons the courses of the moon by the bending of the fingers: ἑτερόπροπα δάκτυλα κάμψας.1) Here we have the fingers as the foundation and expression of the number system, and indeed as a consequence of their connection with material force in general. This finds its confirmation in the statement that this same Minerva is the inventor of number. This has been explained by saying that Athena, the expression of the highest spirituality, could alone have given men number and all the higher science resting on it. But the ground of that connection is a wholly different one, not so much an abstractly spiritual one as rather a wholly sensual-material one. We are not to think of that Athena who has risen to the highest spirituality and comes forth motherless from the head of Zeus, but rather of the nature mother conceived as wholly material herself, the lunar woman Minerva, to whom the fingers are consecrated. Number appears in its connection with Athena as ἀριθμὸς σωματικός. It is innate in matter,2) like law, hence connected with the female side of nature like law, and itself only the expression of the highest law that governs all parts of the material world and at the same time appears as earthly and heavenly Harmonia. In this significance precisely, number enters into closer relation to the moon and the lunar gods. In this significance the fingers are consecrated to Minerva; in it they are Endymion’s means of reckoning the moon; in it, for Aurora-Matuta, the light-radiating, day-bearing attribute; in it, like the moon itself, the bearer of all reckoning of time and of the whole number system, which did not go beyond the five and was so closely akin to πέντε that counting in general was designated by πεμπάσασθαι. With the temples of female deities the reckoning of time was bound up. In Nortia’s Volsinian sanctuary the year’s nail was driven in. Nortia has the nature of a great nature mother, identified at once with earth and mentioned. So in that passage of Macrobius, Sat. 7, 13, used above, where the number six is traced back to the digitus medicinalis complicatus. Further Auson. epist. 7, 6. Ovid. F. 3, 123. Cicero Attic. 5, 21 vers. fin. Juven. 10, 248. On beginning with the left hand Beda, de loquela per gestum digitorum. Marian. in Schol. ad Libr. 1 Hieronym. c. Jovin. It is reported by Plinius 34, 7, 16 and Macrob. Sat. 1, 9 that the Janus image had the fingers of both hands so shaped that together they gave the number of the days of the year (365 according to Macrob., 355 according to Plinius). According to Varro, Janus, who in his nature embraced all stages of generative potency, had twelve altars, according to Marcus Messala the force of cuncta fingendi, which dwells in the fingers in particular. The idea of expressing the reckoning of time on the fingers thus rests here too on the general natural meaning of the hand and its parts. — Jorio, mimica, p. 233. Echtermeyer, über die Finger, was not at my disposal. vers. physic. 2, 249 f.

e: moon, Fortuna-Nemesis,1) and the nail itself has a lunar relation clearly emerging in its connection with Diana and in its use against the putrefaction promoted by moonlight. Through all these remarks the fundamental meaning of the fingers is placed beyond doubt. They show us material natural force as a life-shaping power in the unattainable skill that distinguishes all creatures, hence first female, then also male, and therefore lengthened on images with generative force, always articulated into the conjugal five, and in number, reckoning of time, and harmony outwardly representing the immanent law innate in matter. Hence precisely the tracing back of lyre-playing to the Dactyls and Chiron, as Plutarch attests in de musica, is of deeper significance. Hence the hand is the sign of the mysteries, which are traced back precisely to the Dactyls; for that reason it appears on tombs, like the lyre so closely akin to it,2) as a symbol of initiation into the Bacchic-Orphic orgies; for that reason, finally, it is the expression of all law and of all Aequitas, which Nonnus 41, 344 designates ὄργια θεσμῶν. If we now look back to that Manus Aequitatis,3) which the priest carried in the Isis procession, it gains new significance for us. Only now does its inner connection with the vasculum in formam pupillæ rotundatum, 658, from which the following must find its place here. “In other parts the Egyptian laws may well have their defects; but their law on music is sound, and a remarkable example that it was possible to give laws on this and, with firm courage, to introduce such songs as naturally present what is right and true. That may well be the work of a god or of a man inspired by god: as indeed among the Egyptians too the legend is that these songs, which have been preserved for so many centuries, were composed by Isis. — For however much men in pleasure and pain are inclined always to have new music, this does not easily go so far that they would venture to alter and spoil consecrated melodies merely because they are ancient. In Egypt, at any rate, no one has been able to spoil them; precisely the opposite has happened.” How closely related, however, song-making and music are to legislation is shown by that νομῳδός of the Mazacenes in Cappadocia in Strabo 12, p. 539: χρῶνται δὲ οἱ Μαζακηνοὶ τοῖς Χαρώνδα νόμοις, αἱρούμενοι καὶ νομῳδὸν ὃς ἐστιν αὐτοῖς ἐξηγητὴς τῶν νόμων, καθάπερ οἱ παρὰ Ῥωμαίοις νομικοί (i.e. the jurists entrusted with the jus respondendi). Law and right are by their nature harmony of matter, and therefore inwardly akin to music and orchestics, a revelation of the great concentus of things, which the mystery lyre indicates. Agreeing with this, Lucian de saltat. 14 reports that in Thessaly the highest magistrate was called Leader of the Dance, and that this designation is found there on the statues of famous men. Two are cited: Πρόνκρινε προορχηστῆρα ἁ πόλις. Another says: Εἰλατίωνι τὰν εἰκόνα ὁ δᾶμος εὖ ὀρχησαμένῳ τὰν μάχαν. also Aecetiæ poculum? The Pentas is called Dikaiosyne in Jamblichus 3, 18.

Die runde, milchspendende Brust, !) die mit der linken Hand so wenig Zusammenhang zu haben, ihr so räthselhaft zur Seite gestellt erschien, schließt sich derselben nun als Ausdruck der gleichen Mutter-Jdee an. Hand und Brust zeigen uns das weibliche Naturprinzip in seiner schaffenden, bildenden, gestaltenden, aber auch mütterlich nährenden Eigenthümlichkeit, und auf dieser physischen Grundlage erbaut sich die höhere der Recht und Billigkeit handhabenden Justitia-Fortuna von selbst auf. Was Jsis schenkt, das vertheilt sie auch billig, mit mütterlicher Genauigkeit, ohne Gefährde und List, jedem das Seine, und diese Beziehung wird nun an die linke Hand vorzugsweise angeknüpft. Sie ist also wie Syria Dea justitia et Bquitate insignis, und dadurch wiederum vorzugsweise Mutter. Die Uebereinstimmung beider Gottheiten wird um so beachtenswerther, wenn wir bedenken, daß sie beide, gleich Leda-Nemesis mit dem stofflichen Ur-Ei in Verbindung stehen. Denn auch Jsis ist eigeboren, auf dem florentinischen Canopus selbst in Eigestalt dargestellt und mit vielfältigem Eischmuek geziert. 2) Die Jn seiner Verbindung mit dem weiblichen Naturprinzip kann das Recht selbst nur den Charakter eines Naturgeseßes haben. e: de quo lacte libat, appear in its full justification. The round, milk-giving breast,1) which seemed to have so little connection with the left hand and to be set beside it so enigmatically, now joins it as an expression of the same idea of the mother. One thought governs both symbols. The five fingers of the opened hand can themselves be conceived as milk-giving, as in the myth of Malcander. Hand and breast show us the female natural principle in its creative, forming, shaping, but also maternally nourishing character, and on this physical foundation the higher character of Justitia- Fortuna, who administers right and equity, builds itself up of its own accord. What Isis gives she also distributes justly, with maternal exactness, without deceit or guile, to each his own, and this relation is now attached preeminently to the left hand. She is thus, like Syria Dea, justitia et æquitate insignis, and thereby again preeminently mother. The agreement of the two deities becomes all the more noteworthy when we consider that both, like Leda-Nemesis, stand in connection with the material primal egg. For Isis too is egg-born, and on the Florentine Canopus is herself represented in the shape of an egg and adorned with manifold egg ornament.2) The τε καὶ εὐγενοῦς ᾠοῦ σπέρμα συγγενὲς ἐγεννήθην ἡμέρας. Likewise Isis calls herself the daughter of Cronus, and she too is, with Osiris, the offspring of one maternal womb, hence of one egg. Monuments confirm this. Like the disk, so too the egg sometimes appears between the pair of horns that adorns the head of Isis. So in Montfaucon, antiq. expliquée 2, 143. Especially noteworthy is the Canopus on a gem of the Mus. Florentin. 1, 59, no. 2, with which one must compare another in Causseus Mus. Romanum. tab. 42. On the Florentine stone altogether no fewer than seven eggs appear; one is fastened as an amulet to the necklace and takes the place of the bulla. The six others are distributed in two groups, each of which contains three. Two upright serpents carry one between their bodies; in addition each carries a smaller one on its head. We have here, then, once more the connection of serpent and egg, as on the cameo with the inscription ΥΓΙΑ; and above each of the two groups, as there, a star appears. The Canopus, moreover, itself has the form of an egg, the broad or female end being turned upward. The origin of the Canopus form from the egg can be subject to no doubt; the connection is very clear on a gem in Gorleus pl. 233, no. 491. The Canopic form is found also on Etruscan funerary monuments. So in representations of necyomancy. See the picture in Raoul-Rochette, mon. inéd. pl. 64. p. 371. 372, but also, especially at Clusium, as an independent ash receptacle. This use of the egg form corresponds in a special degree to the religious significance of the egg, and shows it in its close relation to generation and regeneration, as a representation of the physical and the higher ἀρχὴ γενέσεως. — The egg form recurs in Egypt also as a headdress. The colossal head purchased by Belzoni at Karnak, now in the British Museum, shows this egg cap, adorned in front with the royal serpent, in special perfection. Belzoni, p. 184. — The Semiramis egg reminds me of two egg-shaped stones of the British Museum, [PDF 198] — 184 — idea of æquitas can therefore be traced back to the egg as well. Like the female natural principle, it is not only the material primal ground of life but also the expression of maternal justice, of the suum cuique. The same division into two halves distinguished by color assumes, besides the physical, also the, if I may so put it, political significance of the wholly equal right of rule of two brothers called to the throne. They are to rule in turn, one after the other, and Eteocles’ supreme guilt is that he breaks this right, whereas Pollux, following it, voluntarily imparts his immortality to his brother. In the two egg halves from which the caps of the Dioscuri, and likewise heaven and earth, are formed, the thought of the æquum emerges again in another shape, and if the egg is cut through with a hair, or water is handed to the Persian king from an egg, here too we may find expressed once more the idea of the highest equity, which is to prevail in division and to guide the king’s office of judge. According to Egyptian usage the victor in a lawsuit has hung about his neck by the presiding judge the image of Ἀλήθεια which the judge himself wore. Diodor 1, 75. Aelian V. H. 14, 34. Under this image we are to think of the egg-mother Isis in the form of a Justitia-Dike represented with closed eyes. In her name, from her plenitude of power, the judge has given his decision. She herself grants the victory, which restores the right, to the wronged party as arbitra causarum, as æqua lance jura pensitans, a relation through which the ovum anguinum of the Gauls and its force in legal matters are first brought fully to light. Before the egg even the king’s highest authority bows, as the gods bow before Fatum, as Jupiter himself bows before the egg of Night and before the balance, the measure and expression of all justice and equitable distribution. 15. In its connection with the female natural principle, law itself can have only the character of a natural law. What significance attaches to this expression which come from Assyria, and before the great discoveries of the last decade belonged to the few antiquities of the Euphrates lands known in Europe. Bonomi, Nineveh and its palaces, London 1857, p. 6. To all the examples of the egg symbol that India, Assyria, Western Asia, Egypt, Greece, and Italy have furnished us, America is finally added. According to the belief of the Peruvians, three eggs fell from heaven, a golden one, a silver one, a copper one. e: will emerge most clearly from the contrast. Opposed to natural law stand the positive determinations that form the content of a particular civil legal order. We have before us the contrast of jus naturale and jus civile.1) The first and most thoroughgoing difference in which it expresses itself lies in the fact that positive civil law stands hostile and obstructive to the law of purely material life. Serving the higher destiny of man, positive law breaks at many points the law of material life, and withdraws from its dominion more than one domain, which now belongs no longer to the jus naturale but to the jus civile.2) An example will set the idea in its full light. Invincible love drives Myrrha to her father Cinyras. According to the law of matter, which forms the content of the jus naturale, such a union is permitted. But to the jus civile it is repugnant. Lamenting this, the girl speaks thus in Ovid. Met. 10, 321: Di, precor, et Pietas, sacrataque jura parentum, Hoc prohibete nefas: scelerique resistite tanto; Si tamen hoc scelus est. Sed enim damnare negatur Hanc Venerem Pietas: coëuntque animalia nullo Cætera delectu. nec habetur turpe iuvencæ Ferre patrem tergo: fit equo sua filia coniux; It is the law of the material-animal world, as it is recognized by Ulpian in Fr. 1, § 3 D. de justitia et jure (1, 1). If Ulpian among the Roman jurists emphasizes this jus naturale preeminently, his Syrian origin may well have exercised an influence on this. Without doubt Isidore too in his Or. 5, 4, 1 goes back to Ulpian, whose Institutes he seems to have used preeminently. The assumption of a law common to men and the animal world is — on this everything depends — not a philosophical abstraction of a later time, but a remnant of a primal thought of mankind, which has its ground in the factual greater unity of all parts of creation such as dwelt in the primeval ages. Pythagoras and Empedocles, who in everything present themselves so preeminently as the bearers of the earliest ideas of nature, show themselves also, in their connection of the whole animal world, preeminently as the representatives of a general jus naturale, which in the belief in the constant wandering of the world soul through all parts of creation had nothing at all striking about it. Even inanimate creation was made the object of legal procedure, as when the bronze bull at Elis and other objects through which a man had come to harm were made to atone. That idea of unity never perished in Italy, and authors such as Virgil (Georg 4, 227), Ovid. Met. 15, the latter with specific reference to Pythagoras, Seneca Ep. 108, Cicero R. P. 3, 11, Jamblich. vita Pythag. 168. 169, Plinius 8, 42, Cicero Off. 1, 4, 17. 54, demonstrate it in many ways. On all this Voigt’s work das jus naturale der Römer, distinguished by its many-sided learning, affords much instruction, especially in the first volume, pp. 84 f., 286 f., although here too everything seems to me conceived too much in the light of mere philosophical thought and the connection with the oldest views of religion too much neglected.
