Die assyrische Zugehörigkeit Jliums und der assyrische Stamm seines Königshause8 wird von Plato in den Gesetzen 3, p. 685 und Diodor 2, 22 zu bestimmt behauptet , als daß darauf keine Rücksicht genommen werden dürfte. Plato sagt ausdrüclich, die Bewohner von Jlium hätten sich auf die Macht der Assyrer, die Ninus erworben, verlassen, und durch ihre Frechheit den Krieg gegen Troia hervorgerufen. „Denn damals machte der Ueberrest des assyrischen Reichs noch eine ziemliche Figur, und die damaligen Griechen fürchteten jene vereinigte Kriegsmacht so sehr, als wir heut zu Tage den großen König (der Perser) fürchten. Denn die Eroberung Troia's zum zweiten Mal war ein wichtiger Grund zur Klage hegen sie geworden, da diese Stadt ein Theil des assyrishen Reichs war.“ Diodor nennt Priamus einen Vasallen des Königs von Assyrien, und stellt Memnon als den Anführer der assyrischen Hilfsvölker dar. Nach Servius Aen. 6, 650; 9, 643 (gente aub Assaraci) Georg 3, 35 ist Assaracus des Priamus Ahn, - As8araci gens daher die gens Romulea. Diese Zeugnisse, welche man lange mit der größten Verachtung behandelte, hat in der neuern Zeit Walz, in seiner Schrift de Nemeai Grecorum zuerst wieder zu Ehren gezogen. Die Erstrefung des assyrischen Reichs über Vorderasien, namentlich auch über Troia, wird von Ktesias bei Diodor 2, 2 bestimmt bezeugt, und muß als historische Thatsache angenommen werden.
e: Quasque creavit, init pecudes caper: ipsaque cuius Semine concepta est, ex illo concipit ales. Felices, quibus ista licent! humana malignas Cura dedit leges: et quod Natura remittit Invida jura negant. Gentes tamen esse feruntur, In quibus et nato genitrix, et nata parenti Jungitur, et pietas geminato crescit amore. The prohibition of marriage between certain degrees of kinship is a positive enactment, unknown to the law of purely material life. From the dominion of the jus naturale a definite and very important domain of human life has been withdrawn by the jus civile. The latter thus appears as a limitation of the former. From the outset it stands hostile to it, and opens a struggle against it, which with the development of human society and with the unfolding of a higher spiritual life must assume ever greater proportions. We wish to follow this struggle in some principal applications. In the domain of sexual life it takes on a particularly instructive form. To purely material being the exclusiveness of marriage is unknown. Foreign to the animal world, it is wholly opposed to the material creation of lower degrees. In eternal self-embrace the earth brings forth those growths which, without any human aid, ultro et iniussa, come to light from the maternal womb of matter. When Isis and Osiris already mingle in Rhea’s dark womb, this is the expression of that swamp generation which lets ever new reeds arise from the hidden muddy ground and replaces the dying canes by young ones shooting up. That is the Aphroditean natural law according to which some mother goddesses are worshiped ἐν ἕλει, after which Helen herself is named, and on which the epithet ἐν καλάμοις, as well as the sanctity of the swamp plants, rests. To transfer this law to men is the constant striving of Aphrodite and of other primal mothers conceived in Aphroditean terms. She stands hostile to conjugal union. The exclusiveness of matrimonium is hateful to Aphrodite, an object of her enmity and of her displeasure. When Helen, listening to the whisperings of Peitho, follows the seducer Paris and so breaks the law of marriage, she has yielded less to the inclination of her own heart than to the command of the Aphroditean-material impulse, and when Assyrian Troy undertakes her defense, it takes the field for Aphrodite herself and for a religious system resting on Aphroditean materiality.1) It was not for this that Helen was adorned by the primal mother 841. Constat bello Punico secundo exoratam Junonem: tertio vero bello [PDF 201] — 187 — with all the charms that she herself possesses, in order that she should now fall to one man as his exclusive possession and wither away in one man’s embrace. She is to go after ever new men, like Penia, and, like that Arabian king’s daughter whose myth Strabo 16, 783 relates, to fulfill the destiny of matter to the point of weariness, and not to let the frailty of those she has begotten keep her from receiving ever new fecundation. Only so does she fulfill Aphrodite’s law, fulfill the law of matter. Even choice is denied her. As Psyche does not know the form of her mate, as Lamia, the great hetaera, hides her eyes in a bag,1) so too mortal woman is to be at the will of τῷ ἐντυχόντι, and, like the Cretan Gorgo, to feed on a man’s love, not on his destruction.2) This religious idea found its expression especially in the atoning sacrifice of the bride. Aphrodite is injured by the entering into marriage; she must be atoned and so made favorable to marriage through a period of hetaerism to which the girl surrenders herself. Herodotus’s description of the Babylonian custom shows wholly this character, and brings out in particular also the obligation to follow anyone, without will and without choice. This view reaches as far as Italy, as Justin’s account of the vow of the Locrian women and of the reconciliation of Aphrodite thereby intended proves. We find it again in Etruria and on the Balearic Islands. It also underlies the Cyprian institutions, stands in connection with the primal history of Carthage, emerges at the innermost bay of the Adriatic in Cinyras’s a Scipione sacris quibusdam etiam Romam esse translatam. So long did Aphroditean Rome remain conscious of its opposition to Juno. The Assyrian affiliation of Ilium and the Assyrian stock of its royal house are asserted too definitely by Plato in the Laws 3, p. 685 and Diodor 2, 22 for it to be left out of account. Plato says expressly that the inhabitants of Ilium had relied on the power of the Assyrians, which Ninus had acquired, and by their audacity had provoked the war against Troy. “For at that time the remnant of the Assyrian empire still cut a considerable figure, and the Greeks of that time feared that united military power as much as we nowadays fear the great king (of the Persians). For the second conquest of Troy had become an important ground for complaint against them, since this city was a part of the Assyrian empire.” Diodorus calls Priam a vassal of the king of Assyria, and represents Memnon as the leader of the Assyrian auxiliary peoples. According to Servius Aen. 6, 650; 9, 643 (gente sub Assaraci) Georg 3, 35, Assaracus is the ancestor of Priam, Assaraci gens therefore the gens Romulea. These testimonies, which for a long time were treated with the greatest contempt, have in recent times been first restored to honor by Walz in his work de Nemesi Græcorum. The extension of the Assyrian empire over Western Asia, and in particular also over Troy, is definitely attested by Ctesias in Diodor 2, 2, and must be accepted as a historical fact. e: myth, and at Corinth and in other seats of the cult of Aphrodite assumes the form of the dedication of hetaeric hierodules.1) Nonnus remains wholly faithful to this conception when in 41, 335 he has Aphrodite censure Augustus’s penalties for celibacy in the following words: τὸ δὲ πλέον ἔννομος Ἑρμῆς τοῦτο γέρας μοι ἔδωκε, βιαζομένους ἵνα μούνη ἀνέρας, οὓς ἔσπειρα, γάμου δεσμοῖσι σαώσω. These verses form the conclusion of that address in which the anxious Cypris inquires of the heavenly Harmonia about the city of laws, whether it be Paphos or Cypros, or Corinth or Sparta, or rather Berytus, to which the promise applies. She appears here, then, in her relation to law, and precisely in this she takes the field as the defender of the jus naturale of the material world against the determinations of positive legislation. She is the deliverer of men from the bonds with which the jus civile surrounds them. Averse to every compulsion and every exclusive possession,2) she follows only the impulse to union and material love, which abolishes all separation and separate existence, and in its place promotes association and community of life, of bodies, and of goods. From men she demands imitation of her own fundamental law. Woman is to give herself to hetaerism; compulsion to marriage is hateful to her. Those initiated into her mysteries receive the fecundating phallus in return for the meretricium æs that they lay in her lap.3) The ancients called the image of Helen, which was shown to anyone for gold, as we should say for an entrance fee, the meretrix.4) This is the origin of woman’s property, the dos quæ corpore quæritur. It is Aphrodite’s gift, and, like the children, the yield of one’s own sporium. — The contrast of natural-material law and positive law continues in the condition of persons. To the maternal natural principle all inequality, all dependence of one on another, all unfreedom is hateful. What is born from the womb of Mother Earth stands to the great material primal mother in the same relation of childhood. In his Politeia 3, p. 414, Plato exhorts the citizens of his state to that mutual love which we can understand by this the δεσμοὶ γάμου, unless we prefer to recognize in those words the goddess’s aversion to compulsion and fettering as a restriction of natural freedom.

This itself, however, he traces back to the common origin of all from one maternal womb, from the earth, that is, which for this very reason the Cretans designate not as fatherland but call “dear motherland.” According to their material nature, therefore from the maternal side, all men are equal, all free. For this reason manumission takes place in the temple of the great nature mother Feronia. Servius Aen. 7, 799; 8, 564 gives information about this. On Virgil’s words: quis Jupiter Anxurus arvis Præsidet, et viridi gaudens Feronia luco he remarks: Circa hunc tractum Campaniæ colebatur puer Jupiter, qui Anxurus dicebatur, quasi ἄνευ ξυροῦ, id est, sine novacula, quia barbam numquam rasisset: et Juno virgo, quæ Feronia dicebatur. Quam Varro libertorum Deam dicit Feroniam, quasi Fidoniam.1) From the combination of these two testimonies Feronia’s nature results with full certainty. She is the great material nature mother who sends all life into the light from her womb, hence mater and virgo at once, returning every year from perfected maternity to perfected virginity, and for that very reason called Feronia. For Feronia derives, as Perpherees and Medea’s son Pheres derive from fero, to bear, as the ancients (though incorrectly) derive Ceres from gerendis frugibus. It is the concept of physical bearing that is present in ferre and Feronia, as in the Hyperborean Perpherees. The mother bears the birth in her womb, afterward seed and fruit on her body. In a similar way the perfect and participial forms tuli, latum combine the concept of bearing and of material fertility. For tuli attaches itself to that stem τύλος whose meaning we have already brought out above. Latum, however, goes back to lar, las, the designation of the force of natural generation, which, originally resting wholly in matter and conceived preeminently as double, as Lares grundules, underlies so many names such as Larisus and lacus Larius, Larisa, Pe-lasgi, Lastini and Latini, lacus, λάκκος, ferrent. — Feronia at Praeneste birth-mother: Aen. 8, 564.

He is the fecundating Plutus who awakens all life in the lap of the earth, the phallic Jupiter Arcanus, who invisibly performs his work in the depths of matter, at Anxur still conceived preeminently as fecundating force of water, and therefore ruling in the swamp lake named after him. With the tellurian maternal nature the sedile lapideum agrees. To the female natural principle, the ἔδος ἀσφαλὲς ἀεί, the repose of the seated posture corresponds. Hence it is said: Opi sedentes vota concipiunt terramque de industria tangunt in Macrob. Sat. 1, 12. Seated we find, on so many preserved monuments, the mothers of the tomb, in whom the female natural principle has come to expression in its whole significance, embracing life and death. Hence also the stone seat is preserved in tombs, as in the well-known one at Tarquinii, and connected with the Lydian tomb of Geryon seen by Pausanias.1) Hence, finally, woman is called domiseda on inscriptions, and by Luther is even said to be prefigured by nature for a quiet domestic abode. If in all these features Feronia’s material primal-maternal nature cannot be mistaken, it is now of the highest importance for our question that this same mater assumes the significance of a deity upholding freedom and equality among men. In this relation she is called Dea libertorum by Varro, and is brought, correctly in substance, though falsely in etymology, into connection with Fidonia, Fides. In this significance her sedile, which from the outset has a much more general meaning, becomes the thronos libertatis, the asylum that grants freedom. The idea is clear. Whoever seats himself on the goddess’s chair returns to that natural freedom which is inherent in Feronia’s material maternal nature, and which forms an essential part of the jus naturale, of the law governing purely material life. This fundamental idea received its most striking expression in the shearing of the head and in the use of the pileus. The shorn hair is offered to the great mother, who lets it sprout from man’s head as the growths of the earth from her own womb. As the earth-matter in constant self-embrace brings forth the plants, so the same union of both natural potencies brings forth on the human head the hair, on the body of the sheep the wool — hence lana is named from las, ἐρίνεον from ἔρα, terra. It is dedicated preeminently to the generative force of water, the rivers, but is also offered at the tomb to the life-giving chthonian gods [PDF 205] — 191 — as a welcome gift. To the Aphroditean principle of nature, as it prevails in wild, extramarital swamp mating, it stands, moreover, in a special relation. For without human contrivance, sine semine, sine aratro, it comes forth ultro et injussus from the moist depths, and in perpetual renewal hair and reeds are rejuvenated without cease. That is why the Nile rushes are called the hair of Isis, Sari,1) and that is why the nymphs, to whom Feronia also belongs, wear the crown of reeds. In the long, reedlike hair that grows out of Homer’s thighs his illegitimate, purely maternal birth shows itself,2) and in the Laws of Manu, surely in continuation of the same idea, a warning is given against marrying into a family with a heavily haired body, which betrays the rule of unregulated sensuality.3) To all this the offering of the hair to the swamp mother Feronia is joined, and here again we see the connection of physical maternal nature with the idea of universal freedom. The hair offering, which has its ground in that, becomes a solemnity of manumission. The cap, finally, has proceeded from the egg; putting it on is the image of man’s return into the primal egg, and under the dominion of that natural law of freedom and equality which forms the material basic right of the whole creation that has come forth from the egg. From this halving the two caps have arisen which the twins, who set all material creation in motion, wear, and which are sometimes also represented by themselves, joined with the cross, the symbol of tellurian fecundation.1) Thereby the cap becomes the sign of birth from the egg, and thus of the freedom necessarily bound up with it: a significance that it shows also on the head of Olyseus-Nanos, and again in the Bacchic mysteries. The shaven head covered with the egg cap2) shows us man, as it were, reposing in the maternal womb of matter and, like a birth, emerging from it, and therefore also partaking of the freedom that on the side of maternal materiality falls to every creature. Whoever abolishes this breaks the law of Feronia as of Isis, and diminishes the domain of the jus naturale by establishing a positive law hostile to it. From Feronia the slave receives back what human ordinance, those invida jura, had taken from him, the primordial state of material life.3) The same goddess now protects also what she has bestowed. The freedom of the libertus has no protection of the state, any more than a political character, as the older Roman law, too, which as yet grants the freedman no share in citizenship, clearly demonstrates: its protection is a purely religious one, regard for the right of Feronia. In this protective significance she becomes Fidonia, the mother becomes Fides, who keeps faith with her child and, as avenger of all wrong, transfers the respect of men beyond the limits of positive law to that which finds its security only in dread of divine vengeance.4) Thus the maternal principle of nature shapes itself not only into justitia but also into fides, for which, according to Plutarch, Numa erected the first temple, and the material jus naturale into the æquum, and into that fides, corresponds entirely to the description that Lucian gives in the Dialogues of the Gods 26: Everything is the same with the one as with the other, the half egg with the star on the head, the javelin in the hand, the white horse that each has. If by chance they meet one who is being led to death, the life of the condemned man is granted him. But the virgin must swear that she met him by chance and not by design. It is further permitted them to make a will even during their father’s lifetime, and to administer their property without a guardian. So Plutarch in Numa 10. Gellius N. A. 1, 12 adds, probably after Ateius Capito: virgo autem vestalis simul est capta atque in atrium Vestæ deducta et pontificibus tradita, eo statim tempore sine emancipatione ac sine capitis minutione e patris potestate exit, ac jus testamenti faciendi adipiscitur. The dissolution of paternal power is confirmed by Ulpian 16, 5, Gaius 1, 130. 145. Ambros. de virgin. 1, 4, 15; Epist. ad Valentinian. 1, 18, 11. (p. 836. ed. Benedict.) On the similar right of the Flamen Dialis, Tacit. Ann. 4, 16. These privileges are not arbitrary provisions in honorem sacerdotii, but emanations of the divine nature of Vesta. With entry into the atrium Vestæ all restrictions to which positive law subjects women are dissolved of themselves. It is now just as if the girl had never stood in any dependence. The patria potestas dissolves without the mediation of a capitis minutio. The Vestal is as such libera.2) Præterea in commentariis Labeonis, quæ ad XII tabulas composuit, ita scriptum est: virgo vestalis neque heres est cuiquam intestato, neque intestatæ quisquam: sed bona eius in publicum redigi aiunt; id quo jure fiat, quæritur.3) The reason for this provision is clear. Since intestate succession rests on the civil institution of potestas and suitas, it must at the same time fall away entirely with it; if, therefore, the Vestal has made no use of her right to make a will, her property falls to the people, who derive from the primal mother Vesta all their prosperity. To the religious name Amata,4) which belongs to every Vestal in her priestly capacity double name Philotis, Tutela, borne by the leader of the procession. larum cautum est.

e: the Roman tradition attaches a definite expression of mother right, which likewise belongs to the jus naturale. Amata claims against her husband Latinus the right to dispose of Lavinia’s hand. She destines her for her sister’s son Turnus.1) According to mother right it is, after all, the children of the sister for whom the woman implores blessing.2) If this happens in the temple of Leucothea-Matuta, then Venilia, too, is conceived as Salacia, Neptune’s consort.3) There lies, then, in Amata the concept of motherhood in its original loftiness, as bearer at once of the greatest right and of the highest benevolence, and precisely this content is continued in the transference of the word to the Vestal, who in it appears herself as the mortal image of the immortal primal mother Vesta.4) The material-female foundation of the religion of Dionysus develops in the same way into the significance of freedom and equality on earth. Indeed, here the concepts of material life and of freedom coincide so exactly that one word designates both. The different meanings of liber are in fact only a single one. Belonging to a root that in a great number of formations always retains the basic meaning of water, and specifically of the moving, flowing stream that resounds clearly in its course, Liber designates the content of the materially generative force of water, hence the bast of trees, which owes its origin to that force, likewise the children who, sprung from natural force, also continue it,5) and finally the condition of freedom, as it necessarily belongs to material force and to all its births. The root Li appears with various following consonants. Beside g there appears also b, and this again strengthened to p, or resolved into qu. Achilles, the water man, bears as a boy the name Λιγύρων.6) If as Achilles he is the broad, mighty stream calmly rolling on its waves, then as Λιγύρων he is the rippling spring, the clear-sounding little brook, which garrulous and restless out of the Delphic temple service, to refer to Curtius, Anecdota Delphica p. 10, and to pass over entirely the consideration of the asyla, which rest on a similar conception. Latin arbor the tree. Child and tree are products of the male force. The word itself belongs to the stem Ar, (ἄρρην, mas, mars) like arundo, arista, ἀρετή and many others. μαστοῖς οὐ προσήνεγκε.

e: the earth breaks forth. In the river name Liger, and, as I do not doubt, in the name of the people of the Ligurians, the same stem is present, with the same consonant form. Lichas is the name of that rock projecting in the sea;1) Lipara has received from its sea-surrounded position its name, palpably related to liquor, liquesco, and likewise Lilybaeum, Limera, Lixus,2) and others. Of the many relations that offer themselves here in abundance, I wish to point only to the name of the country Libya, which stands in connection with the Ammonian spring god, to λίβερνα, εἶδος πλοίου, to Λίβερνος, the name of the chasm of the earth into which Curtius plunged, to λείβηθρον ὀχετὸς ὑδραγωγικός, to the expression λείβεται and καταλείβεται τοῖς δακρύοις, to the Thracian Λείβηθρα of Orpheus and the Λειβηθρίδες, as nymphs and Muses are called,3) and finally to lichor, and to recall Plato’s connection of the Μοῦσαι λίγειαι with the γένος μουσικὸν τὸ Λιγύων.4) I am convinced that lignum, λίμνη, limus go back to the same stem. This is especially the case with Λικνίτης, a designation of Dionysus himself. The ancients explain the name from the fact that the god at his birth is said to have been laid in the λίκνον, a basket plaited of willows, which served the child as a cradle. Servius, in his scholion on Georg. 1, 166: Arbuteæ crates, et mystica vannus Jacchi, calls the basket a cribrum, and traces that tradition back to the cribrum of the mother Isis, in which she laid down the torn limbs of her consort. From this the original cultic significance of the λίκνον results with certainty. It is, like Vesta’s sieve, like the cask of the Danaids, the earth itself, which takes into itself the generating moisture, and precisely for that reason is conceived as a perforated vessel, now as dolium, now as cribrum, now as vannus. Thus from the perforated willow basket there comes to be the cradle of the god, then the mystic receptacle that holds the mystery of natural generation, on monuments mostly in the form of a serpent, and finally the fruit receptacle, or the winnowing shovel of the farmer that separates grain and chaff.5) In all these turns the λίκνον has an unmistakable relation to the phallic, fruit-generating nature of Dionysus. In its original significance, however, it shows us the god as the fecundating force of water, which γένος μουσικὸν τὸ Λιγύων ταύτην ἔσχετε ἐπωνυμίαν, etc. alius ferebat amphoram (in pompa Isidis). Hesych. λικνίτης. Staveren on Hygin. p. 21.

Als vorzugsweise stofflicher Gott wird er nun auch zum Träger jener Freiheit, die das Leben der rein stofflichen Schöpfung auszeichnet, und nur der positiv menschlichen Gesebgebung, den Cinrichtungen des Staatslebens weicht. e: on the bank of the brook begets and nourishes the willow, and precisely for this reason it cannot be doubted that Λικνίτης and λίκνον rest on the same stem to which lignum also belongs, and which in its basic physical meaning designates the generating moisture. In the designation of Bacchus as Liber pater his generative force resting in the water is thus first of all expressed. Masculinity, however, enters into the relation of son to femininity, as the male Eros, as Enorches comes forth from the egg, as Dionysus himself is conceived as the son of Beroë or of Ino, and as διμήτωρ.1) That is why he is now also called simply the son. This is the meaning of Liber formed in the singular. In Hyginus f. 9 we read: Niobe procreavit liberos septem, totidemque filias. According to the original meaning only the sons, not also the daughters, are liberi, because only they bear the generative force of water within them. Hence Liber the son, as in Quintilian Declam. 11: Liberi ac parentis non alius mihi videtur affectus. If to Liber the designation pater is added, as to Adonis the equivalent Papas, the reason for this lies in the fact that in the son male generation as such is represented, so that the son in fact stands there as the father of all visible creation. As the preeminently material god he now becomes also the bearer of that freedom which distinguishes the life of purely material creation, and yields only to positive human legislation, to the institutions of the life of the state. Hence the word Liber receives the meaning free. Hence Marsyas’s image appears as the sign of the liberæ civitates.2) Hence he is worshiped in Boeotia under the name Eleutherios.3) That is why the cult of Dionysus has also exercised so unmistakable an influence on the democratic development of the ancient world, which raised the lower and neglected est: ut signum sit liberæ civitatis: nam apud majores aut stipendiariæ erant, aut fœderatæ aut liberæ. Sed in liberis civitatibus simulacrum Marsyæ erat, qui in tutela Liberi Patris est. Aen. 4, 58: Patrique Lyæo. Qui, ut supra diximus, apte urbibus libertatis est deus; unde etiam Marsyas, minister eius, civitatibus in foro positus, libertatis indicium est: qui erecta manu testatur nil urbi deesse. A relation of Dionysus to the freedom of the plebeian classes is given by Pausan. 5, 15, 3. With this compare Ἥλιος ἐλευθέριος and Dionysus Σαώτης in Pausan. 2, 31, 8, and the provision of Roman sacral law in Gellius 10, 15. Hyg. fab. 225. Virgil. Ecl. 6, 72: vincula detrahi solita for him who enters the grove of Apollo Grynaeus, as the sanctuary of the Palici, according to Macrob., gave slaves their freedom. the ὕδωρ ἐλευθέριον, Pausan. 2, 17, 1; at Athens Ἐλευθερεύς, Pausan. 1, 29, 2.

o: Stände so sehr gehoben, den Frauen namentlich eine Bedeutung gegeben, die mit den civilen Justitutionen so sehr im Widerspruch stand, und sich mit der auf Freiheit und Gleichheit der ganzen Volksmasse begründeten Tyrannis' eines Pisistratus ') und Cäsar 2) so enge verbunden. Das staatlich-politishe Leben bringt Unterschiede der Stellung, Beschränkung und gänzliche Aufhebung der Freiheit. Diesem gegenüber enthält die Dionysishe Religion eine Zurückführung des Daseins auf das Gebiet « r reinen Stofflichkeit und der bloß leiblichen Existenz, die für alle Glieder der großen menschlichen Gesellschaft dieselbe, ihrer Natur nacH frei und gleich ist. Wenn der staatliche, civile Gesihtspunkt überall Schranken errichtet, die Völker und Individuen trennt, und das Prinzip der Judividualität bis zum vollendetsten Cgoismus ausbildet, so führt dagegen Dionysos alles zur Vereinigung, alles zum Frieden und zur p-zia des ursprünglichen Lebens zurüf. An seinen Mysterien haben Sklaven wie Freie gleichen Antheil, und vor dem Gotte der stofflichen Lust fallen alle jene Schranken, welche das staatliche Leben mit der Zeit zu immer größerer Höhe erhebt. Das Bewußtsein der einheitlihen Abstammung aus einem Stoffe erhäli den Sieg über die positiven Verschiedenheiten und zugleich gedeiht die materielle Entwicklung und die darauf ruhende Liebe zu Genuß und Pracht, wie sie die Dionysishe Religion so bejonders begünstigte, zur höchsten Ausbildung. In allen diesen Richtungen erwahrt Dionysos seine Bedeutung als Lywus. Wie er als zeugender Libor das im Stoffe schlafende Leben weckt und aus den Banden -/ die es gefangen halten, wie das Küchlein aus dem Ei, löst, so hebt er auch alle Unterschiede auf, macht der Feindschaft selbst unter den Thieren ein Ende, und führt in die Schöpfung wieder jenen Frieden, jene Freude, jene allgemeine Gleichheit zurück, die den Alten als das ursprüngliche goldene Zeitalter erschien, und in den Festgebräuchen der Saturnalien, der Dionysischen X65,* und so mancher Safkäischer Feste als Erinnerung vorstaatlicher, rein stofflicher Existenz ihren Ausdruck, ihre zeitweilige Rückkehr fand. Jn dem Weine und seinem Einflusse auf den Menschen schien sich gerade diese Seite der Dionysos-Natur am klarsten zu offenbaren. Wenn er freundschaftliche Vereinigung fördert, geschlechtliches Leben wett, Feindschaften ein Ende macht, Unterschiede aufhebt, und Sorgen bricht, so mochte “man in all dem den AnsdruF der Dionysosökraft wieder erkennen, und die Namen Liber und Lyzeus auch hierauf beziehen und aus des Weines Wirkungen erenen we !) Herod. 1, 64. Welker, Sat. 268 f.
e: classes so greatly, gave to women in particular a significance that stood in such contradiction to the civil institutions, and allied itself so closely with the tyranny of a Pisistratus1) and a Caesar,2) grounded on the freedom and equality of the whole mass of the people. The life of the state and of politics brings distinctions of station, restriction, and complete abolition of freedom. Over against this the Dionysian religion contains a reduction of existence to the domain of pure materiality and of merely bodily existence, which is the same for all members of the great human society, free and equal by its nature. When the civil standpoint of the state everywhere erects barriers, separates peoples and individuals, and develops the principle of individuality to the most consummate egoism, Dionysus on the contrary leads everything back to union, everything to peace and to the φιλία of primordial life. In his mysteries slaves and free persons have an equal share, and before the god of material pleasure all those barriers fall which the life of the state with time raises to ever greater height. The consciousness of unitary descent from one matter wins the victory over positive differences, and at the same time the material development, and the love of enjoyment and splendor that rests on it, which the Dionysian religion favored so especially, prospers to the highest cultivation. In all these tendencies Dionysus confirms his significance as Lyæus. As, in the role of generative Liber, he awakens the life sleeping in matter and frees it from the bonds that hold it captive, like the chick from the egg, so he also abolishes all differences, puts an end to enmity even among the animals, and leads back into creation that peace, that joy, that universal equality which appeared to the ancients as the original golden age, and which found its expression, its temporary return, in the festal practices of the Saturnalia, of the Dionysian Χόες, and of so many Sacaean festivals, as a recollection of prepolitical, purely material existence. In wine and its influence on man this very side of the Dionysian nature seemed to reveal itself most clearly. When it promotes friendly union, awakens sexual life, puts an end to enmities, abolishes distinctions, and breaks cares, one might recognize in all this the expression of the force of Dionysus, refer the names Liber and Lyæus to this as well, and explain them from the effects of wine. Cæsarem pertinet; quem constat primum sacra Liberi patris transtulisse Romam.

Ging man aber weiter, verließ man das Gebiet des stofflihen Lebens, um den freiheitbringenden Gott als einen Erlöser aus der Knechtschaft der Leidenschaft und ds Fleisches zu feiern, so erstieg man eine Höhe der Vergeistigung und Jdealisirung, ähnlich derjenigen, auf welcher die mystica vannus Jacchi als Bild der purgatio animp durch die Mysterien, das Ei als eine Zusicherung höherer geistiger Wiedergeburt , die bachisch-orphische Lehre überhaupt als ein melioris Spei initium aufgefaßt wurde. Man hatte aber damit die äußersten Grenzen der Dionysos-Religion überschritten, und mitten in dem moralischen Verkalle, zu welchem jene nothwendig führen mußte, auf Jenen hingewiesen, der beiusen war, durch des Geistes Wort die Herrschaft des Stoffes zu brechen, und die Freiheit des stofflichen Lebens zu einer höhern göttlichen zu verklären.
e: But if one went further, left the domain of material life in order to celebrate the god who brings freedom as a redeemer from the bondage of passion and of the flesh, one climbed to a height of spiritualization and idealization similar to that on which the mystica vannus Jacchi was conceived as the image of the purgatio animæ through the mysteries, the egg as an assurance of a higher spiritual rebirth, and the Bacchic-Orphic doctrine in general as a melioris spei initium. With that, however, one had overstepped the outermost limits of the religion of Dionysus, and in the midst of the moral decay to which that religion necessarily had to lead, had pointed to Him who was called, by the word of the spirit, to break the dominion of matter and to transfigure the freedom of material life into a higher, divine one. 16.

o: Wir haben bisher gezeigt, in welcher Weise sih das RehHt an das stofflid weibliche Naturprinzip anschließt, und diese Verbindung zunächst für die unterste Stufe des tellurischen Lebens, die rein aphroditische nachgewiesen. Dieselbe erwahrt sich aber auch für die höhere cerealisch-demetrische. Ja auf dieser gewinnt sie eine ungleim höhere Bedeutung. Denn jenes jus naturale, das die Menschen mit der Thierwelt verbindet, ist bestimmt, überwunden zu werden, und einem böhern Rechte zu weichen. Der stofflich-aphroditisce Standpunkt bildet den Ausgang einer Entwicklung, die immer weiter von ihm wegführen, zu immer höherer (Geistigkeit fortschreiten, und den Menschen immer mehr über jene stoffliche Gemeinschaft mit der Thierwelt erheben soll. Das ist das Gesetz aller menschlihen Ausbildung. Es liegt auch der Entwickelung der Religion zu (Prunde, und giebt für diese einen Fortgang, der von unten nach oben, vom Tellurigmus zu der solarisen Lichtwelt des Seins, vom Formlosen zur Form seine Entfaltung nimmt. Ja es ist flar, daß eben diese Entwiklung der Religion auch die des Rechts bedingt und trägt. Denn das religiöse Denken beherrscht nothwendig alle Seiten des menschlihen Lebens, gestaltet Alles nach seinem Jnhalt, und kann nicht nur als der mächtigste, sondern geradezu als der einzige Faktor der Civilisation bezeichnet werden. Welches das Ende dieser Entwilung sein wird, kann Niemand bestimmen. Aber welcher Art ihr Begivn und Ausgangspunkt war, das ist unzweifelhaft. Man hat zwar, und wieder ganz neuerlich, jenes jus naturale, in dessen Natur wir oben einen Einblick eröffneten, als bloße Abstraktion und philosophische Theorie behandelt, ihm alle geschichtliche Wahrheit abgespiochen, und so der Ehre der Menschheit zu Hilfe zu kommen gesucht. Aber daß dasjenige, was man als bloße Abstraktion de [PDF 215]  handelt, wirkliche Zustände und Erlebnisse des Menshengeschleht8 waren, darüber läßt die bestimmte und stets völlig übereinstimmende Tradition der Völker nicht den mindesten Zweifel. Regellose Geschlehtsverbindung, Abwesenheit jedes Eigenthums, überhaupt jedes Sonderrechts irgend welcher Art, Gemeinschaft der Weiber , der Kinder, und als nothwendige Folge davon auch aller Güter, daneben vollkommene, gestalt - und gliederungslose Freiheit aller Geschöpfe, und als einziges Bindeglied unter denselben die aphroditische Lust, Alles das ist so sicher ') als der vorstaatliche Zustand, und jenes Wanderleben, das erst mit dem Tode schließt, und außer dem Grabe keinen festen Punkt, keine heimathliche Stätte kennt. 2) Ja zu der ersten Verbreitung und dem schnellen Wachsthum unseres Geschlehts waren Zustände dieser Art, so tief und so erniedrigend sie jebt auch erscheinen mögen, ohne Zweifel unerläßlich. Eine höhere Gestaltung erhielten Religion und Recht durc den Uebergang zum Acerbau. Das rein aphroditische Prinzip weicht dem cerealishen. e: We have shown so far in what manner law attaches itself to the female-material principle of nature, and have demonstrated this connection first of all for the lowest stage of tellurian life, the purely Aphroditean. The same is confirmed, however, for the higher Cerealian-Demetrian stage as well. Indeed, on this stage it acquires an incomparably higher significance. For that jus naturale which connects men with the animal world is destined to be overcome and to yield to a higher law. The material-Aphroditean standpoint forms the point of departure of a development that is to lead ever farther away from it, to advance toward an ever higher spirituality, and to raise man ever more above that material community with the animal world. That is the law of all human development. It underlies also the development of religion, and gives it a progress that unfolds from below upward, from tellurism to the solar world of light of being, from the formless to form. Indeed, it is clear that this very development of religion also conditions and bears that of law. For religious thought necessarily governs all sides of human life, shapes everything according to its content, and can be designated not only as the most powerful but outright as the sole factor of civilization. What the end of this development will be, no one can determine. But of what kind its beginning and point of departure were is beyond doubt. Men have, to be sure, and quite recently again, treated that jus naturale, into whose nature we opened an insight above, as a mere abstraction and philosophical theory, denied it all historical truth, and so sought to come to the aid of the honor of humanity. But that the things which are treated as a mere abstraction [PDF 215] — 201 — were real conditions and experiences of the human race, the definite and constantly wholly concordant tradition of the peoples leaves not the slightest doubt. Unregulated sexual union, absence of all property, of every special right of any kind whatever, community of women, of children, and as a necessary consequence of this also of all goods, together with this a perfect freedom of all creatures without form or articulation, and as the sole bond among them Aphroditean pleasure, all this is as certain1) as the prepolitical condition, and that wandering life which ends only with death, and apart from the grave knows no fixed point, no native place.2) Indeed, for the first spread and the rapid growth of our race, conditions of this kind, however deep and however degrading they may now appear, were without doubt indispensable. Religion and law received a higher form through the transition to agriculture. The purely Aphroditean principle yields to the Cerealian. With this there enters, in place of community, the exclusive right of an individual, in place of hetaerism marriage, in place of swamp generation and Aphroditean self-sufficient vegetation the laborata Ceres. Carpus and Calamus enter into combat with each other. Nonnus gives the myth surely in the form in which ancient tradition handed it down.3) Drawn by the magic of the golden fruits, Atalanta turns aside from her course, and sacrifices victory and freedom to the enticing possession. The Schœneia virgo, daughter of the rush man, renounces her proud unboundedness and yields to her new lot.4) Among men a culture develops toward which the gods of the pure life of nature behave in a hostile manner. Silvanus threatens destruction to the woman in childbed. Broom, pestle, and ax, tria signa culturæ, protect her against the adversary of all higher human existence.5) The daughters of Pandareus are snatched away by the Harpies would they stand to battle; cities and fixed dwellings they otherwise had none. The tombs are in this nomadic life the only fixed thing. Before death, eternal wandering. So it was written on Trivulzio’s tomb: qui numquam quievit quiescit. Of the Memphites Diodor 1, 51 says that they bestowed little care on their houses, very great on the tombs. The former they called καταλύσεις, which served only a short time, the latter ἀιδίους οἴκους, in which the dead dwells for endless time. The same idea dominates the whole ancient world, which sought to lend the tombs imperishability.

e: “When the merry reapers cut asunder the limbs of Ceres.” The earth has now become wife and mother, and man, who guides the plow and strews the seed, husband and father. The relation of marriage binds the man with female matter, and there is given also for the pairing of the sexes with one another the model of an intimate, lasting, and exclusive community. The earth and mortal woman stand on one line, and γάμος is derived from γᾶ just as γύια, the plowshare, and γυνή, Gaia herself. The male plowshare opens the womb of the earth as of woman; this double deed is at bottom only one, and, toward the earth as toward woman, no longer a passing hetaeric sexual mingling but conjugal union. Not on the satisfaction of sensual pleasure, but on the production of golden fruits is the man’s deed directed. Liberorum quærendorum causa, not ἡδονῆς ἕνεκα, do the sexes unite. Only in this elevation does woman find her repose. In lasting union with Eros, Psyche attains that happiness which she sought in vain to hold fast in unregulated hetaeric mating and in low swamp coupling. We see femininity raised from pure tellurism to the lunar stage of existence, and given over to the man for [PDF 217] — 203 — lasting exclusive possession, like Luna to Sol-Lunus. The children now have, besides the mother, also a father; they are genuine children, like the descendants of the Idaean Dactyls, the Eteo-Cretans. They are διφυεῖς, as the Athenians have been since Cecrops. To this stage of life a new law corresponds. The Aphroditean jus naturale yields to the Cerealian. But the new legal condition, too, attaches itself wholly to the female principle of nature. It retains, even on the new stage, the materially maternal character. Demeter becomes θεσμοφόρος, Ceres legifera, as the pure jus naturale attaches itself to Aphrodite. Indeed, Demetrian law, too, is a true jus naturale, but one that rests on earth-generation regulated by agriculture and not left to itself, on the laborata Ceres, not on the creatio ultronea of Aphrodite. On this stage the conjugal principle of exclusiveness prevails over hetaeric universality. The earth, and after its image mortal woman, gives herself to the man as exclusive property. She is no longer mother in unrestricted universality; she now has this quality in relation to a determinate man, whose seed she receives, for whom she develops the birth, to whom at last she presents the fruits. She is no longer Penia, who goes after ever new men, delights in every fecundation and without cease partakes of it, no longer that daughter who bends without will before the male scepter. She shuns, rather, everything male, succumbs to violence and to rape, and preserves the mystery character of unprofaned matronhood.1) Precisely thereby she becomes the bearer of a higher law, which extends to all relations of life, and may be designated as conjugal mother right. It has been asserted that the θεσμοί of Demeter refer exclusively to the conjugal union of human beings. There is this much truth in it, that marriage in fact forms the center of all Demetrian law. But marriage itself must not be restricted to human beings. It embraces also the man’s relation to the tellurian sown field. It has the double direction toward agriculture and toward sexual union, comprising in one concept, in one mystery, in one law, property and family. Indeed, the relation to woman is subordinated to that to the field, family law to that of agriculture. In the Menexenus, p. 298, is set forth sam numinum, quod Eleusinia sacra interpretando vulgaverit, somnia prodiderunt, visas sibi ipsas Eleusinias Deas habitu meretricio ante apertum lupanar ludere prostantes admirantique et causas non convenientis numinibus turpitudinis consulenti respondisse iratas, ab ipso se adyto pudicitiæ suæ vi abstractas et passim adeuntibus prostitutas.

e: by Plato the proposition, which Plutarch also repeats: it is not the earth that imitates woman, but woman the earth; woman is in general the mortal image of the earth, destined to continue among men, in her place, the work that the earth performed first. In this fundamental conception is rooted the transference of the whole terminology of agriculture to the sexual relations of men. When the deed of the man is called ἀροῦν, σπείρειν, φυτεύειν, γεωργεῖν, the man himself Σπερμώ, φυτουργός, the woman Δαμοννώ,1) the female sown field in Sabine sporium, the offspring sprung from it Spurius, of the same meaning as Σπαρτός, this is not merely a figurative language resting on external comparison, but the expression of that fundamental idea which traces the conjugal union of the sexes back to agriculture and the fecundation of Demeter as to its archetype.2) A remarkable application of the same principle is related by Macrobius, Sat. 1, 15. Verrium Flaccum juris pontificii peritissimum dicere solitum refert Varro, quia feriis tergere veteres fossas liceret, novas facere jus non esset, ideo magis viduis quam virginibus idoneas esse ferias ad nubendum. Here the decision of a question of marriage law is taken from the provisions of agrarian legislation. Demeter serves earthly woman, agriculture marriage, as the model. Here again nature has taken law into her lap. The comparison of the female sporium with a fossa serving the purposes of agriculture here too has more than the significance of a mere image. Both are rather regarded as inwardly of the same meaning. The cultic significance of the fossa emerges from the deed of the Cumaean Malakos,3) and likewise from the tale of the charlatan Alexander’s Asclepius egg. I do not doubt that the underground labyrinthine passages connected with so many hypogea, that the subterraneum rotundum mentioned by Apuleius, Met. 11, that the dark passages of the Cimmerians at Cumae, that finally Ariadne’s labyrinth itself stand in connection with the same sexual conceptions, and I see also in Venus Cloacina or Cluacina the double relation to woman and to the earth, to every fossa purgatoria.4) On such conceptions ἡ κατὰ νόμον ἐπ᾽ ἀρότῳ παίδων ἐλέγετο γίνεσθαι. In the mysteries, moreover, both relations of Cerealian law were conceived wholly as a unity, marriage itself represented as an agrarian relation. The two Eleusinian deities are at once and without distinction a representation of tellurian and of human marriage. The priestess of Demeter shuts herself up with the newly married in the bridal chamber, and impresses on them the θεσμός of the earth mother as the highest law of marriage.1) Thereby every γάμος itself becomes a Cerealian mystery, each one a τέλος θαλεροῖο γάμοιο. Conjugal fidelity is sworn by the Eleusinian goddesses.2) To Ceres legifera Dido sacrifices at her wedding,3) as girls also implore Demeter for a husband.4) All these phenomena are emanations of the same fundamental idea: woman imitates the earth, the γάμος agriculture. In both lies the same mystery. The Demetrian θεσμοί embrace agrarian law as well as conjugal law, indeed they subordinate the latter to the former. If one wishes to designate them as conjugal ordinances, one must give this expression the widest scope, enclosing the whole of agricultural life. Demeter Θεσμοφόρος shows us, then, law again as an emanation of the female principle of nature. If we saw it above linked with Aphroditean nature mothers, it here confronts us as an attribute and emanation of Cerealian maternity. The fundamental idea remains the same; only the stage of culture is different, there the lower, hetaerically conceived, here the higher, conjugal maternity. The female matter that harbors, tends, and develops the seed, and sends the fruit upward, is also the source of the law that regulates the relations of economic life. Therefore Ceres is called legifera in a quite general sense. All law that the cultural stage of agriculture brings with it proceeds from the Cerealian mother. How deeply rooted this conception was is shown by the fact that the temple of Ceres served as an archive of laws.5) It can therefore by no means Augustine, C. In Servius, Aen. 4, 58, Calvus writes: leges sanctas invenit, et cara jugavit corpora connubiis et magnas condidit urbes. I lay particular weight on the expression sanctæ leges. The connection of the sanctum with tellurism, and the idea of the ἀκίνητον lying in it, have already been set forth above. Through both relations sanctitas enters into a more intimate union with the nature of Demeter and her legislation. The laws themselves partake of the goddess’s inviolable being. They are sanctæ like her. The whole of Cerealian law bears the character of religious ordinances, over whose observance the great primal mother herself keeps watch.2) It is therefore in the proper sense θεσμός, an ordinance of divine law, ἐκ θεῶν δοθείς, as Aeschylus, Eumen. 392, adds in explanation. It is not only jus but fas, a pronouncement (from fari) of the primal mother herself, and hence, like the fatum, like the λόγος—for so Lactantius and Tertullian explain the λόγος at the opening of the Gospel of John—eternally unalterable. This character is borne by all those laws kept in the sanctuary of Ceres. They are held to be unalterable and not to be annulled. From the religious protection follows the inviolability of civil institutions. If for the patrician commonwealth that protection lies in obtaining the divine approval through the auguries, as I have shown in my work on the foundations of Roman constitutional law, then for the plebeian community it rests in its relation to the material primal mother Ceres, who at Athens stands in the closest connection with the popular assemblies, to whom at Rome the plebs preeminently belongs, and whose nature has found its expression both in the principle of the old constitutional law: ut quod primum populus jusserit, id ratum esset, and in the provision: actus legitimi nec diem nec conditionem recipiunt. Under the protection of Ceres the community sits in assembly. To the higher consecration that the patriciate possesses, it opposes the inviolability of the material nourishing mother, to the male principle of the former the female principle of the latter. To her temple it entrusts the community treasury, the laws, and the senatus consulta, which are here safe against falsification.3) With pillar in Diodor 1, 27: καὶ ὅσα ἐγὼ ἐνομοθέτησα, οὐδεὶς αὐτὰ δύναται λῦσαι; likewise Plato’s remark on the unalterable maintenance of the songs of Isis (Laws 2, p. 658).

e: custom and ordinance there is joined the founding of fixed dwelling places. Ceres is the founder of cities. So Calvus calls her. As she is the mother of customs and laws, so she is also the mother of fixed seats, and through the union of all these qualities a true Ἀστυνόμη. In her relation to the founding of cities, too, she shows herself true to that character of the sanctum and ἀκίνητον which forms her innermost nature. The walls founded with the use of Cerealian rites stand under the protection of the goddess, from whose womb they ascend into the light like the plants. On account of this relation the walls in Nonnus 41, 360. 370 become the bearers of the great law of fate that Aphrodite learns from Harmonia. She shows her the ἀγλαὰ θέσφατα τοίχου. On the walls the great fatum of the world is written down. They proclaim the law of matter in which they themselves are grounded. Here the same connection of fixed buildings with law is present which is also found again in Ceres. The custom of writing laws down on walls, which African discoveries confirm to us, has thus its deeper ground in ancient religious ideas. On the temple wall of Apollo Ptous at Lake Copais stood, according to Plutarch in the Gryllus, the words “the beautiful Achilles,” and in Lucian, in the Dialogues of the Courtesans, the shipowner Hermotimus writes his declaration of love to a beautiful courtesan on the wall by the city gate. Here, too, Cerealian ideas come to light. To what protection could such expressions of affection be better entrusted than to that of the goddess quæ cara corpora connubiis jungit, and whose being is formed by immovable firmness and unalterable fidelity? In Apuleius we find the speaking tower, which knows all the secrets of the underworld and betrays them to Psyche. It is the announcer of the great Cerealian secrets, like Harmonia’s wall. In a similar relation to Ceres stands Terminus. Issuing from the earth, as the son from the maternal womb, he reveals the male force, is therefore called male, and on the well-known Etruscan mirror is represented with Juventas in phallic form. But, resting in the mother’s womb, he partakes of her sanctitas, and is therefore called preeminently sanctus.1) The ἀκίνητον is what distinguishes him. Thereby he becomes the guardian of the Cerealian laws and is propitiated with the porca lactens. In him all parts of the Cerealian nature come to representation. He is the revelation of the mystery that the mother bears locked within her. He fecundates the field, separates and protects landed property, and defends the immovability that forms the foundation of Cerealian life even against the gods of a newer, more political order [PDF 222] — 208 — of things. With the funerary stelae he shares the same nature. Immovable like the terminus, the funerary pillar proclaims Demeter’s mystery. It is at the same time a representation of the male force pervading it, a λίθος ἔμψυχος, a guardian of her Cerealian law, often also at the same time the terminus that divides lands, and as πυραμίς is itself called by a Cerealian name.1) — The aediles stand forth as priests of Ceres. Their very diverse attributa can all be explained from this character. They stand to the yield of the earth, to the community of the people, to the market, to the buildings, to the administration of justice, in the same relation as the goddess to whom they belong. Their whole sphere of business is of Cerealian nature. But they have their name from the buildings, which here, as in the mural crown, appear in their whole importance for the agricultural life that leads to fixed settlement.2) Having found, then, in Ceres and Demeter, as in Aphrodite, law as an emanation and attribute of the material maternal principle, and having thus demonstrated, for two different stages of life and of culture, that intimate connection of the materiality that bestows wealth and distributes wealth in the concept of one and the same maternity, it now still deserves emphasis that also in the expression jus Quiritium law again enters preeminently into relation with the materially female side of life. From their maternal Sabine descent the Romans are called Quirites, and all private law is treated as Quiritary law. Ex jure Quiritium hunc agrum meum esse aio, says the claimant; ex jure Romanorum would emphasize the paternal side. Roman is the name of the gens Romulea in its political significance, as a political whole, and therefore in its direction outward. Quirites they are according to their material nature. In the expression Populus Romanus Quirites or Quiritium both sides of life enter into connection. over, like Remus, the wall of the newly founded Poimandria, for so, according to Strabo, the Boeotian Tanagra was called. In anger at this Poimander ran to a large stone, which had been embedded there from ancient times and was destined for nocturnal festivals, and tore it from the earth in ignorance. The violation of the sanctum contained in this avenged itself in that the stone struck, instead of Polycrithus, Poimander’s son Leucippus. The same character is borne by the stone mentioned by Pausan. 1, 23, 6. Beside the statues of Hygieia and Athena Hygieia stood a small stone, on which a young man might find room to sit down. Das Recht gehört dieser letztern Seite des Daseins , es ist der Ausfluß des weiblichen Naturprinzips, uud darum von Juno Quiris quiritish. Cbendarum erstreckt es sih auch auf die Plebeier, das 3705, welchem die Formel ex jure Quiritium so gut zusteht als dem Patri« +t, denn nach der stofflich weiblichen Seite sind die Plebeier von den Quiriten in Nichts unterschieden; sie theilen mit ihnen den mütterlichen Ursprung, der in dem Verhältniß zu Ceres, zu Anna-Perenna, zu der veientischen Juno überwiegend hervortritt; während die Patrizier das männlich solarische Vaterprinzip über jenes erheben, sich allein als solche hinstellen, qui patrem ciere possunt, und das Mondzeichen der stofflich leiblichen Geburt auf ihre Shuhe, das Symbol der Naturzeugung, wie es in dem Schuh der Rhodopis-Nitocris, in dem der delpischen Charila, in jenem der Tanaquil-Fortuna, in Perseus und Jason's crepida sich offenbart, zurückverlegen. e: The same Romans are, in their whole extent, Populus Romanus, and in their whole extent Quirites: the former as state, the latter as people; the former according to the male-political, the latter according to the maternal-material side; the former as bearer of the state’s imperium, the latter in their bodily existence. Law belongs to this latter side of existence; it is the emanation of the female natural principle, and therefore, from Juno Quiris, Quiritary. For this very reason it extends also to the plebeians, the πλῆθος, to whom the formula ex jure Quiritium belongs just as fully as to the patrician; for on the materially female side the plebeians are in no way distinguished from the Quirites; they share with them the maternal origin, which stands out predominantly in the relation to Ceres, to Anna Perenna, to the Veientine Juno; whereas the patricians raise the male-solar paternal principle above it, set themselves up alone as those qui patrem ciere possunt, and relegate the lunar sign of material, bodily birth, the symbol of natural generation, to their shoes, as it reveals itself in the shoe of Rhodopis-Nitocris, in that of the Delphic Charila, in that of Tanaquil-Fortuna, in the crepida of Perseus and of Jason. The whole stock of the Opicans, to which the plebeians preeminently belonged, bears, like the Quirites, a name that has maternal descent for its foundation. They are named after the great mother Ops-Tellus, who is placed alongside Bona Dea. The temple of Ops- Diana is raised by Servius Tullius to be the central point of the Latin confederation.1) For all these peoples have in common the maternal-material origin. From this side they enter into community with Rome, while the political side of the imperium remains closed to them. — A further relation of law to the materially female natural principle emerges in the connection of the praetor with Bona Dea. In the account of the event that took place during the festival of the stag antlers but ox horns, Plutarch Qu. rom. 4 tells what Juba and Varro reported. In this myth too, dominion over Italy is linked to Diana’s motherhood. Liv. 1, 45. . . perpulit tandem, ut Romæ fanum Dianæ populi Latini cum populo Romano facerent. Ea erat confessio caput rerum Romam esse. Livy’s allusion to the temple of the Ephesian Diana must not be dismissed as an arbitrary remark of the historian. The connection of central Italy with Anterior Asia will appear to every intelligent and attentive student of ancient history as a highly important element, attested by many testimonies, in the cultural history of the ancient world. Macrob. Sat. 5, 22. The character of the Ephesian temple, that of serving debtors as an asylum, which Plutarch attests at the beginning of his treatise on the admonition that one should beware of borrowing money at interest, connects in a very significant way with the antithesis of the nature mothers and positive law, and with their hostility to compulsion and fetters. 14

o: Bona Dea in Cäsars Wohnung ereignete, berichtet Plutarch, Cxsar 9 bestimmt, daß dasselbe stets in dem Hause eines Consuls oder Prätors pflege gefeiert zu werden. Hierin offenbart sich eine besondere Beziehung jener Göttin, die die Griechen einfach als prrameia Heos bezeichnen, zu dem Wohle des Staats. Aber dieses wird hier nicht nah seiner politisch-männlichen, sondern nach der stofflichweiblichen Seite aufgefaßt. Bona Dea ist das mütterliche Natürprinzip , das allem stofflichen Leben seine Entstehung und seine Nahrung giebt, das alles Gedeihn und allen Reihthum schenkt, und jegliche leiblihe Wohlfahrt befördert. Sie gehört also der quiritischen oder cerealischen Seite des Lebens, wird selbst als Junonis potentia aufgefaßt, mit Ops und Ceres identificirt, als Murcia verehrt, als Salus-Medea mit Hygieens Natur ausgerüstet, und unter dem Namen Maia als magna mater dargestellt, Sie erscheint also als die stofflichemütterliche Grundlage des Staatswohls, der Prätor und Consul in Verbindung mit ihr als die Vertreter dieser materiellen Seite der Volksexistenz. An dieses Verhältniß zu Bona Dea knüpft sich ihre Rechtspflege. Die Ordnung des Güterlebens, welhe den Inhalt des Rechts bildet, ruht als Naturgeseß in derselben Göttin , welche aller jener Güter leßte stoffliche Grundlage bildet. Dieses Geseßh zu erkennen, es auszusprechen , ist des Prätor8 Beruf. Bona Dea als Fauna- Fatua verkündet es ihmz er selbst ist ihr Organ, ihre viva vox, die Saßung selbst ein Edictum. Dieser weiblich tellurische Ursprung des Rechts macht es dem Prätor möglich, mehr dem sachlichen 8quum als dem formellen strictum jus seine Aufmerksamkeit zuzuwenden, und das Civilreht des patricishen Staats zu dem jus naturale des wquum et bonum, und zu jener mit der linken Hand identificirten Justitia, die allen dolus, alle calliditas und astutia ausschließt, und die höhste Elegantia juris in der höchsten mütterlichen wquitas erblit, zurüczuführen. Das Recht selbst ist ein stoffliches Gesetz, es inhärirt also dem Weibe. Bona Dea ist Fe6/uopopos wie die Eleusinische Demeter, das Recht selbst stets weibliches Mysterium, wie die Entstehung alles stofflichen Lebens. Der Geheimdienst orphischer Natur, den die Frauen allein in des Prätors Haus der guten Mutter feiern, umfaßt auc das Recht. Nach dem Scholion zu Theocrit 4, 25 tragen die Frauen und Jungfrauen an der Eleusinischen ua e3s rezers die heiligen Gesehesbüher in Prozession nach Eleusis. Alles Recht ist Saßung Demeters oder der Bona Dea, deren stoffliches Geseß in ihm niedergelegt ist. Darum führen beide Gottheiten den Scepter, und zwar in der linken, erhaltenden weiblichen Hand, beide auch die Rolle, welche in ihrem Verschlusse des Stoffes höchstes Geseß, das Fatum in seinem weitesten Umfange birgt. So erscheint !) Aristoteles bei Lobeck, p. 144.
e: Bona Dea in Caesar’s house, Plutarch, Cæsar 9, reports definitely that it was always the custom for it to be celebrated in the house of a consul or praetor. In this a particular relation of that goddess, whom the Greeks simply designate as γυναικεία θεός, to the welfare of the state is revealed. But this is conceived here not according to its political-male side, but according to the materially female. Bona Dea is the maternal natural principle that gives to all material life its origination and its nourishment, that bestows all prosperity and all wealth, and promotes every bodily well-being. She belongs, then, to the Quiritary or Cerealian side of life; she is herself conceived as the Junonis potentia, identified with Ops and Ceres, worshiped as Murcia, equipped as Salus-Medea with the nature of Hygieia, and represented under the name of Maia as magna mater. She appears, then, as the materially maternal foundation of the welfare of the state, the praetor and consul in connection with her as the representatives of this material side of the existence of the people. To this relation to Bona Dea their administration of justice is tied. The ordering of the life of property, which constitutes the content of law, rests as natural law in the same goddess who forms the ultimate material foundation of all those goods. To recognize this law, to pronounce it, is the praetor’s calling. Bona Dea as Fauna-Fatua proclaims it to him; he himself is her organ, her viva vox, the enactment itself an Edictum. This female-tellurian origin of law makes it possible for the praetor to turn his attention more to the substantive æquum than to the formal strictum jus, and to lead the civil law of the patrician state back to the jus naturale of the æquum et bonum, and to that Justitia, identified with the left hand, which excludes all dolus, all calliditas and astutia, and sees the highest Elegantia juris in the highest maternal æquitas. Law itself is a material law; it inheres, therefore, in woman. Bona Dea is θεσμοφόρος like the Eleusinian Demeter; law itself is always a female mystery, like the origination of all material life. The secret service of Orphic nature that the women alone celebrate in the praetor’s house for the good mother embraces law also. According to the scholion on Theocritus 4, 25, the women and maidens on the Eleusinian ἡμέρᾳ τῆς τελετῆς carry the holy books of laws in procession to Eleusis. All law is the enactment of Demeter or of Bona Dea, whose material law is laid down in it. For this reason both deities bear the scepter, and indeed in the left, preserving female hand, both also the scroll, which in its enclosure conceals the highest law of matter, fate in its widest extent. Thus appears [PDF 225] — 211 — the law of Bona Dea as a mysterious law resting in matter itself, given with matter and as old as it. It is for the praetor, as for the aedile, only to investigate this substantive law, to listen to its revelations, to pronounce them, to choose them as the standard of his own decisions, and to subordinate the political viewpoint as well as that of purely individual conception to the one given in the matter itself. His law becomes a scripta ratio; it contains the revelation of the ratio naturalis lying in the natura rerum. Of the initiates of the mysteries it is not so much spiritual self-activity as rather passive receptivity that is demanded. They have only to receive, and stand before the mystery as listeners. Τοὺς τετελεσμένους οὐ μαθεῖν τι δεῖ ἀλλὰ παθεῖν.1) The praetor takes up a like position toward the material primal mother. He is not the source of law, but only the proclaimer of a natural law that the female natural principle bears within itself. His house is the temple of Bona Dea, as Cadmus on the citadel at Thebes dwells in the house of Harmonia. But on the day of the May festival everything male must avoid the presence of the goddess. Only the women celebrate the nocturnal orgies, which, to use Nonnus’s expression, may be designated as ὄργια θεσμῶν. Woman, like Bona Dea, is the bearer of the material mystery, the content of the Cerealian natural law, man its revelation and proclaimer. He is the secret that has stepped into the light, who learns the primal fate from the mother, as Prometheus learns it from Themis, not from Zeus, from whom it remains hidden. The same views recur in the ideas of the ancients on the origination of speech. It is a law inborn in the maternal matter of the earth. Bona Dea is also Fatua, every Lara a Lala, who bears within herself the power of speech. Only through contact with the earth does the child receive its speech.2) But it attains to revelation among men only through the force that steps into the light, unveiled, in man. The phallic Hermes is the creator and shaper of speech, who as Thoth also records the laws hitherto hidden, and so communicates them to the human race. The names of things themselves are no arbitrary invention, any more than law. They lie mute, as mystery, in the things themselves, are inborn in matter, and as old as matter. It is man’s task to recognize them and to read them out of the thing itself. Moses calls him the greatest who created things, and after sacris adjungi dicunt, quia vox nascenti homini terræ contactu datur. Scimus autem Mercurium vocis et sermonis potentem.

Dieses Selbstreden der Dinge hat eine lezte Aeußerung in dem Gebrauche, die Grabmäler gleich der Jsissäule in der ersten Person wie lebende Wesen sprechen zu lassen: Aus Plato's Phaidrus p. 264 ist die Jnschrift bekannt, welhe auf Midas den Phrygier gemacht worden sein soll. Sie hat hier um so höhere Bedeutung, da nach Macrob. Sat. 1, 12 Bona Dea selbst mit der Midasmutter identificirt wurde. „Eherne Jungfrau bin ich, und lieg an dem Grabe des Midas. Bis nicht Wasser mehr fließt, noch erblühn hochstämmige Bäume, Immer verweilend allhier an dem vielbethräneten Denkmal, Daß auch der Wanderer wisse, wo Midas liege begraben.“ Ehern nennt sich hier die Jungfrau, die Midas Gedächtniß erhält. Die Bedeutung des Erzes in der alten Naturreligion und seine Beziehung zu dem mütterlichen Tellurismus erhält dadurch eine neue Bestätigung. Mit dem cerealischen Kult steht es in besonderer Verbindung. Die wnewx lalces erwähnt Virgil Aen. 4, 513. Bon einer ehernen Sichel hat Drepanum seinen Namen Bei der Städtegründung bedienten sich die Etrusker eines ehernen Pfluges, wie Carminius naß den Tagetica sacra mittheilt.') Daher wurden die cerealischen Saßungen auf Erztafeln eingegraben, und eine ganz cerealishe Naturmutter Cupra, Aphrodite Cypria genannt, zwei Bezeichnungen, die ohne Zweifel mit dem deutschen Kupfer zusammenhängen. Daher gewinnt das Erz auch eine besondere Todesbeziehung. Mit Erz find nah alter Religionsanshauung die Hypogeen bekleidet, wie Dana6's unterirdisches Brautgemach und Athene Chalcioikos Tempel. Stücke des ws rude finden sich in großer Anzahl in den Gräbern, neuerlich wieder in den öfter erwähnten pränestinischen der casa Barberini. Omnino autem ad rem divinam pleraque enea adhiberi Solita, multa indicio unt; et in his maxime Sacris, quibus delinire aliquos, aut devovere, aut denique exigere morbos volebant.
