e: him the one who recognized and shaped their names, and Eusebius, in the Præparatio Evangelica 11, 6, has developed this primal idea of mankind further, and has shown it also to be a Platonic doctrine. The same idea is taken into account by Lucretius, de nat. rer. 5, 1040, when, in a highly noteworthy discussion of the origin of speech, not brought out by Grimm in his Geschichte der Sprache, he sets up the proposition: aliquem tum nomina distribuisse rebus, et inde homines didicisse vocabula prima, Desipere est, and, instead of a single individual, assigns to the whole race the task, Pro vario sensu varias res voce notare. This self-speaking of things has a last echo in the custom of letting the funerary monuments, like the column of Isis, speak in the first person like living beings. From Plato’s Phaedrus p. 264 the inscription is known that is said to have been made for Midas the Phrygian. It has all the higher significance here because, according to Macrob. Sat. 1, 12, Bona Dea herself was identified with the mother of Midas. “Maiden of bronze am I, and I lie on the tomb of Midas. As long as water still flows and tall-stemmed trees still bloom, Ever abiding here at the much-bewept monument, That the traveler too may know where Midas lies buried.” “Of bronze” the maiden here calls herself, she who preserves the memory of Midas. The significance of bronze in the ancient nature religion and its relation to maternal tellurism thereby receive a new confirmation. It stands in a special connection with the Cerealian cult. The æneæ falces are mentioned by Virgil, Aen. 4, 513. From a bronze sickle Drepanum has its name. In the founding of cities the Etruscans made use of a bronze plow, as Carminius reports from the Tagetica sacra.1) Hence the Cerealian enactments were engraved on bronze tablets, and a wholly Cerealian nature mother was called Cupra, Aphrodite Cypria, two designations that are without doubt connected with the German Kupfer. Hence bronze also acquires a special relation to death. According to the ancient view of religion, the hypogea are lined with bronze, like Danaë’s subterranean bridal chamber and the temple of Athena Chalcioecus. Pieces of æs rude are found in great number in the tombs, most recently again in the often-mentioned Praenestine ones of the casa Barberini. Omnino autem ad rem divinam pleraque ænea adhiberi solita, multa indicio sunt; et in his maxime sacris, quibus delinire aliquos, aut devovere, aut denique exigere morbos volebant. To this attaches the bronze maiden of Midas.

o: frau an. Wenn hier das Erz redend eingeführt wird, so verbindet fich dieß mit der Heiligkeit des Erztons, die den alten als eine Offenbarung des in dem Stoffe schlafenden Naturgeseßes gilt. Das ados //ovv des corcyräishen Weihbildes zu Dodona, der Cureten wra crepitantia, unter deren Klang das Zeuskind ans Licht tritt, der Schall der Tyrrhenischen Tuba, des Jsischen Sistrum, der Salischen Schilde, jeder Ton, den ein Erzgefäß von fich giebt, verkündet als stumme Sprache das latente Mysterium des Stoffes, wie es die eherne Jungfrau an Midas Grab in Worten ausspricht, wie es auch die ehernen Geseßestafeln darlegen. In dem Erze kommen also alle Seiten des mütterlihen, namentlich cerealisch gedachten Naturprinzips zur Datstellung : wir sehen in ihm den Stoff . in seiner lebenspendenden , ebenso in seiner das Leben wieder zurüknehmenden Potenz: wir sehen ihn überdieß das Geseß verkündend , das ihn durchdringt. Das Erz ist, was Ceres selbst, zugleich der Reihthum, und das Gesetz, das seine Vertheilung auf Erden ordnet und bewacht. Darum hat Ws et libra in dem Verkehrsleben eine so hohe Bedeutung erhalten, daß auf ihm alles Nexum beruht, von ihm alle Rechtskraft abhängt. Auch die Wage muß ehern sein, und mit dem Erzstück berührt werden. Wenn sie unter dem Schlage tönt, so erhält alles, was die Partheien dazu sprechen, die Bedeutung einer cerealischen Saßung, einer lex, deren Verlegung eine Verlehung der stofflichen Naturmutter und ihres in dem Erzklang kundgegebenen Willens selbst enthalten würde. Die wnea libra zeigt uns die Naturmutter als Geberin, als gerechte Vertheiletin, dadurch auch als Lenkerin und Vermittlerin alles Güterverkehrs. Auf dieser, wenn ich so sagen darf, stofflichen Bedeutung der Wage ist dann die höhere, in welcher sie die abstrakte Gerechtigkeit bezeihnet, und zum Attribut der justitia wird, aufgebaut. Wir sehen also in der Wage dieselbe Verbindung der Begriffe von Recht und Gerechtigkeit mit dem stofflichen Naturprinzip, welche uns in den Urmüttern, in Ceres, Syria, Aphrodite selbst entgegen trat.
e: If here the bronze is introduced as speaking, this connects with the sanctity of the bronze tone, which for the ancients counts as a revelation of the natural law sleeping in matter. The χαλκὸς ἠχοῦν of the Corcyraean votive figure at Dodona, the æra crepitantia of the Curetes, to whose clangor the child Zeus steps into the light, the sound of the Tyrrhenian tuba, of the Isiac sistrum, of the Salian shields, every tone that a vessel of bronze gives forth, proclaims as mute speech the latent mystery of matter, as the bronze maiden at Midas’s tomb pronounces it in words, as the bronze tablets of law also set it forth. In bronze, then, all sides of the maternal natural principle, conceived above all as Cerealian, come to representation: we see in it matter in its life-giving and equally in its life-reclaiming potency; we see it, moreover, proclaiming the law that pervades it. Bronze is what Ceres herself is, at once wealth and the law that orders and guards its distribution on earth. For this reason æs et libra have acquired so high a significance in commercial life that all nexum rests on it, and all legal force depends on it. The scale, too, must be of bronze, and be touched with the piece of bronze. When it rings under the blow, everything that the parties say to it acquires the significance of a Cerealian enactment, of a lex, the violation of which would amount to a violation of the material nature mother herself and of her will, made known in the sound of bronze. The ænea libra shows us the nature mother as giver, as just distributor, and thereby also as director and mediator of all traffic in goods. Upon this, if I may say so, material significance of the scale is built the higher one, in which it designates abstract justice and becomes the attribute of justitia. In the scale, then, we see the same connection of the concepts of law and justice with the material natural principle that confronted us in the primal mothers, in Ceres, Syria, and Aphrodite herself.

o: Bona Dea, deren Verbindung mit dem Rechte wir bisher erläuterten, giebt“ mir noch zu zwei Bemerkungen Veranlassung. Wir haben dieselbe nach Ma- crobius 1, 12 Vorgang mit Juno zusammenstellt. Nun erscheint aber diese unter einem Beinamen, der jene ihr eigenes Gese verkündende Natur des weiblichen Stoffes besonders hervorhebt, In allen Nachrichten, die wir über Juno Moneta besißen, tritt diese Göttin immer in derselben Natur, als mahnende, des Stoffes Gesey den Menschen verkündende Macht, uns entgegen. Aber diese Eigenschaft darf nicht in abstrakter Unkörperlichkeit gedacht werden. Moneta trägt vielmehr, gleich Fatua, in sich die ganze Stofflichkeit des Mutterthums, die sih nicht nur in Mahnungen und Offenbarungen, sondern allgemein in der Spende jegliches materiellen Wohlergehns kundgibt, Sie tritt darum zu dem Staatswohl in ein  [PDF 228]  ähnliches Verhältniß wie Bona Dea. Der Begriff des Rechts und seiner Handhabung verbindet sich auH mit Moneta. Zum Bau ihres Tempels wird von dem Senat die Area, wo des M. Manlius Capitolinus Haus gestanden, angewiesen. Hatte er den Umsturz der Freiheit angestrebt, und dadurch das stofflich weibliche Rechtsprinzip verleßt, so soll diejenige Gottheit, welche als der Jnhalt eben dieses Rechts gilt, auf der gleichen Stätte ihren Wohnfiß erhalten. Der Tempel selbst war von F. Camillus im auruncischen Kriege gelobt worden.) Warum gerade der Moneta? J< denke, weil sie dem gerechten Kriege Sieg verleihen sollte. Sie erscheint so überhaupt ganz in der Natur einer Victoria, die dem Verlekten beisteht, und seine Unternehmung begünstigt.?) Von Suidas wird Moneta gerade zu mit der justjtia in bellis identificirt. Sie straft die injuria, schädigt den, der andere verkürzt, und giebt durch die Verhängung der Strafe. ihren Unwillen zu erkennen. Dadurch mahnt fie fortwährend zur Gerechtigkeit, zur Befolgung ihres mütterlihen Gesees. Der Name Moneta geht also selbit aus ihrer Eigenschaft als Trägerin der höchsten mütterlichen Gerechtigkeit hervor. Darum heißt auch Apoll Moneta, weil er durh Pest Ungerechtigkeit rächt, und zur Sühne auffordert. Jeßt gewinnt die Beziehung der Moneta zur Prägung der Münzen ihre richtige Erklärung und tiefere Bedeutung. Nicht weil die Münze an irgend ein Ereigniß erinnert =- denn diese Bedeutung des Gepräges ist keine ursprünglihe -- auch nicht, weil das Gepräge eine Garantie des völlig richtigen Werthes knthält -- denn diese konnte durch Abwägen ebenso, vollkommen geleistet werden =-, sondern weil das geprägte Geld zunächst als Aequivalent der in Rindern und Shaafen von Alters her zu leistenden Multen eingeführt wurd«, mithin die Sühne einies begangenen Unrechts, die Ausgleichung eines zugefügten Scadens, die Erstattung eines Verlustes seine nächste Bestimmung war, darum ' wurde die Prägstätte in Juno Moneta's Heiligthum verlegt, und dem geprägten Gelde, so wie dem Stempel und der Münzstätte der Göttin Namen geliehen. In allen diesen Aeußerungen bewahrt also Juno Moneta ihren Charakter als höchste justitia, in welchem fie auf der Burg selbst, gewissermaßen als Hüterin des Staats, ihren Siß erhält. Wir haben wieder die gleiche Verbindung des weiblich- stofflichen Naturprinzips mit der Gerechtigkeit, welche wir nun schon fo oft gefunden haben. Nur wird hier die Mütterlichkeit niht sowohl als bloßer Träger des höchsten Geseßes, sondern vielmehr als verfolgende, und für die Sühne des Unrechts selbst sich erhebende Macht in dem Wesen einer die gestörte Naturordnung wieder herstellenden Nemesis-Erynnis gedacht.
e: Bona Dea, whose connection with law we have so far elucidated, gives me occasion for two further remarks. Following the lead of Macrobius 1, 12, we have placed her together with Juno. Now Juno appears under an epithet that especially stresses that nature of female matter which proclaims its own law. In all the reports we possess about Juno Moneta, this goddess confronts us always in the same nature, as a power that admonishes, that proclaims to men the law of matter. But this quality must not be conceived in abstract incorporeality. Moneta bears within herself, like Fatua, the whole materiality of motherhood, which makes itself known not only in admonitions and revelations but generally in the bestowal of every material well-being. She therefore stands to the welfare of the state in a [PDF 228] — 214 — relation similar to that of Bona Dea. The concept of law and of its administration connects with Moneta as well. For the building of her temple the Senate assigns the area where the house of M. Manlius Capitolinus had stood. If he had aspired to the overthrow of freedom, and thereby violated the materially female principle of law, then the deity who counts as the content of this very law is to receive her dwelling on the same site. The temple itself had been vowed by F. Camillus in the Aurunican war.1) Why precisely to Moneta? I think, because she was to grant victory to the just war. Thus she appears altogether in the nature of a Victoria, who stands by the wronged and favors his undertaking.2) By Suidas Moneta is straightaway identified with the justitia in bellis. She punishes injuria, harms him who curtails others, and by the imposition of punishment gives her displeasure to be known. Thereby she admonishes continually to justice, to the observance of her maternal law. The name Moneta, then, proceeds itself from her quality as bearer of the highest maternal justice. For this reason Apollo too is called Moneta, because by pestilence he avenges injustice and summons to atonement. Now the relation of Moneta to the minting of coins receives its true explanation and deeper significance. Not because the coin recalls some event — for this significance of the stamp is not an original one — nor because the stamp contains a guarantee of the entirely correct value — for this could be achieved just as perfectly by weighing —, but because minted money was introduced at first as the equivalent of the fines to be paid from of old in cattle and sheep, and consequently the atonement for a wrong committed, the compensation for harm inflicted, the restitution of a loss, was its nearest purpose, therefore the mint was placed in the sanctuary of Juno Moneta, and the minted money, as well as the die and the mint, were lent the name of the goddess. In all these manifestations, then, Juno Moneta preserves her character as the highest justitia, in which she receives her seat on the citadel itself, in a sense as guardian of the state. We have again the same connection of the female-material natural principle with justice that we have by now found so often. Only here maternity is conceived not so much as mere bearer of the highest law as rather as a power that pursues, and rises up itself for the atonement of wrong, in the nature of a Nemesis-Erinys restoring the disturbed order of nature.

o: Eine zweite Bemerkung liefert mir die Auffassung der Bona Dea als Murtia. Gellius N. A. 5, 6 berichtet, der kleine Triumph, die sogenannte ovatio, gelte der Murtia, und die von dem Sieger getragene corona ovalis besiehe aus Myrthenlaub. ') Hier sehen wir die Feier des Sieges, mithin den Sieg selbst mit dem weiblichen Naturprinzip, und der stofflichen Seite des Staates in Verbindung gebracht. Dieß findet seine Bestätigung in dem Scaafopfer, das der ovatio ihren Namen gegeben.?) Wir können diesen kleinern Triumph gerade wegen seiner religiösen Verknüpfung mit Murtia den plebeischen nennen, und ihn dadurch von dem großen oder patrizischen, in welchem der Sieger als Sonnengott und mit allen Attributen dieser höchsten väterlichen Lichtmacht ausgerüstet, zum Capitolinischen Tempel heranfährt, unterscheiden. Murtia bewahrt auch hier ihren, dem jus naturale so innig verwandten Charakter. Das zeigen die einzelhen Fille, in welchen die ovatio zur Anwendung kommen soll. Ovandi autem, schreibt Gellins 5, 6, ac non triumphandi causa est, quum aut bella non rite indicta, neque cum justo hoste gesta sunt; aut hostium nomen humile et non idoneum est, ut gervorum piratarumque?) aut, deditione repente facla, impulverea, ut dici Solet, incruentaque victoria obvenit. cui facilitati aptam esse Veneris frondem crediderunt, quod non Martius, ged quasi Venerius quidam triumphus esset. Damit stimmt Festus v. ovalis corona überein. Dem weiblichen Naturprinzip sänd die Bestimmungen des positiven Rechts zuwider. Es vereinigt sich mit der natürlichen Seite des stofflichen Lebens, und tritt daher so oft in den Vordergrund, äls der Krieg wegen Mangel der Beobachtung des positiven Fecialrechts oder wegen anderer ähnlicher Defecte den Charakter eines justum et legitimum bellum nicht in Anspruch nehmen kann. Jn einem solchen Falle betheiligt sihß an der Siegesfeier nur der Stand der Plebeiexr und das ihm zugehörende Ritterthum, während dem Rindopfer des Triumphes der ganze Staat beiwohnt. Das Plebeierthum steht eben seines rein stofflichen Charakters wegen mit dem weiblichen Naturprinzip in genauerem Zusammenhangz das Patriziat hat einen höhern Charakter. Es besißt die höhere Sonnenweihe, und verbindet sich mit dem väterlichen Prinzip des himmlischen Lichts, kraft dessen in ihm das Jmperium des Staats ruht. Bona Dea-Murtia trägt nah Festus auch den Namen Damia, ihre Priesterin heißt Damiatrix, ihr Opfer Damium. Hier sehen wir fie als Tellus. Denn Damia hat, wie wir oben bemerkten, die Bedeutung der Fruhterde. Damia und Auxesia verbinden sich zu Trözen wie Demeter und Kora,
e: A second remark is furnished me by the conception of Bona Dea as Murtia. Gellius N. A. 5, 6 reports that the lesser triumph, the so-called ovatio, was dedicated to Murtia, and that the corona ovalis worn by the victor consisted of myrtle foliage.1) Here we see the celebration of victory, and hence victory itself, brought into connection with the female natural principle and the material side of the state. This finds its confirmation in the sacrifice of a sheep that gave the ovatio its name.2) Precisely on account of its religious linkage with Murtia we may call this lesser triumph the plebeian one, and thereby distinguish it from the great or patrician one, in which the victor, as sun god and equipped with all the attributes of this highest paternal power of light, drives up to the Capitoline temple. Murtia preserves here too her character, so intimately akin to the jus naturale. This is shown by the individual cases in which the ovatio is to be applied. Ovandi autem, writes Gellius 5, 6, ac non triumphandi causa est, quum aut bella non rite indicta, neque cum justo hoste gesta sunt; aut hostium nomen humile et non idoneum est, ut servorum piratarumque3) aut, deditione repente facta, impulverea, ut dici solet, incruentaque victoria obvenit. cui facilitati aptam esse Veneris frondem crediderunt, quod non Martius, sed quasi Venerius quidam triumphus esset. With this Festus v. ovalis corona agrees. The provisions of positive law are repugnant to the female natural principle. It unites with the natural side of material life, and therefore comes to the fore whenever the war, for want of observance of the positive fecial law or because of other similar defects, cannot lay claim to the character of a justum et legitimum bellum. In such a case only the order of the plebeians and the equestrian order belonging to it take part in the victory celebration, whereas the whole state attends the ox sacrifice of the triumph. Plebeiandom stands, precisely on account of its purely material character, in closer connection with the female natural principle; the patriciate has a higher character. It possesses the higher solar initiation, and unites with the paternal principle of heavenly light, by virtue of which the imperium of the state rests in it. Bona Dea-Murtia bears, according to Festus, also the name Damia, her priestess is called Damiatrix, her sacrifice Damium. Here we see her as Tellus. For Damia has, as we remarked above, the meaning of the fruitful earth. Damia and Auxesia are joined at Troezen like Demeter and Kore, [PDF 230] — 216 — As Damia, Bona Dea appears once more in her closer connection with the plebeian element of the state. She is the mother of the δῆμος, which plebeiandom precisely forms. 17.

o: Die Verbindung des Rechts mit dem weiblichen Naturprinzip seßt sich in merkwürdigen Erscheinungen fort, die nur durh Anknüpfung an den aufgestellten allgemeinen Gesichtöpunkt ihr richtiges Liht erhalten. Mit den so allgemein herrschenden Jdeen über Entwürdigung des weiblichen Geschleht8s im Alterthum stehen gewisse nicht zu bezweifelnde Angaben über ihre Theilnahme an dem Richteramte in dem schneidendsten Gegensaße. Jn Elis ist es ein collegium matronarwn, das den Streit der Eleer mit den Pisanern als höchste richterliche Autorität schlichtet. In dem Bündniß , das Hannibal mit gewissen gallischen Völkerschaften abschließt, stand die Bestimmung, es sollte im Falle des Streits über Auslegung desselben die höhste Entscheidung einem Collegium gallische Matronen vorgelegt werden. Jn dem Streite der böotishen Cadmeer mit dem dodonäischen Orakel verlangen die Priesterinnen des legtern, es sollten zu der richterlichen Behörde eben so viele Weiber als Männer zugezogen werden. Zu Athen richten über Neptunus und Minerva's Streit neben den Männern auch +. Frauen, und Aristophanes ECcclesiazusen und The8smophoriazusen erscheinen als eine Parodie wirklich erlebter älterer Zustände. Bei einem Weibe holen die Germanen den Entscheid auch in Fragen völkerrechtlicher Natur, Erscheinungen, die ich in meinem Mutterreht näherer Betrachtung unterworfen habe. Haben wir oben dieß weibliche Naturprinzip als Träger des dem Stoffe eingebornen Rechts erkannt, so sehen wir hier die Matronen mit der Rechtspflege betraut, und selbst das Ret verwaltend. Sie übernehmen das Amt der tellurischen Urmutter, wie sie dessen physische Bestimmung durch die Geburt fortsezen , und an ihrer Stelle erfüllen. Es kann keinem Zweifel unterliegen, daß diese matronale höchste Rechtöspflege einen Hauptbestandtheil jener Gynaikokratie bildet, welche die Religionsidee des stofflich-weiblichen Naturprinzips in das Staatsleben überträgt, und den Urzustand der menschlichen Gesellschaft gebildet zu haben scheint. Wir finden sie bei den Lyciern, auf Creta, bei den karisch-lelegischen, bei den libyschen Stämmen, und wie bei deutschen Völkerschaften, so auch bei den Kantabrern. Als sterbliches Bild der großen Naturmutter genießt die Matrone besonderes Ansehen und einen geheiligten Charakter, der von jener auf sie übergeht. Unverleßlichkeit zeichnet sie aus. Sie tritt zwischen die kämpfenden Partheien und alle Waffenthat ruht sofort. So finden wir sie auf den balearischen Inseln, und wer die hierüber  [PDF 231]  erhaltene Schilderung Diodor's mit des Livius Erzählung von dem Auftreten der Sabinerinnen zwischen den Reihen der kämpfenden Römer und Sabiner vergleicht, sindet eine so vollkommene Uebereinstimmung beider Erscheinungen, daß sein Glaube an die Richtigkeit auch dieser Tradition eine neue Stüße erhält. Die hohe Stellung der sabinischen Frauen hat auch einen Nachklang in jener Erzählung Plutarch's Qu. rom. 82 gelassen, wonach in ihrem Bündniß mit den Römern die Bestimmung enthalten war, es sollte kein Römer seine Frau zu der Arbeit des Kochens oder Mahlens nöthigen. Dieß mußte jenen Völkern als eine Beeinträchtigung der hohen Stellung erscheinen, welche die Matrone in Haus und Staat einnahm. Je fremdartiger solche Sitten den spätern Zeiten waren, um so echter ist ihre Ueberlieferung. Mag darüber in einem Vertrage entschieden worden sein oder nicht: als Zug des alten Lebens ist die Rachricht unzweifelhaft. Sie entspricht vollkommen jenen Zuständen, die die Gynaikokratie begründeten, und in dem Richteramte der Frauen ihren höchsten Ausdruck fanden. Als den römischen Matronen das Recht des currus entzogen werden sollte, schübte sie Themis-Carmenta. Der hierüber bei Plutarch Qu. r. 53 erhaltene Mythus zeigt uns die Matrone wieder als der Urmutter Ebenbild, an ihrer Weihe theilnehmend, von ihr besonders gehütet. Jede Verlezung der Weiblichkeit rächt die Mutter Erde. In dieser ausschließlichen Verbindung des weiblich-stofflichen Urprinzips mit der sterblichen Mutter, ruht die besondere Beziehung, welche die Erynnien, diese tellurischen Urmütter , mit der Rache des verlezten Weibes verbindet. Unbekümmert um das höhere apollinische Vaterrecht, das die Sühne bringt, verlangen sie Orestes Blut, das ihnen gehört nach jenem alten Recht und Gese der mütterlihen Erde , welches sich auch in Alcmäons Verbannung auf ein neugebornes Shlammeiland in gleicher Entschiedenheit offenbart. Aus dem Zusammenhang mit dem weiblich - stofflichen Urprinzip leitet die Mutter jene besondere Heiligkeit ab , die sie umgiebt. Sie ist der gebärende Stoff, der das Mysterium der Dinge in sich schließt, der das Naturgeseß in sih trägt, bei dem es der Mann erkunden muß, wie Zeus bei Themis, der es in Orakeln verkündet, in Richtersprüchen enthüllt, der durch sein Erscheinen jeder feindlihen Begegnung der Männer Halt gebietet, der überall als das Prinzip der Vereinigung, des Friedens, der Ruhe erscheint, und ebendadurch inmitten des wilden Kampfes kriegerischer Urstämme als das wohlthätige Prinzip der Ordnung, als der wahre Mittelpunkt der ersten Gesittung, als die zusammenhaltende, versöhnende und ordnende Macht dasieht. Gegenüber dem Kriege ist die Mutter der Friede, gegenüber dem Kampfe die Versöhnung, gegenüber dem herumschweifenden Leben des Mannes die häusliche Niederlassung, gegenüber dem Entscheid der Waffen der friedliche des Rechts, gegenüber dem  [PDF 232]  Erkämpfen das Bewahren, gegenüber der Gewalt die Harmonie. Darum gehört auch alles Eigenthum dem Weibe. Wie aller Reichthum dem Stoffe entspricht, so gehört alle Habe dem stofflichen Weibe. Wie Hermes den gefüllten Beutel Fortunen in den Schooß legt, so bringt der Mann der Mutter Alles, was sein Arm erringt, zum Eigenthum dar. In dem System der Gynaikokratie ruht hierauf alles Erbrecht. Nur die Töchter erben, nicht die Söhne. Nur auf den Töchtern ruht die Alimentationspfliht, nicht auf den Söhnen. Auf die Shwesterkinder vererbt die Herrschaft, wie auc) noch die Römerinnen in Matuta's Tempel um der Schwesterkinder Heil und Seegen bitten. Der Mann hat Schwert und Bogen, und den Arm zum Erwerb. Mag er diesen auf der Jagd und im fernen Kriege, mag er ihn wie die rußigen Doz0us in der Schmiede, wie die ozolishen Locrer als Hirten , wie die Aegypter am Webstuhl gewinnen: was er erwirbt, fällt der Mutter in den Schooß, erbt von ihr auf die Töchter allein, der Stoff auf den Stoff, die erwerbende Kraft auf die Söhne, denen die Frau das Gut zubringt. Au hier zeigt sich das Recht mit dem Weibe verbundtn, nicht nur, indem es dasselbe in sich trägt, niht nur, indem es als Schiedsricterin es verkündet und handhabt, sondern auch indem es seinen Gegenstand, die stofflichen Güter an seine Person knüpft und nur in der weiblichen Linie fortpflanzt. e: The connection of law with the female natural principle continues in remarkable phenomena that receive their proper light only through linkage with the general standpoint set up. With the generally prevailing ideas about the degradation of the female sex in antiquity, certain undoubted reports of its participation in the office of judge stand in the sharpest contrast. In Elis it is a collegium matronarum that settles, as the highest judicial authority, the dispute of the Eleans with the Pisans. In the alliance that Hannibal concludes with certain Gallic tribes there stood the provision that, in the event of a dispute over its interpretation, the supreme decision should be laid before a college of Gallic matrons. In the quarrel of the Boeotian Cadmeans with the Dodonaean oracle the priestesses of the latter demand that as many women as men be called into the judicial body. At Athens, in the quarrel of Neptunus and Minerva, women too sit in judgment alongside the men, and Aristophanes’ Ecclesiazusae and Thesmophoriazusae appear as a parody of older conditions actually experienced. From a woman the Germans obtain the decision even in questions of the nature of international law, phenomena that I have subjected to closer consideration in my Mutterrecht. If we recognized above this female natural principle as the bearer of the law inborn in matter, so we see here the matrons entrusted with the administration of justice, and administering law itself. They take over the office of the tellurian primal mother, as they continue her physical vocation through birth, and fulfill it in her place. There can be no doubt that this supreme matronal administration of justice forms a chief component of that gynecocracy which transfers the religious idea of the material-female natural principle into the life of the state, and seems to have constituted the primal state of human society. We find it among the Lycians, in Crete, among the Carian-Lelegian and the Libyan tribes, and, as among German peoples, so also among the Cantabrians. As the mortal image of the great nature mother the matron enjoys special esteem and a sacred character, which passes to her from the latter. Inviolability distinguishes her. She steps between the combatant parties and at once all deeds of arms cease. So we find her in the Balearic Islands, and whoever compares the [PDF 231] — 217 — account preserved by Diodorus on this subject with Livy’s narrative of the intervention of the Sabine women between the ranks of the fighting Romans and Sabines finds so perfect an agreement of the two phenomena that his belief in the correctness of this tradition too receives a new support. The high position of the Sabine women has also left an echo in that narrative of Plutarch’s, Qu. rom. 82, according to which the provision was contained in their alliance with the Romans that no Roman should compel his wife to the labor of cooking or grinding. This must have appeared to those peoples as an impairment of the high position that the matron occupied in house and state. The more alien such customs were to later times, the more authentic is their transmission. Whether this was decided in a treaty or not: as a trait of the old life the report is beyond doubt. It corresponds perfectly to those conditions that founded gynecocracy and found their highest expression in the office of judge held by women. When the Roman matrons were to be deprived of the right of the currus, Themis- Carmenta protected them. The myth preserved about this in Plutarch Qu. r. 53 shows us the matron once more as the image of the primal mother, sharing in her initiation, specially guarded by her. Every violation of womanhood Mother Earth avenges. In this exclusive connection of the female-material primal principle with the mortal mother rests the special relation that links the Erinyes, these tellurian primal mothers, with the vengeance of the injured woman. Heedless of the higher Apollonian father right that brings atonement, they demand the blood of Orestes, which belongs to them according to that ancient right and law of the maternal earth, which reveals itself with equal decisiveness also in Alcmaeon’s banishment to a newly born island of mud. From the connection with the female-material primal principle the mother derives that special sanctity that surrounds her. She is the birth-giving matter that encloses within itself the mystery of things, that bears the natural law within itself, from whom man must inquire it, as Zeus from Themis, who proclaims it in oracles, unveils it in judgments, who by her appearing commands a halt to every hostile encounter of men, who everywhere appears as the principle of union, of peace, of rest, and precisely thereby, in the midst of the wild strife of warlike primal tribes, stands forth as the beneficent principle of order, as the true center of the first civilization, as the power that holds together, reconciles, and orders. As against war the mother is peace, as against combat reconciliation, as against the roving life of man the domestic settlement, as against the decision of arms the peaceful decision of law, as against the [PDF 232] — 218 — winning by combat, preservation; as against violence, harmony. For this reason all property also belongs to woman. As all wealth corresponds to matter, so all possessions belong to material woman. As Hermes lays the filled purse in the lap of Fortuna, so man brings to the mother, as property, everything that his arm wins. In the system of gynecocracy all law of inheritance rests on this. Only the daughters inherit, not the sons. Only upon the daughters rests the duty of maintenance, not upon the sons. Dominion passes by inheritance to the sisters’ children, as even the Roman women in the temple of Matuta still pray for the welfare and blessing of their sisters’ children. Man has sword and bow, and the arm for acquisition. Whether he gains this in the hunt and in distant war, whether he gains it like the sooty Ψολόεις in the smithy, like the Ozolian Locrians as herdsmen, like the Egyptians at the loom: what he acquires falls into the mother’s lap, passes by inheritance from her to the daughters alone, matter to matter, the acquiring force to the sons, to whom the woman brings the property. Here too law shows itself bound up with woman, not only in that it bears the same within itself, not only in that as arbitress she proclaims and administers it, but also in that it ties its object, the material goods, to her person and propagates it only in the female line. So the material jus naturale brings it with it, and the same reveals itself in the exclusive regard for maternal descent, according to which the children bear the name of the mother, as among the Lycians; the nobility of birth is measured only by the female ancestors, as among the Locrians; the same in the admission of marriage between the nearest relatives, between brother and sister, mother and child; the same in the right of the maiden to dispose of her own hand, to choose the husband of her own accord, indeed, as among the Cantabrians, also to give her brothers in marriage. The material-female standpoint dominates this whole law. Motherhood is not only the bearer of the principle of law, it also determines its content, and stands in exclusive connection with the goods, the object of legal life. Precisely thereby woman becomes the scepter-bearing queen, the bearer of the potentia that confronts the political imperium as the epitome of material power. Thereby the mother becomes the Creusa of her lineage, therefore the sole source of nobility, therefore, as an immortal, joined to a mortal man, therefore in the Naupactia and Eoiai the guiding thread of all heroic genealogy. In Plato there is found the remark that the seed is very often transformed into the nature of the mother by the soil to which it is entrusted, but never does the land pass over into the nature of the seed, and this agrees with the account of Aeschylus and Euripides, in which they carry through the mother’s closer connection with the [PDF 233] — 219 — child, entirely. In this physical truth lies the foundation of that whole mother right whose individual aspects we have briefly indicated. Gynecocracy thus presents itself as jus naturale in the proper sense, as law of material creation. It is no positive institution, but a natura ductum, developed natura duce, nulla ratione, nullaque doctrina.1) It rests on the view that, as the æs receives its impress from the die, so man’s seed receives its stamp from woman’s moneta.2) It is the Jus terræ, which in Roman law too is opposed to the jus seminis. He who sows a foreign field does not gain the fruits; they fall to the owner of the ground: jure terræ non jure seminis. The same holds of building on foreign ground and soil. The same of the fecundation of a slave woman, the same of illegitimate mating, where the spurio editus, the sown spurius, follows the maternal earth. The principle of Aphroditean-hetaeric life is carried over into the conjugal relation. Cerealian law does, to be sure, give the child also a father, makes it a διφυής, a legitimate offspring. But in this relation of exclusiveness the maternal matter has the upper hand over the paternal incorporeal force, as at the lunar stage of religion Luna has over Lunus, who recedes behind her. Over against this female jus naturale Rome founds her family and her state on the higher immaterial law of fatherhood. It wrests itself free from the material natural law that attaches itself to the female natural principle, and founds its family, and as the consistent extension of it its state, on the basis of the paternal imperium, which, apart from the Gallograeci of Asia, no other people has developed and maintained in so decided a manner. With this law Rome enters into history. For this very reason she is from the day of her foundation more a state than a people, from the first day dominated by the grip of the imperium, and holding to it always until the completion of her world-historical task. The material-female natural principle forms no unified state, only peoples and natural wholes, no political bodies. It produces only external union, no concentration. It communicates its own nature to the peoples it rules; gives them the tendency toward the development of material life, which the Hellenic tribes carry through to the farthest limit of idealization, the Asiatic and Egyptian to the most sunken materialism; promotes the development of the arts and sciences, which, like navigation, astronomy, poetry, and all erotic [PDF 234] — 220 — refinement of life, attach themselves preeminently to the Aphroditean- Dionysian cult; is, in uncorrupted times, a mighty lever of valor, which finds in the encouraging love of woman its highest spur and the greatest reward of chivalry; carries also a very vigorous element of political conservatism within itself, so that gynecocratic peoples in particular are praised and extolled as εὔνομοι: but with all these qualities, in part excellent, it nevertheless remains always in matter, and entangled in a development of material, natural life that is now more refined, now more material: whereas the Roman principle, in the paternal imperium on which family, state, and world dominion are founded, raises to the throne a political idea of wholly incorporeal nature, and subordinates to it the female-material side of the existence of the people. Thereby its private law too acquires more and more spiritual content. Whoever follows its progress will recognize the elevation from the material-maternal character to the immateriality of the paternal principle in all its parts, in the development of adoption, in the doctrine of inheritance, in the fiction of a personality reaching beyond death, holding the property together, as it were animating matter, in the ever-advancing legal shaping of merely factual relations, and in a great number of particulars. In the political idea of the imperium lies that higher spiritual content which Rome possesses beyond all the peoples of the ancient world. When this faded more and more toward the end of the Republic, that inclination to the material-female side of life emerged with unbridled force. Now those Asiatic-Egyptian cults in which the maternal natural principle predominates found so rapid an entry and so powerful a diffusion. Now Rome had to live through the spectacle to which she had never been accustomed, feminam præsidere signis romanis. What a contrast to the earlier time, which excluded women even from representation in court, which promoted subjection through the guardianship of the sex and through the restriction of their right of inheritance, to which it counted as an ill-omened event when once a woman had appeared speaking in the Forum, and which allowed woman so little connection with the state that even the taxation of woman’s property counted as a sacrilege. Whoever does not conceive the patria potestas and the patrem ciere of the patricians in contrast to the material mother right and the wholly material formation of the other peoples will never be able to appreciate their whole significance; nor will it come to his consciousness what special difficulties the spread of the Christian doctrine was bound to meet precisely in the Roman idea of the state.

e: 18. A whole class of monuments on which the egg occupies a significant place has remained excluded from our account so far. I mean the representations of the circus games, which form the content of many sarcophagus reliefs. A complete enumeration of them would be pointless. It suffices to single out a number of the most important. One finds them assembled in Visconti, Museo Pio-Clementino vol. 5. tab. 36–43 and on the tavole d’aggiunta to the 11th volume of the Annali dell’ Instituto di correspondenza archeologica. Guattani, notizie sulle antichità di Roma per l’anno 1785. Ottobre tav. 3. On a high scaffold, supported now by four, now by two columns, egg-shaped bodies appear, set up now in the number seven, now in the numbers five and ten. Another structure, entirely corresponding, carries an equal number of dolphins. The nature of these objects can be subject to no doubt, because eggs as well as dolphins are not seldom singled out among the appurtenances of the circus in written testimonies. To win a secure foundation for what follows, the pronouncements of the ancients are first to be assembled. Cassius Dio 49, 43 names the eggs and dolphins together: κἂν τῷ ἱπποδρόμῳ σφαλλομένους τοὺς ἀνθρώπους περὶ τῶν διαύλων ἀριθμὸν ὁρῶν, τούς τε δελφῖνας καὶ τὰ ὠοειδῆ δημιουργήματα κατεστήσατο ὅπως δι᾽ αὐτῶν αἱ περίοδοι περιδρόμων ἀναδεικνύωνται. Agrippa, to whom this account refers, seems to have made some new, expedient arrangement with regard to the dolphins and the eggs and their setting up in the circus. For the use of eggs at the circus games does not derive from him. Already for the year 578 of the city it is attested by Livy 41, 32. (Censores Q. Fulvius Flaccus et A. Postumius Albinus locaverunt) et carceres in circo et ova ad notas curriculis numerandis et — —. The remaining part of the passage is so corrupt that a tolerable restoration of it has so far been attempted in vain. Here too there is no talk of the introduction of a new usage. Only the structural restoration of the individual parts of the circus, among them also the eggs, is ordered by the censors. The ὠοειδῆ δημιουργήματα seem accordingly to have been made of wood or of baked clay1) and to have been of considerable size. Particular attention is deserved by Varro R. R. 1, 2. In that conversation which he says he held in the temple of Tellus at the feriæ Sementinæ with C. Fundanius and other friends, C. Licinius Stolo says the following: Nam non modo ovum illud sublatum [PDF 236] — 222 — est, quod ludis Circensibus novissimi curriculi finem facit quadrigis, sed ne illud quidem tum vidimus, quod in Cereali pompa solet esse primum.1) These words show with certainty that at each circuit of the chariot teams one of the eggs was taken down from the scaffold on which they were set up, so that with the completion of the seventh circuit the last one vanished. Sublatum cannot without strain be explained otherwise. When Visconti puts forward the opinion that it was not so much that an egg was removed each time, but, conversely, that one was set up, several reasons can be urged for this. First, the representation on individual monuments in which the presentation of the victor’s wreath and the full number of eggs appear side by side. Moreover, however, the following words of Cassiodorus, Var. 3, 51: Nec illud putetur irritum, quod metarum circuitus ovorum erectionibus exprimatur quando actus ipse multis superstitionibus gravis, ovi exemplo, geniturum se aliqua2) profitetur. Et ideo datur intelligi, volitantes atque inconstantissimos inde mores nasci, quos avium moribus aptaverunt. Yet several objections can be raised against the probative force of these representations. The artist must have been free to indicate the sum of the circuits by affixing the full number of eggs, without seeing himself hindered by the completion of the contest, which of course presupposes the bestowal of the victor’s crown. Cassiodorus’s words, however, are not entirely certain. Instead of the decisive erectionibus, Salmasius, Plinianæ exercit. ad Solinum p. 640, reads, after old manuscripts, exceptionibus, and proposes to emend this to exemptionibus, while others give preference to ereptionibus. At any rate, the passage falls short of full probative force in that it speaks not of the successive erection or removal, but in general of the significance of the erected eggs and the relations tied to them. Accordingly there is no reason to depart from the removal of the egg after the completion of each individual circuit, assumed already by earlier writers, like Bulenger and Salmasius, and by later ones, like Raoul-Rochette and Friedländer.3) — To the eggs of the circus, finally, the following passage of Juvenal, Sat. 6, 589–591, is to be referred. Plebeium in Circo positum est et in aggere fatum. Quæ nullis4) longum ostendit cervicibus aurum Consulit ante phalas, delphinorumque columnas, An saga vendenti nubat, caupone relicto.

e: While the rich turn for divination to the Phrygian augur or to Indian Brahmans, and buy their oracles with money, the plebeian woman, whose neck no costly jewelry covers, goes to the circus, and there inquires of the eggs and dolphins the voice of fate concerning her future husband. Phale designates the ὠοειδῆ δημιουργήματα of Dio Cassius. If only eggs can be associated with the dolphins, then also everything that the ancients remark about Falæ proves a fundamental meaning that finds its full application in the ovoid form of those Demiurgemata. According to Nonnus 2, 114, Fala is turris lignea, according to Servius Aen. 9, 705 simply turris. Festus: Falæ dictæ ab altitudine, a falando, quod apud Etruscos significat cælum. Among the Greeks we find φάλαι, which Hesychius explains as ὄρη, σκοπιαί. Thus we arrive, for fala, at the meaning of a rounded elevation, at the top, of a body projecting above the surface of the earth, and this it is that enables the word also to designate those ὠοειδῆ δημιουργήματα. Unmistakable is its kinship with palus, stake, φαλλός, and the divus pater Falacer. The stake that rises out of the earth, the conical stone formed like an omphalos, is the image and expression of the generative natural force that penetrates the matter of the earth. In φαλλός both relations lie united: the external one of elevation, according to which the phallic Dionysus is called ὀρθός,1) and the internal one of the generative force, which finds its expression in that image. Falacer is accordingly a god of the generative natural force represented in phallus form, which is confirmed by his association with Pomona.2) A perfectly corresponding parallel is furnished by Τύλος; for in this word too the meanings of a bulging elevation, and of the male generative force represented by it, are united, concerning which I refer to a special section of my Mutterrecht. Accordingly I do not doubt that by his falæ Juvenal understood the scaffolds crowned with the seven egg-shaped rounded bodies, as we see them represented on the sarcophagi mentioned. e: her marriage, while the rich women buy by large payment the favorable pronouncement of a foreign charlatan. That precisely the eggs and the dolphins, the animals of the generative Neptunus, are used for such a divination is explained by itself in the light of what was remarked earlier. As ἀρχὴ γενέσεως the egg stands in the closest relation to marriage and generation. Among the superstitiones that Cassiodorus mentions, the practice of the women of the lower people alluded to by Juvenal may also be included. The ovi exemplo geniturum se avem shows that the original significance of the egg lived on still in popular tradition. It appears in the circus also as ἀρχὴ γενέσεως, and can for this very reason be brought into so close a connection with the egg of the Cerealian pompa. It is in the circus too a representation of the female natural principle, and older than the bird-birth that breaks forth from it, winged and swiftly flying onward, like the quadriga from the carceres, in unconquerable desire of becoming. This is the idea that Cassiodorus recognizes in the connection of the egg with the circuit of the chariots. The race itself, he says — for this is what is to be understood by actus — gives us to know that from each of the erected eggs a lightly winged bird-birth will emerge. The swiftly flying four-horse team appears here as the image of egg-birth. As the bird breaks through the shell of the egg and, freed from its enclosure, tries the force of its wings, so the four-horse team storms forth, impatiently and with winged course, from the carceres that enclose and restrain it, and thereby gives us to know what relation the erected and removed egg has to the race itself. If in this connection the original significance of the egg and its relation to the circus games have been preserved with remarkable purity, then, on the other hand, the relation of the swift flight of the quadriga, compared to the bird, to fickleness of customs is a continuation and development of the fundamental idea which does not belong to it at all, and had its occasion in the conditions of the later time. The effect of the circus games, that is Cassiodorus’s idea, consists in this, that they make the customs of the people like those of birds. Volitantes atque inconstantissimi inde mores nascuntur. In the words that follow, instead of avium maribus, avium moribus is to be read. The whole connection of this passage, so little understood hitherto, is now clear. Cassiodorus says in the context the following: the erection of the eggs, whose successive removal corresponds to the individual circuits, is as little without meaning as everything else that the circus and its games offer us. Manifold superstition attaches itself to the relation of the egg to the race. In my opinion the birth of a bird is indicated to us by the egg, and the [PDF 239] — 225 — circuit of the four-horse team is itself the image of this event. But at the same time we are also taught what influence the circus games exert on customs. The life of the people becomes like that of birds, fickle and inconstant, like that of the restless and unresting winged inhabitants of the air. In this sense too, from the eggs of the circus, insofar as they direct the games and announce their actual undertaking, a race of birds is born, namely the fickle and inconstant people itself that looks on at them. From the testimonies considered so far the following propositions result. The eggs stand in an inner connection with the circus games. Their setting up had, to be sure, also an external purpose, namely to remove every doubt about the number of completed circuits, and to give both the competitors themselves and the spectators certainty about it at every moment. To attain this purpose it was also indispensable to have ovoid bodies, artificially made and of considerable size, set up on a high scaffold instead of the all too small natural eggs. But this external purpose by no means exhausts the relation of the egg to the circus and its games. This could just as well have been achieved by some other objects. If eggs in particular were chosen, and from of old, the ground of such a choice rests in the religious significance of the egg itself. To each circuit of the meta corresponds an egg. At each circuit one of them is removed. This inner relation of the egg to the racing was not entirely obscured even in later times. In many a superstitious practice of the people, particularly of its lower, plebeian classes, the old consciousness lived on, and so far as we see from Cassiodorus, from Juvenal, and from Varro, it was always the thought of the maternal, Cerealian primal principle of tellurian creation, of marriage and birth, of the female ἀρχὴ γενέσεως, that found its expression, now purer, now more unclear and obscured, in such popular views. It is now our task to bring fully into the light the original idea that governs the connection of the eggs with the circus games. Earlier remarks have long since led him who followed my exposition to the right path. I recall here in particular what has been remarked about the Dioscuri and the Elean Molionidae. Both pairs of brothers have sprung from the mother egg. Both are distinguished by the unattainable swiftness with which they fly along on horse and chariot. As mighty racers and charioteers they come forth from the maternal primal egg. If in this the seed of all things lay enclosed in the deepest rest, now from the opened shell the visible creation emerges, and in this everything is 15

e: restless, eternal motion. The life of tellurian generation endures no standstill. In it everything comes to be and passes away. It was of this that Heraclitus, according to Aristotle, Metaphysics 4, 5, 26, used the image of the river, saying that one cannot step twice into the same river, to which Cratylus replied with censure that one cannot do so even once. Of this too the physicists asserted that, because of the eternal flux of the world of the senses, nothing at all could be said about it, and that existence in general must rather be denied it. Between two poles material life moves. Its realm is not that of being but of becoming and passing away, of the eternal alternation of two colors, the white of life and the black of death.1) Only through the equal mixture of the two is the continuance of the material world secured. Without death no rejuvenation is possible, and in the eternal labor of nature the destroying force is no less indispensable to the preservation of ever-young life than the creative and generative one. Indeed, at no moment can the positive force subsist without the negative. Only what the latter dissolves can the former restore. Death is therefore not the opposite but the helper of life, just as the negative pole of magnetism forms not the opposite of the positive but rather its necessary complement, without which the latter too would at once vanish, and life would have to yield to nothingness.2) Two forces, then, govern tellurian creation and by their cooperation assure the progress of things. Together they were born. As twin brothers they go forth from the same egg. At equal pace they run side by side. A two-horse team they have mounted; it is their doubled effort, directed to the same goal, that assures them invincible speed. Actor’s sons, the Molionidae, owe the victory of their team precisely to this united effort. Swift as an arrow it flies along. Swift as an arrow, too, is the course of the tellurian world of appearance. The rapidity with which the two united forces sweep creation onward has found its expression in the speed of the chariot that the Molionidae drive. In the progress of the motion the team always returns again to its point of departure, like the circular line, whose completion is lost in the Euripides recalls in the Ion, 1007–1023. Pallas gives Erichthonius two drops of the blood of the dying Gorgon. The one brings death, the other healing. Highly expressive too is Vitruvius’s account, 8, 3, of the tomb that Archelaus erected to Euripides. It lay at the confluence of two streams, of which the one contained deadly water, the other healing water.

e: beginning. If one of the forces drives straight ahead, the other turns aside and leads back again. The completion of every existence is a return to its beginning, and in every distance from the point of departure there lies at the same time a renewed approach to it. Two directions are bound together in a manner just as inexplicable as the two forces themselves to which they correspond. The result of their combined force is the circular course in which all tellurian life eternally moves. The image of this circular course is the circuits of the chariots, which with the utmost speed fly around the metae in order to return to the point of departure, and then to traverse the same space anew. By this two things are now made clear: first, the connection of the egg with the chariot racing of the circus; second, the correspondence that connects the completion of each single circuit with the removal of one egg at a time. If the ἀρχὴ γενέσεως lies enclosed in the egg, the two-horse team shows the motion of the creation that has stepped into the light from the womb of matter. With each return to the point of departure the circuit of one existence is completed, and a new one is about to begin. Come into being, grown, vanished is the offspring of one egg; a new one takes the place of the one removed, and so in the unforeseeable series of the generations there follows always one after another, always the brood of one egg after that of the other, and always with that unattainable speed which is presented to us in the myth of the Molionidae as the result of the union of two forces, of two twin brothers uniting their effort. Now it is clear what we indicated above: how close Cassiodorus’s thought, actus ipse, ovi exemplo, geniturum se avem profitetur, is to the original and true significance of the circus egg. The team bursting forth from the carceres is rightly represented as an egg-birth. As the chick from the egg, so the team hastens winged out of the prison that until now set bounds to its lust for becoming. What was hidden becomes visible; what was motionless passes now into restless haste. With the first moment of existence begins that unrest which forms so decided a contrast to the stillness and immobility that formerly reigned in the egg. So Pegasus, the winged horse, breaks forth neighing from the Gorgon’s bleeding trunk; so the black horse of the Phigalians from the womb of Ceres,1) so the wild Scythius, whom the scholiast to Pindar, P. 4, 246 calls Σκύφιος, from the depths of the earth, like the water of the spring, which from its source onward, never resting, never pausing, rolls wave upon wave in hurrying haste.2) Not meaningless [PDF 242] — 228 — in fact is the erection of the eggs in the circus. Nec illud putetur irritum, quod metarum circuitus ovorum erectionibus exprimatur. The idea of generation from maternal primal matter, the birth of a chick that comes into the light only to succumb very soon to the law of matter, governs the circus egg no less than the one that is carried at the head of the Cerealian pompa. The people watching the games recognizes in the swift flight of the teams, and in the corresponding disappearance of the upraised eggs, the spectacle that all tellurian life presents, the law that governs its own existence; and when it awards the palm of victory to the one who surpasses the others in speed, it confesses thereby that the highest glory of a people and of every individual man consists not in the longest duration of existence, not in the longest possible prolongation of it, but in the mightiest unfolding of force, which is always accompanied by the swiftest consuming. Into his description of the Roman circus Tertullian de spectac. 8 has taken the remark: ova honori Castorum attribuunt. We see from this that our juxtaposition of the circus games and their eggs with the Dioscuri and with the mother egg, from which the mounted, swift-footed twins, the brother-kings of creation, to whom the horse is consecrated, issued, was fully justified. Though the relation of the circus egg to that of Leda-Nemesis may seem no less arbitrary than the similar relation of that egg which hung from the roof, bound in fillets, in the Laconian temple of the Leucippides, yet the whole fullness of the idea that lies in the circus egg is nevertheless thereby quite rightly brought out. The alternation of life and death, the night that takes the day into itself in order to give birth to it again, rejuvenated, out of itself, the speed that irresistibly sweeps on the stream of life as soon as it has once emerged into the light from the mother egg: all this is the physical fundamental idea of the Leda egg and its twin birth, all this too the content of the circus games and their eggs. 19.

o: Der Gedankenkreis, in welchem sich diese Vorstellungen bewegen , beherrscht auch alle übrigen Theile des Circus, alle damit verbundenen Heiligthümer, Kulte und Einrichtungen. Die Naturkraft in ihrer dreifachen, tellurischen, lunarischen, solarischen Stufenfolge, in ihrer doppelten, weiblich-passiven, männlich-aktiven Potenzirung, in ihrer zwiefahen Aeußerung als belebende und als zerstörende Mat, hat in dem römischen Circus eine so vollkommene und so mannigfaltige Darstellung gefunden, daß er als wahres Pantheon gelten und von den Kirchen [PDF 243]  vätern den Gläubigen ihrer Zeit vokzugsweise al8 unrein und sorgsam zu meidende Stätte der heidnishen Dämonenwelt bezeichnet werden konnte. ') Hat das weibliche Naturprinzip in Murtia, in Cybele, in der Muttertrias Seia Segetia Tutilina in Pollentia, Libera, Ceres einen die aphroditische sowohl als die cerealische Stufe des stofflihen Lebens umfassenden Aus drus erhalten, 2) so ist die männlich zeugende, lebenerweckende und befruchtende Potenz als tellurische Wasserkraft in Consus-Neptunus, als himmlische Lichtmacht dagegen in den Obelisken und manhen andern Einzelnheiten, auf welche wir später zurükfkommen, zu erkennen. Die Verbindung der tellurishen und der solarishen Stufe der Naturkraft ist eine Erscheinung, die besondere Beachtung verlangt. Scwierigkeiten vermag sie uns nicht mehr zu bereiten. Haben wir doh jene beiden Grade der Naturzeugungskraft selbst in einer und derselben Gottheitsgestalt verbunden gesehen, AHill, Dionysos und manche andere Götter als Träger der tellurischen Wassermacht, zugleih aber auch als Herrn des himmlischen Lichts erkannt, und die scheinbare Unverträglichkeit des Wassers und Feuers von den Alten selbst als eine auf dem Gebiete der Mythologie nicht zulässige Behauptung bestritten gefunden. 3) Die männlichezeugende Kraft beruht auf mehr als einem Faktor. Ihre physische Grundlage ist das himmlische Liht nicht minder als die Feuchtigkeit der Tiefe. Aus der vereinten Einwirkung auf den weiblichen Erdstoff geht alle tellurische Fruchtbarkeit hervor. Doch wird auf den verschiedenen Stufen der religiösen Entwicklung bald die <thonische, bald die uranishe Mat, bald das Wasser, bald das Licht, bald das neptunische , bald das solarische Element in den Vordergrund treten. Einer stofflihern und darum tiefern Auffassung gilt das Wasser, einer unstofflihern und darum reinern Anschauungsweise das immaterielle, gewichtlose Sonnenliht als Siß und Träger der befruchtenden Kraft. In den Heiligthümern und Kulten des römischen Circus erscheinen die f) Tertall. 3pectac. 8, Quot igitur in habitu loci ipsius idolatrias recognoscis ? -- Animadyverte, Christiane, quot numina immunda possederint circum.
e: The circle of thought in which these conceptions move governs also all the other parts of the circus, all the sanctuaries, cults, and institutions connected with it. Natural force in its threefold, tellurian, lunar, solar sequence of stages, in its twofold, female-passive, male-active potentiation, in its twofold expression as vivifying and as destroying power, found in the Roman circus a representation so perfect and so manifold that it could count as a true pantheon and be designated by the Church Fathers [PDF 243] — 229 — to the believers of their time preeminently as an unclean place of the pagan world of demons, to be carefully avoided.1) If the female natural principle has received in Murtia, in Cybele, in the mother triad Seia Segetia Tutilina, in Pollentia, Libera, Ceres an expression embracing both the Aphroditean and the Cerealian stage of material life,2) the male generative potency, which awakens life and fecundates, is to be recognized as tellurian force of water in Consus-Neptunus, but as heavenly power of light, on the other hand, in the obelisks and in many other details to which we shall return later. The connection of the tellurian and the solar stage of natural force is a phenomenon that demands particular attention. It can no longer cause us difficulties. For have we not seen those two degrees of the force of natural generation united in one and the same divine figure? Achilles, Dionysus, and many other gods we recognized as bearers of the tellurian power of water and at the same time as lords of the heavenly light, and the apparent incompatibility of water and fire we found disputed by the ancients themselves as an assertion not admissible in the domain of mythology.3) The male-generative force rests on more than one factor. Its physical foundation is the heavenly light no less than the moisture of the depths. From their united action on the female matter of the earth all tellurian fertility proceeds. Yet on the different stages of religious development now the chthonian, now the uranian power, now the water, now the light, now the Neptunian, now the solar element will come to the fore. To a more material, and therefore deeper, conception, water counts, to a less material, and therefore purer, way of viewing, the immaterial, weightless sunlight counts as the seat and bearer of the fecundating force. In the sanctuaries and cults of the Roman circus there appear the Christiane, quot numina immunda possederint circum. August. C. D. 4, 8. e: Neptunian and the solar stage of force side by side, and while some of the ancients declare Neptune to be the lord,1) others with equal decisiveness bring Sol into the foreground and perceive in the individual institutions of the circus a preeminently solar relation.2) Neither of these two conceptions may be denied or diminished in its significance. The tellurian-Neptunian element maintains its significance to the last, and is by no means displaced by the ever more decided emphasis on the solar. To the female primal egg there stands at the side, as the representation of the awakening potency, a chthonian male god, who rules and works in the moist depths of matter, hidden in the darkness of the earth, a true Zeus Arcanus, comparable to the Puer Jupiter Anxurus,3) a demon of the phallic force, from whom Murcia expects her fecundation, a god of hidden counsels. Subterranean is his altar, Neptunian his nature, his physical foundation the moisture that penetrates the depths of the earth, his consecrated animal the horse, the image of the generative waters, the games celebrated in his honor true Ἱπποκράτεια or Equiria.4) In the moist valley between the Aventine and the Palatine munera, Saturno attributa sunt, ludi scenici Libero, Circenses Neptuno. — Salvianus 8: Colitur Minerva in gymnasiis, Venus in theatris, Neptunus in circis, Mars in arenis, Mercurius in palæstris. — Serv. On this custom Plutarch, Qu. rom. 45 — Consus seems to go back to Consivius, the name under which Janus was invoked, and thus to conserere, physical fecundation. Thus [PDF 245] — 231 — Murcia, a primal mother conceived as Aphroditean, had her cult. The luxuriant meadowland bore the stone of the gods, the Metæ Murciæ, and the neighboring Aventine itself the name Murcus. As a chthonian demon Consus stood at the mother’s side, as Eros stands beside Aphrodite, whom she addresses in Virgil as mea magna potentia. He is her Virbius, her Adonis, her Euamerion, her Sosipolis, the beloved and fecundator without whom Murcia can do nothing; he dwells with her in the depths, rests in her womb, apud metas sub terra delitescit. This place Tarquin chose for the erection of his circus, and there can hardly be any doubt that it was precisely the veneration, native to that valley, of Murcia and her πάρεδρος Consus that determined the choice. The stage of religion to which this cult, and the games now entering into connection with it, belong, can be subject to no doubt. It is the tellurian-Neptunian, which conceives the force itself as chthonian power of water. The horse and chariot races held in its honor are, in agreement with this conception of the force itself, celebrated preferably in luxuriant moist meadowlands, on the banks of brooks and rivers. The proximity of that element which was regarded as the seat of the force, as the bearer of the generative Lar of the earth, had itself to appear as the presence of the deity, and when now on the bank the swift horses flew by, as Pindar emphasizes of the Elean games in the first Olympian Ode, one could see in the turning of the wheels, in the hurrying stride of the foaming racers an image of the water itself, which in the midst of an immovable nature alone enjoys the privilege of unstoppable haste. The connection of the circus games with water, with rivers, swamps, moist grassy lowlands emerges everywhere, and especially at Rome. e: the Equiria were celebrated on his meadow in the lowland of the Tiber. The swampy, grassy plain, which the river fecundates with its yellowish waters and which it also often inundates with its floods, was assigned to the god preeminently as his property. Here his games were held. Within sight of the river the horses raced, the image of the water, the symbol of the god (ἵππιον ὕδωρ, Nonnus 41, 229). The river itself wreathed the course, while swords, the divine image of Mars, were planted as metae.1) According to the same idea Virgil, Georg. 3, 13–20, promises to hold games for the emperor on the green meadow on the bank of the Mincius, a hundred four-horse chariots. Greece will give up the Alpheus and hasten to Mantua. Et viridi in campo templum de marmore ponam Propter aquam, tardis ingens ubi flexibus errat Mincius, et tenera prætexit arundine ripas. e: looks on at the game.1) Horse, chariot, wheel have a Neptunian relation to water. The victorious right-hand horse falls to the god as a sacrifice. The bleeding trunk is fastened to the wall of the Regia and adorned with rings of bread, images of the blessing of the harvest, which one also provided with the sign of the wheel.2) The rivers and the chariot races were bound together by so close a relation that even such games as were held at a distance from water were nevertheless thought of in connection with it. At Anagnia there is a circus maritimus. Liv. 9, 42. Concilium populorum omnium habentibus Anagninis in Circo, quem maritimum vocant. But Anagnia is an inland town in the land of the Hernici; the designation of its circus as maritimus is therefore not geographical but sacral. It contains the acknowledgment that the circus games are dedicated to the generative element of water, whether it appear as Neptunus, as Consus, or as Mars. It is possible that a small body of water that lay nearby, or was purposely led thither for the purpose, was given the name mare. This would have fully accorded with ancient practice. So we find in Plutarch de virtt. mull. in fine an example in which a tomb was brought into connection with water by an artificial conduit, because it was customary to erect for the dead their resting place on the bank of the life-generating element. So too in Lydia, according to Pausanias 1, p. 87, a little stream bore the name Oceanus, and its connection with the tomb of Geryon shows that one actually saw in it the image of the great Ocean. In connection with the circus maritimus of the Anagnians I wish to point to a report about the sign of the wheel: Festus, p. 348. Summanalia, liba farinacea in modum rotæ ficta. On this, Passeri, pict. Etr. 3, 282 sqq. Zoëga de obeliscis 228. Hesych. Ἐλασιβρόντα. How much attention must be paid to the form given to the festival cakes is shown by many reports, among others Plutarch de Is. et Osiride. The wheel belongs among the most significant symbols of antiquity, and therefore already among the ancients, as Clement reports in the Protrepticus, occasioned special treatments. Whoever collects the particulars will find that it, like the majority of symbols, has first of all a physical meaning, and embraces in this all sides of natural force, the chthonian-Poseidonian and the heavenly-solar, hence both that of swift passing away and that of becoming, but that one then advanced from the physical to the abstract, figurative meaning, as it emerges especially in the wheel of Nemesis. The more exact discussion does not belong here, but in an account of the ancient symbolic language, for whose knowledge the time since Payne Knight, on symbolical language, has furnished all too little. — On Summanus, whom the Glossarium Labb. explains by Προμηθεύς, see Martian. Ἔχελος ἥρως. ὡς δὲ ἔνιοι, ἐπίθετον ἥρωος, ἐπὶ τοῦ ἕλος παρακεῖσθαι τῷ ἥρῳ. ἔστιν δὲ ὁ Ἀθηναίων ἱππόδρομος Ἐνεχελιδών. ἐν ᾧ ἱππικοὶ ἤγοντο ἀγῶνες. καὶ ναὸς Ἴλου. — Etymol. magn. Ἐνεχελιδώ, τόπος Ἀθήνησι, σταδίων ὀκτώ, ἐν ᾧ αἱ ἱπποδρομίαι. ἀπό τινος Ἐχέλου. Cf. s. v. Ἔχελος. There was, then, a Heroon of Echelus, which lay on the shore of a swamp lake. The Heroon itself formed a part of the Athenian hippodrome, which accordingly bore the name Enechelidon. The chariot race thus took place in the neighborhood of a body of water, and was held in honor of the generative Consus-Echelus who rules in the swamp. The name itself is without doubt connected with ἕλος, as Ἴλος with ἰλύς. So too Euripides in the Hippolytus, 207–210, 213, joins lake and racecourse, and places both under the protection of Artemis. On the seashore Hippolytus drives his team of horses along, when Poseidon’s bull brought him destruction. For this reason Euripides, lines 1072–1074, has the chorus sing that henceforth the Amazon’s son will no longer guide the Enetian racers, no longer hold, on the lake, with the swift horse the circuit of the racecourses. In the beautiful description of the Greek camp that is found in the Iphigenia Aulidensis, Achilles is depicted as he, the fleet racer, on the sandy seashore leaves the four-horse team behind in the run. Lines 204–212. Indeed, in the Ἀχιλέως δρόμοι the river beds themselves appear as racecourses, as indeed the name and conception of Achilles demonstrate the complete identity of the course of the world and the motion of water. Now we shall also appreciate the whole weight of the remark of the scholiast on Pindar’s ἄριστον μὲν ὕδωρ, when he emphasizes that the poet’s thought runs thus: as water occupies the first place among the elements, so too the Olympian agon, consecrated to the water of the Alpheus, has greater dignity than all the other contests of the Hellenes.

e: A very remarkable example of the retention of the Neptunian relation, even for such circus games as were celebrated at a distance from water, is furnished by the ludi capitolini, as they appear on two glass images communicated by Buonarroti, osservazioni sopra alcuni frammenti di vasi antichi di vetro, ornati di figure, trovati nei Cimiteri di Roma, Firenze 1716, plates 30, 31. On both the victors of the Capitolina are represented with all the attributes of a river god. I wish to describe here in more detail the picture of plate 30. With the upper body half bared the victor reclines, with his right hand grasping a bundle of reeds, in his left the cornucopia. The left arm rests on an overturned vase from which a rich stream of water wells forth. At the victor’s side, with her left arm embracing the man’s shoulder, sits a female figure, whose significance we shall discuss afterward. Beside her, closing the picture, there appears, overtopped by tall reed stalks, a boy’s figure, who [PDF 249] — 235 — in his gathered garment offers fruits of the most various kinds to the victorious pair. Three little winged genii fill the air above the heads of the reclining figures. One hovers above the victor’s head. The bellied vessel that he holds bears on its front the inscription ΚΑΠΕΘ, as proof that the victory celebrated here was won in the Capitoline games. In the hands of the second of the genii one sees an open garland of flowers, which likewise is being offered to the victor. The third, finally, carries in his arms a bundle of rods, which seem to me to have much less the appearance of palm branches than of swamp stalks. Around the upper curve of the picture one reads the acclamation: — — RIS VIVAS VALEAS VINCAS. — RIS evidently forms only the final syllable of the name, whose beginning has become illegible. Except for quite slight differences, the picture of plate 31 (our pl. Romulus. Plutarch Quest. rom. 50 connects the custom, still observed in his time, of setting up and offering for sale Sardians at the Capitoline games with the war of Romulus against Veii. In Tertullian de spectac. 5 Romulus is expressly named as the first organizer of the Capitoline games. Dehinc idem Romulus Jovi Feretrio ludos instituit in Tarpeio, quos Tarpeios dictos et Capitolinos Piso tradidit; post hunc Numa Pompilius Marti et Robigini fecit (nam et Robiginis Deam finxerunt); dehinc Tullus Hostilius, dehinc Ancus Martius et ceteri, qui quotque per ordinem et quibus idolis ludos instituerint, positum est apud Suetonium Tranquillum, vel a quibus Tranquillus accepit. Fest. v. Sardi venales. After the departure of the Gauls, among other religious ordinances the holding of the Capitoline games was also decreed. Liv. 5, 50: ludi Capitolini fierent, quod Jupiter optimus maximus suam sedem atque arcem populi romani in re trepida tutatus esset; collegiumque ad eam rem M. Furius dictator constitueret ex iis, qui in Capitolio atque arce habitarent. These Capitolini are also mentioned elsewhere. Cic. ad Quint. fratr. 2, 5. That the Capitoline games were celebrated in honor of Jupiter, Tertull. de spect. 11 emphasizes once more: Olympia Jovi, quæ sunt Romæ Capitolina. Plin. 27, 7 gives the following report: De usu eius (apsinthi) convenit, herbæ facillimæ atque inter paucas utilissimæ, præterea sacris populi Romani celebratæ peculiariter; siquidem Latinarum feriis quadrigæ certant in Capitolio victorque absinthium bibit, credo, sanitatem in præmio dari honorifice arbitratis majoribus. Here we are informed of a custom that can solve for us the riddle of the purpose of those glass vessels. Might they not have been intended to hand to the victor the drink of absinthium? Pliny’s remark, Sanitatem in præmio dari, agrees perfectly with the acclamation Vivas valeas vincas. On the relation of [PDF 250] — 236 — of that god. He assumes the nature and form of that deity in whose honor the games are celebrated. Thus what we remarked above is perfectly confirmed: games of a circus nature, even where their celebration does not take place on a riverbank, are nevertheless always thought of in connection with the element of water and with rivers, just as the currus too contains a decidedly Neptunian relation.1) That the ludi Capitolini are now traced back preeminently to the Alpheius, that river which Elis especially venerated and which it set in the closest connection with the divine force of Zeus,2) gives the glass paintings mentioned a still higher significance. This too finds its justification in other reports. The Olympia and the Capitolina are put together by Tertullian de spectac. 11. Olympia Jovi, quæ sunt Romæ Capitolina. Likewise by Cassius Dio 79, 10. Also the custom of depicting the victor himself, as we find it here for the Capitoline games, derives from Olympia, as Pausanias and Plinius 34, 4 inform us. But not only the Capitoline games, but all circus games in general are traced back to the model of the Olympian celebration and to Pelops and Oenomaus. Thus Cassiodor 3, 51 introduces his remarks on the circus games with the words: Primus enim hoc apud Elidem Asiæ civitatem Oenomaus fertur edidisse, quod postea Romulus in raptu Sabinarum, necdum fundatis ædificiis, ruraliter ostentavit Italiæ. Similarly Sidonius Apollinar. Carm. 23: Elei simulacra torva campi exercent spatiantibus quadrigis. Nonni Dion. 19, 150. οὐ δρόμος ἱπποσύνης, οὐκ Ἤλιδος εἰσὶν ἀγῶνες, οὐ δρόμος Οἰνομάου γαμβροκτόνος. On the well-known words of Horace: Metaque fervidis evitata rotis, Acron remarks: Circenses agonici in honorem Jovis Olympici sunt inventi apud Elidem. See besides Virgil. Georg. 3, 13–20. 180 and Dionys. Hal. 7, 73. To the same idea is joined the choice of Alpheus as the image of the victor of the Capitoline Sanitas to the celebration of the games and to the religious idea contained in it will be spoken of later. — The Capitolina received a renewed significance through Domitian. Sueton, Domit. 4: Instituit et quinquennale certamen Capitolino Jovi triplex, musicum, equestre, gymnicum et aliquanto plurium, quam nunc est, coronatorum. In this new form they were first celebrated in the twelfth year of the emperor’s reign, in A.D. 86. Later their mention is not rare. They occur often on inscriptions and coins, on which Scaliger on c. 4 of Domitian and Buonarroti pp. 219–220 are to be consulted.
