e: games. This one is thereby traced back to Pelops. From this the female figure is explained who, on our glass pictures, is depicted at the side of the Capitoline victor, lovingly embracing him. To take her merely generally as the victor’s consort, and to explain her embrace as an expression of joy over the prize carried off, would by no means exhaust the idea. Rather we have here to recognize Hippodamia, won by Pelops in the race with Oenomaus, and thereby released from her father’s hands and restored to her higher female destiny. A youthful consort must stand at the victor’s side, if the model of the Olympian agon is to be completely recognized in the Capitoline games and their prize vessel.1) Thereby the games themselves appear as the foundation of the first higher culture, grounded in agriculture and marriage, and it gains heightened significance when the Capitolina are traced back to the founder of the Roman state and of marriage with the Sabine daughters, as the Olympia are to the union of Pelops with the daughter of Oenomaus. The Achaean Pelops for his part leads back again to Asia, especially to Lydia; for Pelops is called a Lydian.2) Now, that the chariot races were known to the Lydians is attested by a very remarkable proof preserved in the myth of the meeting of Gyges and Lixus.3) From the Lydian emigrants, moreover, the ancients derive the naturalization of the circus games in Etruria,4) and from there an Etruscan prince brought them to the Romans. Thus an immediate connection between Rome and Asia is established, and the tracing back of the Capitoline games to the Lydian Pelops and his victory in the plain of the Alpheus, the swampy Elean lowland, is explained also by the historical connection of the lands and peoples. In view of these occurrences the Neptunian relation of the Roman circus and of the games celebrated in it no longer appears as an isolated phenomenon, but rather as an expression of that general idea which assigns to the generative force its seat in the tellurian waters. To this element point the dolphins, whose connection with the eggs now her the sovereignty, forms the prize of victory in so many examples. Cf. e: explains itself. Delphinos Neptuno vovent, says Tertull. de spectac. 8. In the circus the god of the generative waters appears not in anthropomorphic form but in the shape of a fish, as indeed the cult practices and cult representations of the circus have remained faithful preeminently to an earlier, more ancient, more original stage of religion. With the dolphins Cassiodor 3, 51 connects the mention of the Euripus. Euripus maris vitrei reddit imaginem, unde illic delphini equorei aquas interfluunt. By Euripus is here understood not an actual water channel but rather the intermetium, the spina, which extended between the two metae in the middle of the circus and divided it lengthwise into two halves. One must conceive it as an agger held by two side walls, on whose height were set up the many objects required for the celebration of the sacred games, and the images of the gods, among them especially Cybele, præses Euripi, and the tres aræ.1) If now this earthen dam is nevertheless conceived as an image of the sea, and brought into connection with the dolphins, those inhabitants of the waters, well disposed to man and distinguished by the greatest speed, there lies in this again an idea corresponding to the original maritime nature of the circuses. In elaboration of the same thought the Euripus of the circus was compared with that Euripus which separates Euboea from the mainland of Boeotia. The sevenfold ebb and flow that drives the water of the strait up and down seemed to correspond to the sevenfold circuit of the teams, to the seven eggs and seven dolphins, and to express perfectly the thought of the waves of existence flowing eternally back into themselves. Εὔριπος ὠνομάσθη ἡ μέση τοῦ ἱπποδρόμου κρηπὶς ἐκ τοῦ θαλαττίου Εὐρίπου, καὶ τῆς ἑπτάκις αὐτοῦ διαυλοδρομίας· οὕτω γὰρ ἐπ᾽ ἐκείνου φασὶ συμβαίνειν. So Joannes Lydus, p. 4, Schow. οὐδὲ ἡ τῶν ὑδάτων φύσις ἔξω τῆς δυνάμεως τῆς ἑπτάδος ἀπολέλειπται· ὁ γοῦν Διονύσιος ἐν ταῖς Κτίσεσι φησί, τὸν χαλκιδικὸν Εὔριπον, ἑπτάκις καθ᾽ ἡμέραν στρεφόμενον, κατὰ μόνας τὰς ἑβδομάδας ἵστασθαι. p. 28 Schow. Other passages of like content are given by Salmasius p. 638. In fact Seneca in Hercule Oetæo sets up the sevenfold flood of the Euripus as the rule: Euripus undas flectit instabiles vagus Septemque cursus flectit, et totidem refert. Greek authors, such as Joannes Antiochensis and Cedrenus (in Salmasius p. 638), explain the name euripus from the similarity which the spina seemed to them to have with water enclosed on both sides by the mainland. Gregory Nazianzen, on the other hand, mentions for the circus of Constantinople a [PDF 253] — 239 — subterranean hidden water channel that could justify that designation: ἱππικὰ βασίλεια καὶ κάλλη στοῶν, καὶ τὸ ἄπυστον τοῦτο ἔργον ὁ ὑποχθόνιος καὶ ἀέριος ποταμὸς, καὶ ὁ λαμπρὸς στύλος οὑτοσὶ καὶ ἀπόβλεπτος. According to Suidas in Σεβήρῳ the Byzantine hippodrome moreover contained a lavacrum Zeuxippi, which Ismenius and Manasses also praise as an especially beautiful work. Its connection with the Draconteum and with a seated Athena justify the comparison of this Zeuxippus with Erichthonius, the serpent-footed demon of the tellurian waters, to whom the four-horse team is traced back in a very significant manner.1) Through all these particulars the essential connection of the circus games with the tellurian waters receives ever new confirmation.2) Indeed, their relation to the fertility of the land and to the blessing of the harvest remained, down to the latest times, in the consciousness of the pagan world. It is very remarkable that ideas of tellurian fertility were also connected with the colors that the contestants wore, and that one especially observed in the choice of the horses, and that relations to the causæ elementorum were found. Not only did one relate the colors themselves to the seasons and to those elements which become important precisely for the yield of the crops; one saw also in the victory of the individual colors the omens of the coming blessing of the harvest or of impending infertility. Especially noteworthy is a saying of Joannes Antiochensis, which one finds with several similar ones in Salmasius p. 634: ἐβάλλοντο κλῆροι, καὶ ὃς ἔλαχεν ὑπὲρ τῆς γῆς ἀγωνίσασθαι ἐφόρει χλοανόν, ὃς δὲ ὑπὲρ τῆς θαλάσσης κυανόν. ἐπετίθει δὲ Οἰνόμαος ἔπαθλον τὴν ἑαυτοῦ θυγατέρα, καὶ ὁ νικηθεὶς ὑπὸ τοῦ πλήθους τῶν θεωμένων ἀνῃρεῖτο. Εἶχον οὖν σημεῖον οἱ τότε, καὶ εἰ μὲν τὸ χλοανὸν ἐνίκα τῆς γῆς εὐφορίαν ἤλπιζον καὶ οὕτως ἐγίνετο. εἰ δὲ τὸ κυανόν, τῆς θαλάττης εὔπλοιαν, καὶ ηὔχοντο οἱ μὲν γεωργοὶ τὸ χλοανὸν νικᾶν, οἱ δὲ ναύτιλοι τὸ κυανόν. Even if the individual presuppositions, combinations, and meanings of the colors, about which one finds much in Tertullian de spect. 9 and Isidor Orig. 18, 41, appear wholly arbitrary and without justified foundation, nevertheless the idea of a general connection of the circus games with the fertility of the earth, and the belief in it, so deeply rooted and bound up with passionate outbursts that Cassiodor also describes, Lydus p. 4, Apuleius Metam. 6, p. 123. According to Nardini 3, p. 245, the remains of this sanctuary were discovered tra il cerchio massimo e’l monte Aventino. Now near the Porta Capena, thus quite close to that temple, lay the Aqua Mercurii, on which Ovid F. 5, 670–692. Thus here too the connection of the circus with water is shown, and it is explained why, according to Stesichorus’s account, the Dioscuri receive their horses from Hermes.

If we sum up these discussions, they yield a result that agrees perfectly with the significance of the eggs developed above. If these appeared to us as the ἀρχὴ γενέσεως, destined to let all things of visible creation issue from their dark womb in a never-ending succession of generations, then the deities of the circus that surround them, and the games that accompany them, are a representation of the great forces whose action on the maternal matter of the earth completes the work of fecundation and of the eternal rejuvenation of all things. In this direction of the circus games toward the generative, life-giving force, the opposite direction toward the destroying and annihilating potency is necessarily included. Thereby the races become true funeral rites, and this their somber side comes to the fore the more, the more, in the conception of the force itself, Neptunian tellurism had retained its significance. In Consus, in Summanus, in the Canicidium, in the Dii magni, valentes, potentes,2) the relation to death emerges very definitely. But quite generally too the funerary significance of the ancient festal games is emphasized, so by Tertullian de spectac. 6: Nam et a primordio bifariam ludi censebantur, sacri et funebres, id est Diis nationum et mortuis. Sed de idolatria nil differt apud nos, sub quo nomine et titulo, dum ad eosdem spiritus perveniat, quibus renuntiamus, licet mortuis licet Diis suis faciant. Proinde mortuis suis ut Diis faciant. So too by Cyprianus de spectac. p. 3. ed. Joannes Cistert. Quis ludus sine sacrificio? quod certamen non consecratum mortuo? For all the great national games of the Greeks this latter saying has its full correctness. At the funeral rites of Azan one saw the horse races first in Arcadia.3) Archemorus is celebrated at Nemea, Melicertes-Palaemon through the Isthmian games. The Olympian games are linked to the funeral rites of Oenomaus, on which one finds the testimonies collected in Argoli on Panvinius, de ludis circensib. p. 4, or, as by Ausonius in the Eclogues,4) conceived as the funeral games of Pelops. Now if such an individual connection is lacking for the Roman Archemori Nemea colunt quinquennia Thebæ, Isthmia defuncto celebrata Palæmone notum, Pythia placanda Delphi statuere draconi.

Darin findet die Aufnahme der Circusrennen und anderer Spiele unter die Grabdarstellungen, wie sie auf den Wänden Cornetanischer Hypogeen, in den genannten Sarkophagreliefs, und auf etruscischen Aschenbeh?'tern in so manigfaltiger Form wiederkehrt, ihre Rechtfertigung und Erklärung. Was von Sculptur-Darstellungen der Circusspiele auf uns gekommen ist, entstammt alles der Gräberwelt. Die Scenen, in welchen die höchste Kraftäußerung des vollsten Lebens, der höchste Genuß des Daseins sich ausspricht, haben an der Stätte des Todes eine vorherrschende Funerärbedeutung angenommen. Wenn Eier und Delphine einen hervorragenden Bestandtheil der Grab-Ornamentik bilden, so scheint ihre Uebertragung auf die Circusspiele damit unvereinbar. Und do sind diese beiden Anwendungen nur zwei Aeußerungen derselben Grundbedeutung. Als ich im Vatican die mit den Circusreliefs geshmückten Sarkophage zum ersten Male sah, und einem mich begleitenden, jeht verstorbenen Archäologen die Frage vorlegte, in welcher Beziehung denn nun diese Vorstellungen zu Grab und Tod ständen, war derselbe sehr verlegen, und gab das offene Bekenntniß ab, daß die Kunsterklärung sich um Aufhellung dieses Punktes wenig bemüht habe, vielmehr alle ihre Anstrengung auf die Erklärung der Einzelnheiten, auf Wiedererkennen der Carceres, der Sonnensäule, der Meta, der Parabaten, der vielen Heiligthümer und Symbole richte, und ihre Aufgabe für gelöst erachte, sobald die Uebereinstimmung der erhaltenen Zeugnisse mit der Darstellung der Dankmäler nachgewiesen sei. Sollte sich aber die archäologische Neugierde noch weiter erstreen, und über die Grenzen des Dargestellten hinaus den stummen Monumenten die Frage über ihr Verhältniß zu der Gräberwelt vorlegen, und so gewissermaßen Rechenschaft über ihre Verwendung zu Funerärzweken verlangen, so könne man ja gar mancherlei Beziehungen denken. Sollten denn nicht die in solhen Sarkophagen Beigesekten vielleicht selbst ausgezeichnete Wagenlenker gewesen sein, oder gar in den Circusspielen ihren Tod gefunden haben? Sollte nicht vielleicht schon der Gedanke genügen, daß, ja die Circusspiele die mächtigste Leidenschaft der Römer gewesen, daß sie oft zu Partheiungen und blutigem Kampf geführt hätten, und daß eben daher der- Wunsch entstanden sei, nach dem Tode noh eine Erinnerung an die während des Lebens so oft genossenen Freuden erhalten zu sehn. Wolle man aber noh weiter gehen , so biete ja das Leben selbst die schönste Vergleichung mit solchen Wettkämpfen, ihren Anstrengungen, ihren Erwartungen, ihren getäuschten Hoffnungen, dar. Ob denn nicht die stürzenden Desultores, die zertrümmerten Bigä, 16
e: circus games, the general funerary significance emerges especially in the laying bare of the subterranean altar of Consus, in the cult of Summanus and its wheel-shaped, Plutonian bread cakes, as well as in the Canicidium. Therein the admission of the circus races and of other games among the tomb representations, as it recurs in so manifold a form on the walls of Cornetan hypogea, in the aforementioned sarcophagus reliefs, and on Etruscan cinerary urns, finds its justification and explanation. Whatever sculptural representations of the circus games have come down to us derives wholly from the world of the tombs. The scenes in which the highest expression of force of fullest life, the highest enjoyment of existence, speaks itself out have taken on, in the place of death, a prevailing funerary significance. If eggs and dolphins form a prominent component of tomb ornamentation, their transference to the circus games seems incompatible with it. And yet these two applications are only two expressions of the same fundamental meaning. When I saw in the Vatican for the first time the sarcophagi adorned with circus reliefs, and put to an archaeologist who accompanied me, now deceased, the question in what relation, then, these representations stood to tomb and death, he was very embarrassed, and made the open confession that the interpretation of art had taken little pains to clarify this point, but rather directed all its effort to the explanation of the particulars, to recognizing the carceres, the column of the sun, the meta, the parabatæ, the many sanctuaries and symbols, and considered its task solved as soon as the agreement of the surviving testimonies with the representation on the monuments had been demonstrated. Should archaeological curiosity, however, extend still further, and beyond the limits of what is represented put to the mute monuments the question of their relation to the world of the tombs, and so to speak demand an accounting of their use for funerary purposes, one could think, to be sure, of all sorts of relations. Might not those interred in such sarcophagi perhaps themselves have been distinguished charioteers, or even have met their death in the circus games? Might not perhaps the thought suffice that the circus games were indeed the mightiest passion of the Romans, that they had often led to factions and bloody strife, and that for this very reason the wish had arisen to retain after death a memory of the joys so often enjoyed during life? And if one wished to go still further, life itself offered indeed the most beautiful comparison with such contests, with their exertions, their expectations, their deceived hopes. Might not the falling desultores, the shattered bigæ, 16

Sie bemüht sich viel weniger um das Verständniß der Jdee, als um Entwilung einer oft Staunen erregenden Erudition, die aber: gerade durch die Massenhaftigkeit des angehäuften Materials den gänzlihen Mangel leitender Grundideen nur noh fühlbarer
e: the overturned vessels recall the fortunes of human existence, which founds the victory of one on the ruin of many, which always leads only a few to the goal, which hurls quite a few into the abyss early on, one at the very beginning of the contest, another at the moment when the palm of victory seemed secured to him? I confess that among all the explanations proposed this last allegorical interpretation appealed to me most by its inner truth. Now, however, even it appears to me very secondary. “To decide larger, general questions one must, to avail myself of a wise saying uttered by Plutarch, take one’s standpoint higher.” As sarcophagus pictures the circus games have no other significance than the games actually celebrated; and these refer to material force, first of all to natural generation, conceived wholly in tellurian terms, which includes in itself all the factors that cooperate in the creation of the earth, and embraces life and death, matter and force, and which forms the content of the idea of deity itself. In this significance the games themselves have a predominantly funerary character; in this they take their place beside the great national games of the Hellenes, which through their connection with famous dead appear as true funeral rites. In this they recall those numerous funeral games of which myth makes mention, and which are so often represented on Etruscan cinerary chests. All the games have the character of funeral rites, those celebrated in the circus, in the Terentum of the Tiber, on the shore of the Mincio, no less than the Olympian ones in memory of Pelops, the Nemean around the tombstone of Archemorus, the Isthmian in honor of Palaemon, the Lydian around the monument of Lixus. The meta is always a tombstone and as such the monument of a tellurian Dameon, a λίθος ἔμψυχος, who as Taraxippus frightens the horses, as meta sudans proclaims his relation to the generative moisture of the depths. On this general religious significance rests the admission of the games into the world of the tombs, whether they adorn, as at Corneto, the walls as painting, or, as on our sarcophagi, the funeral chests themselves as reliefs. In the funeral rite, however, the whole of natural force is glorified in its twofold potency, bringing life and death. Death appears bound up with life, and even as its ground. Therefore the symbols of life are so frequent in the tombs; therefore the phallic Priapus on the inscription of the Campana columbarium calls himself at once mortis et vitai locus. Therefore the circus games, too, are a representation of the united force of both, and of the eternal cycle of tellurian creation brought forth by their union. That is the fundamental idea to which our sarcophagus representations attach; that the idea which the world of the tombs disclosed to them. And upon this a higher one is erected, that of deification, of apotheosis. Augustus’s admission [PDF 257] — 243 — among the immortals is to be proclaimed by the games on the shore of the Mincio. The highest idea of the circus reliefs is therefore this: that the dead man has now passed over into the company of the gods and put on the garment of immortality, of which further discussion is to follow at the close of this treatise. Measured against this relation, all those personal explanations drawn from the rank or favorite occupation, the manner of death of the one interred, appear as petty expedients of an archaeology little familiar with the fundamental ideas of the ancient view of life, and no better than many similar attempts that undertake to explain mystery scenes, such as those of the Cumaean tomb, or symbolic accessories, such as the dice,1) hands, shoes, and much else of the kind, from personal circumstances of the buried. Allegorical interpretation is, to be sure, by no means foreign to ancient times,2) and has also been practiced in many ways by the profoundest minds. Indeed, it seems, when faith and understanding of the oldest religious way of thinking vanished, to have overgrown everything, and to have contributed much to securing continuance for the traditional tomb representations. The foundation of the mortuary symbolism it nevertheless by no means forms, and may never be chosen as the starting point of interpretation. 20. What we have reproached in the preceding remarks as an essential defect of the archaeological interpretation of ancient tomb monuments applies to the whole literature that the last centuries have produced on the games of the ancients, in particular on the circus games. It strives far less for an understanding of the idea than for the development of an erudition often astonishing, which, however, precisely through the massiveness of the accumulated material makes the complete lack of guiding fundamental ideas only the more palpably over also into Christian use, I have treated in an essay in the Annali dell’ Instituto per l’anno 1858. The symbolic part of the world of the ancient tombs is one of the most beautiful and yet scarcely trodden regions of archaeology. The seven-stringed lyre, formerly known to the Greeks as well, had fallen out of use in Hellas. Rome, then as now still ever faithful to what has been handed down in religious practices, retained it. Dionysius does not fail to emphasize this adherence to old usages especially in the case of the circus games. The nakedness of the athletes, the use of a third horse joined freely to the yoked pair, the race of the parabatae, all these practices, likewise known to the Hellenes but abandoned by them, continued unchanged in Rome, like the use of the seven-stringed lyre; from which it follows that the Romans did not first take all these things from the Hellenes, but rather retained them even after they had fallen out of practice among the latter.1) The three odd numbers named (3, 5, 7) must necessarily stand in an inner relation to the significance of the circus and its games developed by us above. The idea that governs them can be no other than precisely that from which the circus games themselves sprang. And this agreement is in fact a complete one. If in the circular course of the teams we have recognized a representation of the fundamental law of all tellurian generation, its motion produced by two cooperating forces, and the continuance lying in this motion itself, then in the first three odd numbers the same property of visible creation makes itself known once more. All three belong to the world of appearance, to the world of becoming and passing away, like the egg and what proceeds from the egg. In all of them we find the idea of motion, not that of rest, such as dwells in the Monas. If the one belongs to the solar world, to which all composition and divisibility remain alien, to the divinity in which absolute simplicity dwells, to which only rest, eternally unchangeable essence, and timeless being pertain, then the three odd numbers, by contrast, designate the entry of the Monas into the change of the sublunary world, in which everything is subject to eternal becoming, eternal motion, eternal cycle between two opposed and yet connected [PDF 261] — 247 — poles. It is the world of matter that the three, the five, the seven represent, but not the world of resting, dead matter, but of matter awakened to life through fecundation and thereby given over to constant motion. If, accordingly, the numbers named have a common domain to which they belong, that of the world of appearance, and a common property that they express, namely that of motion and of the life that appears only in this form, yet each of them develops the general idea in its own particular way, each in a different tendency. Force takes shape as the triad through its own nature, directed toward generation; as the five through the necessity of the union of both sexual potencies; as the seven through its dependence on the law of the cosmos. As Trias and as Pempas the generative natural force, the source of motion in the world of becoming, appears following only its own inborn drive, the inclination toward the sexual act that constitutes its being, obedient to it alone, directed only toward its realization; as Heptas, on the other hand, it subjects the untamed drive of nature to an ordering, regulating law that is of higher origin than itself. If it appears in the Trias in the highest fullness of force and in the perfect development of its content, in the Pempas, on the other hand, as the indissoluble union of the two potencies required for every generation, then in the Heptas its previously unregulated sway is subordinated to the harmony and the moderating influence of uranian orchestics. It is no longer left to itself and to its own wild drive, but has entered upon the course of the great cosmic order. Yet it may also be that the τριπλάσιον is used by the ancients in its proper sense. ἡ γὰρ ὑγρὰ φύσις, ἀρχὴ καὶ γένεσις οὖσα πάντων ἐξ ἀρχῆς, τὰ πρῶτα τρία σώματα, γῆν, ἀέρα καὶ πῦρ, ἐποίησε.” Here the three appears as a necessary property of the force of natural generation, grounded in its drive toward multiplication, which forms its real being. It thereby itself becomes the designation of the ἀρχὴ καὶ γένεσις or ἀρχὴ τῆς γενέσεως, and is suited for that very reason quite especially to the representation of the phallic force of an Osiris-Dionysus and to connection with the egg, which is itself designated as ἀρχὴ γενέσεως. If in the Monas the divine force appears as the principle of the world of being, the Trias shows it as the origin of the world of becoming. The one becomes three through its entry into matter, whose animating and moving principle it henceforth forms. The Trias belongs wholly to the idea of natural generation. It is the ἀρχὴ καὶ δύναμις as γόνιμον; it is the material primal force in its direction toward generation. For this reason the Osiris-phallus is necessarily threefold, for this reason Dionysus, too, is threefold, for this reason the whole world of the material gods is in general triplex, that of the female no less than that of the male.2) At the head of things there always stands a threefold ἀρχή, whether ἔδοξε τρία ἔχειν αἰδοῖα, δοῦλος ὤν, καὶ ἐγένετο ἐλεύθερος· καὶ ἀνθ᾽ ἑνὸς ὀνόματος τρία ἔσχεν, δύο τε ἀπελευθερώσαντος προσλαβὼν ὀνόματα. ἀλλὰ τοῦτο ἅπαξ ἐγένετο. We recognize here the significance of the three names that the Romans gave to boys. taria circum effigiem duco: Numero deus impare gaudet. The idea of multiplication through generation leads into the infinite and, strictly speaking, is subject to no limit that could be expressed by any number. Its being consists, indeed, in the infinity of progress, in a never-exhausted multiplication. If now the three is chosen preeminently before every other number to designate such infinity, the ancients base this significance on a particular property of it, and indeed on that which is emphasized by Aristotle right at the beginning of his four books on the structure of the heavens: “Of magnitude, that which extends in one direction is a line; that which extends in two directions, a plane; and that which extends in three, a body,1) and besides these there is no other magnitude, because the ‘three’ is as much as ‘all,’ and ‘thrice’ as much as ‘on all sides.’ For, as the Pythagoreans also say, the All and the Whole are bounded by the three, since in end and middle and beginning lies the number of the All, and end, middle, and beginning make three. In taking from nature, then, its laws, as it were, we apply that number also in the sacred observances relating to the gods.2) idem est enim Apollo, qui Liber Pater, qui Sol. unde ait Lucanus: Cui numine mixto Delphica Thebanæ referunt Trieterica Bacchæ: unde in eorum sacris erat Phœbadum Baccharumque conventus. Jn diesen Bezeichnungen aber, wie gesagt, sind wir, weil die Natur selbst so darauf hinführt, ihr nur gefolgt.“ In dieser Stelle stimmt Aristoteles, was die Bedeutung der Drei betrifft, vollkommen mit Plutarch überein. Die Drei, sazen beide, hat außer der beschränkten, rein arithmetischen, auch noh eine zweite Bedeutung, in welcher sie jede Beschränkung , jede Zahl hinter sich zurückläßt, nnd in den Sinn von "All*, „Alles“, „Vollkommen“ übergeht. So erscheint sie in dem rouauapes, welches niht dreimalseelig, sondern allseelig, vollkommenseelig, bedeutet. Darin aber wird Aristoteles unterrichtender als Plutarch, daß er die zweite Bedeutung der Drei auf die Natur und ein allgemeines Naturgeseß zurückführt, sie also nicht als eine uneigentliche, sondern vielmehr als eine selbstständige, 8» proe begründete stoffliche Bedeutung darstellt. Worin dieser Vorgang der Natur liegt, sagt uns der Stagirite deutlich. Die Drei erfhafft den Körper, der sich ja nach drei Seiten ausdehnt, und außer Linie, Fläche, Körper giebt es keine andere Gestaltung mehr. Darum ist die Drei die Vollkommenheit, das All und Alles. Zu demselben Resultat gelangen die Pythagoreer von einer andern Seite her. Denn fie sagen, zu dem All gehört die Vereinigung von Ende, Mitte, Anfang, und dieses ergiebt wiederum die Dreizahl. Demnach erscheint die Drei eine somatische Zahl , -wozu sie die Natur selbst gemacht hat. In dieser Bedeutung bezeichnet sie das All, das Alles, die Vollkommenheit, in ihr wird sie selbst zur vollkommenen, die erste ungerade zur ersten vollendeten Zahl. e: We distribute, moreover, even the linguistic designations in just this way. For ‘two’ we also call ‘both,’ and ‘two men’ also ‘both men.’ But ‘all’ we do not call them; only with three do we pronounce this word for the first time. In these designations, as has been said, we have only followed nature, because nature itself leads to it.” In this passage Aristotle agrees completely with Plutarch as regards the significance of the three. The three, both say, has, besides the limited, purely arithmetical significance, also a second significance, in which it leaves behind every limitation, every number, and passes over into the sense of ‘All,’ ‘Everything,’ ‘Perfect.’ So it appears in the τρισμάκαρες, which means not thrice-blessed, but all-blessed, perfectly blessed. In this, however, Aristotle becomes more instructive than Plutarch, in that he traces the second significance of the three back to nature and a general natural law, thus presenting it not as an improper significance, but rather as an independent, material significance grounded ἐν φύσει. In what this procedure of nature consists, the Stagirite tells us clearly. The three creates the body, which indeed extends in three directions, and besides line, plane, body there is no other configuration. For this reason the three is perfection, the All and Everything. The Pythagoreans arrive at the same result from another side. For they say that to the All belongs the union of end, middle, beginning, and this yields in turn the number three. Accordingly the three appears as a somatic number, which nature itself has made it. In this significance it designates the All, Everything, perfection; in it the number itself becomes perfect, the first odd number the first completed number. In the same significance it unfolds into the triangle, and indeed into that most perfect of all triangles under whose form the Egyptians and the Pythagoreans conceive the nature of the universe, in which the lowest side contains 4 parts, the side standing at right angles to it 3, and the side opposite the right angle 5, and in which, according to the Pythagorean theorem, the squares of the first two taken together have as much area as the square of the last alone.1) In the same significance the triangle appears on that image of the phallic Poseidon whose It is noteworthy that the ter beatus is here placed together precisely with the triplex telete and the expression felix, faustum, salutare. mensib. 2, 7. ἐν δὲ σχήμασι τὸ ὀρθογώνιον τρίγωνον ὑποτίθενται στοιχεῖον τῆς τῶν ὅλων γενέσεως. e: of the All, and all these relations appear not in ideal abstraction but as properties of matter, as manifestations and forms of material life. The idea of infinity combines with that of limitation; the ἀρχή is confronted by a τελευτή, and both move around a μέσον, which as the enduring element amid the change of the two poles,1) and therefore in pictorial representations, as on the Canopus described above, appears prominent through its size. Precisely thereby the number three becomes the mystery number. Even if it is correct, what Jahn urges against Böttiger, that the number three alone does not suffice to demonstrate a mystery significance, because it has found a far more extensive application, it is nevertheless indisputable that of all numbers only the three can express the fundamental idea of the mysteries, the eternal continued working of force in visible creation, and the hope of a higher rebirth tied to its perfection. For the three receives the significance of completion and of divinity. August. de Civ. Dei 7, 9 cites, probably from Varro, the sentence: Penes Janum sunt prima, penes Jovem summa. Now Zeus is designated as the third, that is, the greatest: Aeschylus suppl. 27: σωτὴρ τρίτος. Choeph. 242: τρίτος πάντων Ζῆν. Eumen. 751: τοῦ πάντα κραίνοντος τρίτου σωτῆρος. Likewise in Suppl. 678 the commandment of reverence toward parents is called τρίτον, that is, the greatest. Thus tertius is synonymous with summus, the number three directly a designation of the divine is lacking. e: nature, which as the abiding element in motion towers over the material world and its constant revolution. This property belongs preeminently to the heavenly powers of light, which are enthroned high above the change of tellurian matter, where it does not reach. In this sense the three is so preeminently ascribed to Apollo and Dionysus. In this sense the former is also called Hecatos,1) a designation meant to emphasize the remoteness in place, the summum. In this sense the Flamen Dialis is not to climb beyond the third rung of the ladder; he would otherwise raise himself above the height of the god of light. Now the application of the three in the Bacchic mysteries appears in its higher spiritual significance. It proclaims to the initiate the participation allotted to him in the eternal power of the Lord, to whom he has given himself through initiation. The number three of the eggs especially bears this meaning in itself. It shows the mysteries as the means of pressing through to divinity. The initiate will be raised through death to the completion of the Trias. Thus the number three is the number of salvation, of σωτηρία, as it makes itself known especially also in the proverb: the third helps. It is therefore called the number of the upper, the Olympian gods, while the two belongs to the chthonian powers.2) It passes itself into the significance of light, becomes like light the paternal number, and is called pater.3) Female materiality recedes entirely into the background. Thus the Trias in its highest development designates the perfected paternal luminous nature, the eternal force of creating, in which Dionysus and Apollo appear as the saviors and healers of the human race, as conquerors of tellurism and its transience. In this significance the three is the mystery number, in this significance the triquetra, as it also appears on funerary vessels, e.g. on a bowl of the Vienna Cabinet, is a sign of Bacchic initiation. of Apollo was fifteen feet high, the multiplication of three by five is to be recognized in this. Hence also preeminently the placing of Apollonian sanctuaries on high mountain peaks, as above Casinum on the site of the present Benedictine monastery, which has so commanding a position. o: Die Jdee der Zeugung und der durch sie hervorgerufenen Bewegung in der stofflichen Welt kehrt wieder in der Fünf. Aber hier nimmt sie eine andere Richtung an, als bei der Drei. Zeigt die Trias die ao;/7 als Vervielfältigung durch Zeugung, so liegt in der Pempas das Streben nach Verbindung und Mischung. Beide ungerade Zahlen stellen uns den Stoff dar in seinem Triebe nach Vervollkommnung und Selbstergänzung. Beide aber nach zwei verschiedenen Seiten: die Drei nach der Seite vollkommener Entfaltung durch das All, die Fünf nach jener der Verbindung des Getrennten, der Verschmelzung zweier geschlechtlicher Gegensäße. Die Bewegung der Trias ist also eine multiplicative, bei welcher die Grundzahl stets dieselbe bleibt, die der Pempas eine additionelle, deren Wesen Aristoteles Metaph. 14, 6, 3 als Mischung bezeichnet. Jene geht aus von der Einheitlichkeit der Kraft, diese von der Scission derselben. ') Jene entwikelt Einheitliches, diese führt Getrenntes zur Einheit zurück. Jene ist also selbst noch eine einheitliche Zahl, die große Eins, untheilbar, und in jedem ihrer Theile die ganze Trias; diese dagegen ist eine zusammengeseßte Zahl, entstanden aus der Verbindung zweier verschiedener Größen, die in ihr auch nach der Vereinigung zu unterscheiden sind. Die Drei hat keine Theile, wohl aber die Fünf. Die Vollkommenheit der beiden Zahlen ist also ganz verschiedener Natur: die der Drei eine äußere körperliche Darstellung der potentiell in der Kraft enthaltenen innern Bollkommenheitz die der Fünf eine solche, welche die in der Kraft eingetretene Trennung vorausseßt , und diese nun als überwunden und besiegt darstellt. Demnach steht die Trias der unstofflichen Monas in demselben Verhältniß näher, in welchem die Linie von der Natur des Punktes weniger sich entfernt als die Fläche oder der Körper. Mit der Eins ist die Drei darin verwandt, daß sie die Kraft wie jene in ihrer innern Einheit und Vollkommenheit auffaßt, in ihr keine (Geschlechter unterscheidet, überhaupt überckdie Bestandtheile derselben nicht nachforscht. In der Fünf dagegen wird die doppelte geschlechtliche Potenzirung der Kraft selbst vorausgesept, und statt von der Monas , von der Duas, statt von der Cinheit und Eintracht, von der Zweiheit und Zwietracht ausgegangen. Ebendarum ist die Fünf eine viel stofflichere Zahl als die Drei. Somatisch sind sie zwar beide, denn sie zeigen uns beide die Kraft in den Stoff eingegangen, und den Stoff bewegend , aber der Fortschritt von der Einheit der Kraft zu der Zweiheit ruht auf der Betrachtung der geschlecht-

e: The idea of generation and of the motion called forth by it in the material world returns in the five. But here it takes a different direction than with the three. If the Trias shows the ἀρχή as multiplication through generation, then in the Pempas there lies the striving toward connection and mixture. Both odd numbers represent matter to us in its drive toward perfection and self-completion. But they do so from two different sides: the three from the side of perfect unfolding through the All, the five from that of the connection of what is separated, of the fusion of two sexual opposites. The motion of the Trias is thus a multiplicative one, in which the basic number always remains the same; that of the Pempas an additive one, whose nature Aristotle, Metaph. 14, 6, 3, designates as mixture. The former proceeds from the unity of force, the latter from its scission.1) The former develops what is unitary, the latter leads what is separated back to unity. The former is thus itself still a unitary number, the great one, indivisible, and in each of its parts the whole Trias; the latter, by contrast, is a composite number, arisen from the combination of two different magnitudes, which are to be distinguished in it even after the union. The three has no parts, but the five does. The perfection of the two numbers is thus of a wholly different nature: that of the three an outward corporeal representation of the inner perfection contained potentially in force; that of the five one that presupposes the separation that has entered into force, and now represents this as overcome and vanquished. Accordingly the Trias stands nearer to the immaterial Monas in the same relation in which the line departs less from the nature of the point than the plane or the body. With the one the three is akin in that it grasps force, like that, in its inner unity and perfection, distinguishes no sexes in it, and in general does not inquire into its constituents. In the five, on the other hand, the double sexual potentiation of force itself is presupposed, and the starting point is not the Monas but the Duas, not unity and concord but duality and discord. For this very reason the five is a far more material number than the three. Somatic they are indeed both, for both show us force entered into matter and moving matter; but the progress from the unity of force to duality rests on the consideration of the sexual [PDF 270] — 256 — difference, as the organisms of animal creation show it,1) while the unity of force belongs not to physical corporeality but to a presupposed Monas. The five therefore leads us deeper into the world of appearance than the three. It shows us not only the motion of eternal becoming that prevails in it, of the constant multiplication of the same ἀρχή; it descends yet a stage further into the realm of the world of becoming, and recognizes in force itself a composition of two materially distinct potencies, the male and the female, and consequently also a second law of motion, namely that which strives to overcome that discord and always to unite again what is separated. Thus it comes about that the five is now not only conceived as marriage, but is itself also called φύσις. For it shows us force as it presents itself physically in the world of appearance, namely separated into two corporeal forms, not as it can be conceived before corporeal configuration, without entry into matter. This perfection of the corporeal world of generation the three is unable to represent. In the Trias we see force only multiplying itself, but not splitting itself into bodies of different sexual formation; in the five, on the other hand, this scission is presupposed and canceled through reunion. The concept of material sexual union emerges in all the accounts of the ancients as the distinguishing mark of the Pempas. Some things on this have already been adduced earlier. In Plutarch’s work de Ei apud Delphos Eustrophus, to whom the development of the mathematical significance of the E is put in the mouth, adds to his manifold instructive remarks on the Pempas c. 8 also the following: “because the five arises from the first male and the first female number, the Pythagoreans, on account of the similarity, called it marriage.” Isis et Osiris 56: “The five is partly like the father, partly like the mother, because it consists of three and two.2)” The same lies in the report cited above from Plato’s Laws, that at wedding celebrations five guests are to be invited, no more, no fewer. The same in the five wax candles of the Cerealian aediles, while the praetors carry only three,3) and in the Quincuncialis ordo in Plin. 17, 78. essence. two and three, but here multiplicative, that justifies the concept. Therefore children who have father and mother in common stand in the relation of the five. So Joseph and Benjamin, the sons of Jacob by Rachel. In recognition of this significance it says in Moses 1, 43, 34: “and Joseph had dishes of honor brought from himself to them (his brothers), and the dish of honor of Benjamin was greater than the dishes of honor of them all, fivefold. And they drank, and became drunk with him.” For Jacob’s ten other sons were by three other mothers, Leah, Bilhah, Zilpah (1, 35, 23–25). According to Moses 1, 45, 21 the same Benjamin receives five festal garments. The significance of sexual union lies also at the basis of the five days of the Sacaean festivals,1) of the five classes of the Roman people, which appears in them united like man and wife, of the Censura quinquennalis,2) in particular also of the number five of the Idaean Dactyls, to whom Achilles belongs as Pemptus, and, through the mediation of Hercules Idaeus, of the five-year period of the Olympic games.3) On the monument of Alyattes on the shore of the Gygaean swamp lake, which the Lydian hetaerae had for the most part erected, stood five phallic cones. As many pyramids were shown by the Porsenna tomb at Clusium, and the same number by the still preserved tomb by the road near Albano.4) With the birth of Minerva the Argive-Faliscan Quinquatria are connected.5) They are the festival of the consecration of the trumpets, whose significance for generation and fecundation we have already emphasized above,6) also a matrons’ festival celebrated in spring, of a Saturnalian-natural character.7) Five is therefore preeminently consecrated to the moon, for in the moon the double formation of nature appears in indissoluble hermaphroditic union. With the fifth number, then, the idea of material generation is connected, and this is not canceled but rather confirmed by the transfer of the dark side of material force onto it.1) According to Egyptian mythology Mercury played at draughts with the moon, won from it the seventieth part of each light, and composed from these the five intercalary days which the Egyptians celebrate as the birthdays of their five gods, Osiris, Arveris, Typhon, Isis, Nephthys, who is also called τελευτή, Ἀφροδίτη, and Νίκη. — Fifteen times (3×5) greater than earthly births are the offspring of the moon women, who come forth from the moon eggs. — According to Mosaic teaching the creation of the animals was begun on the fifth day, on which Müller on Philo, de mundi opificio § 20, p. 236 is to be compared. — The same idea of generation belonging to the five continues in the thirteen, which is explained from the union of two and three, both raised to the square. By addition, says Plutarch de animæ procreatione e Timæo 12, the following remarkable combinations result: 2 and 3 make 5; 4 and 9 make 13; 8 and 27 (namely 2×4 and 3×9) make 35,2) which are especially distinguished by the Pythagoreans in the theory of tones. From the roots 2 and 3 arises the square 13, the cube 35. Since therefore 13 and 35 rest on the same basic numbers 2 and 3, which form marriage, the basic significance of the five must repeat itself also in thirteen and thirty-five. The 13 appears as the expression of the great year of generation in the myth of Io, to whom Prometheus in Aeschylus foretells the birth of the redeemer Heracles in the 13th generation, and to this attach themselves many other similar applications of the same number, which I compile in my Mutterrecht.3) age, is added. e: The 35, as the highest development of 2 and 3, underlies the number of the Roman tribes, which as the highest limit could not be exceeded, and those 35 children of Rhegium in Pausanias. Like the number of the five classes, it has a purely material significance, comprehending in itself the two potencies of the Roman commonwealth, and thus attaches itself confirmingly to the developed idea of the Pempas. — Once more the basic significance of marriage returns in the following conception: Plutarch Is. et Os. 56: “The Egyptians have in all likelihood imagined the nature of the universe chiefly under the image of the most beautiful of all triangles. So Plato too seems to have made use of this symbol in his books on the State, where he sketches the picture of the married state. This triangle consists of three such sides, where the lowest contains four parts, the one standing at right angles on it three, and the one lying opposite the right angle five, and where the squares of the first two taken together have exactly as much area as the square of the last alone. (4² + 3² = 5².) Here one must imagine the side standing perpendicularly on the base line as the man, the base line itself as the woman, and the one lying between the ends of those two as the child begotten by the two.”1) Here, then, the five appears once more as marriage, namely as the child representing the union of father and mother, in whom the materially separated sexual potencies return ever again to original unity; and from this is explained why the Elean matrons, who otherwise appear in the number sixteen, celebrate their games in every fifth year and weave the splendid Junonian garment in every fifth year.2) From the basic significance of the five it follows now that this second odd number is preeminently a numerus naturalis and justifies the designation φύσις to a special degree. The union of the two sexes for generation belongs exclusively to physical-animal life, to the domain of purely material existence. For that very reason it becomes, in the number of the fingers, a sign of natural justice; for that very reason it can be attributed to the likewise material censorship, to the transactions of the mancipatio, to the Cerealian aediles in the five cerei, never to the civil praetorship.3) For that very reason it assumes a preeminently γιγνόμενον, τὸ δ᾽ ἐν ᾧ γίγνεται, τὸ δ᾽ ὅθεν ἀφομοιούμενον φύεται τὸ γιγνόμενον. καὶ δὴ καὶ προσεικάσαι πρέπει, τὸ μὲν δεχόμενον, μητρί, τὸ δ᾽ ὅθεν, πατρί· τὴν δὲ μεταξὺ τούτων φύσιν, ἐκγόνῳ. The mother he calls, p. 350: γενέσεως τιθήνην ὑγραινομένην καὶ πυρουμένην: p. 349: ἕδραν παρέχον ὅσα ἔχει γένεσιν πᾶσιν.

e: female nature, as is revealed in its connection with Minerva,1) with Hera, with Rhea, with Nephthys-Aphrodite, and in the birth-giving force of the fingers. It thereby becomes the basis of the female series of numbers, which proceeds from 5 to 10,2) 50, 100,3) and enters into a decisive opposition with the male series 3, 6, 12. From the material significance of generation there now emerges that significance, appearing in many applications, of the limitation of the material world by the five. If the generating force consists of five parts, which now present themselves as five elements, then what is generated itself cannot possibly exceed the number five. This significance of the five is especially emphasized by the ancients. Most noteworthy on this are the expositions in Plutarch de defectu oraculorum c. 35–37, de Ei apud Delphos c. 7– 16, and in Macrob. Somn. Scip. 1, 6. p. 31. 32 Zeune, Philo, de mundi opificio § 20. To single out particulars, it is found application. A relation to the conjugal sexual significance is shown by the following provisions: Dotem deductis quintis singulorum liberorum nomine repetere posse. Vaticana fragm. § 108. The quinquennii præscriptio is applied in the crimen adulterii and in the querela non numeratæ dotis, and before the lapse of five years the woman who is charged with the divortium may not marry again. On these and many other applications Cuiac. Op. t. 1, p. 543. — On quinque testes: Gaius 1, 119; 2, 104. Ulpian. 19, 3. 20, 2. e: especially remarked that the five is that number which nature preeminently employs in all things, according to which it creates everything, divides everything, orders everything. “So we have in ourselves five senses, and just as many powers of the soul, and on each hand five fingers; the most fertile seed is divided fivefold, for one has never heard that a woman has borne more than five children at once.1) Egyptian mythology says that Rhea bore five gods, and thereby it is meant to be indicated that from one matter five worlds arose. In the universe the earth is divided by five zones, and the heaven by five circles. — Also the revolution of the planets is fivefold, since the sun, Venus, and Mercury have only one. In general there prevails in the arrangement of the world the same harmony that we notice in the positions of the five tetrachords, the highest, the middle, the conjoined, the disjoined, and the superior. And so in singing, too, there are only five intervals, namely the diesis, the half tone, the tone, the tone and a half, and the double tone. In this way nature seems to wish, in all its arrangements, reb. dubiis (34, 5) and Julian in Fr. 36 De Solut. (46, 3) Si pater meus prægnante uxore relicta decesserit, et ex causa hereditaria totum hoc, quod patri meo debitum fuisset, petissem, nihil me consumsisse quidam existimant; si nemo natus sit recte me egisse, quia in rerum natura verum fuisset, me solum heredem fuisse, Julianus notat; verius est me eam partem perdidisse, pro qua heres fuissem, antequam certum fuisset, neminem nasci, aut quartam partem, quia tres nasci potuerunt, aut sextam, quia quinque; nam et Aristotelem scripsisse, quinque nasci posse, quia vulvæ mulierum totidem receptacula habere possint, et esse mulierem Romæ Alexandrinam ab Aegypto, quæ quinque simul et tum habuerit incolumes; et hoc et in Aegypto affirmatum est mihi. e: far rather to employ the number five than, as Aristotle (de cœlo 2, 4) maintains,1) the spherical form.” — In agreement with this, Eustrophus remarks: “In the whole of nature the five matters most of all, which is why the wise call counting πεμπάζειν.”2) Macrob.: Illa vero quinario numero proprietas excepta potentiæ ultra ceteras eminentis evenit, quod solus omnia quæque sunt, quæque videntur esse, complexus est. Pursuing the same idea, πάντα and πέντε are declared identical, and of this etymology what holds of so infinitely many others holds: it is derived from the thing, not the thing from it, and therefore, the more forced it seems, so much the more probative for the idea itself. With the five the whole series of numbers is closed; it designates, then, the All, and furnishes the terms πεμπάζειν and πεμπάσασθαι, whereby counting in general, and not merely counting up to five, is expressed. “Passing over many other such matters,” Eustrophus continues, “I wish only to cite Plato, who, at the place where he maintains that there is but one world, adds that if this world is not the only one, there can certainly in all be no more than five worlds.”3) Since the perfect force, composed of masculinity and femininity, contains five elements, what these create cannot possibly exceed the number five. From this follows the relation of the Trias and the Pempas. Both designate the material All, but the three presents it in its infinite extension, the five in its limitation, the former in its divinity, the latter in its material articulation.4) He is called thrice blessed whose perfect blessedness is to be expressed in its whole fullness. He cannot be called five times blessed, because that would express perfection in its finitude and limitation.5) “It is the five, says which we emphasized above. Somn. Scip. 1, 16, p. 37: Virgilius nullius disciplinæ expers, plene et per omnia beatos exprimere volens ait: O terque quaterque beati. The two numbers 3 and 4 are multiplici inter se cognationis necessitate sociati, as Macrob. p. 36 puts it. This rests on the significance that the Pythagoreans gave to the Tetractys, on which see Macrob. S. Sc. 1, 16, p. 32, p. 37, 2. 2, p. 131. Platonis Timæus p. 352 sqq. Bipont. Plut. de placit. philos. 1, 3. Hutten 12, p. 342 sqq. Here Pythagoras calls the Tetractys Παγὰν ἀεννάου φύσεως ῥίζωμά τ᾽ ἔχουσαν. Philo de mund. opif. § 15–18. Ὁ γὰρ ἐντελεχείᾳ δεκὰς, τουτὸ τετρὰς, ὡς ἔοικε, δυνάμει. Parallel passages from Philo and literature are given by Müller, p. 211. Lucian pro lapsu inter salut. 5, Vitar.

Die Fünf also ist jener sinis, quem intra citraque nequit congistere rectum, und daher das revraypauuor den Pythagoreen Darstellung des vpraivzw, deren sie siH in den Briefen bedienten.*) Darum führte Domitian die Umläufe auf fünf, nicht auf sechs und nicht auf vier zurück. Aber die Vier ist die Vollkommenheit potentiell, die Drei actuell gedacht (Arist. Metaph. 9, 8). Tie Tetracty3 wird dadurch unkörperlicher und geistiger als die Trias, Sie eignet sich besonder3 zur Bezeichnung der Sonnenkraft , wie denn die quadrigw]w der Sonne gehören, am vierten Tage die Gestirne erschasfen werden, aus der Vier die Pyramide, des himmel: anstrebenden Feuers (Ovid. altum flamma petit. Bild hervorgeht, Die Vier ist daber am meisten gottähnlich , vollkommen, gleichmäßig uud gercht wie Gott, darum der höchste Shwur, die Quelle - der Zahl und aller Dinge. e: the same Eustrophus, that does not let the species of animate creatures rise to infinity, but has limited all living beings to only five kinds.” This very relation of the five and the three is to be observed on our tomb painting. Three eggs we see here, and beside them five ephebes.1) The reverse, five eggs and three ephebes, is inadmissible. In the three eggs the divine perfection of the material force is represented according to its inner infinity; in the five ephebes, what it creates, in its limitation and formation. Thus the five fingers of the creative hand show the force not in its infinite plenitude of power, but in its subjection to a finite limit, which it does not exceed. The same idea lies in the Greek ἢ πέντε πίν᾽, ἢ τρὶς πίν᾽, ἢ μὴ τέτταρα. This Plautus in the Stichus expressly traces back to the five fingers of the hand: Quot cyathos hos bibimus? St. tot quot digiti sunt in manu. Pliny 28, 6 mentions the same law: Numerum quoque quaternarium prodidit Demetrius condito volumine, et quare quaterni cyathi sextariive non essent bibendi. In the πέντε πίν᾽ there lie at once fullness and measure, limitation within multiplicity. Four cups it may not be, because otherwise perfection is not attained; six, too, it may not be, because otherwise the boundary that nature has set for herself, as in the fingers, in the five senses, in the five zones, and according to which she has created and ordered the All, would be overstepped, and the necessary harmony of things thereby disturbed.2) Therefore Plato, too, says expressly: five wedding guests, none more and none fewer. The five, then, is that finis, quem intra citraque nequit consistere rectum, and hence the πεντάγραμμον was for the Pythagoreans the representation of ὑγιαίνειν, which they used in their letters.3) Therefore Domitian reduced the rounds to five, not to six and not to four. Therefore, too, the missus had to be fixed at 24, so that for the ærarius auctio 4. The idea of perfection is shared by the three and the four, as by the seven composed of both. But the four is perfection thought of potentially, the three actually (Arist. Metaph. 9, 6). The Tetractys thereby becomes more incorporeal and more spiritual than the Trias. It is especially suited to designate the force of the sun, as indeed the quadrigæ belong to the sun, the stars are created on the fourth day, and from the four there arises the pyramid, the image of the heavenward-striving fire (Ovid. altum flamma petit. Jambl. myst. 5, 11. 12. p. 214–216 Parthey.). The four is therefore most like God, perfect, equable, and just as God is; hence it is the highest oath, the source of number and of all things. Plut. de Ei apud Delph. 13, the arcana vis. Macrob. p. 36: inter arcana venerantur. 1843. p. 1–6. 25.

Dieß kann auch so ausgedrükt werden: Durch Einkleidung in eine bestimmte Zahl wird die Formlosigkeit des Unendlichen überwunden. Die Alten sagen gleichbedeutend: die ungerade Zahl überwindet die gerade, zu weler fie hinzutritt.
