For this very reason the number of the elements, too, must be limited to four, so that the fifth place, that of the soul, which is to set the dead body in motion, may remain open. “For the five has as many advantages over the four as the animal has over the lifeless body.”1) Now by the fact that the five limits infinity, it acquires a preeminent kinship with the idea of form, of articulation, and of the harmony lying therein. Infinity is by its nature formless and unregulated. The imparting of form always contains a limitation, and conversely every limitation necessarily contains articulation and form. This may also be put thus: through clothing in a definite number the formlessness of the infinite is overcome. The ancients say to the same effect: the odd number overcomes the even to which it is added. The view on which this rests is set forth with great clarity, precisely for the five, by Plutarch in his work on the decline of the oracles, c. 35: “But now I ask you to consider attentively with me this circumstance also, that of the two highest principles, I mean the one and the indefinite two, the latter is the primal matter of all shapelessness and disorder, and is therefore called infinity;2) the former, however, by its nature defines and limits the empty, groundless, and indeterminate element of infinity, gives it a shape, and brings it about that it can at least in some measure bear and accept the designation proper to sensible things. These principles become visible first in number, or, to speak more properly, multitude is not a number at all unless, like the form to matter, it is added to the indefinite infinity and now more, now less is separated from it. Only then, determined by the one, does every multitude become a number; but if one takes the Mosaic story of creation. After heaven and earth have been created on the first four days, the creation of the animals begins on the fifth with that of the fishes and birds. On Moses, Genesis 1, 20–23, Philo de mundi opificio § 20 remarks: Τὰ θνητὰ γένη ζῳοπλαστεῖν ἐνεχείρει, τὴν ἀρχὴν ἀπὸ τῶν ἐνύδρων ποιούμενος ἡμέρᾳ πέμπτῃ, νομίσας οὐδὲν ὄντως ἕτερον ἑτέρῳ συγγενὲς, ὡς ζῴοις πεντάδα. Διαφέρει γὰρ ἔμψυχα ἀψύχων οὐδενὶ μᾶλλον ἢ αἰσθήσει· πενταχῇ δὲ τμητὸν αἴσθησις, κ. τ. λ. On this Müller, p. 236. The four is here taken in its material significance as στερεόν. Philo p. 16. σπεύδει δ᾽ αὐτῷ τῶν ἀρχῶν ἡ μὲν ἐπὶ τὸ ποιητικὸν αἴτιον καὶ εἰδικὸν, ὅπερ ἐστὶ νοῦς ὁ θεὸς, ἡ δ᾽ ἐπὶ τὸ παθητικόν τε καὶ ὑλικόν, ὅπερ ἐστὶν ὁ ὁρατὸς κόσμος. From this side, too, the two is the female-material principle, the three the male form-giving principle, as we shall find the contrast a few pages further on.

o: Eins weg, so verwirrt die unbestimmte Zwei alles wieder, und hebt Verhältniß, Maß und Grenzen gänzlich auf. Weil nun die Form nicht eine Zerstörung der Materie ist, sondern vielmehr jedem Subjekte Gestalt und Ordnung mittheilt, so müssen auch nothwendig in der Zahl beide Prinzipien sich befinden, aus welcher die erste Verschiedenheit oder Ungleichheit entspringt. Denn das unbestimmte Prinzipium bringt die gerade, das bessere aber die ungerade Zahl hervor. Die Zwei ist die erste gerade, und die Drei die erste ungerade Zahl. Aus diesen beiden entsteht die Fünf, die ihrer Zusammensegung nach beiden gemeinschaftlich, in Ansehung ihrer Kraft aber ungerade ist. Da das Sinnliche und Körperliche seiner Zusammensegung wegen durH die: Gewalt der Verschiedenheit in mehrere Theile getheilt wird, so durfte die Zahl derselben weder die erste gerade, noch die erste ungerade sein, sondern eine dritte, die aus diesen zusammengeseßt ist, damit sie von beiden Prinzipien, sowohl demjenigen, das die gerade, als dem, das die ungerade erzeugt, ihre Entstehung bekäme. Denn es ging nicht an, daß das Eine von dem Andern getrennt würde, weil beide die Natur und Kraft eines Prinzipii haben. Wie nun beide mit einander vereinigt wurden , so bes hielt das bessere Prinzipium die Oberhand über die das Körperliche trennende Unbestimmtheit, septe derselben Shranken, und stellte, da die Materie einmal zwischen beiden getheilt war, die Einheit in die Mitte, um zu verhindern, daß das All nicht in zwei Theile getrennt würde. So entstand die Menge der Welten durch die Verschiedenheit und Ungleichheit des Unbestimmtenz aber die Kraft des sich stets Gleichen und Bestimmten machte diese Menge ungerade. Das Ungerade nun ist von der Art, daß es die Natur nicht weiter, als es gut und nüßlich ist, sich ausdehnen läßt. Denn wäre die Eins rein und unvermischt, so würde in der Materie gar keine Trennung sein; da aber die Eins mit der theilenden Kraft der Zwei vermischt worden, so hat die Materie dadurch eine Theilung und Zerschneidung bekommen, doch mußte es dabei bleiben, weil die gerade Zahl durchß die ungerade überwältigt wurde." Wie man nun auch über diese Deduktion urtheilen mag, der Saß, der durch fie hegründet werden soll, ist klar, und früher da, als die nachhinkende Erklärung. Die. Fünf auferlegt dem Unendlichen Einschränkung, dem Formlosen Form, dem Ungegliederten Gliederung; sie hemmt die unbegrenzte Ausdehnung der stofflichen Welt, und seßt ihr Schranken. Sie ist es, die durch die Verbindung der Ungeraden mit der Geraden, die Theilung des Alls in zwei Hälften verhindert. Sie zeigt uns also den Stoff in seiner Richtung auf Zusammenführung des Getrennten und Entgegengesegten, in seiner Tendenz nach Gestaltung, Begrenzung und stets sich gleichbleibender, harmonischer Regelung. Ebendadurch bekundet sie fich als den vollkommensten Ausdruck der stofflichen Schöpfung. Denn sie zeigt uns nun  [PDF 280]  die Materie in allen ihren wesentlihen Eigenschaften: in dem Bedürfniß nah geschlehtlicher Einigung und Wiederaufhebung der eingetretenen Scission von Mann und Weib; ebenso in ihrer Einschränkung und Endlichkeit, in ihrer Unzertrennlichkeit von Form und gegliederter Gestaltung, zuleßt in ihrer Harmonie und Gesetzmäßigkeit, welche alle Theile der Schöpfung, die himmlischen und tellurischen, die göttlichen und die menschlichen, die seelischen und die körperlichen durchdringt, und in jener Bewegung, die den Jnhalt des Lebens bildet, ewig dieselbe Gleichmäßigkeit erhält. Darnach kann die ganze Fülle der Jdee bemessen werden, welche in der Bezeichnung der Fünf als pros enthalten ist. Die Welt der stofflichen Zeugung hat in der Pempas ihren vollsten Ausdrud zefunden. Die Bewegung und die ewig gleiche Geseßmäßigkeit derselben, die volle Natürlichkeit des Werdens und Vergehns, das ist die ganz somatisch gedachte Fünf, und eben diese Bedeutung legt Aristoteles in der Methaphysik 5, 4, vergl 9, 8, dem Aus8druck por:s bei. Wie nun dieser werdenden sublunarischen Vilt das stete Rüclaufen in sich selbst, die ewige Rückkehr zu dem Ausgangspunit eigen ist, so ermangeln die Alten nicht, auch diese Seite der Fünf hervorzuheben. De Ei apud Delphos 8. „Die Fünf heißt pros, in so fern fie durch die Multiplication mit sich selbst gleichsam in sich zurückkehrt. So. wie die Natur, nahdem sie das Samenkorn des Weizen empfangen und erweicht hat, nach und nah vielerlei Formen und Gestalten hervorbringt, wodurch sie das Werk vollendet, und zuleßt den Weizen darstellt, so daß sie am Ende des ganzen Geschäfts den Anfang wiedergiebt, ebenso pflegt sich auh die Fünf und Sechs (2 + 3;- 233) mit sich selbst multiplicirt, zu erhalten und wieder hervorzubringen, da hingege alle andere Zahlen, wenn sie multiplicirt werden, sich durch Vermehrung in andere Zahlen verwandeln. Denn 6>»<6 ist 36, und 5>C<5 ist 25. Indessen geschieht dieß bei der Sehse nur einmal, und auf eine einzige Weise , daß fi von sich selbst ein Quadrat macht; bei der Fünf hingegen kann es in der Multiplication, und besonders in der Addition mit sich selbst, wodurch sie auß wechselsweise die Zehn hervorbringt, immerfort geschehen, so daß sie hierin dem Wesen, das die Welt regiert, ähnlich ist. =- Auf gleiche Weise pflegt auch die Zusammenkunft der Fünf mit sich selbst Nichts Unvollkommenes oder Fremdes zu erzeugen, sondern sie hat ihre bestimmte Veränderungen, weil sie entweder sich selbst, oder die Zehn, d. h. entweder etwas Eigenes oder etwas Vollfomments hervorbringt." Dazu besonders Jo. Lydus de mensid. p. 23 Schow. Aber es bleibt noch eine andere Beziehung der Bezeichnung pro:s übrig, die besondere Hervorhebung verdient. Die Fünf gehört der 1hierisch-animalischen Welt. Sie kömmt also dem Menschen nur nach seinem animalischen Theile zu. Mit andern Worten: Als Pempas erscheint der Mensch nach der Seite, welde  [PDF 281]  er mit dem Thiere gemein hat, niht nach derjenigen, welche ihn über das Thierreich erhebt. Die Fünf ist also die lunarische oder psychische Stufe, welche zwischen der somatisch-tellurischen und der solarischen des vovs in der Mitte steht. Darum beginnt die Thiershöpfung am fünften Tage. Die Thiere haben die fünf Sinne, welhe dem Psychischen, nicht dem Geistigen angehören, mit dem Menschen gemein, und die Bezeichnung dieser Lebensstufe mit der Fünf wird von Philo 65. 20 ausdrüFlich hervorgehoben. Als Pemptus ist Achill nicht solarisch, sondern [unarisch, wie er auf der Mondinsel Leuke mit Helena psychisch verbunden lebt, also der Sinnenmensch, nicht der geistige. Fünf ist die Ehe nicht nah ihrer geistigen, sondern nach ihrer animalischen Auffassung, als natürliche Geschlechtsverbindung, wie sie auch die Thiere üben, denen die verschiedene Geschlechtögestaltung mit dem Menschen gemeinschaftlich ist. Daher ist auch die außereheliche Begattung der Sakäen eine Fünf, nicht weniger als das Connubium, ja dieses ist die Fünf nur nach seiner natürlichen Seite. Wenn die Pempas daher als pros bezeichnet ist, so wird darin das rein Menschliche nicht inbegriffen , und nur das Lunarisch-Psyhische, das alles Animalische verbindet, hervorgehoben.
e: one away, the indefinite two confounds everything again and abolishes relation, measure, and limits altogether. Since, then, form is not a destruction of matter but rather imparts shape and order to every subject, both principles must necessarily be present in number, from which the first difference or inequality arises. For the indefinite principle brings forth the even number, the better one, however, the odd. The two is the first even number, and the three the first odd. From these two arises the five, which by its composition is common to both, but with regard to its force is odd. Since the sensible and the corporeal, on account of their composition, are divided into several parts by the might of difference, their number could be neither the first even nor the first odd, but had to be a third, composed of these, so that it might receive its origin from both principles, from the one that generates the even as well as from the one that generates the odd. For it was not possible for the one to be separated from the other, since both have the nature and force of a principle. As soon as both were united with each other, the better principle retained the upper hand over the indefiniteness that divides the corporeal, set limits to it, and, since matter was once divided between the two, placed unity in the middle, to prevent the All from being split into two parts. Thus the multitude of the worlds arose through the difference and inequality of the indefinite; but the force of that which is ever the same and determinate made this multitude odd. The odd, now, is of such a kind that it does not let nature extend further than is good and useful. For were the one pure and unmixed, there would be no division at all in matter; but since the one has been mixed with the dividing force of the two, matter has thereby received division and cutting apart, yet it had to stop there, because the even number was overpowered by the odd.” However one may judge this deduction, the proposition that is to be established by it is clear, and older than the halting explanation. The five imposes limitation on the infinite, form on the formless, articulation on the unarticulated; it checks the unbounded extension of the material world and sets limits to it. It is the five that, by the union of the odd with the even, prevents the division of the All into two halves. It shows us, then, matter in its tendency toward the bringing together of the severed and the opposed, in its inclination toward shaping, delimitation, and a harmonious regulation ever remaining the same. By this very fact it proves itself the most perfect expression of material creation. For it shows us now [PDF 280] — 266 — matter in all its essential properties: in the need for sexual union and for the abolition again of the scission that has set in between man and woman; likewise in its limitation and finitude, in its inseparability from form and articulated shape, and finally in its harmony and conformity to law, which pervades all parts of creation, the heavenly and the tellurian, the divine and the human, the psychic and the corporeal, and in that motion which constitutes the content of life preserves forever the same regularity. By this the whole fullness of the idea may be measured that is contained in the designation of the five as φύσις. The world of material generation has found its fullest expression in the Pempas. The motion and its eternally identical conformity to law, the full naturalness of becoming and passing away, that is the five conceived wholly somatically, and precisely this significance Aristotle attaches to the expression φύσις in the Metaphysics 5, 4, cf. 9, 8. As to this becoming, sublunary world there belongs the constant running back into itself, the eternal return to the point of departure, so the ancients do not fail to bring out this side of the five as well. De Ei apud Delphos 8. “The five is called φύσις inasmuch as, by multiplication with itself, it as it were returns into itself. Just as nature, after receiving and softening the seed grain of wheat, gradually brings forth manifold forms and shapes, whereby she completes the work and at last presents the wheat, so that at the end of the whole business she gives back the beginning, so too the five and the six (2 + 3; 2 × 3), multiplied by themselves, are wont to preserve and reproduce themselves, whereas all other numbers, when they are multiplied, are changed by increase into other numbers. For 6 × 6 is 36, and 5 × 5 is 25. Yet in the six this happens only once, and in a single way, that it makes a square of itself; in the five, on the contrary, it can happen continually in multiplication, and especially in addition with itself, whereby it also produces the ten alternately, so that in this it is like the being that governs the world. — In the same way the conjunction of the five with itself is wont to produce nothing imperfect or alien, but has its determinate alterations, because it produces either itself or the ten, i.e. either something proper to it or something perfect.” On this especially Jo. Lydus de mensib. p. 23 Schow. But there remains yet another relation of the designation φύσις that deserves particular emphasis. The five belongs to the animal world. It therefore pertains to man only according to his animal part. In other words: as Pempas man appears on the side which [PDF 281] — 267 — he has in common with the animal, not on that which raises him above the animal kingdom. The five is therefore the lunar or psychic stage, which stands midway between the somatic-tellurian stage and the solar stage of the νοῦς. For this reason the creation of the animals begins on the fifth day. The animals have the five senses, which belong to the psychic and not to the spiritual, in common with man, and the designation of this stage of life by the five is expressly emphasized by Philo § 20. As Pemptus, Achilles is not solar but lunar, as he lives psychically united with Helen on the lunar island of Leuke, hence the man of the senses, not the spiritual man. Marriage is five not according to its spiritual but according to its animal conception, as natural sexual union, such as the animals also practice, whose differing sexual formation they share with man. Hence the extramarital mating of the Sacaea, too, is a five, no less than the connubium; indeed the latter is the five only according to its natural side. When the Pempas is therefore designated as φύσις, what is purely human is not included in this, and only the lunar-psychic, which unites all that is animal, is emphasized.

o: Stellen wir nunmehr die beiden ersten ungeraden Zahlen, deren Verhältniß zu der Bewegung des Lebens in der stofflichen Welt wir bisher erläuterten, nochmals nebeneinander, so ergiebt sich eine Erscheinung, die besonders hervorgehoben zu werden verdient. Wir sehen nämlich nun die Drei von der Ungeschlehtlichkeit, in welcher sie als Trias erschien, übergehen in die Bedeutung der männlich-zeugenden, aktiven Naturpotenz. Als Theil der Fünf ist die Drei männlich, als selbstständige Trias geschlehtslo8. Dieser Fortschritt in der Bestimmung des Geschleht8 hängt damit zusammen, daß die erste Entwiklung der Kraft, welche zu der Drei führt, eine Untersuchung der Bestandtheile der Zeugung nicht vornimt. Erst in Folge einer zweiten Entwiklung, die zu der Fünf führt, wird die geschlehtliche Bildung der Drei genauer fixirtz; ein Fortschritt, mit welhem ein ähnlicher der Kultsteine übereinstimmt. Denn auch diese haben ursprünglich keine Andeutung der Geschlechtlichkeit, und erhalten eine erkennbare phallische Bildung erst im Fortschritt religiöser Entwicklung. Ebenso die Drei. Anfänglich geschlechtslos findet die Trias auf männliche und weibliche Gottheiten gleiche Anwenduug, ja insofern ursprünglich das weiblich-stoffliche Prinzip an die Spiße der Dinge gestellt wird, erscheint sie zunächst als Grundzahl der Muttergottheiten. Jeht aber wird ihr ebenso bestimmt die Beziehung zu der männlichen Kraft beigelegt, und diese Bedeutung durchß den Gegensatz der weiblichen Zwei erläutert. Eustrophus ist darüber sehr bestimmt. Da alle Zahlen in gerade und ungerade eingetheilt werden, so ist die Eins in Ansehung ihrer Kraft beiden gemeinschaftlich. Daher macht sie auch in der Addition die ungerade  [PDF 282]  zur geraden, die gerade zur ungeraden, und man pflegt die zwei als Anfang der geraden, die Drei aber der ungeraden Zahl anzusehn. Durch die Vermischung beider miteinander wird die Fünf erzeugt, und diese hält man mit allem Recht in Ehren, weil sie zuerst aus den ersten Zahlen entsteht, und sie wird die Che genannt, wegen der Aehnlichkeit der geraden Zahl mit dem Weibt, der ungeraden mit dem Manne.!') Denn bei Zerlegung der Zahlen in gleiche Theile, steht die gerade gänzlich von einander, und läßt gleichsam einen der Empfängniß fähigen Raum und Prinzip in sich selbst zurück; bei der Theilunz der ungeraden Zahl aber bleibt allemal zwischen den beiden Hälften etwas übrig, und in so fern kömmt ihr eher als der andern Zahl eine Zeugungöfkraft zu; sie behält auch, wenn sie mit der andern vermischt wird, stets den Vorzug, obne ihn je zu verlieren. Denn aus beiden wird durch keine Verbindung eine gerade Zahl, sondern allemal eine ungerade.“ Dieses, und was Plutarch den Eustrophu? weiter zur Begründung der Männlichkeit der Drei , der Weiblichkeit der Zwi, vortragen läßt, mag auf sich beruhen. Die Geschlechtsverschiedenheit beida Zahlenformen selbst ist von dem Werth oder Unwerth der Erklärung unabhänziz. Sie offenbart sich in dem römischen Gebrauche, den Mädchen am akten , den Knaben am neunten Tage ihren Namen zu geben, ebenso in der Beziehung der ungeraden Zahl auf die olympischen, der geraden auf die <thonischen Götter, die hierin die Natur der Mutter-Erde annehmen, und in der Sitte, den Knaben drei, den Mädchen nur zwei Namen beizulegen.?) Jn der Duas tritt die erste Seission der Einheit hervor. Sie ist das Prinzip der Trennung, der Feindschaft, des Zwiespalts. Sie erscheint daher bald als Darstellung der beiden sich en!gegenstehenden Pole der Kraft, der schaffenden und der vernichtenden, der dunkeln und der hellen Naturseite, bald aber auch als Ausdruck der geschlechtlichen Scissfion, und in Folge davon als Bild des Weibes, welches ebenso an der Spiße der sichtbaren Dinge steht, 'wie die Zwei die Zahlenreihe eröffnet. Als Ausdruc der Seission wird die Zwei zur bösen Zahl, welche, wenn sich selbst überlassen, ein Auseinanderfallen der Eins oder des einheitlichen Alls herbeiführen würde. Sie ist nicht schaffend, sondern auflösend, wie sie denn auch die Grundlage der völlig theilbaren Zahlen eröffnet. Jhr gegenüber erscheint die Drei als Herstellunz der Einheit, bewerkstelligt durch die Monas, welche der Zwei sich anschließend,
e: If we now place side by side once more the first two odd numbers, whose relation to the movement of life in the material world we have so far explained, there results a phenomenon that deserves particular emphasis. For we now see the three pass from the sexlessness in which it appeared as Trias into the significance of the male-generative, active natural potency. As part of the five, the three is male; as independent Trias, sexless. This advance in the determination of sex is connected with the fact that the first development of force, which leads to the three, does not undertake an investigation of the components of generation. Only as a result of a second development, which leads to the five, is the sexual formation of the three more precisely fixed; an advance with which a similar one in the cult stones corresponds. For these too originally have no indication of sexuality, and receive a recognizable phallic form only in the progress of religious development. So too the three. Originally sexless, the Trias finds equal application to male and female deities; indeed, insofar as the female-material principle is originally set at the head of things, it appears at first as the basic number of the mother goddesses. But now the relation to the male force is assigned to it just as definitely, and this significance is explained by the contrast with the female two. Eustrophus is very definite on this point. Since all numbers are divided into even and odd, the one, with regard to its force, is common to both. Hence, in addition, it also makes the odd [PDF 282] — 268 — to the even, and the even to the odd, and the two is regarded as the beginning of the even number, the three, however, as that of the odd. By the mingling of both with one another the five is generated, and this one holds in honor with every right, because it arises first from the first numbers, and it is called marriage, on account of the likeness of the even number to woman, of the odd to man.1) For when numbers are divided into equal parts, the even stands wholly apart, and leaves behind in itself, as it were, a space and principle capable of conception; in the division of the odd number, however, something always remains over between the two halves, and to that extent a generative force pertains to it sooner than to the other number; it also retains, when it is mingled with the other, the preeminence always, without ever losing it. For from the two no union ever produces an even number, but always an odd.” This, and what Plutarch has Eustrophus further advance to establish the masculinity of the three and the femininity of the two, may be left aside. The difference of sex between the two forms of number is itself independent of the worth or worthlessness of the explanation. It reveals itself in the Roman custom of giving girls their name on the eighth day, boys on the ninth, likewise in the relation of the odd number to the Olympian gods, of the even to the chthonian, who in this take on the nature of Mother Earth, and in the custom of giving boys three names, girls only two.2) In the Duas the first scission of unity comes forth. It is the principle of separation, of enmity, of discord. It therefore appears now as the representation of the two opposed poles of force, the creative and the annihilating, the dark and the bright side of nature, now again as the expression of sexual scission, and in consequence of this as the image of woman, who stands at the head of visible things just as the two opens the series of numbers. As the expression of scission the two becomes the evil number, which, if left to itself, would bring about a falling apart of the one, or of the unitary All. It is not creative but dissolving, as it also opens the foundation of the wholly divisible numbers. Over against it the three appears as the restoration of unity, accomplished by the Monas, which, joining itself to the two, eighth? At the end it says: “One must add this also, that just as the eight is a cube of the two, the nine the square of the three, so women bear only two names, men, however, three.” On this the passage cited above on the three-phallic formation of the male.

o: Untheilbarkeit bewirkt. Jn der Drei kehrt die Duas zur stofflich entwidelten Einheit zurück , wie das Kind die Naturen von Vater und Mutter verbindet und ihre Trennung überwindet. So wird die Drei der Zwei gegenüber zur guten, schaffenden Zahl. Sie ist darum den olympischen, wie die Zwei den <thonischen Göttern zugeeignet. Sie ist das osinishe, bachische Prinzip gegenüber dem typhonischen, das in der Ocnusfabel weiblich gestaltet erscheint. Damit hängt zusammen, daß die gerade Zahl dem Prinzip der Ruhe, die ungerade Drei dem der Bewegung entspricht. Die zeugende Potenz ist es, auf welche alle zivyo«s der sihtbaren Welt zurückgeht, während der weiblich empfangende Stoff in den Eigenschaften desselben, dem der Oertlichkeit, des Raumes, und mithin der stofflihen Ruhe sich spiegelt. Darum eben sind nur die ungeraden Zahlen Zahlen der Bewegung, die geraden umgekehrt Zahlen der Ruhe, wie die Vier sowoh( den todten Körper als die in sich ruhende vollendete Quelle des stofflichen Alls darstellt. So wird die Zwei der Drei, die Vier der Fünf, der Kubus dem Kreise entgegengeseßt. Wenn die Vier dem phallischen Merkur, die Aht dem zeugenden Neptun und dem Poseidonssohne Theseus gewidmet erscheint, so sind diese beiden männlichen Götter in solcher Zahlennatur noh als von dem Stoff beherrsHt und in der Bewegungslosigkeit des Telluri8mus selbst gedacht: eine Auffassung , die durH den Kubus des obenerwähnten Poseidon-Bildes vollkommene Bestätigung erhält. Auf dem ruhenden Würfel ist das Dreieck , das die zeugende und bewegende Kraft des Phallus darstellt, wie die im Laufe befindliche bachische triquetra, abgebildet. Aus diesem Gegensaß der geraden und der ungeraden Zahl wird nun erst die ausschließliche Verbindung der leßtern mit den Circusspielen in ihrer ganzen Bedeutung klar. Denn da hier die Bewegung der erscheinenden Welt, wie sie aus der Befruhtung des Stoffs hervorgeht, zur Darstellung gebracht werden sou: so ist es eben die zeugende und bewegende Ungerade, die in den Circusspielen vorherrschen muß.
e: brings about indivisibility. In the three the Duas returns to materially developed unity, as the child unites the natures of father and mother and overcomes their separation. Thus the three, over against the two, becomes the good, creative number. It is therefore assigned to the Olympian gods, as the two to the chthonian. It is the Osirian, Bacchic principle over against the Typhonian, which appears in the fable of Ocnus given a female form. Connected with this is the fact that the even number corresponds to the principle of rest, the odd three to that of motion. It is the generative potency to which all κίνησις of the visible world goes back, while the female receptive matter is mirrored in its properties, that of locality, of space, and hence of material rest. For this very reason only the odd numbers are numbers of motion, the even conversely numbers of rest, as the four represents both the dead body and the perfected source of the material All reposing in itself. Thus the two is opposed to the three, the four to the five, the cube to the circle. When the four appears dedicated to the phallic Mercury, the eight to the generating Neptune and to Poseidon’s son Theseus, these two male gods are in such a nature of number still conceived as dominated by matter and as themselves in the motionlessness of tellurism: a conception that receives perfect confirmation from the cube of the picture of Poseidon mentioned above. On the resting cube the triangle that represents the generative and moving force of the phallus is depicted, like the Bacchic triquetra in motion. From this contrast of the even and the odd number the exclusive connection of the latter with the circus games first becomes clear in its whole significance. For since here the motion of the phenomenal world, as it proceeds from the fecundation of matter, is to be represented, it is precisely the generative and moving odd that must predominate in the circus games. 22.

e: With the first two odd numbers, three and five, the seven is connected. Before we subject it to a closer consideration and seek to establish its significance, it is necessary to preface a remark on the age of its adoption into the circus games. In Dio Cassius 37, 18 there is found, namely, an account that might easily give occasion for doubt. On the occasion of the Jewish custom of hallowing the seventh day, and of the advantage which Pompey drew from it in the siege of Jerusalem, the historian expresses himself as follows: τὸ δὲ δὴ ἐς τοὺς ἀστέρας τοὺς ἑπτά, τοὺς [PDF 284] — 270 — πλανήτας ὠνομασμένους, τὰς ἡμέρας ἀνακεῖσθαι, κατέστη μὲν ὑπ᾽ Αἰγυπτίων, πάρεστι δὲ καὶ ἐπὶ πάντας ἀνθρώπους, οὐ πάλαι ποτέ, ὡς λόγῳ εἰπεῖν, ἀρξάμενον. οἱ γοῦν ἀρχαῖοι Ἕλληνες οὐδαμῇ αὐτὸ (ὅσα γε ἐμὲ εἰδέναι) ἠπίσταντο· ἀλλ᾽ ἐπειδὴ καὶ πάνυ νῦν τοῖς τε ἄλλοις ἅπασι καὶ αὐτοῖς τοῖς Ῥωμαίοις ἐπιχωριάζει, καὶ ἤδη καὶ τοῦτο σφίσι πάτριον τρόπον τινά ἐστι, βραχύ τι περὶ αὐτοῦ διαλεχθῆναι βούλομαι, πῶς τε καὶ τίνα τρόπον οὕτω τέτακται. Here the spread of the Hebdomades over Greece and Rome is placed in a very recent time and traced back to Egypt. Now the passage of Cassiodor 3, 51, communicated earlier, reports that the seven laps of the circus were introduced ad similitudinem hebdomadis reciprocæ, from which the conclusion seems to follow that the application of the number seven to the circus games, their eggs and dolphins, is not original but of later origin. But this conclusion is refuted at once by the fact that Varro in Gellius already emphasizes the septem curricula solemnia; that, further, the seven-stringed lyre of the circensian pompa is named an ancient sacral usage customary in all ceremonies and is traced back to the seven-stringed Orphic lyre itself; that Venus promises septem savia suavia to him who would bring back to her Psyche, the runaway slave, to the metæ murciæ; and that, finally, the number seven appears at Rome, in many applications, as an ancient holy number: in the seven hills, the festival of the Septimontium, the seven pignora imperii, the septemviri epulonum, the sevenfold renewal of the plebeian games, the seven times three tribes, the seven times three shields of Mummius, the observance of the seventh day in the planting of the vine; whence it follows that the sevenfold number of the laps, too, is original and stands wholly independent of the adoption of the Hebdomades as a number of days. What Dio Cassius alone designates as a custom previously unknown in the Occident and come only shortly before his time into general diffusion is the distribution of the seven planets over seven days and the designation of the latter by the names of the former. If this usage is traced by him to Egypt,1) where the number seven holds so high a position,2) Joannes Lydus, on the other hand, goes custom mentioned by Plut. de Is. et Os. 52, according to which the sacred cow is led seven times around the temple, “because the sun completes its course from the winter to the summer solstice in the seventh month;” the significance of the numbers 2 + 7 and 4 + 7, Plut. Is. et Os. 42; the death of Mycerinus in Herod. 2, 133: six years he would live, it was prophesied, in the seventh he would die. The sun, thought of as force, has the number four. Plut. Is. et Os. 39. The seven young of the cat mentioned as the highest number of its births. Plut. Is. et Os. 63, the septem dies cærimoniosi at the birth of Apis. Ammian. Marc. 22, 15. The seven forms the basic number of the Egyptian circles of gods, to which an eighth is added as father. He who comprehends the seven children is called Esmun, the Eighth. Bunsen has devoted particular attention to this subject, Aegyptens [PDF 285] — 271 — back to the Chaldeans, Philostrat in vita Apoll. 3, 13 to the Indians, which more recent travel reports and researches confirm also for other peoples of eastern Asia. If, then, no probative force can be conceded to the account of Dio Cassius for a late introduction of the number seven into the circus games, and no connection at all can be assumed between the designation of days by the names of the heavenly bodies and the sanctity of the number seven in general, then on the other hand Cassiodorus’s expression septem metis certamen omne peragitur ad similitudinem hebdomadis reciprocæ is likewise unable to raise a serious difficulty. By this Hebdomas the number of seven days is not to be understood, and Cassiodorus is by no means to be interpreted as though the seven laps had been introduced after the model of the custom, spread from Egypt, of dividing the week into seven days. Rather the whole context of the passage shows that the Hebdomas or number seven can refer only to the seven planets and the spheres corresponding to them. For Cassiodorus undertakes to demonstrate for the individual parts of the circus games a decidedly uranian-sidereal significance. The seasons, the twelve signs of the heavens, the moon, the sun, the morning star and the first light, the three zones, the rising and the setting receive their determination and representation, and in such surroundings the Hebdomas, too, can Stellung in der Weltgeschichte 5, 198 f. 336; 6, 4 f., Mainardus, Studien über den Zusammenhang der ägyptischen und griechischen Religion, p. 37, 38. Both the former and the latter always return to their point of departure, like the waves of the Euripus, which the flood drives forward and the ebb draws back again. So reciprocus stands in Plinius 2, 97: æstus amnis reciproci; 9, 57: amnis reciprocus; Varro L. L. 6, 5: tela reciproca, i.e. such arrows as fly back as they were shot off. After these preliminary remarks we pass to the discussion of the number seven and its significance itself. Its sanctity is acknowledged by the most diverse authors and is often emphasized in the most emphatic manner. “The seven consecrated to Apollo,” remarks Ammonius in Plutarch on the inscription Ei in the temple at Delphi, “would require more than a day to enumerate all its forces.” No less admiration for it is displayed by Varro in Gellius, Noct. Atticæ 3, 10. In connection with the Mosaic story of creation Philo, in the work on the creation of the world, discusses at length all the distinctions of the Hebdomas, and introduces his account with the words, § 30: τὴν δὲ ἑβδομάδος φύσιν οὐκ οἶδ᾽ εἴ τις ἱκανῶς ἀνυμνῆσαι δύναιτο, παντὸς οὖσαν λόγου κρείττονα. It is to him the holiest of all numbers, and by an etymology current elsewhere as well is traced back to σέβομαι. With the same reverence it is treated by Macrobius, Somn. e: equally at home among the different tribes.1) Any attempt to assign a definite local home to the Hebdomas, which appears everywhere, and to recognize this perhaps in Egypt, or in Palestine, or in India, would be untenable, although Jewish authors, misled by the vanity of their patriotism, have often fallen into such an error. For since it did not escape them that Greeks and Romans too paid manifold homage to the number seven, they recognized therein a homage rendered to the divinity of the Mosaic law by the whole rest of the world; indeed, to make the agreement still greater than it really was, even forgery of ancient Greek texts seems not to have been disdained. Well known and much discussed are the accounts of Josephus and Philo. In the second book against Apion the former expresses himself thus: Οὐ μὴν ἀλλὰ καὶ πλήθεσιν ἤδη πολὺς ζῆλος γέγονεν ἐκ μακροῦ τῆς ἡμετέρας εὐσεβείας· οὐδ᾽ ἔστιν οὐ πόλις Ἑλλήνων οὐδ᾽ ἡτισοῦν, οὐδὲ βάρβαρον οὐδὲ ἓν ἔθνος, ἔνθα μὴ τὸ τῆς ἑβδομάδος, ἣν ἀργοῦμεν ἡμεῖς, τὸ ἔθος οὐ διαπεφοίτηκεν. Philo in the book on the creation of the world seems nevertheless to attach a similar meaning to his more vaguely held words: Τιμᾶται δὲ (ἡ ἑβδομάς) καὶ παρὰ τοῖς δοκιμωτάτοις τῶν Ἑλλήνων καὶ βαρβάρων, οἳ τὴν μαθηματικὴν ἐπιστήμην διαπονοῦσιν. While these two authors are content to bring the manifold recognition finitely much else, belongs to the Semitic tribes of the East, and goes back to the primeval times of Asiatic culture and observation of the heavens. This first diffusion over the lands of the ancient world, although perfectly certain, cannot come into consideration here, because it recedes into times of which no report has reached us; it belongs to a general phenomenon, before which men for so long deliberately closed their eyes, namely that Asiatic civilization has become the foundation of all ancient culture. This original diffusion from Asia has no connection with the assumption of a transmission from the Orient to the peoples of Greece and Italy that took place only in historical times. If I maintain the former, I deny the latter, without thereby denying that the scientific treatment and investigation of the number seven by the Greeks and Romans was first called forth by their later acquaintance with the Orient. The use of the number seven is older than its scientific contemplation. — A most remarkable application of the number seven is found in Eustath on Dionys. Pereg. V. 76. e: of the religious significance which the number seven found among Greeks and non-Greeks into a general connection with the Jewish hallowing of the seventh day, the Jew Aristobulus directed his effort to demonstrating a far more extensive agreement between Hebraism and Graecism. According to him, the religious significance of the seven was supposed to have found its expression among the Greeks too, from of old, in the same hallowing of the seventh day that underlay the Jewish sabbatism. What he adduced for this is in Clemens Stromata 5, p. 513. Oxon., and from there passed into Eusebius, Præpar. Evang. 13, 12. 13. They are verses of Hesiod, Homer, Linus, Callimachus, whose forgery is in part obvious, as in the following, ascribed to Homer and Linus: Ἕβδομον ἦμαρ ἔην, καὶ τῷ τετέλεστο ἅπαντα. — Ἑβδομάτῃ δή οἱ τετελεσμένα πάντα τέτυκται — in part, though hard to detect, nevertheless demonstrated by Valckenaer de Aristobulo Judæo, Philosopho Peripatetico, § 38. p. 116 ff. ed. Luzac. Lugduni Batav. 1806.1) To the Greeks and Romans the hallowing of the seventh day in the Jewish manner was wholly foreign, as many utterances show, e.g. Juvenal Sat. 6, 158; 14, 105, Rutilius, Itinerar. 1, 391, Ovid, Ars am. 1, 416. Rem. amor. 219, Horat. Sat. 1, 9, 69, (the much discussed tricesima sabbata, on which Acro and the opinions of more recent writers collected by Orelli), Persius Sat. 5, 18, Sueton. Aug. 76, Seneca Ep. 95 medio, Tacit. Hist. 6, 4. Cf. Plutarch, Sympos. 4, 5, and de superstit. 3 (Hutten 8, 59), especially Tertullian ad nationes 1, 13, Apologet. 16. If, then, we are compelled to oppose the Jewish authors cited and their accounts called forth by national-religious interest, it must on the other hand be conceded that their statements about the general diffusion sumption of conscious forgery. Nevertheless I openly confess that precisely this result, from another side, again presents me with the greatest difficulties. How could such forgeries remain unnoticed? Homer, Hesiod, Linus, Callimachus were authors whom at Alexandria men not only read but, for the most part, probably learned by heart; and how do scholars like Clement and Eusebius stand in relation to such a deception? One of two things: either they appear as ignoramuses or as accomplices. Two qualities that both fit the character of their writings poorly. Forgeries were indeed very common in the ancient world, and one has reason to wonder that the present predominantly negative tendency of mind has not yet undertaken a compilation of the numerous testimonies which the works of the ancients offer for literary deceit; but upon Eusebius and Clement such suspicion is cast nowhere. When Varro declares that one should assert nothing with absolute certainty, this principle seems to me, at least in the face of doubts, to have full justification. It is impossible to untie a knot if one does not know how it was tied. This Aristotelian saying holds above all of the question before us, which is still surrounded by so much mysterious obscurity.

e: of the sacral character of the number seven are in perfect agreement with what has already been adduced of Greek and Roman custom. The sanctity of the number seven is the same among all the peoples of antiquity. In this there is no difference between Greeks, Romans, Egyptians, Jews, Indians. Where they differ from one another is only in the significance that they attached to the Hebdomas in their cult practices. The transfer to the number of days, and the hallowing of every seventh day connected with it, as well as the naming of the days after the planets, is not original with the Romans and Greeks, but a custom that penetrated from outside only late.1) But even this was not without all foothold. On the contrary, among the Hellenes too an application of the seven to the seventh day appears, and indeed one that, like all the Jewish festivals, is brought into connection with the revolution of the moon. The seventh day of the month is consecrated to Apollo, as the eighth to Poseidon.2) The testimonies of the ancients are perfectly definite on this. In Plutarch’s Table Talk 8, 1 Florus says that on Plato’s birthday one must not pass over in silence Carneades, one of the most worthy heads of the Academy. Both, he says, were born at a festival of Apollo: the former at the Thargelia in Athens, the latter during the Carneian festival at Cyrene.3) “The one as well as the other,” he adds, “is celebrated on the seventh day, and you prophets and priests call the god himself, because he was born on this very day, Hebdomagetes (as Valckenaer de Aristobulo 37, p. 115 emends the usual Ἑβδομαγένην). Therefore, it seems to me, those who ascribe Plato’s begetting to Apollo do this god no insult at all, who by means of Socrates, as of another Chiron, has formed for us in this man a physician against the gravest diseases, I mean the passions.”4) Ἑβδομαγέτας the god is called also in Aeschylus, Seven against Thebes, line 780: καλῶς ἔχει τὰ πλεῖστ᾽ ἐν ἓξ πυλώμασιν, fifth book of Euseb. e: τὰς δ᾽ ἑβδόμας ὁ σεμνὸς ἑβδομαγέτας ἄναξ Ἀπόλλων εἵλετ᾽. The connection of the number seven with Apollo’s Delian birth is celebrated by Callimachus in the Hymn to Delos 249–255. For seven times the song-rich swans of the Pactolus circle the island, and they had not yet begun the eighth song when the youthful god stepped forth into the light. The boy then strung the divine lyre with as many strings as the number of times the swans had raised their song at his mother’s birth pangs. — Compare with this what Ptolemæus Hephæstio lib. 7 in the Fr. h. gr. 4, 513 reports of the birth of Zeus: Θεόδωρος ὁ Σαμοθρᾷξ τὸν Δία φησὶ γεννηθέντα ἐπὶ ἑπτὰ ἡμέρας ἀκατάπαυστον γελάσαι, καὶ διὰ τοῦτο τέλειος ἐνομίσθη ὁ ἕβδομος ἀριθμός. The hallowing of the seventh day applies to every month, as appears from the scholion on Aristophanes Plutus 426. ἡ τετρὰς ἐνομίζετο τοῦ Ἑρμοῦ, καὶ καθ᾽ ἕκαστον μῆνα ταύτῃ τῇ ἡμέρᾳ ἀπετίθεντο τῷ Ἑρμῇ.1) ἔξω γὰρ τῶν ἑορτῶν ἱεραί τινες τοῦ μηνὸς ἡμέραι νομίζονται Ἀθήνησι θεοῖς τισίν, οἷον νουμηνία καὶ ἑβδόμη Ἀπόλλωνι, τετρὰς Ἑρμῇ, καὶ ὀγδόη Θησεῖ.2) Gellius 15, 2 and Lucian Pseudologista 16 give information on the manner of observing this seventh Apollonian day. Gellius: Is (ex Creta homo) in conviviis juvenum, quæ agitare Athenis hebdomadibus lunæ solemne nobis fuit, simulatque modus epulis factus, et utiles delectabilesque sermones cœperant, tum silentio ad audiendum petito loqui cœptabat.3) Lucian says that the name Ἑβδόμη suits a man who likes to turn everything into a jest. ὁ δὲ Ἑβδόμην (εἶπεν), ὅτι ὥσπερ οἱ παῖδες ἐν ταῖς ἑβδόμαις, κἀκεῖνος ἐν ταῖς ἐκκλησίαις ἔπαιζε, καὶ διεγέλα, καὶ παιδιὰν ἐποιεῖτο τὴν σπουδὴν τοῦ δήμου. Without mention of the day’s celebration, the seven is more often ascribed to Apollo. Plutarch Symp. 9, 3: Ἡ δὲ ἑβδομὰς τῷ Μουσηγέτῃ προσκεκλήρωται. Censorin. de die nat. 14. Fuerunt etiam, qui utrumque reciperent numerum (sc. κλιμακτῆρα vitæ humanæ) et undequinquagesimum (7 × 7) et octogesimum unum (9 × 9); et minorem nocturnis genesibus, majorem diurnis adscriberent. Plerique aliter moti, duos istos numeros subtiliter discreverunt, dicentes septenarium ad corpus, novenarium ad animum pertinere. hunc medicinæ corporis et Apollini attributum; illum Musis; quia morbos animi, quos adpellant πάθη, musica lenire ac sanare consueverit. Particular attention is deserved also by the following statement in Plutarch’s letter of consolation to Apollonius, in Hutten 7, 335: “Agamedes and Trophonius had built the temple at Delphi, and now asked Apollo for a reward. He promised to give it to them on the seventh day, and admonished them that they should meanwhile [PDF 291] — 277 — treat themselves well. They obeyed the command, lay down to sleep on the seventh night, and died.” The number seven now transfers itself, in the most manifold application, to everything Apollonian. The seven-stringed lyre is traced back to Orpheus.1) On the Amyclaean throne, in the economy of Polygnotus’s paintings at Delphi, the seven prevails, no less than at Olympia in the division of the chest of Cypselus, on the throne of Zeus, and at Rhodes in the size of the Colossus of the Sun,2) on Lesbos in the number of the leaders in Plutarch Conviv. sept. sapient. c. 20. In the tenth Greek question, in connection with his explanation of the month Bysios as Pysios, from πύθεσθαι, to ask, Plutarch relates the following: “To this explanation the old popular legend also corresponds. For in this month the oracle is said to have originated, and the seventh day is held to be the birthday of Apollo, and is called πολυφθόος, not because on that day a certain kind of cake, called φθοῖς, is baked, but because on that day Apollo gave answer to many questions. For only in later times was it permitted to consult the oracle in every month, but earlier the Pythia, according to the report of Callisthenes and Alexandrides, used to prophesy only once a year, namely on this day.” This leads us to the verse of Hesiod, Works and Days, 770, which Aristobulus places at the head of his proofs taken from Greek poets: Πρῶτον ἐνὴ τετράς τε καὶ ἑβδόμη ἱερὸν ἦμαρ Τῇ γὰρ Ἀπόλλωνα χρυσάορα γείνατο Λητώ. Compare with this Lydus de mensib. p. 26. Schow. Μάρτυς Ὀρφεὺς λέγων Ἑβδόμη, ἣν ἐφίλησεν ἄναξ ἑκάεργος Ἀπόλλων, which is probably taken from the Orphic περὶ Ἡμερῶν (Lobeck, Aglaopham p. 428–432). Further Proclus in Tim. 3, 168: ἡ μονὰς καὶ ἑπτὰς ἀριθμοὶ νοεροί τινες· ἡ μὲν μονὰς αὐτόθεν νοῦς, ἡ δὲ ἑπτὰς τὸ κατὰ νοῦν φῶς, καὶ διὰ τοῦτο ὁ περικόσμιος νοῦς μοναδικός τε καὶ ἑβδοματικός ἐστιν, ὡς φησιν Ὀρφεύς. Finally the following statements also come into consideration: Diogenes Laërt. Plato 2: καὶ γίνεται Πλάτων, ὥς φησιν Ἀπολλόδωρος ἐν χρονικοῖς, ὀγδόῃ καὶ ὀγδοηκοστῇ ὀλυμπιάδι Θαργηλιῶνος ἑβδόμῃ, καθ᾽ ἣν Δήλιοι τὸν Ἀπόλλωνα γενέσθαι φασίν. Boeckh. C. J. 1, p. 465. The Antiochenes, according to Libanius Declam. T. 1, 236, venerated Apollo and Artemis on the same day, namely the seventh, whereas otherwise, as the scholion on Aristophanes Plutus and Iamblich. 5, 152 attest, Artemis had the sixth, Apollo alone the seventh day.1) These two are also joined in Theophrast. char. 14 and in Dionys. Art. 3, 243: ἑβδόμῃ καὶ ἕκτῃ ὅτι ἱεραὶ τοῖν θεοῖν.2) The Apollonian seven is repeated in Orestes and in the solar hero Heracles. To both the stature of seven cubits is ascribed. Of this we possess the testimonies of Herodot 1, 68. 69. Gellius 3, 10, Solinus c. 1, p. 7, Philostrat Her. 1, 2, p. 28. Boiss., as indeed the perfect measure of the body was generally fixed at this height, on which Plautus Curcul. 3, 70 (statua septempedalis) and the septipedes Burgundiones in Sidonius Apollinaris, as well as other passages collected by Salmasius on Solinus p. 31, give information. Finally I call attention to Pausan. 2, 7, 7. Apollo and Artemis are propitiated by the offering of seven boys and seven girls. By all these testimonies the sanctity of the number seven and its connection with Apollo, as well as with the seventh day of every month, is raised above all challenge, and at the same time demonstrated in its originality. 23. Now we have cleared the way to penetrate into a correct understanding of the significance that distinguishes the number seven. If the three showed itself as ἀρχὴ καὶ γένεσις, the five as φύσις and γάμος, so the seven is τελεσφόρος, and this according to the Greek conception as well as the Jewish. Six birth pangs Latona has to endure until in the seventh Apollo can step into the light. Seven times the swans circle the island singing, and before they begin the eighth circuit, the god has come into appearance. With him the work of the mother stands completed. The lord of creation, the great hero of light, crowns the realm which he enters, and even before the seventh day reaches its close, all is perfect. Six days the preparation lasts, the seventh [PDF 293] — 279 — brings the completion. In the same significance the number seven appears in the Mosaic story of creation. It is the seventh day on which God completes his work which he has made, and on which he rests from all his work which he made creating. (Moses, Genes. 2, 1, on which passage see Bunsen in the first half of the first volume of his Bibelwerk; the leaf bears no page number.)1) For this reason the seventh day is called by Philo ὁ τοῦ κόσμου γενέσιος or γενέθλιος, καθ᾽ ἣν τὸ τοῦ πατρὸς ἔργον τέλειον ἐκ τελείων μερῶν ἀναφανέν.2) Likewise τελεσφόρος, i.e. bringing to maturity and completion. Καλεῖται δὲ ἡ ἑβδομὰς ὑπὸ τῶν κυρίως τοῖς εἰωθόσιν ὀνόμασι χρωμένων καὶ τελεσφόρος, ἐπειδὴ ταύτῃ τελεσφορεῖται τὰ σύμπαντα.3) Philo de septenario: Ἑβδομὰς δ᾽ ἀμιγέστατος, καὶ φῶς (εἰ χρὴ τἀληθὲς εἰπεῖν) ἑξάδος. ἃ γὰρ ἐγέννησεν ἑξάς, ταῦθ᾽ ἑβδομὰς τελεσφορηθέντα ἐπεδείξατο.4) That which is perfected comes into being last. It is there not at the beginning but at the end. Therefore Apollo and creation in their perfected glory cannot come to birth on the first day, but only on the seventh. The development is the same as in the bodily birth of man, in which likewise the seventh month appears as τελεσφόρος. It always proceeds from below upward, from the imperfect to the perfect. In this sense the gods have their birthday festivals, as the Quinquatria have been cited as Minerva’s natale, and as, beside the Ἀπόλλωνος καὶ Ἀρτέμιδος γοναί, others are mentioned: Ἀφροδίτης γοναί, Ζηνὸς γοναί, Ἀθηνᾶς γοναί, Πανὸς γοναί.5) The ancients place the dedication of temples on a line with birth. They are the birthday festival of the god who rules in them. The work itself must come first; the dedicatio is the γενήσιος τοῦ θεοῦ, and as such belongs to the Fasti.6) According to this conception the elapsing of the seventh day is not required. Since the work belongs to the first six, which alone are generative, it suffices, in order to fulfill the destination of the seventh, if it merely dawns, and thus shows the completion, τὸ φῶς τῆς ἑξάδος. Apollo’s birth is complete before the seventh sun sets, before the seventh circuit ends, the seventh song dies away. Moses assigns the completing and the resting to the same day. From this conception the Roman principle dies is repeated in Plato Timæus p. 386, Bipont. and Plut. Sympos. 3, 1.

This meaning of the ἑβδόμη, and consequently of the ἑβδομάς, recurs in all those applications by which the ancients carry through the physical-natural meaning of the number seven. The Hebdomas of the stages of age in human life is especially emphasized. So by the physician Hippocrates2) according to Censorin Dies Nat. 14, Macrob. Somn. Scip. 1, 6. p. 44. Philo, de opif. mundi § 36. Aristot. Polit. 7, 14, 11. In the presentation of the Solonian elegies, too, the seven plays a great part. These distichs, which one recognizes in Herodot. 1, 32, have been preserved for us by Philo § 35, are mentioned by Censorin, Dies Nat. 14, Eusebius 12, 12. 13, Ambrosius Epist. 6, 39,3) and are discussed more fully by Müller on Philo, pp. 313–318. In place of the septies decem, decies septem anni appear here as the εὐκταῖον τοῦ βίου τέλος, as in Psalm 90, 10. In this application to the development of human life the τελεσφόρος δύναμις ἑβδομάδος lies quite clearly before us. In seven cycles existence is completed; the last brings the desirable end of life. The Hebdomas thereby passes over into the meaning of the measure of earthly things. Thus we have already found it above as the limit of bodily length; thus it appears further in the number seven of births: the seven daughters of Deidamia,4) the seven children of Niobe,5) the seven boys and seven girls whom the earth brought forth in the third birth,6) the seven Cynosures,7) the seven Cyclopes (Strabo 8, 372), the seven daughters of Amphion and the seven gates of Thebes corresponding to them (Hygin. f. 68), the seven gates of Mithras (Beyer on Selden 1, 6), the seven offspring of Thetis,8) among whom Achilles, the most perfect, is called Septimus; so too in the seven boys and girls who every ninth year go as tribute to Crete,9) in the seven islands, the seven Centaurines, the seven Achaean heroes, the seven persons involved in Agamemnon’s murder;10) again in the septemplex clypeus Apollod. 3; in the commentary of Meursius on Lycophron in Müller’s Lycophron, vol. 1, 1199.

If, further, the seventh day is decisive in all illnesses and is therefore called κριτικός or κρίσιμος; if the halcyonic brooding days are seven; if in the cycle of seven larger or smaller periods of time all growth, all bodily change, even female purification and death from hunger, attains a definite completion: then here too we see the Hebdomas again as τελεσφόρος, so that the six, as in the Mosaic story of creation, creates and leads toward ripeness what the seven then presents completed in all its parts. The applications emphasized are all the more instructive for the number seven of the circus laps, since they bring the idea of completion into connection with that of motion and of material growth, and belong wholly to the domain of material becoming and passing away. We see from this that the seven, which differs so essentially from the three and the five, nevertheless agrees with these first two odd numbers in this, that, like them, it belongs to the realm of the creation that appears, advancing in eternal motion and eternal growth, and therefore, like them, is a somatic number, existing in things, not outside them. But here we have arrived at the point where the Hebdomas separates from the Trias and the Pemptas and assumes a nature to which those cannot rise. The seven, within whose limits all things of the tellurian world move and undergo all the changes prescribed to them, is of uranian origin; its first and most prominent manifestation in Rufum 1, 185.

e: is an astronomical one. In the sevenfold number of the planets and in the seven spheres in which they complete their course, the motion of the tellurian creation, which follows the same law and measure, is prefigured. From heaven the harmony of the seven has descended into the things of a deeper, more material region. From above it governs the tellurian world, whose motion is guided and harmoniously developed by that of the uranian. “It is impossible that any motion should exist that does not agree with the motion of some star.” “The revolution of the planets brings forth all phenomena.” These utterances of Aristotle (in the Metaphysics 12, 8, 9. 15) contain a primal thought of humanity that wholly governs the mode of contemplation of the ancient world.1) In its highest uranian revelation the seven is now less material than in the tellurian, and indeed less so in the same proportion in which the stars are purer than earthly beings and stand closer to the perfect immateriality of God than the earth does. True, the stars too still belong to the sensually perceptible world, but they have a greater kinship with eternal substance than the tellurian has, to which the world of sensuality surrounding us belongs.2) They are themselves divine bodies, and the science that occupies itself with them is the one best suited to lead the spirit to the unmoved source of all motion, to the Aristotelian primal circle. Between this purely intellectual being and full materiality the stars stand in the middle. More material than the former, less material than the latter, they partake of the nature of both, act by virtue of their materiality upon matter, and indeed with the greater force the nearer their spheres approach the earth, but at the same time, by virtue of their immateriality, lead upward to the highest source of light.3) In the double nature of the stars the number seven too shares, in consequence of its astronomical origin. Without stripping off materiality, it nevertheless penetrates to its farthest boundary, and so mediates the transition from the sensual into the supersensible ἐπίγεια ἤρτηται κατά τινα φυσικὴν συμπάθειαν, ὁ τῆς ἑβδομάδος λόγος ἄνωθεν ἀρξάμενος κατέβη καὶ πρὸς ἡμᾶς, τοῖς θνητοῖς γένεσιν ἐπιφοιτήσας. συμπάθειαν πρὸς ἀέρα καὶ γῆν. — § 38. init. e: world. Belonging to earthly things and to heavenly appearances alike, it unites in itself both boundaries of the universe and thus forms the nodus omnium rerum. The middle position between the ἐπίγεια and the ἀσώματα καὶ νοητά that belongs to the uranian seven may be compared with that which, according to Plato’s views, falls to the mathematical domain between the sensual and the ideal.1) Here greater purity is ascribed to the mathematical that appears in the heavenly bodies than to that in the tellurian ones. The same idea leads to the proposition that in the stars form outweighs matter. When it is said in Aristotle, Metaphysics 12, 8, 25, that the highest form has no matter, then, conversely, tellurian things are matter without form, a thought which the Bithynian Ares myth cited above makes quite vivid. In the stars both meet, matter and form; the former they have in common with the tellurian creation, and on this community rests the sympathy2) that binds the two spheres of the universe; the latter, on the other hand, derives from that highest form to which no matter clings. Thus the sidereal seven appears now, preeminently before the other numbers, as the expression of perfected form, and, inasmuch as harmony and beauty are grounded in form, the Hebdomas itself now becomes καλλίστη and ἁρμονικωτάτη,3) the rhythmic motion of the heavenly bodies the expression of the most beautiful form and of perfected harmony. Revealed in the stars and their dance, it is destined to guide every motion of the lower creation, to bring it into accord with itself, descending from stage to stage to pervade all matter, and to subject its wild force to the law of beauty, of rhythm, and of perfected proportion. So there is confirmed in the most perfect way what we set forth above as the distinguishing feature of the seven over against the three and the five: that, namely, alongside the common idea of motion in cœli, quam vocant συμπάθειαν. e: the world of sensual appearance, which underlies all the numbers considered, the seven nevertheless, by virtue of its higher uranian origin, takes the lead of the other two numbers, ruling and guiding them, as the supreme law revealed in the stars.1) If the Trias and the Pempas present force in the fullness of its content, in the seven it appears obedient to a higher law. It is Pegasus, whom Athena teaches to rein and to guide, Ares, who subjects his overflowing male force to the rules of orchestics. In participation in the seven, the motion that forms the essence of life in the earthly creation appears traced back to the divine model of the stars, and by that alone partakes of order and of regulated progress. For this reason the Ἑπτὰ enjoys that Σεβασμός which is ascribed to it alone.2) It is the highest visible expression of the divine law, revealed in the purest of the perceptible bodies, the stars, which themselves partake of divinity. It can therefore be regarded as the expression of the highest sovereignty, according to Macrobius as the numerus qui omnia gubernat. In this meaning the seven is the number of the sun. Among the seven spheres, in whose orbits the seven planets move, that of the sun stands out as ruling. Helios is the king of heaven, as the Homeric Hymn 17 greets him; the stars are his retinue, which grows pale at the appearance of the prince. He alone is as much as the whole remaining host; alone he strides on, in undivided and uncontested greatness.3) In the sun the seven unites with its source, the Monas. Sol himself follows in his motions the law of the seven,4) according to which he guides, as himself, so also the moon.5) For Luna, like everything uranian, like Pleiades and Atlantides and everything tellurian, is wholly governed by the septenarius numerus. In this highest tracing back the seven meets the Monas, as indeed the sayings of the ancients already communicated above declare that no number has so intimate a kinship with the one as the seven, which in Apollo also takes its place beside that one. e: solar Hebdomas bears all the attributes that belong to the eternal, unchangeable source of light. Like light itself it is immaterial, wholly of an incorrupt and incorruptible nature. Not directed toward generation, it appears as the representation of the pure masculinity that stems from the sun and of its spiritual luminous nature. In this meaning it is joined with Pallas-Athena and is itself called πάρθενος, ἀμήτωρ, ἁγνεία. It is, like the virgin who is said to be well disposed toward everything male, πλὴν γάμου τυχεῖν, sprung in unitary nature from the head of Zeus, perfect as the word from the mouth.1) In this wholly spiritualized meaning it belongs especially to the metaphysical purity of the Apollonian nature. In this meaning it becomes the number of joy, the Apollonian seventh day of the month and the birthday of a Carneades and a Plato. e: destruction, consecrated at Olympia,1) all of which evidently place the solar number in the foreground in its meaning directed toward rule and political hegemony. In many applications that private law offers, especially in the septem signa testamentorum,2) the same idea of sovereignty is recognizable clearly enough, notably in contrast to the application of the number five. 24. Turning again, enriched by the insight into the higher nature of the number seven, to the circus games, we find that these now for the first time gain their full and highest significance. Governed by the Hebdomas, they assume all those higher relations that rest in the sacred number. The motion of visible creation, which is represented in the swift flight of the teams, appears borne and regulated by the harmonious motion of the stars, the law that governs the tellurian world as an effluence of a higher divine order of things. The earthly becomes a likeness of the heavenly; the spirit, led on from the eternal destruction that governs the former, is carried to the contemplation of a world in which the eternity of the cycle is accompanied by no destruction, whose motion points to a mover, whose harmony and beauty point to a highest source of perfected form. Overcome appears the dark violence of the powers that rule in the depths of the earth. Victorious and ruling, the gods of heavenly light come forth. In their praise the games are celebrated. Everything takes on a uranian relation. In everything the phenomena of the heavenly cosmos are recognized. Cassiodor 3, 51 calls the games of the circus an expression of the star cult,3) and when he assigns to each single act of them a definite relation to the heavenly bodies and their course, he lends expression in this only to the general popular belief. In the seven circuits one recognizes the cœli clupeo. — Hence the shields of the Caeretan tomb, now in the Gregorianum at Rome, from whose center the horned head of Bacchus looks out. e: image of the revolution of the seven heavenly spheres, whose harmony is repeated in the seven-stringed lyre of the circus pompa and in its tones. The four-horse team is brought into connection with the nature of the sun by virtue of the perfected incorporeality of the tetractys, as already in the triumph of Camillus, while the two-horse team is assigned to the maternal lunar nature, which is related to the disunion of matter. The solar rises above the lunar, so that even the team of mules, as it was originally in use according to the testimony of Festus, has everywhere disappeared, except at the Consualia. For mules stand in a close relation to the moon. Between the ass and the horse, the animal of unregulated material force, and the noble winged steed guided by Athena, the mule occupies an intermediate position, just as the moon, which unites a higher and a lower nature in itself, stands between sun and earth, and the sterility of both seems to have offered a further point of comparison.1) Now, however, natural force is raised to its highest stage. The paternal principle of the sun stands there ruling, and whereas on the tellurian stage Consus appeared in a subordinate position as the πάρεδρος of Murcia, female materiality in the moon now recedes into the background before the greater power of the sun. — If the general solar significance of the number seven is thus to be recognized in the seven circuits, the seven eggs, the seven dolphins, and the seven-stringed lyre, then that side of its nature in which it appears as τελεσφόρος becomes especially important. In this quality it gives the circus games a quite special consecration, the correct conception of which is of the highest importance. We have come to know the solemnity of the great races as funeral games, and have recognized in them the idea of a cult offered to the highest lord of life. Now this double relation to death and life receives its closer determination. As τελεσφόρος, the number seven that rules in the circus shows tellurian life as the time of birth of a higher existence. The completion that it brings lies in the passage to a higher sidereal existence. As, according to Varro in Plutarch Qu. rom. 11,2) the Roman who turns around at his father’s grave connects with this the thought of the elevation of the dead to divinity primum putatur cœptum currui vehiculoque adjungi. e: so too the completion of the seven circuits expresses the passage of earthly existence to a higher sidereal existence. The life of the body itself takes on the meaning of a time of birth, death that of an act of birth which lets a new being of divine nature come forth. As after six birth pangs Apollo steps into the light in the seventh circuit of the swans, so the sevenfold circling shows that the seven ages of man are themselves only the birth pangs of a divine being. When the seventh circuit begins, the dead man has come into being as Hebdomagetes in the realm of light.1) Thus it is not the sad lot of death of everything that has become that governs the circus games as their final thought; rather, above it there rises, consoling, the certainty of an immortality prepared by it. The words of a fragment of Euripides find their place here: “Who knows, remarks the poet, whether life is not what is called dying, and living death? Unhappy are the living, but nothing torments the dead; their woe has departed.” The same holds for the egg. It is not the downward-going birth into material life, but the upward-leading one, from the material into an immaterial existence, that is recognized as the highest idea in its setting up and its removal. If at birth the genius leads the soul of man into the change of matter and into all its deceit, then death, through the annihilation of the coarse garment, conducts it back to the stars and raises it to a uranian existence in which, united with the heavenly lord of the pure stars, it shares in the glory of the prince of light.2) The hope of such an elevation to sidereal life is expressed in many ways by the initiates on their epitaphs, of which we have already adduced several examples earlier. “I am joined to the heavenly host, for the god was my guide,” we read on that epitaph of the fisherman of Marseilles.3) The same thought is shown by the circus sarcophagi, which we therefore without hesitation ry palm won in the race with the idea of bodily destruction. The same I remark [PDF 305] — 291 — in general, the manifold emphasis on the world of the stars in the tombs, the use of the white color in initiation and in mourning: everything proclaims the thought of a birth of light mediated through the death of the body, in contrast to which tellurian life appears as the time of birth completed according to the law of the number seven. The material primal egg is now, in a higher sense, ἀρχὴ γενέσεως. It shows the birth of man no longer only in its limitation to the narrow bounds of corporeal existence, but as the ground of an eternal existence that develops out of the tellurian, and hence the motion in the stream of the appearing sensual creation as preparation for a participation, removed from the motion of becoming and passing away, in the eternity of the realm of light, whose kingship rests in Apollo and Dionysus.1) In accord with this, uranian significance is ascribed to the egg itself. It stems from heaven, to which it leads its births back. Egg-bearing are the moon women. From heaven falls that egg into the Euphrates which gives the Syrian Aphrodite her origin. In the egg-birth and the egg caps of the Dioscuri the same connection of the stars with the egg emerges, which has often found artistic representation. On the Pompeian paintings we see the starry garment of the female nature mother combined with the representation of the egg on the lower half of the painting. In imitation of this uranian origin we found the egg also in temples, hanging down from the tholus and, like the stars, floating freely in the airy space. Thus it itself partakes of the pure nature of the stars and lies, like them, on the boundary of two worlds, the material one of the earth, the immaterial one of light. Precisely thereby it is able in one act to bestow two births, the tellurian and the sidereal; thereby too it receives its purifying, lustrating force. Thereby it is suited to be the center of the mysteries,2) thereby for connection with about the beautiful picture in Stackelberg, Gräber der Hellenen 2. Here it now proclaims the connection of the sensually palpable with the supersensible world of light, of corporeal existence with that which follows it, of death with life, of the tellurian with the uranian sphere. The two worlds and existences that in the tomb join hands, and whose inner relation forms the object of all those riddles that the entering of the place of death suggests, these appear also joined in the egg; and in the relation of the chick to it the correspondence of corporeal and heavenly existence is recognized. As the egg must perish in order to give origin to a being that wings bear aloft to heaven: so the life of the body is consecrated to death, if the initiate is to be raised to sidereal existence in the train of his heavenly god.1) 25. Returning, enriched with these views, to the Pamphili tomb painting, we find that the colors too in which it is executed gain sense and meaning. Blue, red, and yellow are the only ones of which the artist made use.2) The colors named have, all of them, a solar significance. Light and color stand in an inner connection, so that the latter can be called an embodiment of the former. From this it follows, shows itself in the seven days which the souls spend in the Platonic meadow (Plato Republic 10, 616), in the sevenfold immersion of the head in the lustrating spring in Apuleius, probably also in the seven-day duration of the festival of Demeter in Pausan. 7, 27. 3 and in the septem fabæ in Ovid. F. 2, 574. The Karlsruhe Museum possesses several of them. To think of a jest is forbidden by the gravity of the tomb. If one wishes to recognize a satirical conception, this may well not contradict the ancient cast of mind. It always lets parody follow at the heels of earnestness. In the description of the great festival games with which Rome celebrated the victory over the Latins, Dionysius Halicarn. 7, p. 352 brings out very definitely the combination of satire with earnestness as a peculiarity of the ancient conception, and in the Laws Plato declares that earnestness without the corresponding jest is incomplete and unintelligible. Just for that reason parodies of the mysteries, such as those in Aristophanes’s Birds and their cosmogony, were not so offensive to the ancients as they might seem to us. Thus satire itself receives a serious character, and this one cannot deny to the said bird-men either. They too have a Bacchic relation to the mysteries. — With the picture of the bird breaking forth from the egg may be compared the flying up of the eagle, as it was represented at Olympia, and to which the simultaneous sinking of the dolphin corresponds. e: that color must stand in the closest relation to the highest solar divine nature of Dionysus. Its symbolic application, moreover, seems to agree admirably with the purely symbolic significance of the Pamphili painting. Among the colors predominantly ascribed to the sun the red takes the first place. In the work on the tenets of the philosophers 3, 5 Plutarch remarks that among the colors of the rainbow the red always takes the first place, and that it comes from the bright and brilliant ray of the sun falling on the raindrops and being refracted in them. In the triumph of Camillus, Livius 5, 23 emphasizes at one and the same time the team of the sun and the complexion of the victor painted with red ocher. From Plutarch Qu. rom. 98 there emerges the custom of the Romans of painting the Capitoline image of Jupiter red. The same color is attested especially for Dionysus. With red ocher the wooden carved image of him at Phelloë in Achaia was painted, and likewise the one at Phigalia in Arcadia.1) According to Macrob. Sat. 1, 18 the image of Dionysus at the festivals of the god wore πέπλον φοινίκεον πυρὶ ἴκελον, and if this garment is traced back to Orpheus, then the use of the red color in the mysteries is certainly expressed in this. In a red garment Bacchus appears also on a Herculanean painting (Pitture d’Ercolano T. 2. tab. 13. 16), and likewise on another that Philostrat Imag. 1, 15 describes, and for which Welcker p. 299 adduces the similar statements of Hymn. Homeric. 7, 5, Proclus in An. V. P. T. 2, p. 446, Nonnus Dionys. 20, 228, Lucian Bacchus C. 1. Ovid met. 3, 554. Typhon, who according to Firmic. Matern. de errore prof. relig. p. 3 ed. Bursian was conceived as force of fire, is called red in color in Plutarch Is. et Os. 29, and likewise gold, on account of its reddish color, is put in close relation to the sun. — For the determination of the blue color there serves a statement of Macrob. Sat. 1, 19 on the Egyptian representations of the sun. The images of the sun god the Egyptians paint now with a blue color, now gleaming white. The white sun they call Sol superus, the blue Sol inferus. Inferus, however, the sun is called in inferiore hemisphærio, hence as Dionysus in contrast to Apollo, as Macrob. Sat. 1, 18 designates that distinction. Blue appears also among the colors of the rainbow, and indeed after the red, because the ray of the sun that produces it is already more clouded and darkened.
