e: appearance as a ὑδρογονικὸν σημεῖον proclaims the fullness of the year’s blessing.1) However much the melilotum has risen to a preponderant significance in the religion, life, and art of the Nile land, the remaining swamp plants nevertheless take their place beside it with equal holiness. The papyrus in particular comes forward significantly. In a vessel made of papyrus Isis sails over the swamps,2) to seek out the body of her consort, torn to pieces by Typhon. Hence it is said to come about, Plutarch reports, Is. et Os. 17, that no crocodile does harm to those who travel on the Nile in such vessels made of papyrus, whether from fear or from reverence for the goddess. In this account the close connection of the primal mother Isis with swamps and swamp generation emerges most clearly. With right, therefore, the adornment of the lotus is ascribed to her. On a relief published by Caylus in the Recueil she appears seated in the midst of a thicket of reeds, as Horus too is sometimes shown not only resting on the lotus cup but even wholly overshadowed by such cups,3) and the body of Osiris resting on a crocodile and being carried to a region marked as swampland by reeds.4) If papyrus vessels are considered inviolable by the crocodile, this view can have its origin only in the holiness of that water reed. So too the Ioxids hold inviolable those plants in which the fair daughter of Perigune sought protection, reeds and wild asparagus: an ordinance handed down to them from the maternal side, because hetaeric sexual union knows only the material connection. With the papyrus vessel of Isis is to be compared the head of Adonis, formed of the same reed, which swims every year from Egypt, in Lucian, de dea Syria 7, and likewise the sutilis cymba of Charon, the ferryman of the underworld. The swamp nature of the primal water of the underworld, to which all life returns, corresponds perfectly to the idea of a skiff plaited of reeds.5) The holiness which the ancient religion ascribed to the material is revealed in this feature as well. Charon, who sails it, is the lion of the swampy deep, who bears within himself all the generative force of tuum — sutili cymba deducit commeantes. In Lucian’s veræ historiæ a skiff of asphodel stalks appears. Plinius 16, 27 describes scirpi and papyrus. From the former the village ἡ Σκιρποῦ on the swampy shores of Lake Copais, next to the ruins of the temple of the Charites, has its name. — On the similar names Θρύον and Θρυόεσσα Strabo 8, 3, 24.

G. 4, 478) von dem durch ruhelose Eile ausgezeichneten fließenden Strome ausdrücklich hervorgehoben wird. 2) Jn Charon und seinem rißenreichen Shilfkahne haben wir also einen neuen Ausdruck der Bedeutung des Sumpfschlammexk, der in ihm entspringenden Sumpfpflanzen, und beider Beziehung zu der in Zeugung und Untergang gleich waltenden Naturkraft. Auch diese Charontishen Vorstellungen stammen zweifelsohne aus dem schilfreichen Nil-Lande, dem Ocnus, die Danaiden und so vieles Andere angehört. =+ Die Beziehung des Sumpilebens zu der zeugenden Naturkraft führt zu der Annahme gewisser mit Weissagunz ausgerüsteter Wasserpflanzen. An die gleiche Anffassung schließt sic) die dem leisen Geflüster des Shilfröhrihts in manchen Sagen beigelegte Bedeutung an. In dem schönen Mythus von Pan's Liebe zu der Nonacrinischen Syrinx bei Ovid Met. 2, 639--712 tritt zu gleicher Zeit die dem Sumpfröhricht beigelegte Göttlichkeit, die Bedeutsamkeit der durch den leisen Luftzug hervorgerufenen Töne und der Zusammenhang der doppeltröhrigen Pfeife, wie sie Pan , Marsyas und der großen Sumpfmutter Neith-Athene, der Göttin der Tritonia palus als Attribut beigegeben wird, mit der alten Naturanschauung von der Heiligkeit der Sümpfe in sehr belehrender Weise hervor. Nicht weniger Beachtung verdient der Mytbus von der Liebe des zeugungsfkräftigen Priapus zu der schönen Lotis,%) und von
e: the mud. For Charon, whose connection with the stem Ar we have already pointed out above, is expressly attested as the Macedonian name of the lion; the lion, however, as a representation of the phallic force, and therefore sometimes also formed phallically, is brought into an entirely natural connection with the tellurian waters, especially according to Egyptian conception,1) and is therefore placed together with the horse by Horus: a comparison in which the difference between the stagnant, motionless swamp ground (tarda palus Virg. G. 4, 478) and the flowing stream, distinguished by restless haste, is expressly stressed.2) In Charon and his chink-ridden reed skiff we have, then, a new expression of the significance of swamp mud, of the swamp plants that spring up in it, and of the relation of both to the natural force that holds equal sway in generation and destruction. These Charontic conceptions, too, doubtless originate in the reedy Nile land, to which Ocnus, the Danaids, and so much else belong. — The relation of swamp life to the generative force of nature leads to the assumption of certain water plants endowed with prophecy. Thus in the fable of Psyche the green reed appears speaking. In human fashion it shows the much-tried girl the way to the golden sheep’s wool for which Venus has sent her out.3) With this one may compare the speaking calamus that betrays Midas’s ass’s ears, as well as the report of Julius Valerius (Res gestæ Alexandri 3, 40) about Indian wondrous and oracular trees, of which the male prophesy by day, the female by night. The significance attributed in many legends to the soft whispering of the reed beds attaches to the same conception. In the beautiful myth of Pan’s love for the Nonacrian Syrinx in Ovid, Met. 2, 689–712, there emerge at the same time, in a most instructive way, the divinity attributed to the swamp reeds, the significance of the sounds called forth by the gentle breath of air, and the connection of the double-reed pipe, as it is given as an attribute to Pan, Marsyas, and the great swamp mother Neith-Athena, the goddess of the Tritonia palus, with the ancient view of nature concerning the holiness of swamps. No less attention is deserved by the myth of the love of Priapus, mighty in generative force, for the fair Lotis,4) and of ward the sea with the mummy of Osiris. Die üppige Vegetation feuchter Tiefen zeigt den Stoff in seiner unbesiegbaren, nie erfüllten Sehnsucht nach Begattung und stets frischer Zeugung. Der. Hetärismus tritt also hier nicht nur in seiner Regellosigkeit, sondern nicht weniger in der Unerschöpflichkeit seines erotischen Einigungstriebes hervor. Nie ruht das Werk der stofflichen Kraft. e: that of Acis for Galatea.1) Both receive their full explanation only through their connection with the ancient swamp cult. To pluck the swamp flower appears as an outrage against its holiness, which the Ioxids therefore carefully avoid, and for which Dryope pays with a heavy punishment. Acis is wholly covered by the clod of earth that Polyphemus hurls after him. But the water dissolves the ground, and from the chinks of the burst mass reeds grow forth. As a horned river god Acis, too, rises from the waves. Reeds wreathe the pair of horns that adorns his brow, like that of Epidius Nuncionus.2) As in his name, which is related to Acca, Achelous, Achileus, Acheron, Inachus, and others, so too in the horns is revealed the force of the tellurian waters that call forth the reeds out of the matter of the earth. It is very significant that in all these mythic formations hetaeric sexual love forms the center. Thereby the equation of the latter with swamp life is confirmed anew, and the Egyptian myth of Mycerinus’s sojourn in the swamps, of Typhon’s hiding place in the mud grounds, of the mighty footprints of Perseus in the soft earth, likewise the Egyptian mourning custom of smearing the face with moist earth,3) become intelligible. The luxuriant vegetation of moist depths shows matter in its invincible, never-satisfied longing for mating and ever-fresh generation. Hetaerism thus emerges here not only in its lawlessness, but no less in the inexhaustibility of its erotic impulse to union. The work of material force never rests. Already in Rhea’s womb Isis and Osiris embrace. Without respite Penia strives for the favor of ever new men. Life seems doubled. In seven years the Egyptian king passes the double span of time. But with the greatest development of force goes hand in hand the swiftest consumption of it. Mycerinus, who thought to deceive the oracle, now himself brings about its fulfillment. This is the expression of hetaerism as it presents itself in the swamp world and in every lawless mating. The rose, quick to lose its scent, is its Aphroditean symbol. But all those myths, too, of the mingling of son with mother, of daughter with father, of Dionysus with Prosymnus, and of the exposure of the newborn in stagnant waters, belong to swamp life and to that stage of religion which chooses the former as the measure of its conception of the generative force of nature. The mating [PDF 344] — 332 — in the dark, which is often expressly stressed,1) and whose significance we established above in Psyche’s dragon husband, belongs, like the unwitting deed of Oedipus, to the purely tellurian-Poseidonian stage of religion. In the dark womb of the deep takes place that generation whose lawless luxuriance is hateful to the pure powers of heavenly light, and justifies the designation luteae voluptates, which Arnobius employs. It is significant that to the name Larisa, too, there attaches the myth of a similar assault on the chastity of the daughter by the father;2) for the designation Larisa has as its physical foundation alluvial river land, in which the same union of water and earth is present as in moist swamp grounds.3) To the Aphroditean swamp cult of the Nile land corresponds that materialism which emerges in the hetaerism of the Pallades, in the sexual excesses of its festivals, in sibling marriage, in the requirement of corporeal fecundation for the validity of marriage, in the preponderance of the female-material principle over the incorporeal-male, for which I have assembled the testimonies in my Mutterrecht. The poem of Helen’s sojourn in Egypt, as Herodotus and Euripides in particular tell it, whatever its origin may be, rests on a deeply grounded inner kinship of her Aphroditean figure with the foundation of Egyptian views of nature. For as a hetaeric swamp mother Helen, like Hella, is represented not only by her name (ἕλος), but also by her lunar nature and by her transposition to the sea-washed Leuce, to which Philostrat heroïc. 19 ascribes the nature of an island of mud.4) Like Helen, Latona too enters into connection with the swamp cult. In the swamps of Buto Horus is brought up by her. The tracing of Horus back to the mating of siblings in the night-filled moist grounds of the earth, that of Harpocrates to Osiris dwelling in the underworld, leave no doubt about the chthonian foundation of the two beings who issue from such a union, and this finds its confirmation in the offering of legumes, in the significance of the finger and the tongue, as in the bald head adorned only by a lock. e: as a representation of the creative and nourishing generative force. For this reason it has become no less significant for Harpocrates than for Angerona-Volupia.1) The tongue, however, is regarded by the Egyptians as a representation of the moist deep, because, according to Horapollo’s explanation, it always rests in moisture and in the dark enclosure of the cavity of the mouth. The Latin designation lingua, which rests on the root Li, established by numerous formations as the designation of moisture, proves how original and widespread precisely that view of nature must have been. When, then, in the month of Mesore the firstlings of the legumes are offered to the god Harpocrates and it is said at the same time: γλῶσσα τύχη, γλῶσσα δαίμων,2) this cult act has at first a physical-natural meaning. It shows the god in the significance of the great natural phallus, which has its seat in the tellurian moisture of muddy grounds. In this material sense he is called δαίμων, the god who holds sway in the earth, in this also τύχη, the primal mother attending the birth, as Egypt conceives the moon as τύχη nascentium.3) In the union of τύχη and δαίμων the tongue is represented as androgynous, as the bearer of both sexual potencies, just as we have found the swamp, and the moon, which is set equal to the swamps, in the same hermaphroditic nature. The significance that the ancients give to the finger and the tongue for Harpocrates is not the original one, but one derived from it. The finger laid on the mouth now stamps the god as the god of silence, who by his own bearing recommends to men too discretion and the prudent use of the tongue, because on this the fortune and fate of the individual depend.4) Of the thoughts combined in this conception, that of the silent Harpocrates-Sigalion likewise has a physical-natural truth. Wherein this lies emerges from another feature of Egyptian mythology. At Abydus Osiris is buried, and this site is so much distinguished above the other burial places of the god that the richest and most distinguished Egyptians especially liked to have themselves buried there, in order to share one burial place with their lord. At the burial place of the lord of all tellurian generation soundless stillness reigns. The noise of life has died away, everything has returned to the repose of first nature. Mute is Memnon, the great giver of sound, who possesses in the same Abydos his most famous Memnonium, and who is called by the Egyptians Ismandes-Osymandyas, the speaking, sounding stone. Strabo 17, 813. Creuzer, Symb. 2, 38. 39. Parthey 201. Wilkinson 4, p. 346. Here silence appears synonymous with grave and death. It is the night side of nature, and stands with sound and noise in the same antithetical relation in which we have found darkness and light, night and day, black and white. According to this connection Harpocrates appears not only as the phallic god of life, but equally as lord of death, as Sigalion,1) as he indeed was begotten by the dead, subterranean Osiris, and, like Hecate, takes delight in the legumes that enclose their kernel in a dark husk. Indeed, through the darker side of his nature the relation to the swamps gains new significance. The luxuriance of hetaeric generation, which prevails in them, lets death and destruction emerge, through an antithetical interaction well intelligible to us, with a double significance precisely here. The most luxuriant life consumes itself most quickly. If it knows how to make fourteen years out of seven, it thereby promotes swift destruction, and plays into the hands of death. Thus through his phallic swamp nature Harpocrates and his finger become also a representation of the night side of life, the soundless Sigalion, who sees the plants that sprout in rapid succession sink back with equal swiftness into the soundless, dark2) swamp depths, or also that Priapus whom the gate inscription of the Campana tomb designates as pene destricto Deus mortis et vitai locus. All these ideas recur in the Roman Angerona, who by her connection with Volupia, her worship ad navalia (Varro L. L. 5, 3), and her finger laid on her mouth, makes herself known as a hetaeric swamp mother like Acca Larentia,3) worshiped in the Velabrum, but reveals this nature preeminently in the stress on the dark death side of life on earth. In tellurism the idea of death prevails over that of generating and giving life. At this stage of religion destruction, perishing, and mourning over the swift fading of all existence predominate. Acca Larentia, the blooming hetaera, receives in her tomb in the swamps of the Velabrum the cult of the dead. The cruel Sphinx holds sway over the race of the Σπαρτοί sprung from the teeth of the swamp dragon, whose fate the famous riddle represents in all the desolation of the existence of the lower, unwept creation. In vain Mycerinus seeks to escape the death lot that threatens him, and as Isis ever anew bewails the death of Osiris, so in Egypt the melancholy Linus song first arose, and a trait of melancholy contemplation of nature is noticeable, which emerges in the Egyptian memento mori, the passing around of the dead Maneros-Pelusius at banquets, in the cry Maneroti, and in the myth of the early death of the young favorite of Isis.1) The serpent bite as cause of death, the unforeseen destruction in gathering truffles or ostrich eggs on the shore of the Syrtes, the fall into the water when plucking an onion,2) the mourning song of the reeds gently stirred by the wind, and many similar images show us how closely the thought of death and early destruction is connected with the contemplation of swamps and of swamp life. If Harpocrates-Sigalion’s twofold relation to life and death has developed according to precisely this view of nature, and so has given divine expression and personal shape to that mightiest but lowest stage of tellurian generation, as it comes before the eyes in reeds and rushes, so that the name Pelusius or Palaistinus, the swamp man, would suit him too, then the idea of weakness and incomplete formation of the lower parts of the body receives its natural explanation. In this idea lies the same thought that has also received its artistic expression in the incompletely formed legs of Erichthonius and of other earth-born beings. Through his serpent feet Erichthonius proclaims his origination from the moist depths to which the dragon belongs. The same significance attaches to the incomplete figure that is stressed in the lower parts of the body of Harpocrates. Like those animals which emerge incompletely from the Nile mud and, according to Ovid’s description,1) show a union of animate and crude earthy parts, the moist deep has produced in Harpocrates a being that has reached full development only in its upper half, and in its lower half retains the nature of the ὕλη2) and material connection with it. If this accords with the origination of the god from the self-embrace of the moist dark matter of the earth, it finds in the nature of the swamp plants, in the lotus especially, so exact a correspondence that the religious representation appears to have followed the natural model as that swamp growth presents it. But in the weakness and incomplete formation of the lower limbs yet another property of tellurian natural powers is to be recognized. They share with the matter to which they belong the repose and immobility that has been recognized in the ἀκίνητον of the Camarinian swamp lake as in the lion of the subterranean waters, unsuited to swift pursuit, and that constitutes the content of the Sanctum or ὅσιον in its real, original meaning. For Harpocrates this thought finds its full confirmation in the closely joined legs with which he is represented in some works of art,3) as well as in the seated posture that others give him. The δύο πόδες συνημμένοι (Horap. 2, 3) are an expression of tellurism precisely by stressing the incapacity for self-movement. Nah dieser Auffassung erscheint Harpocrates als eine völlig entsprechende , naturgetreue Darstellung der in den Sümpfen waltenden Natur« kraft und ihrer Produkte, der Sumpfpflanzen. Ju der niedern unbeweinten Schöpfung ist jene Trennung der Geburt von dem Mutterleibe des gebärenden Stoffes , wie sie die animalische Welt auszeihnet, nom nicht eingetreten. Die Erdzeugung ist nom nicht zur Beweglichfeit durhgedrungen. Die ziryog der höhern Schöpfung ist: der Pflanzenwelt als einer tiefern ursprünglichern Stufe der Naturzeugung versagt. Der schlammigen Hyle eignet ShHwere und Bewegungölosigkeit. Die Vegetation, welcher sie Entstehung gibt, theilt dieselbe Eigenschaft. Von ihr geht sie auf diejenigen Göttergestalten über, welche jener Stufe des Naturlebens entsprechen, und die generative Kraft nach ihrem Vorbilde gestalten. Demgemäß steht die Schwäche der untern Glieder mit Hatpocrates phallischer Kraft durhaus nicht im Widerspruch, Vielmehr zeigt sich nun, wie beide Eigenschaften in demselben Wesen zusammentreffen. Kraft der Zeugunz und örtliche Gebundenheit gehen auch in dem Sumpfe Hand in Hand, und in dem üppig aufschießenden Lotus offenbart sich zu gleicher Zeit die noch unztbändigte Fülle der stofflichen Urkraft, die unvollkommene Bildung der mit der Materie verbundenen tiefern Körpertheile, und die dadurch bedingte träge Ruh, welche die tiefste Stufe freiwilliger Erdzeugung auszeichnet. Wir werden durh diese Betrachtung in den Stand geseßt, eine Eigenthümlichkeit der verschiedenen Oenusdarstellungen in ihrer Bedeutung zu würdigen. Der seilflehtende Greiß ist überall in ruhender Haltung dargestellt. Sißend oder auf der Erde knieend verrichtet er sein Werk. Jeder Gedanke an Bewegung ist ausgeschlossen. Dadurch wird seine tellurische Sumpfnatur in derselben Weise angezeigt, wie die des Harpocrates durH die Shwäche und Gebrechlichkeit der untern Glieder. e: signifies progress in religion; it rests on the contemplation of the heavenly luminaries, to which eternal motion is as peculiar as immovability and firm attachment to the clod are to the tellurian hyle and its plant world. According to this conception, Harpocrates appears as a wholly corresponding, true-to-nature representation of the natural force that holds sway in the swamps and of its products, the swamp plants. In the lower, unwept creation, that separation of birth from the maternal womb of birth-giving matter, which distinguishes the animal world, has not yet taken place. Generation from the earth has not yet pressed forward to mobility. The κίνησις of the higher creation is denied to the plant world as a deeper, more primal stage of natural generation. Heaviness and immobility belong to the muddy hyle. The vegetation to which it gives origin shares the same property. From this it passes to those divine figures which correspond to that stage of the life of nature and which shape the generative force after its model. Accordingly, the weakness of the lower limbs is by no means in contradiction with the phallic force of Harpocrates. Rather it now becomes evident how both properties meet in the same being. Force of generation and local boundness go hand in hand in the swamp as well, and in the luxuriantly shooting lotus there is revealed at one and the same time the still untamed fullness of the primal force of matter, the imperfect formation of the lower parts of the body bound up with matter, and the sluggish repose conditioned thereby, which distinguishes the lowest stage of spontaneous generation from the earth. By this consideration we are put in a position to appreciate the significance of a peculiarity of the various representations of Ocnus. The old man plaiting rope is everywhere shown in a posture of rest. Seated or kneeling on the ground, he performs his work. Every thought of movement is excluded. Fettered to the same spot, he performs through aeons the work that never ends. Thereby his tellurian swamp nature is indicated in the same way as that of Harpocrates is by the weakness and infirmity of the lower limbs. The chthonian nature has driven artistic representation to many other equivalent modes of expression as well. Seated or reclining are the earth deities represented, above all the great mothers of the tomb.1) At the Thesmophoria the women rest on the bare earth.2) To the Dea Tellus a vow can Veron. p. 51, no. 9. Virgil. Aen. 11, 787. Strabo 12, 2, 7.

e: be made only while seated.1) With the knee pressed to the earth, in Euripides’ Troades 1296–1299 the chorus with Hecuba calls upon the dead husbands in the underworld.2) According to Pausan. 8, 48, 5, the Tegeans had an image of Eileithyia with the epithet Ἐν γόνασι, with which an altar of the earth was connected. In this position the daughter of Alces was said to have endured the pains of birth. On her knees the earth herself implores Zeus for rain.3) In the constellation Engonasin,4) which is connected with Ariadne’s crown, the same idea has been transferred from the earth to the heavens. At Latona’s giving birth the island, hitherto floating, receives its firmness; with fettered legs the generative ass is shown on the Egyptian festival cakes, and the earth mothers Damia and Auxesia are shown kneeling.5) Everywhere the seated, reclining, kneeling posture appears as the artistic expression of the same idea, of the local boundness, firmness, and immobility grounded in tellurism, in a word of that ἀκίνητον which is proper to stagnant waters and their plant world, and which is declared inviolable by the oracle. Therefore the kneeling Ocnus agrees completely with the surroundings of swamp plants in which we see him in the Campana painting. More and more, all the particulars of the remarkable representation shape themselves into a unified idea. In the swamp, out of swamp plants, the old man plaits his rope, and thus sets before our eyes in pictorial expression the work of natural generation, as it has been accomplished without cessation in the dark depth of the mud for aeons. In this conception Ocnus appears as a true Pelusius, Peleus, Palaistinus. We could also call him Schoeneus: a speaking name, which in the Greek world of legend enters into connection with mythic formations of physical-material generative significance,6) and which gives us the key to understanding the Roman rush men,7) the choice of swamp plants for the preparation of the couch,8) τοὺς ἐμοὺς καλοῦσα νέρθεν ἀθλίους ἀκοίτας. e: and those mother goddesses of Aphroditean nature who, venerated ἐν ἕλει and ἐν καλάμοις, are thereby set beside the reed-covered Isis and Helen,1) and who in their nature present that double relation, already pointed out, to swamp vegetation and to hetaeric sexual union. By the combination of all the examples named so far, not only the religious significance of the swamps and swamp plants but in particular also the Egyptian origin of the representation of Ocnus is raised above all doubt.2) The idea that gave this natural symbol its origination agrees so completely with the fundamental view of the Egyptian religion, with the nature of the land, and with the prominent role that swamp and swamp plants play in the life and cult of the Nile valley, that the representation of the panegyris at Acanthus, as Diodorus describes it, can to a certain extent be designated as a summation of the Egyptian conception of the life of nature, of its origination and its continuance. If this result is in itself already worthy of notice, it becomes still more significant in that it carries the origination of the natural symbol that concerns us back into the earliest antiquity, one may say into the primeval ages of human culture. To these alone the simplicity of the representation and the crudeness of the plaiting of a coarse rope seem to correspond, as against the conception of an artful weaving by the powers of nature. The rope crudely twisted together from swamp plants shows tellurism in all its nakedness. The generative force of nature still appears wholly in the chthonian-Poseidonian conception. The dark powers of the depth alone come forward. An elevation of material force from the moisture of the soil to the heavenly light, a progress from the earth to the sun, has not taken place. If in the number of the priests who daily pour the Nile flood into the perforated cask of Acanthus there is a connection of the power of water and of the sun, of the Poseidonian and the uranian conception of natural force, month, likewise in Ephesus: Boeckh, Corp. Fischer, die in den aus dem Flußschlamme allmälig sich bildenden Sumpf- und morastreichen Niederungen des Nil-Landes ihr Leben fristen, müssen das Symbol des geflochtenen und wieder aufgelösten Stries zuerst au8gedacht und an ihren Festen bildlich dargestellt haben. Von diesen pflanzte es sic auf künftige Geschlechter fort, ohne doh je zum Gegenstand eines Mythus zu werden. Keine Erzählung knüpft si an Ocnus und sein Seil. e: and a clear reference to the revolution of the sun is present, then every such connection falls away for the swamp rope. It shows us only the phallus borne by the Nile floods, not the Osiris sheltered in the arms of the sun,1) only the resting swamp lion. It grasps the life of nature at the stage of its greatest wildness and primitiveness, not at that of orderly agriculture, which heeds the movement of the sun and the stars and depends on the course of the seasons. By this very fact it enters into connection with those conditions of culture that precede the transition to agriculture, its cultivation, and the regulation of life conditioned by it. Fishermen, who eke out their lives in the lowlands of the Nile land, rich in swamps and morasses, that form gradually from the river mud, must have been the first to devise the symbol of the plaited and again unraveled rope and to represent it pictorially at their festivals. From them it was transmitted to future generations, without ever becoming the subject of a myth. No narrative attaches to Ocnus and his rope. At all times the representation of Acanthus has preserved in full purity the character that it had from the first: among Greeks and Romans too it shows itself without any unfolding in mythical narrative, as a pure symbol. 7. The relation of Ocnus to the tellurian waters and their force of generation finds its full confirmation in the Mantuan myth. From the swampy banks of the Nile stream we come to those of the Eridanus, which gives the Po plain its fertility, reaches the sea, like the Nile, in seven mouths, is called by the Celts Padus, by the earlier Ligurian tribes Bodincus, Βόδεγκος (fundo carens), the bottomless river, filled with mud and shallows, but is often given by poets the general name Eridanus (in which Era, terra is not to be mistaken).2) In the as Alberti, Palmer, Voss prefer Βέδεγκος, Βόδεγκος. Likewise Βόχερυσος in Theo on Aratus, Phain. 359, p. 84 Bekker is corrupt. It is noteworthy that purely German words are found in ancient Italy. As here Boden, so we find Grund in lares grundules, Morgen in μόργιον, πλέθρον γῆς according to Hesychius, whence Morgetes, Kuh in the northern Cevæ, as, according to Columella, the small Alpine cows, whence the cheese-rich Cebanum in Pliny, are called. — Flumen Bodincus corresponds to lacus Fundanus near Formiae. As an earth stream or fat stream Ister too is explained by Grimm in the Geschichte der deutschen Sprache.

Lassen wir aus diesen Angaben Alles das bei Seite, was ethnographische Beziehung zeigt, und beschränken wir uns darauf, des mantuanischen Ocnus religiöse Natur zu ermitteln. Diese ergiebt sich aus der genealogischen Zurücführung auf Manto und Teiresias mit voller Bestimmtheit. e: Po plain we meet Ocnus again, and indeed in a divine nature that corresponds in every respect to the one recognized in the old rope plaiter. Among the heroes who come to the aid of Aeneas in the war against Turnus, Ocnus too is named. Aen. 10, 198: Ille etiam patriis agmen ciet Ocnus ab oris Fatidicæ Mantus et Tusci filius amnis; Qui muros matrisque dedit tibi, Mantua, nomen; Mantua, dives avis, etc.1) In Eclogue 9, 59 the same founder of the swamp city of Mantua is called Bianor. On the words Namque sepulcrum incipit apparere Bianoris, Servius remarks: Hic est, qui et Ocnus dictus est: de quo ait in decimo: Fatidicæ Mantus et Tusci filius amnis. Conditor Mantuæ. Dictus autem Bianor est, quasi animo et corpore fortissimus: ἀπὸ τῆς βίας καὶ ἀνορέης. With this compare the commentary on Aen. 10, 198. Ocnus. Iste est Aucnus, quem in Bucolicis Bianorem dicit, ut: Namque sepulcrum incipit apparere Bianoris. Hic Mantuam dicitur condidisse, quam a matris nomine appellavit: nam fuit filius Tyberis et Mantus, Tyresiæ Thebani vatis filiæ, quæ post patris interitum ad Italiam venit. Alii Mantos filiam Herculis vatem fuisse dicunt. Hunc Ocnum alii Auletis filium, alii fratrem, qui Perusiam condidit, referunt; et ne cum fratre contenderet, in agro Gallico Cesenam, quæ nunc Bononia dicitur, condidisse: permisisse etiam exercitui suo, ut castella munirent, in quorum numero Mantua fuit. Alii a Tarchonte, Tyrrheni fratre, conditam dicunt: Mantuam autem ideo nominatam, quod Etrusca lingua Mantum Ditem patrem appellant, cui etiam cum cæteris urbibus et hanc consecravit. Let us set aside from these reports everything that shows an ethnographic relation, and confine ourselves to determining the religious nature of the Mantuan Ocnus. This emerges with complete certainty from his genealogical derivation from Manto and Tiresias. Tiresias appears wholly in the nature of a subterranean Consus, of a Cerus manus or Creator bonus,2) of a Jupiter Soranus,3) who bears within himself the generative force of tellurian matter. Like the moist depth, he unites in his nature the twofold potency of nature, male and female. As over the former, so over him too eternal darkness Borborus, a river at Pella in Macedonia according to Plutarch, may be connected with the present-day bourbon, mire (hence the pun bourbonner et s’embourbonner). The earth-bearing nature of these rivers is described by Callimach. in Apoll. v. 108–110. that the two city names Mantua and Mantinea belong to one stock.

His seat is in springs; the serpent whose shape he assumes is inwardly akin to him.1) As the son of Udaeus, the Moist One, he belongs to the race of the Σπαρτοί, who arose fatherless from serpents’ teeth and in the necklace of the pair of dragons proclaim their descent from the maternal womb of the earth. To the Cadmeans he prophesies victory if the last of the draconteum genus will devote himself to death. But when the Epigoni avenged the defeat of their fathers, and the hard-pressed Cadmean Σπαρτοί at last succumbed to their fate, he too met his destruction. The maternal race of the sown men vanishes from Boeotia. Thus there declares itself in Tiresias that conception of tellurian generative force which takes hetaeric swamp mating as its model. In the race of the Σπαρτοί the children, like the swamp reed, have only one mother, the earth. The sower (Semo Sancus) who scattered the seed steps forward as little as the father does in relation to the spurius. In the Oedipus myth this stage of religion appears joined with all that lutea voluptas which we emphasized above as a necessary property of swamp life. For Oedipus, who does not know his father, who fecundates his mother and loses his sight, himself belongs to that fatherless race of the Σπαρτοί, and in his swollen foot, in the legend of his finding on the seashore, and in the father’s name Laius, he makes himself known as a representation of the tellurian primal force of generation. As the prototype of the draconteum genus and of the stage of religion belonging to it stands Tiresias. In him we recognize the same divine nature that confronted us in the swamp man Ocnus. There can therefore be no doubt that the Mantuan Ocnus represents the same deity as the old rope plaiter. Now the derivation of Bianor from the daughter of Tiresias, in the sense of the mother right of the chthonian Σπαρτοί, and the naming of the city after the mother’s name become significant, and the bringing in of the Pelasgian-Tyrrhenian Dis-Mantus intelligible, who in his Plutonian Hades nature unites both sides of tellurian force, the giving and the taking,2) and through his Charontic significance leads back again to the aged Ocnus. If the identity of the divine nature of both Ocni has thus emerged, then Nem. 1, 91. Diod. 4, 66. Pausan. 9, 33, 1. Od. 10, 492. Spanh. on Callim. lav. Pallad. 81. the connection of the cult of Hades with the great fertility of Elis, which seemed incomprehensible to Demetrius of Scepsis in Strabo 8, p. 344.

e: the situation of Mantua in the midst of swamps and morasses becomes doubly noteworthy. Thereby Ocnus-Bianor enters here too into the closest connection with the nature of the land, with swamp and swamp generation. The ship that carries the king bears the image of the Mincius, whom green river reed wreathes, and Ocnus has a stream, like the Thracian Rhesus, for his father. With Protomantis Gaea, the primal mother Earth, the Tuscan stream unites. From their mingling springs Ocnus-Bianor, who accordingly, like the reed, stands there as the son of the moist πηλός, as Pelusius-Schoeneus. Hence Bianor is an interpretation that perfectly designates the nature of Ocnus. The force that the name emphasizes is the generative primal power of matter, to which the phallic formation of a Priapus, a Harpocrates, a Dionysus corresponds. The same conception underlies also the centaur name Bianor, which is cited together with Chthonius. In a similar sense we find Valens,1) Valesius,2) Andraemon, Virbius, Iphis, Kratos,3) Σθένεια,4) and many others. Especially instructive is what Plutarch, de Is. et Os. 37. 42, reports on the name of Osiris. Ἀρίστων τοίνυν ὁ γεγραφὼς Ἀθηναίων ἀποικίαν ἐπιστολῇ τινι Ἀλεξάρχου περιέπεσεν, ἐν ᾗ Διὸς ἱστορεῖται καὶ Ἴσιδος υἱὸς ὢν ὁ Διόνυσος ὑπὸ Αἰγυπτίων, οὐκ Ὄσιρις, ἀλλὰ Ἀρσαφὴς (ἐν τῷ ἄλφα γράμματι) λέγεσθαι, δηλοῦντος τὸ ἀνδρεῖον τοῦ ὀνόματος. ἐμφαίνει δὲ τοῦτο καὶ ὁ Ἑρμαῖος, ἐν τῇ πρώτῃ περὶ τῶν Αἰγυπτίων. ὄμβριμον γάρ φησι μεθερμηνευόμενον εἶναι τὸν Ὄσιριν. — 42: Ὁ γὰρ Ὄσιρις ἀγαθοποιός, καὶ τοὔνομα πολλὰ φράζει, οὐχ ἥκιστα δὲ κράτος ἐνεργοῦν καὶ ἀγαθοποιόν, ὃ λέγουσι· τὸ δ᾽ ἕτερον ὄνομα τοῦ θεοῦ τὸν Ὄμφιν εὐεργέτην ὁ Ἑρμαῖος φησὶν δηλοῦν ἑρμηνευόμενον. The weight of these remarks is wholly independent of their linguistic correctness. Yet the present state of hieroglyphic studies by no means entitles us to call such definite statements into doubt, and to reject the designations Ἀρσαφής and Ὄμφις “because at present not interpretable hieroglyphically.” Both are firmly established in the manuscripts. Hence Ἀρσαφής is retained by Jablonski, Panth. P, 1, p. 289, Wyttenbach, Hutten, and Parthey, p. 231, just as the addition ἐν τῷ ἄλφα γράμματι may be neither struck out as a gloss, with Reiske, nor made meaningless, with Parthey, by the reference to the alphabetical order of Ariston’s work. All the interpretations, now, that are given for Osiris, Arsaphes, Omphis in the passages cited place in the foreground the phallic masculinity, and the beneficent, wealth-giving force lying in it, of the Egyptian Zeus-Neilos. The expressions τὸ ἀνδρεῖον, τὸ ὄμβριμον, κράτος ἐνεργοῦν καὶ [PDF 357] — 345 — ἀγαθοποιόν, to which the explanation of the name Osiris given by Hermes Trismegistus, σωμάτων ἑκάστου ἔθνους ἡγεμὼν καὶ ἰσχύος καὶ ῥώμης καθηγητής, corresponds,1) all point to the male causality of material generation, to the γόνιμον καὶ τρόφιμον (Plut. Is. 51) and its unweakened fullness, which is designated by Lucian, de saltat., with reference to the phallic Mars, as πέραν τοῦ μετρίου σκληρόν, and by Plutarch, l. c., as ἐξορθιάζων τῷ αἰδοίῳ (foedius excitata natura). Of warlike valor, of which the most recent translator, Parthey, thinks, there is no question. In the same sense the Ionian Poseidon on the Mannheim bronze is called Ἀρχὴ τῶν πάντων, an expression that corresponds to Plutarch’s Ἀρχὴ καὶ δύναμις. With his hand pointing to the phallus, the θεὸς γενέσιος gives those words their quite definite meaning. He too appears as Ἀρσαφής-Bianor, as a representation of the κράτος ἐνεργοῦν καὶ ἀνδρεῖον. To see the god of generative water designated as ἀρχή corresponds to that Egyptian-Ionian doctrine which conceives water itself as ἀρχή, αἴτιον, πρώτη ζωή, and in this sense as ἄριστον. From ἀρχή and ἄριστον that addition too, ἐν τῷ ἄλφα γράμματι, can now be explained in its full meaning. The letter ἄλφα corresponds to the concept and meaning of ἀρχή. It takes the first place among the letters, rejects, as the grammarian Protogenes expresses it in Plutarch, Table Talk 9, 2, every placing after, and always seeks the beginning due to it. In this way it becomes identical with ἀρχή itself. But it coincides with it in a second respect as well. Ἄλφα is the basic vowel with which water is designated. We find it, with various consonants following, in aqua, apa, Ἀπιδανός, Apis (bull and bee), aspirated in Epaphus, apium, aper, aca (Acis), Acca (Larentia), Achelous, Achileus, Acheron, Achaia, Acharnae, Apii, and Achrades (according to Plutarch the juicy pear), Ach (the Birnbaumer Ach near Bregenz), and without any consonant at all in the little stream of Unterwalden that the natives call the A-water. Between the high vowel I and the deep O, U, A occupies the middle. Thereby it becomes the designation of the resting mass of water, while the stem Li corresponds to wetness set in motion and thereby clear-sounding, Ul, Ud (uligo, udus, Olyseus, Olane) to the stagnant, sluggish mass of the swamp, the tarda palus. In consequence of this relation to water, A now becomes also the basic vowel for the words that serve to designate generative masculinity. Leaning on the following R, it forms the stem syllable Ar, which here takes the first place. It is found as the designation of the γενέσια δύναμις in ἄρρην, Ἄρης, aries (Ovid F. 4, 771. salax) Ἀρετή (whence Heracles [PDF 358] — 346 —

We gather from this that ἀρχή too carries within it the physical basic concept of generative water, and that the general meaning beginning has grown out of the material one of origin. In connection, now, with this meaning of the A vowel, Plutarch, or already his authority Ariston, emphasizes as significant that Ἀρσαφής was formed and written ἐν τῷ Ἄλφα γράμματι; no other vowel is to be found in the word than ἄλφα; for how closely η coincides with α is shown already by that old Pamphylian Ἦρ, the son of Ἀρμένος, whose vision Plato relates in the Republic.1) I do not now wish to decide whether Plutarch’s remark is to be treated as grammatical trifling, or whether, as the syllable Ἀρ lets us believe, it offers a reliable point of support for the explanation of Ἀρσαφής; enough that the thought of the Greek has become clear, and that the sense of the letter Ἄλφα, on the one hand in its relation to water and to the doctrine of the origin of all things from the moist, on the other in its relation to the meaning of the word Ἀρσαφής as a ὀνόματος τὸ ἀνδρεῖον δηλοῦντος, has been brought closer to our consciousness. How familiar combinations of this kind were to the ancient grammarians is shown precisely by the table talk of Plutarch just cited: Cur A principem inter literas locum obtineat, which the interpreters of that statement about Arsaphes should have remembered. From that conversation the following remark of Ammonius in particular deserves consideration: “How, he retorted to Plutarch of Chaeronea, how is it that you, as a Boeotian, do not here take the part of Cadmus, who is said to have placed alpha before all the other letters because the Phoenicians call the ox by the word alpha (ὅν φασι τὸ ἄλφα πάντων προτάξαι, διὰ τὸ Φοίνικας οὕτω καλεῖν τὸν βοῦν), an animal that, they believe, takes among the necessities of life not the second or third place, as Hesiod (Works, line 403) will have it, but the first?” The juxtaposition of alpha with the bull leads us once again into the midst of the circle of ideas we have developed. For the bull bears the generative force of water within him, and is therefore in this wholly material sense the alpha of nature. The hymn with which the women of the Eleans summon the god with the bull’s foot out of the water, to the sound of trumpets, that he should come to them and grant them fertility, has been preserved by Plutarch in Qu. Gr. 36, with which Is. et Os. 34 and Theseus 16 are to be compared. In agreement with this, Bacchus is called πάσης ὑγρᾶς φύσεως κύριος, Βουγενής, and even Βοῦς or Ταῦρος, as in the cry ἄξιε ταῦρε, ἄξιε [PDF 359] — 347 — ταῦρε, as he is also shown on Greek coins of Magna Graecia and in Nonnus pouring the fecundating jet of water from his mouth.1) In this sense he is the alpha of nature, Ἀρσαφής-Bianor, the god of the primal waters, mighty in generation. When Christ lays claim to the meaning of alpha for himself, his saying, “I am the A, I am the origin,” gains its whole weight only when we bring it into contrasting connection with that Phoenician and generally ancient conception of the physical-sensual meaning of the first letter. The ultimate causality of things is not the force placed in matter, but the highest God, who has communicated it to matter, and who is therefore entitled to claim the alpha for himself alone. For comparison with these remarks on water as the seat of force, the word Nar and the name Nero offer themselves. Nar designates water. With this meaning it is found in many expressions: in Nar, the river name, Narcissus, Nereus, Νηρεῖς, Ναρκαῖος, Athena Ναρκαία (Pausan. 5, 16, 5), Narycii Locri (Geo. 2, 438), νηρός, ναρός, especially in the word τὸ νερόν, which later and present-day Greek uses exclusively for water.2) From moisture the nose too is called nares. How far the root reaches is shown by Narajana, the oldest designation of Mesopotamia. The same word, however, is also a designation of force, as in Nerien Martis, and in Nero, as Gellius N. A. 13, 22, Sueton. Tiber. 1, and Lydus de magistr. 1, 23, demonstrate, hence also used for milites, as on the Bantine Table, l. 29. 31. 8. By this elucidation of Plutarch’s statements on Osiris-Arsaphes, the physical-material significance of generation of the Mantuan Ocnus-Bianor has, I hope, been established, and the Poseidonian-tellurian stage of natural force that he personifies raised above all challenge. Only now can the historical connection with Boeotia, which Servius indicates in the passages transcribed, be touched upon in a few words. Through Manto, the daughter of Tiresias, the Mantuan Ocnus is brought into connection with the Cadmean race of the Σπαρτοί. Strabo 7, p. 326, Gieseke, thrakisch-pelasgische Stämme, p. 59), and so form a chain of settlements that mediates the passage to northern Italy. If the Phoenician colony in Mantua thereby gains every probability, there are added in confirmation the presence of the Cinyras myth and of Asiatic cult practices at the innermost Hadria, the connection of the Ligurians with the inhabitants of the Po country as well as with Boeotia, and finally the prominence of the number seven, on the one hand in the Boeotian Tiresias myth, on the other in the remarkable Ligurian legend already touched upon. The morasses formed by the Mincio and the Po gave the fugitive, homeless Thebans a position secured against attack, the possession of which has always been of the greatest importance to all subsequent immigrants and conquerors down to the present day. In the series of peoples who crowded here, and whose considerable number led Virgil, the Mantuan, to the expression Mantua dives avis, sed non genus omnibus unum, the Thebans are named in the first place. Servius: Bene dives avis, quia non ab Ocno, sed ab aliis quoque condita fuit: primum namque a Thebanis; deinde a Tuscis; novissime a Gallis, vel ut alii dicunt a Sarsinatibus, qui Perusiæ consederant. Sed non genus omnibus unum. Quia origo Mantuanorum et a Tuscis venit, qui in Mantua regnabant, et a Venetis, nam in Venetia posita est, quæ et Gallia Cisalpina dicitur. Through this whole series of peoples the worship of the Theban-Cadmean Ocnus- Bianor was maintained. Even in Virgil’s time his tomb was still extant, as at Ilium that of Ilus, at Sardis that of Lixus,1) whom, after the fall of the Assyrian Heraclids, the native Mermnads surrounded with equal veneration. It may seem striking that the Tuscan Tiber is woven into the genealogy of this Theban-Mantuan god. For that the Mantuan poet reports the native legend incorrectly, or that Servius referred the Tuscus amnis to the Tiber without reason, is equally unacceptable. I see in this a confirmation of that assumption which follows the Cadmean-Phoenician Gephyraeans as far as Latium, and which, appealing to J. Lydus de mensib. p. 45 ed. Schow, emphasizes in particular for this the identity of the priestly character and of the river cult as it was practiced by the Phoenician Gephyraeans at Athens and by the Pontifices at Rome. If in this passage the water on whose bridge the Athenian Gephyraeans offer their cult to the Palladium is called Σπερχειός, then by it the Thessalian river of this name is certainly [PDF 361] — 349 — not to be understood, but the cult designation of a native Attic water is to be recognized, as Attica too possessed its own Eridanus. Strabo 9, 397. Then, however, the derivation from σπείρω, which in any case is not doubtful, appears in its whole significance. The Gephyraean cult is dedicated to water as the seat and bearer of the generative power of nature: a conception of religion that becomes manifest, with ever the same meaning, in the likewise Phoenician-Gephyraean Demeter Ἀχαιίη,1) in the sacrifice of the rush men, and in the legend of the Aegidae in Pindar, Pyth. 5 and 9, of the Cyrenaic clod of earth that comes from the Syrtes and slips into the sea near Aegidian Thera, as well as in the high significance that Phoenician cosmogony grants to the water-soaked πηλός.2) Thus for the historical part of the Ocnus myth a result has emerged that adds to the inner agreement of the rope-plaiting and the Mantuan Ocnus-Bianor a historical connection of the tribes so widely separated in place. The representation of the aged rope plaiter in the Lesche at Delphi, where Tiresias too was seen depicted, lets us suppose that he was a figure native to central Greece; his connection with the Mantuan Cadmeans, that he belongs to the Phoenician circle of religion, and came with the Phoenician colony to Hellas, and with its emigrating remnants to the Po country. Thus Phoenicia now ranks beside the Nile land related to it,3) and it gains heightened significance if, as the statement of Pausanias allows us to conclude with certainty, the Ocnus symbol was native also among the Ionians of Asia Minor. We are thereby led into a circle of peoples who connect us with the earliest culture of the human race, and who are suited to secure for the natural symbol of the rope-plaiting swamp man the highest antiquity, reaching back beyond the beginnings of history. 9.

e: Of the statements of Servius about the Mantuan Ocnus-Bianor one remains that is able to supplement and confirm our discussions so far. Instead of Ocnus the grammarian uses alternately Aucnus, an alternation that occurs in numerous examples, such as Claudius-Clodius, auriga-origa, caudex-codex, caules-coles, saurix-sorix (Serv. G. 2, 30), [PDF 362] — 350 — and which finds its repetition in the more recent transformation of Au into O, as in Auximum — Osimo, Aufantus — Ofanto, Laus Pompeia — Lodi, as well as in the pronunciation of Romance peoples. Accordingly the syllable Auc is to be regarded as a word stem, and in Aucnus the meaning of augere, auctare is to be recognized. The insertion of the n has its analogue in the aorist formation of individual verbs (ἱδρύνθην from ἱδρύω, ἀμπνύνθη from ἀναπνέω, and the like); the difficulty, however, that might be drawn from the quantity has no claim to consideration, because the measure of the vowels was certainly established and regulated only much later than the word had received its formation in the mouth of the people, so that here purely empirical observation, which judges the possibility of a derivation by the comparison of similar phenomena, alone may be taken as the guide.1) What gives the proposed etymology full certainty is the use that the ancients make of the expressions augere, auctare, auctus, which agrees completely with the meaning ascertained for Aucnus-Ocnus. If Ocnus is the representation of the tellurian generative force that creates all life and brings it to ripeness, then augere, auctare, αὐξάνειν are met with in a great number of passages as designations of this same nourishing and augmenting nature of matter. Lucretius, whose usage becomes especially instructive through the Aphroditean-Epicurean standpoint that he takes, furnishes thoroughly decisive examples: 1, 50: Nam tibi de summa cœli natura Deumque Disserere incipiam, et rerum primordia pandam. Ut omnes natura creet res, auctet alatque, Quoque eadem rursum natura perempta resolvat. In the same sense there is 6, 168: arboris auctus; 2, 572: nec porro rerum genitales auctificique motus perpetuo possunt servare creata. With the same reference to the growth of tellurian bodies Plutarch says, Is. et Os. 35: ὅτι δ᾽ οὐ μόνον τοῦ οἴνου Διόνυσον, ἀλλὰ καὶ πάσης ὑγρᾶς φύσεως Ἕλληνες ἡγοῦνται κύριον καὶ ἀρχηγόν, ἀρκεῖ Πίνδαρος μάρτυς εἶναι, λέγων· Δενδρέων δὲ νόμον Διόνυσος Πολυγαθὴς αὐξάνοι, ἁγνὸν φέγγος ὀπώρας. Plato Timæus p. 331, Bip: ὅταν τὸ τῆς αὔξης καὶ τροφῆς ἔλαττον ἐπίῃ ῥεῦμα. p. 326: τὸ δὲ λοιπὸν ὑμεῖς, ἀθανάτῳ θνητὸν προσυφαίνοντες, ἀπεργάζεσθε ζῷα καὶ γεννᾶτε, τροφήν τε διδόντες αὐξάνετε, καὶ φθίνοντα πάλιν δέχεσθε. Pausan. 7, 22, 5: Μελάνιππον δὲ παῖδα Ἄρεως καὶ Τριταίας οἰκίσαι τε καὶ αὐξῆσαι τὴν πόλιν, καὶ θέσθαι τὸ ὄνομα ἀπὸ τῆς μητέρος. Diodor. 3, 51. Pausan. 5, 14, 4. Of the growth of the Nile Plutarch, Is. et Os. 75, uses αὔξησις. The same meaning recurs in a considerable number of proper names, which appear now as independent designations of gods, now as epithets. At Epidaurus, [PDF 363] — 351 — on Aegina, and at Tarentum we find the two earth mothers Αὐξησία and Δαμία, of wholly Cerealian standing, on which see Pausan. 2, 30, 5; Herod. 5, 82. 83. Hesych. v. Δάμεια. On the stem and meaning of Δαμία (Δαμοννώ, Damiatrix, Archidamia, Damium, Δᾶ) we have spoken above. Of Dionysus Αὐξίτης Paus. 8, 26, 2 speaks: Εἰσὶ δὲ καὶ Διονύσῳ ναοί, τὸν μὲν καλοῦσι πολίτην, τὸν δὲ αὐξίτην, for which the explanation is contained in the Pindaric δενδρέων νόμον αὐξάνοι. In the same sense Pan, who is often given phallic form, is called Αὐξητής, hymn. Orphic. 10, 11. Likewise Zeus, h. Or. 14, 8. Hermes Αὐξίδηνος in Hesych. s. v., Gaea Αὐξιθαλής and φερέκαρπος, h. Or. 25, 3. Likewise Demeter, h. Or. 39, 10. Adonis-Papas, h. Or. 55, 6. Asclepius, h. Or. 66, 5. A nymph Αὐξίτροφος, h. Or. 50, 12. As Attic Graces Paus. 9, 35 names Αὐξώ and Ἡγεμόνη; Αὐξώ is also invoked in the Attic citizens’ oath, which likewise designates her as a city mother who grants life and prosperity. And it is the Charites who, as great earth mothers, fill the barn with provisions, the table with abundance of nourishment, and through superfluity life with convivial joy.1) Somewhat longer attention is required by the Elean Augeas, whose name and myth are equally eloquent. Among the Greeks we find Αὐγέας and Αὐγείας, among the Romans Augeas, Augias, Augeus.2) The relation to the fertility of the earth emerges for this son of Eleus from his wealth in herds, from the dung, and from its connection with the water of two rivers, the Alpheius and the Peneius. In this Augeas shows himself as Deus Stercutus, with whom he is also equated, as Mutunus-Priapus or Saturnus, who bears within himself the generative force of the water-soaked dung, and who grounds, augments, and furthers all growth.3) He is the phallic force resting in the dung of the earth and generating all life out of itself, like the Egyptian dung ball, and in this sense the Deus Laconian city name after Homer, in Pausan. 3, 21, 5. I note further that Maia, after which Μαίονες or Μῄονες, likewise contains the concept of augmenting, making greater. p. 412. Schol. Pind. Ol. 10, 30. The equation with Stercutus in Plin. 17, 9, 6. Ovid. F. 3, 292. The combination of Stercutus with Saturnus is given by Macrob. S. 1, 7. p. 238, with Mutunus (which recalls the Μοῦθ and Μῶθ of the Egyptians and Phoenicians), Tertull. Apol. 25. Lactant. de falsa rel. 1, 20, p. 132. Bünemann; with Priapus, August. C. D. 4, 11. Arnob. adv. gent. 4, p. 131. 133. Cf. Salmas. Exercc. Plin. in Solin. C. 16, T. 1. p. 219. — Son of Eleus-Aleus, Paus. 5, p. 377. — On the Orphic Jupiter Stercoreus and the religious significance of cow dung: Selden de diis Syr. p. 305. Beyeri addit. p. 119. ed. Lips. 1672. — On the idea of the generation of the beetle, the great creative source of life, from a ball of dung hidden under the earth: Porphyr. de abstin. 4, 9. Horapollo 1, 10. Diese Natur findet in der Bezeihnung Augeas ihren sprehenden Ausdruck. Der Name des Elishen Stercutus schließt sich also den andern uns schon bekannten Aleus, Peneus , Alfeus , Larisus, welche alle in jenem sumpfigen, üppig fruchtbaren Küstenstrich begegnen, in sehr bezeichnender Weise an. So haben wir also den Stamm, auf dem Aucnus-Ocnus beruht, in einer großen Zahl von Götternamen stets mit derselben Grundbedeutung gefunden. Der Wortsinn stimmt mit dem Inhalt der Gottheitsnatur vollkommen überein. Darin liegt der größte Beweis für die Richtigkeit der Etymologie. Das auctare findet überdieß in der dildlichen Darstellung des seilflehtenden Greises eine genau entsprechende Versinnlihung. Ohne Unterbrehung der Arbeit obliegend, fördert Ocnus beständig sein Werk. Unter seinen Händen wächst das Seil. Ohn' Aufhören wird es gemehrt. Au in der Beziehung des Bildes auf einen fleißigen, arbeitsamen Hausvater wird. der Gedanke der argos festgehalten, und durch den Gegensatz der verschwenderischen, das Errungene stets mindernden Ehefrau nur um so nadrülicher hervorgehoben. Bild und Name decken sich vollkommen. Sie sind beide gleich spreßend. Daher kann es nicht auffallen, daß Aegypten sich mit der Darstellung der Aktion begnügt zu haben scheint. Diodor wenigstens giebt keinen Namen, und die wirkliche Vorstellung der Handlung spricht dafür, daß zu Acanthus fein solcher üblih war. Er kann erst entstanden sein, nachdem die lebendige : Darstellung zum todten Bilde geworden war. Das Symbol selbst ist weit älter als der Ocnus-Name, der unter dem Einfluß der Volksaussprache diejenige Gestalt erhielt, in welcher er zulept in der Schrift festgeseßt und überliefert worden ist.
e: fœcundus, the son of the nourishing father Aleus, a true Trophonius (from τρέφειν), who hides in subterranean chambers the fullness of the tellurian treasures. This nature finds its eloquent expression in the designation Augeas. The name of the Elean Stercutus thus joins, in a very significant way, the others already known to us, Aleus, Peneus, Alpheus, Larisus, which all occur in that swampy, luxuriantly fertile coastal strip. So we have found the stem on which Aucnus-Ocnus rests in a great number of divine names, always with the same basic meaning. The sense of the word agrees completely with the content of the divine nature. Therein lies the greatest proof for the correctness of the etymology. The auctare finds, moreover, an exactly corresponding embodiment in sensible form in the pictorial representation of the rope plaiter. Without interrupting his labor, Ocnus ceaselessly advances his work. Under his hands the rope grows. Without end it is augmented. Even in the relation of the picture to a diligent, industrious father of the household the idea of the αὔξησις is retained, and is brought out all the more emphatically by the contrast of the prodigal wife who always diminishes what has been won. Picture and name coincide perfectly. Both are equally eloquent. Hence it cannot be surprising that Egypt seems to have contented itself with the representation of the action. Diodorus at least gives no name, and the actual representation of the action argues that at Acanthus none was in use. It can have arisen only after the living representation had become a dead picture. The symbol itself is far older than the name Ocnus, which under the influence of popular pronunciation received the form in which it was last fixed in writing and handed down.

e: From the basic idea of auctare there can be derived all those meanings that the ancients connect with the word ὄκνος. The proper name and the conceptual ὄκνος form a coherent whole. Their meanings stand in inner connection and give a connected series of ideas. Transferred to the moral domain of reflection and scrutiny, the idea of augmenting and continuing to work takes the shape of that of scruple, of irresolute postponement, of hesitation. In a similar way the idea of postponement, and of the renewed deliberation thereby made possible, as it is present in the forensic term ampliatio, has attached itself to ampliare, which in its physical-sensual meaning corresponds exactly to αὐξάνειν. From irresolution comes hesitation, which puts everything off to the following day and has received its scenic personification in ὄκνος as αὔριος δαίμων. Hesitation itself can pass as a sign of sluggishness and [PDF 365] — 353 — laziness, but may also lie in external causes, such as the exhaustion of the warrior. Thus there results that translation of the proper name Ocnus by Piger, which we found in Pliny, and which is contained also in the conceptual ὄκνος, as well as in the verbal ὀκνέω (Herod. 7, 50). When elsewhere Ocnus is compared to the man who invented the fortification of camps, in order to hide behind rampart and ditch, there converge in this idea all the relations found so far in the word ὄκνος: scruple, irresolution, fear, slackness.1) The abstract ideas indicated, developed from the physical meaning of auctare, present the spectacle, not rare in the history of words, of a complete reversal of sense. From the diligent furtherer and augmenter of his work there becomes at last the sluggish or irresolute man of tomorrow, who lacks all courage, resolution, and energy. Words cannot escape such a transformation of sense. Symbolic representations, on the other hand, are less accessible to it. They oppose to such transformations the immutability of pictorial expression. What alone appears possible in respect of them is misunderstanding and arbitrariness of interpretation. To both the Ocnus symbol has fallen victim in antiquity in many ways. As the people in the course of time became more and more alienated from the old views of nature and religion, it sought wholly external explanations. For such, the sense of the word seemed at first to offer a point of support. The idea of sluggishness that lies in ὄκνος was transferred to the old man in the picture who plaits rope. But since the assumption of sluggishness stands in decided contrast with the representation itself and with the unremitting working of the chief figure, one took refuge, in order to overcome the manifest contradiction, in the idea of punishment and retribution. Through never-ending restless labor Ocnus must after death atone for the fault of sluggishness shown in life. If no great misdeed can be proved against him like that which the Danaids, placed at his side, committed, or for which the son forgetful of his duty, depicted by Polygnotus, is chastised by his father, then a generally vicious disposition must serve as a makeshift, and this seemed sufficiently emphasized in the name. In the working old man the lazy youth was to recognize his future, the cowardly warrior hiding behind walls to revive his manly valor. To such conceptions, misled by the sense of the word, in which, significantly enough, only Roman authors take part, there attach themselves others which, with the meaning of the word, 23

The explanation that the Delphic guides gave Pausanias takes the picture as a whole, and attaches itself especially to the contrast of sex between the male Ocnus and the female she-ass. It becomes remarkable by showing us what fate was finally prepared for the profound symbolic images of earlier times by a generation wholly estranged from ancient wisdom. Yet more recent writers have declared themselves in agreement with this childish trifling, and have spun it out still further by the assumption of a concealed allusion of the painter to his own domestic circumstances. The proverbial saying of the Ionians, ὁ ἀνὴρ οὗτος συνάγει τοῦ Ὄκνου τὴν θώμιγγα, with which they designate as contemptible every labor that brings neither gain nor profit, gives more information about the tendency of mind of that tribe, which had at last fallen victim to the most luxuriant materialism, than about the inner content of the representation, and furnishes an example of those likewise proverbial Ἰωνικαὶ ῥήσεις. 10.

e: Having thus followed all the turns that the word Ὄκνος underwent as a proper name and as a conceptual designation, and having discussed their relation to the pictorial representation, there remains, in order to conclude this side of the investigation, only the consideration of the augural meaning of the same expression. Pausanias, to whom the picture of the rope plaiter, and in particular also the name Ὄκνος written beside it, appeared very enigmatic, assembles everything that could possibly serve to clarify the obscurity. Thus he first relates the silly explanation of the Delphians, and then communicates from his own knowledge the Ionian proverb and its sense, and finally the augural meaning of the bird Ὄκνος. To find two things so far apart designated by one name seems to have surprised him himself no less than it strikes the present-day reader as strange. Did Pausanias, then, think of the possibility of contributing, by the mention of the bird Ὄκνος, to the elucidation of the rope-twisting Ὄκνος? The only connection besides that of the name that might be recognized in the account of Pausanias can be found in the common relation of both Ὄκνοι to religion and cult. As the rope-plaiting Ocnus in the Lesche at Delphi necessarily acquires a religious significance, so the bird Ὄκνος too is put in connection with the augural discipline and presented as an augural name. We must hold fast to this point of agreement, and now wish to try to develop its whole content. It is in fact the religious significance that connects the two Ὄκνοι [PDF 367] — 355 — and justifies and explains the identity of the name for two beings and phenomena so different externally. Ὄκνος is assigned to the genus ἐρωδιός. In this Aristotle, Hist. an. 9, 10, and Hesychius agree: Ὄκνος, εἶδος ἐρωδιοῦ. Ἐρωδιός is described by Suidas as follows: εἶδος ὀρνέου, ὁ πελαργὸς λεγόμενος ἢ ὅμοιος αὐτῷ, ἐλωδιός τις ὤν, παρὰ τὸ ἐν ἕλεσι διατρίβειν, τουτέστι καθύγροις τόποις. On this see Etym. magn. s. v. Schol. Il. 10, 274. Lycophr. Cass. v. 597. Salmas. Plin. Ex. 1, p. 41. 64.1) The swamp nature emphasized here finds its confirmation in the fact that the Septuagint too renders the stork by Ἐρωδιός (Psalm 103, 19), and that Pliny, 18, ult., attributes to the palustres fulicæ (Ovid. Met. 8, 625) those properties that Theophrastus emphasizes in the ἐρωδιός. If these genera of birds are counted in the genus ἐρωδιός on account of their swamp nature, ardea appears on the other hand as the Latin word corresponding exactly to the Greek expression. The identity of the two forms is obvious. Ἐρωδιός, Sicilian ἀρωδιός, hence ardea, as merulus and merula, luscinius and luscinia. Pliny 10, 60, 79 prefers the diminutive form ardeola. Hesych. gives as a further word formation ἄραμος, for which ἄραρος is doubtless to be read. The stem syllable Ἀρ, whose relation to the generative phallic force we emphasized above, is thus established. It recurs in Ἄσιδον, which according to the same Hesychius is used for ἐρωδιός or ῥωδιός, which with the Asia palus rests on the same stem and the same view of nature, and which finally, according to Lex. Origen. p. 191. Martian (Ἀσίδα ---- ὁ ἐρωδιός, πελαργὸς λέγεται or λεγόμενος), is likewise used of the stork. The swamp nature of the ardeæ is emphasized in that well-known passage of Virgil that depicts the approach of the storm. G. 1, 361. e: Deserit, atque altam supra volat ardea nubem. to which Servius adds Lucan: aut siccum quod mergus amat: quodque ausa volare ardea sublimis pennæ confisa natanti, while Salmasius, 1, p. 65, demonstrates most clearly the imitation of the Aratean description in which ἐρωδιός is used for ardea. After these statements the determination of the religious meaning of the bird ὄκνος presents no difficulty any more. This most beautiful and largest of all swamp herons appears as the bearer of the tellurian generative force resting in the mud of the morasses. He is the natural phallus embodied in animal form. The religious meaning of the swamps that he inhabits passes to him himself. Therefore his name is formed from the stem [PDF 368] — 356 — Ar, and therefore the male and the female sex, as they interpenetrate in the swamp, are alternately attributed to him. Hence the designation Ὄκνος also appears fully justified. The king heron is not only the symbol, he is himself the content of that natural generative force resting in tellurian moisture. In him antiquity recognizes the divine augmenter and promoter of all growth. In this nature he joins the rope-plaiting Ocnus and the Mantuan Ocnus-Bianor as an identical divine figure. However different these three beings may be in their outward appearance, their inner nature is just as perfectly identical, the view of religion from which they have all proceeded just as wholly unified. The moisture of the depth appears as the physical foundation of all three Ὄκνοι. To swamp and swamp life they all stand in the most intimate relation. With rushes and reeds the water heron shares the same divinity. It is he whose phallic force becomes manifest to the eyes of men in that luxuriant vegetation. On this physical significance rests his augural one. As a divine animal, Ὄκνος-ardea guides the founding of cities. After him the Rutulian Ardea has its name. The king heron is its founder, the father of its people (Bohlen, Ind. 1, 193), the giver of all the blessing of the earth, its divine ruler. So he appears in the founding myth, as Hyginus, according to the testimony of Servius (Aen. 7, 412), presented it in his work on the origin of the Italian cities, and as he, according to Ovid’s account in the Metamorphoses 14, 572 f., reappears at the last destruction of the city by Hannibal. For out of the ashes there rises a bird never seen before; the ash color of its plumage, the shrill tone of its voice, the leanness of its elongated form, all is an expression of mourning for the destruction of the city of the same name. Nomen quoque mansit in illa (præpete) urbis, et ipsa suis deplangitur Ardea pennis. We recognize in this the description of the Ardea pellos of Pliny 10, 60, 79, which derives its name from πελλός, fuscus, and might equally be called ardea cinereus. Indeed it is precisely this color of mourning that may have given Ovid the occasion for his poem. For what he reports is his own invention, and is therefore presented by Servius on Aen. 7, 412 in this sense, and in contrast to the anciently transmitted founding legend, as fabulosa narratio. The name of Ardea seems to underlie also the designation of the people, Rutuli, Ῥοτυλοί. Instead of ἐρωδιός, Hesych. and Etymol. magn. s. v. Ἐρωδιός give, citing Hipponax, ῥωδιός. The Aeolic dialect often changes ω into ο (ὥρα-ὄρα; ὠτειλή-ὀτειλή) or into υ (χελώνη-χελύνη; τέκτων-τέκτυν; Ὅρμινα- Ὕρμινα in Strabo 8, 3, 10), so that ῥωδιός expanded into Rutus, and this, as Volscus into Volsculus, Aequus into Aequiculus, [PDF 369] — 357 — Tuscus into Tusculum, into Rutulus. The designation of a people after its θεὸς γενέσιος is a very general practice of the Pelasgian tribes, deeply grounded in the paternal nature of the generative god; Strabo 5, 221 expressly notes that the custom of adopting special names after heroes was particularly usual among them, and hence had sprung from their very view of religion. It emerges, however, not only in the names of individual Pelasgian tribes but also in the collective name Pelasgians, Pelargians, Pelarge. I have already remarked earlier that this word is compounded of πέος and lar, as the Pelasgian city name Larisa, the son of Pelasgus, Laris, and the Pelasgian royal name Lar, Lars, Larius, Γέλας irrefutably demonstrate.1) The combination of πέος and lar gives the idea of generative masculinity a double expression, as it is also found in Λακεδαίμων, in Erichthonius, in Ἄραρος. Thus the people is named after the generative earth phallus, and is necessarily of the same name as the stork. In the proud and beneficent inhabitant of the swamps2) the divine bearer of the force dwelling in them is beheld and venerated. He is the Pelasgian god himself, their king, their leader, their father, their giver of names. In the Pelasgian land of the Peneus he is, according to Plutarch’s testimony, held sacred and inviolable even in later times,3) for which reason he is placed on a level with the sacred water birds of the land of the Nile. The same significance he has for the Lelegian tribe. This name arose, like Λελάντιον πεδίον, from the reduplication of the root syllable La, which has been preserved in this simple form in Lelegian Laconia.4) Now τὸ λελέγι appears as a designation of the stork still in use in the present popular speech of the Greeks. It thus gains the greatest probability that the Lelegian people, too, stands in the same relation to the stork as the Pelasgian, with which Strabo joins it as πλανητικόν. Thereby that account, communicated by the Samian Menodotus in Athenaeus 15, p. 671 (Fr. h. gr. 3, 103), of the natus Laris. — Pelarge, the priestess of initiation, Pausan. 9, 5, 6. She is called Potnei filia; a pregnant sow is sacrificed to her. — Strabo 9, 1, § 18: ὑπὸ τῶν Ἀττικῶν Πελαργοὶ προσηγορεύθησαν διὰ τὴν πλάνην. Dionys. Arch. 1, 18 in fine. e: first founding of the celebrated Samian sanctuary of Hera by Leleges and nymphs acquires a new meaning. The wonder of the founding becomes perfect only when we understand by Leleges not men but the divine bird itself.1) Storks, united with the nymphs, carried out the oldest building, as bees put together the little Delphic temple from wax and feathers, doves the sanctuary at Dodona, herons that of Diomedes in Apulia.2) The nymphs join the storks, and to both, as a complement, attach themselves the Samian cult of a hetaeric Aphrodite venerated ἐν ἕλει and ἐν καλάμοις, and the significance of the succulent willow nourished by water. Swamp and swamp plants appear in the same religious significance as among the Pelasgians, and Hesychius’s statement Λελεγίες, κόχλακες ἢ κοχλώδεις τόποι is no longer unintelligible. The Leleges lead us to the Aetolians3) and to the birds of the Aetolian Diomedes. The kinship of the Leleges and Aetolians emerges from Dionys. Arch. 1, 13. Thereby the Aves Diomedeae too are drawn into the circle of the Pelasgian phallic religion, and placed on a line with the swamp herons of Ardea, the storks of the Pelasgians and Leleges. They are called in Solin. p. 13. Salm. fulicæ; forma illis pæne quæ fulicis. Stephanus Byz., Antigonus, Servius call them outright ἐρῳδιοί; Lycophron and Ovid compare them to swans. The swamp nature is thus beyond doubt for these also, and λάρος, which the ancients equate with fulica, brings us back once more to the root word of the Pelasgians and Leleges.4) Their dwelling place on the island by Garganum, their dripping wings, with which they moisten the interior of the sanctuary, are features of the myth in which one recognizes the same Poseidonian nature, and which recur in perfect correspondence in the birds of Achilles on the lunar island of Leuke in Philostrat her. c. 19. As now the Pelasgians and Leleges appeared to the ancients themselves under the image of those animals that clothe their religion with divinity, as the Ardeates and Rutulians bear the name of the heron, and Cupavo, the Ligurian prince on the lower Po, bears on his head swan plumage as a sign of his descent (Aen. 10, 188), so the companions of Diomedes also receive the form of the swamp herons, which prove hostile to all non-Greeks. In all the features cited there is revealed the same view of nature that gave the king heron its name Ὄκνος, and the whole race of birds to which it belongs its religious significance. We can designate this conception as the Pelasgian, and in [PDF 371] — 359 — it recognize an expression of that phallic cult which is expressly ascribed to the Pelasgians, and which, through the αἰδοῖον erected in the midst of the Lernaean swamp lake, declares its relation to the generative moisture of the depths.1) Ardea itself is traced back to the Pelasgian Argos, to which the Aetolian Diomedes also extends; and since we find the latter again in Venetia, while on the other hand the Leleges and the Lelegian sanctuary on Samos stand in connection with the land of the Nile, all those points at which Ocnus and the divine veneration of the swamp herons are joined enter into a closer relation. — With the Pelasgian name that of the Tyrrhenians is equivalent in its religious significance. For this is traced back by the ancients themselves to Tylos, the son of Earth;2) but Tylos is made recognizable, through a series of connections which we assemble in the Mutterrecht, as the personification of the force of generation, likewise conceived as wholly tellurian. For this reason it becomes very noteworthy that the Pelasgian Ardea is called the city of Turnus, comes to power with him, and falls with him too. For Turnus, like Juturna, like Tolus, and the chthonian Hermes-Trophonius that occurs on the Etruscan mirror, TURMS AITAS, is by etymology and significance precisely that Tylos of the Tyrrhenian stock, and the relation of the swan augury to his fate, as Aen. 12, 244 f. tells it, is in full agreement with the Tyrrhenian-Pelasgian conception. Finally we find Ardea, the city of the swamp heron, brought into connection also with Odysseus. Like Latinus, Ardeus is called the son of Odysseus and Circe.3) This juxtaposition, too, leads back again to the idea of a tellurian phallus, to the generative force of swamp mud, and to the religious significance of the swamp birds. In Italy Odysseus took on the form of a pygmy equipped with a mighty generative member, such as the land of the Nile knows. He was called Nanos, as Odysseus and Laertes also bear within them the significance of generation. With Ardeus the hero Ἐρῳδιός is to be set side by side. Antoninus Lib. 7 draws from Boeus. His account becomes especially instructive in that it connects Ἐρῳδιὸς Σχοινεύς, lets the father Αὐτόνοος be transformed into Ὄκνος, and sets the swamp birds together with the swamp plants against the cultivation of the soil, thus reproducing the whole circle of ideas in which we are moving. the Annali dell’ Instituto, and by the Tylonia gens, as well as by Aphrodite Tydo, who occurs in Nicolaus Damascen.
