e: Odysseus’s Πηνελόπη joins Circe-Medea in the significance of a weaving nature mother. What she weaves by day the following night undoes again. The Aphroditean nature emerging here has left an echo in that myth of the surrender of Ulysses’ consort to the whole row of suitors, of her union with the chthonian Hermes, and of the birth of Pan. It is repeated, however, also in her equation with the many-colored golden duck, which the ancients call πηνέλοψ. She is said to have been raised by birds of this kind when Periboea, her mother, exposed her. In their company she appears on vase paintings.1) Thereby the Penelops receives the same religious significance as Penelope, and the name of the spring, πηνελοπεία, its explanation. The one shows in the form of a duck what the other shows in human representation. The identity of the name of both is no accident, πηνέλοψ not merely joined quite externally with πηνελόπη as a name hieroglyph, even if in the end no other relation might any longer be intelligible. In Penel there emerges the stem πέος, penis, as we find it, with varying quantity of the vowel, in a great number of formations in Peneus, Penus, Penates, Peneleus, Pales, Pelops, in πέλις, πελώρια,2) πέλανα, πηλός, παλίκοι, palus, Pallas, παμύλια3) πέλαγος, the Palaemonids, the Peleiades, πελάγων in Pausan. 6, 21, 7, and the earlier name Arnea (ἐν τῷ ἄλφα γράμματι), which Penelope bore at first, will now no longer appear so remote. If the scholiast on Od. 4, 797 in Creuzer 2, 520 derives Penelope from πένεσθαι τὸ λῶπος, this much is certainly correct in it, that πένεσθαι belongs to the same stem as Penelope. From the never-resting activity of the force of nature the idea of toiling, as it lies in πένεσθαι, arises quite of itself. The picture of the rope-plaiting Ocnus sets the connection of the two thoughts vividly before our eyes. The highest exertion distinguishes him. He appears himself as πενέστης or πένης, and the poverty of his attire supports the thought of the harassed life of the ἐγχειρογάστορες. Were we to give the consideration of the swamp life revealed in the animals, and of its religious significance, still further development, there would offer itself, for ever greater confirmation of the ideas put forward, the swan, the goose, the duck, as they unite with Dionysus, the lord of the moist Lycophr. Thereby so firm a standpoint has been created that the peculiarities of our painting not yet considered offer their solution quite of themselves. The old age of the chief figure seems indeed to correspond little to the idea of a Bianor; nevertheless the religious significance of the rope plaiter presents a side to which it attaches itself pre-eminently. We cited above that the older founding legend of Phoenician Berytus calls the Aphroditean Beroë coeval with the earth and of one origin with Aion. This conception recurs in the beneficent nymph of the Numicius, who dispenses warm loaves, in Anna Perenna, whose name has been preserved in those regions as Anna Petronella, just as in the Volscian regions Camilla is still given to children today as a baptismal name. The myth portrays her as a wrinkled old woman, which becomes especially significant for us in that it belongs to Bovillae, the city of the Julian cult of Aphrodite. Anna, the material primal mother who holds sway in the Numicius, whose festival is called by Ovid, very significantly, geniale,1) is as old as the earth, in which she, from the beginning of things, well disposed toward mortals, performs her work.2) Like Aphrodite-Beroë she has the same origin as Aion; like the Moira Eileithyia she is older than Cronus. The idea of the highest old age lies in her innermost nature. But as nature combines in itself the seemingly most irreconcilable opposites, so here too the thought of age does not exclude that of youth and its bloom. By her beauty Beroë arouses the strife of the gods, and yet she is not inferior to Aion in age. Like the earth she is ancient and eternally young, fresh and glorious like creation, no otherwise than on the first day. In the same way the concepts of motherhood and of perfect virginity, to which it returns in its yearly rejuvenation, unite in the earth. Pausan. 2, 38, 2. In this domain all opposites vanish. What is most irreconcilable always passes over into its opposite. As the two poles of existence, as the two sexual potencies, combine into unity, so the highest old age and the most blooming youth, maternal fertility and virginal chastity enter into the closest union, so that Penelope’s double conception, and the phallus cult in the service of chaste Vesta, can give no offense. They are properties of the same being, present in and with each other. The creative force of Juventas has, through the centuries that have furrowed Perenna’s Silius 8, 50 f. Macrob. S. 1, 12.

Still she arouses the amorous desire of Mars, eager to beget,, who suspects behind the mask of youth no such gray old age. (Ovid. F. 3, 657 f.)1) In all these features she is the faithful counterpart of Ocnus. To him also the aeons, with which he keeps pace, have, like bald Nereus, like the subterranean longævus Terentus,2) impressed the unmistakable stamp of the highest old age. And yet he performs always with the same diligence and the same success the work that has an origin contemporaneous with the earth itself. The idea of the highest force and of the highest age go hand in hand. We find the same combination of both qualities in the Celtic Ogmius-Heracles, whose representation Lucian has preserved in his προσλαλιά (Ed. Bip. 7, 312). The comparison of Ocnus and Ogmius is instructive in several respects. In the picture that Lucian describes, Ogmius was represented with the signs of the highest old age. His Charontic look, and the remark γέρων ἐς τὸ ἔσχατον, are features that correspond also to our conceptions of Ocnus. But the highest old age did not exclude the highest force. The lion skin, the club, and the band of captives recall the invincible Heracles, whose name Lucian also chooses as the most fitting Greek designation. With bodily strength the picture seemed to bring into connection the force of eloquence. The chain by which the old man drew the band of captives behind him was fastened at one end to the tip of his tongue, at the opposite end to the ears of his companions, a very graspable intimation of the omnipotence of the word, which hands over the hearers to the speaker, as it were, as will-less captives, for his possession. In this way the Celt in Lucian grasps the allegory of the representation, and that he was not thereby setting up some wholly arbitrary explanation, but was adhering to a native Gallic conception, is proved by the Ogham script, which evidently derives its name from Ogmius, the god of eloquence. This attribution now has an inner connection with that first one, of bodily force and strength. We need not think here of the mighty influence by virtue of which the power of speech often accomplishes more than bodily athleticism. Good words are better than bad strokes, Octavius. The connection of word and force lies much deeper. Most clearly it meets us in Hermes- Mercury, who, precisely in his relation to word and speech, is compared by Lucian to the Gallic Ogmius. The phallic god of the tellurian generative [PDF 376] — 364 — force, who unites in himself the luminous and the nocturnal side of the life of nature, and, like the Dioscuri, wanders eternally to and fro between the two poles, is also the giver of the word, and is therefore called on the herm of the Villa Albani sermonis dator.1) The gift of speech and the life of the body spring from the same force. They are bestowed on man by nature, and are so much of material-chthonian origin that the newborn becomes a partaker of the word only through contact with the earth. In consequence of this conception the faculty of speech attaches itself to the phallic nature of Hermes. As the bearer of the force of earthly generation he is also the origin of speech, which receives its embodiment in him. Hence his pillars are speaking stones of the gods, the writings they bear Hermes’s revealed word: a conception that underlies not only Egyptian views,2) but emerges equally in the use of Greek herm pillars as law tablets, in the Asclepius pillars covered with writing, in the speaking tower of the fable of Psyche, and has found a long-lasting expression in the custom of introducing pillars and funerary monuments as speaking in the first person, as well as in the use of walls for the proclamation of the secrets of fate. The union of the generative and the speaking force in one being is beheld in the tongue. We pointed above to the physical significance in nature of the γλῶττα. From its position in the moisture, which Egyptian hieroglyphics especially emphasize in it, it has received its name and likewise its meaning, uniting both sexual potencies, from τύχη-δαίμων. At the same time, however, it is the bearer of the word, embodied speech, and in the union of this double physical and spiritual potency the perfect expression of the Hermetic divine nature. In Lara-Larunda-Lala the same conception recurs. The stem on which this designation rests has become familiar to us in many ways as an expression of the generative force lying in the moist matter of the earth. The nymph Lala thereby becomes the representation of tellurian motherhood in its significance of generation. But with this the idea of speech now combines, so that the faculty of speech appears as a potency connected with the chthonian generative force.3) If we apply this conception to the picture of the Gallic Ogmius- portance in several respects for the present subject. e: Heracles, the role that the tongue plays here appears first in its full significance. The force of speech here too attaches itself to the physical foundation of the bodily strength displayed in generative fullness. The comparison with the Greek Hermes becomes a thoroughgoing one, governing all stages of his divine nature. Ogmius is first of all the representation of the generative force of nature, such as both the lion and the Greco-Italic Heracles- Italus bear within them, with the green club and the cornucopia of the blessing of harvest. The extreme old age and the Charontic look that Lucian emphasizes form, precisely in union with that physical significance in nature, a parallel perfectly corresponding to the rope-plaiting Ocnus. In both, the inexhaustibility of generative force enters into connection with the idea of the highest old age. The aeons, by which the old man’s age is reckoned, show the fullness of life diminished by no lapse of time. Charon himself is in his foundation nothing other than the generative water lion of the tellurian swamps, into whose chaos all life returns, as it has its origin from the moisture; his hammer is the bearer not only of destroying but equally of creative, healing force.1) But, coeval with matter, he assumes the appearance of a primeval origination, and, akin to the dark depths of mud, his appearance receives the wild look of those thickets to which man never turns his tending care. — If we wish to search for further analogies, Orphic theology in particular offers one. It is all the more noteworthy since it goes back precisely to that primeval age to which the Ocnus symbol belongs. I have earlier, pp. 110, 141, mentioned the Orphic Heracles, who is called Χρόνος ἀγήρατος and is joined with Ananke-Adrasteia, who spreads through the All. The coin of Camarina represents him as a bearded old man with the primal egg, which owes its origination to his πατρικὴ δύναμις. He is represented through his attributes as the content of the primal generative force, but at the same time is formed as an old man. The swan with the inscription MAPA, whose meaning we explained above, and the bearded human head of Dionysus-Hebon lead us here too back to the swamps and their relation to creation from moisture. What gives the Orphic representation special significance, however, is the identification of the creative Heracles with Chronos.2) In this, time appears as an attribute of becoming, moving creation: a conception whose inner correctness Aristotle too recognizes in the Metaphysics, in that he sets up the proposition mysteries of Juno of Falerii.

e: that for the world of becoming the idea of time is as indispensable as that of timeless eternity is for the world of being.1) The former is an attribute of becoming; it is becoming’s necessary companion, the form in which it appears. Chronos therefore appears as the representation of matter in development, set in motion. Only where there is becoming and passing away is there also time. Where the former does not reach, there is no time either. Where there is no movement, there is no development, and hence no time, which Plato aptly calls the movable image of eternity. “The human race and all time together are of one nature: the former runs on with the latter, and will endure alongside it, and is in this way immortal, in that it always leaves behind children and the children of those same children, whereby all time remains one and the very same, and through constant becoming has a share in immortality.” (Plato, Laws 4, p. 721, on which the eighth of Plutarch’s Platonic Questions must be consulted.) According to this conception the force that generates, and through generation sets matter in motion, appears as Chronos. If, then, the dragon-shaped Heracles, surrounded by a lion’s head and an ox’s head, receives the name of time, he is thereby most emphatically represented as the originator of material life, as the fecundating natural phallus that calls everything into existence. The generative force takes shape as time. Heracles, who by his first phallic deed gives the impulse to the movement of becoming, appears as Χρόνος, πατὴρ χρόνου,2) and is therefore winged, like all movement of the world of becoming, hastening swiftly on, like all life in time. The same transition of the material idea of generation into that of χρόνος recurs in the name of the compassionate nymph of the Numicius. Anna attaches herself to Annus. The ancients emphasize this unmistakable etymological connection; but the way in which they conceive it is not suited to exhaust the whole fullness of the thought. Perenna forms a significant complement to Anna, also in the phrase Anna et Perenna (Gell. N. A. 13, 22). If the former designates the division of time, Perenna emphasizes the duration extending over all the parts, and the repetition proceeding in eternally uniform sections. If Anna gives the unity, Perenna gives its unlimited multiplication. We can compare with this the Elean μήτηρ ἰσοδρόμη. In the designation ἰσοδρόμη the primal mother appears as an Anna Perenna who accompanies at equal pace the movement of the life that has proceeded from her womb. Strabo 9, 440. With ὥσπερ οὐδὲ τὸ νοητόν, αἰῶνος. Rochette, Hercule p. 15, 2; 94–96. — Soph. Antig. 608.

e: the first becoming she began her course, with the progressing one she has continued it. She too can therefore be conceived as winged time, as Σάρδαν recurs as Σάρδις, Ἰάρδαν, year.1) However long the movement has already lasted, the swiftness has nevertheless not slackened, and no weariness has set in. Sedula in old age as in youth, Anna gladly hears the good wishes of many years of life, for which, at her festival, an equal number of cups is emptied, as if the idea of the ἰσοδρομεῖν were to receive a pictorial expression. As Χρόνος ἀγήρατος Heracles too is a never-tiring Isodromos- Perennus, and is therefore represented on Cilician coins as Δρομεύς, carrying the material egg away in swift course. Ageless time shows once more the combination of old age and youthful bloom that we found in the assumption of an ancient and yet eternally fresh force of nature. Indeed, in the garb of time, which always keeps equal pace with material life, the intimate kinship of those two seemingly mutually exclusive opposites steps forth first in its full truth and justification. For Ocnus, however, there results from the consideration of the Orphic Χρόνος ἀγήρατος a meaning that attaches itself most closely to his conception as πατρικὴ δύναμις, and shows us this in the garb of the oldest religious ideas. Γέρων ἐς τὸ ἔσχατον, he is yet ἀγήρατος, primeval and Bianor at once, sedulus like the wrinkled nymph of the Numicius, a true γραῖα, Isodromos-Perennus as she is Perenna, keeping equal pace with the movement of life, and never tiring. How intimately this nature is connected with the work assigned to him is plain. Like creation, moving onward in eternal becoming, eternal passing away, the rope, too, that issues from Ocnus’s hands is at no moment the same. As the river there pours its waters into the sea and here receives a replacing inflow from the spring, no otherwise the rope diminishes at one end while it grows at the other. Under this double influence river and rope stand in never-ending movement. They thereby become the image of becoming creation, whose eternal change Heraclitus compares to that of flowing water. As movement has time as its necessary companion, so Ocnus, who incites and sustains it, becomes Χρόνος, and in this nature Ἰσοδρόμος, who always keeps equal pace with the movement of life, and in every coil of his cord, as ἀγήρατος, with the deceptive mask of youth νέον δὲ Σάρδιν τὸ νέον ἔτος ἔτι καὶ νῦν λέγεσθαι τῷ πλήθει συνομολογεῖται· εἰσὶ δὲ οἱ φασί, τῇ Λυδῶν ἀρχαίᾳ φωνῇ τὸν ἐνιαυτὸν καλεῖσθαι Σάρδιν. The form Ἰάρδαν is found in Elis, where Ἰαρδάνου λειμὼν καὶ τάφος is very remarkable. Strabo 8, 347. Pausan. 5, 5, 5 reports that an Ephesian told him that the Ἀκίδας (one thinks of Acis) was called Ἰάρδαν in ancient times. Paus. 5, 18, 2; 6, 21, 5. Raoul-Rochette Hercule p. 45.

e: steps again before the eyes of men. Himself imperishable, he is the originator and witness of the perishability of the work that issues from his hands. If he creates on untiringly, yet it falls to his lot to suffer the pain of giving, with all his generation, nothing but ever new nourishment to death. According to this connection the concept of mourning joins that of time. The destruction of all his children fills the father with deep pain. We find this thought in moving expression on a Roman funerary monument that Raoul-Rochette first made known, Monuments inédits Pl. 77. 4. p. 407. Here Cornutus, mourning the destruction of his eight children, appears in the figure and bearing of aged Saturn, and corresponds to those words that the chorus addresses to Peleus in Euripides, Andromache 1185: Ὦ κακὰ παθὼν ἰδών τε δυστυχὴς γέρον, Τίν᾽ αἰῶν᾽ εἰς τὸ λοιπὸν ἕξεις; The inscription Hic ego sum Cornutus doliens cum filiis dulcissimis octo agrees so completely with the details of the pictorial representation that one might perhaps be justified in taking Doliens rather as a proper name than as an epithet. The example is all the more noteworthy since Saturnus-Cronus presents the inner connection of the three ideas considered so far, of phallic natural generation, of time, and of pain, in the most unmistakable way, and sets all of them before us in the garb of the highest old age.1) The name Anius could therefore find application to him. So is called that Delian priest of Apollo who vainly seeks to conceal from Anchises, the Trojan beloved of Aphrodite, the destruction of his five children. From ἀνία he is called Anius, a Doliens, like Bellerophon, who after the destruction of his race wanders alone on the Aleian plain, a Cinyras, to whose happiness nothing was lacking but childlessness: felix si sine prole fuisset.2) Anius leads us to the meaning of the word Anio, Anien. This river, which Virgil G. 4, 369 also counts among the subterranean ones, reveals itself as a river of sufferings and of pain, like Ἀχέρων, which, though etymologically incorrect, is yet in meaning aptly interpreted as ὁ ἄχεα ῥέων. e: an element of death and an expression of pain, into which in the end all the bliss of the earthly creation dissolves.1) On the height of the Sipylian rock face Niobe mourns, in eternally trickling springs, the destruction of all her births: an image of primal mother Earth, of whose many children in the end not one is left to her. e: Surrounded by the bones of the dead, of decaying men, Homer (Od. 12, 41 f.) shows us the song-rich Sirens. The blooming daughters of Achelous see everything that the water generates transformed into mold and dust. Their song becomes a lament for the dead, like the roar of the ocean that reaches their ears, an ever uniform moaning of grief (Euripid. Suppl. 80– 87). They themselves, in the youthful bloom of perfected beauty, appear as a representation of the thought of the tomb, as they are so beautifully described in Euripides, Helena 169–178, and as guardians of the Plutonian laws according to Plutarch’s (Symp. 9, 13) highly remarkable account. The most luxuriant life is dominated by death. What Ocnus weaves through the aeons is all doomed to destruction. His diligence profits him nothing. With the joy of creating he combines the deep seriousness that the contemplation of the fate of all tellurian creation produces in the soul of the old man. Euripid. Hippol. 1104–1106. Medea 1096–1104. 12.

e: These thoughts, to which the ancient world of myth lends the most moving expression in thousands of images and funerary monuments, have prepared us for the consideration of the second main part of our Ocnus pictures. To the creating and increasing activity there is opposed a dissolving and diminishing one. Two forces work against each other in eternal enmity. Two streams meet with equal violence. Through their opposed cooperation creation is kept in its eternal youthful freshness. The small end of the rope, which holds the middle between the creative and the destroying principle, is that visible creation which, caught up in never-resting movement, remains the same at no moment either. Compared with what has long since returned into the dark womb of the earth, the visible end sinks to insignificance. What is the number of the living beside the incalculable hosts of the dead? What is the span of the time allotted to them beside the aeons, which the fleeting moment of the present constantly enlarges? With justice, therefore, the dead are called the more numerous, plures, πλείονες. When the oracle made known to the commonwealth of the Megarians, shaken by the expulsion of the kings, that all misfortune would then be averted ἢν μετὰ τῶν πλειόνων βουλεύσωνται, a heroon was erected to the dead in the middle of the council house, in correct interpretation of the word. Pausan. 1, 43, 3. Anth. Pal. T. 1, p. 530. Plaut. Trin. 2, 2, 14. Plut. Alex. 64. Jul. Valer. R. G. Al. M. 3, 18 ed. Mai. Whoever possesses an overview of all time and of all being cannot possibly think human life anything great. Plato, Republic 6, p. 486. It sinks rather to a deceptive mask worn for a small moment. Instead of her husband [PDF 383] — 371 — Laodamia embraces an image.1) The mortal Helen is Aphrodite’s shadow. Beneath the veil of youth lies hidden the wrinkled brow of the primal mother. What seems real is not the real; becoming is the opposite of being. All these ideas, whose ancient expression has already met us in many ways in the first treatise, attach themselves to the sight of the small end of the rope, which alone remains of the labor of the centuries. Another series of thoughts is stirred by the representation of the destroying principle before the festival assembly of Acanthus. If the plaiting is the work of one individual, the unraveling is assigned to a plurality of men. Unitary and always the same is the work of the generative force, but destruction takes a thousand forms. If in the serpent bite and in the myth of the black man who appears at the back of his victim the treachery of death, snatching away from the midst of the most harmless life, is brought out, then in the plurality of the dissolving men, by contrast, the manifoldness of the means is indicated that the destroying principle knows how to employ in combating the creative one. And yet the united exertion of all adversaries is not able to carry off the victory over the generative force, any more than the latter succeeds in removing the former entirely from its path. In this conception the representation of Acanthus corresponds perfectly to the fundamental view of Egyptian religion. According to the theology of the Egyptians there are two forces opposed to each other, which however are not of equal power. The good being has the upper hand, yet cannot wholly annihilate the evil. Indeed, Isis is so convinced of the necessity of the destroying force that she, of her own resolve, grants freedom to the captive Typhon, and so of herself calls forth again the eternal struggle of the hostile forces. Plutarch, from whose work on Isis and Osiris 19, 45 f. what has just been reported is taken almost word for word, holds the assumption of a conflict of two opposed fundamental forces to be not only ancient but just as much universally diffused, and to be deposited equally in the systems of Zoroaster, of the Magi, of the Greek philosophers, despite all difference of form and expression. “Ancient is the opinion — which has been propagated from the theologians and lawgivers to the poets and philosophers, and which, even if its first originator cannot be named, is nonetheless no less certain and reliable, since it rests not on mere legends and rumors but is taught everywhere in mysteries and sacrifices, among Greeks as among barbarians — that this universe is neither, without reason, without understanding [PDF 384] — 372 — and without government, left to chance, nor governed by a single rational being as with a rudder or rein; that further, since in many things good and evil are mixed with one another, or, to speak properly, nature has nothing at all pure and unmixed, a single steward cannot possibly, as it were out of two casks, like a tavern keeper, mix the drinks and distribute them to us; but that there must be two distinct primal beings and opposed forces, of which the one leads to the right hand and straight ahead, the other however turns about and drives back. Hence human life, and, if not the whole world, at least this sublunary earth, is so unequal, so manifold and subject to changes. For since nothing is wont to happen without cause, but the good cannot be the cause of evil, the evil must have its own cause and origin just as well as the good.” (C. 45.) In Typhon’s battle with Horus this duality of contending forces has found its mythic expression, as in the cult act of Acanthus its symbolic one. “Typhon’s destroying force, the Egyptians teach, does not always keep the upper hand; often it is overcome and bound by the generative force, and just as often it tears itself loose again and fights with Horus. This one, however, is the world surrounding the earth, in which destruction and production alternate with each other.” According to this conception, to the 24 gods whom Arimanius shuts up in the primal egg, 24 others begotten by Horomazes stand opposed in hostility. After these are conceived the two eggs handed by Cronus to Hera, after these the two drops of blood that Pallas entrusts to Erichthonius. For of them the one brings death, the other healing. When Euripides, Ion 926, expressly stresses that the goddess’s double gift was not mixed, this again presents that doctrine of the independence of the two hostile fundamental forces, and repeats the distribution of the creative and the destroying principle to two separate figures, as the Ocnus symbol contains it. Enmity and war now appear as the father, king, and lord of all things. We stand before the doctrine of Heraclitus, who rebukes Homer for the fact that through his wish Would that discord were wiped out among gods and men, he unawares curses the origin of all things, which arose solely through strife and enmity. If we sum up all these remarks, there results the most complete agreement of the Ocnus symbol with the view of the oldest, especially the Egyptian, theology concerning the struggle of two separate forces, which meet everywhere, set destroying against creating, passing away against becoming, evil against good, and through their enmity [PDF 385] — 373 — secure eternal movement and constant rejuvenation to the visible world.1) From both sides the greatest exertion is summoned up. For the force of the two opposed streams must correspond perfectly. The slightest inequality on the one side or the other would have to disturb the balance, bring the egg held upright by the two dragons to a fall, and in the end wholly abolish the uniform progress of earthly generation. Therefore Horomazes sets against the creations of Ariman an equal number of his own; therefore Penelope and the daughter of Tarchutius unravel each night exactly as much of their web as they accomplished through the day. The slightest inequality of the two opposed acts would inevitably have to end by putting a term to the further activity of the force of nature, either through complete destruction or through complete consummation of creation. With this exact correspondence another goes hand in hand. To plaiting is opposed unraveling, to the giving of form the taking of form, and so, in agreement with the processes of the life of nature, that requirement of the most complete correlation of the creative and the destroying, of the binding and the loosing deed is conscientiously fulfilled. 13. The complete elucidation of the Ocnus symbol now still requires the consideration of the animal that has been chosen on our tomb paintings for the representation of the destroying principle of nature. While at the Panegyris of Acanthus a plurality of men confronts the rope plaiter, all the paintings, whether actually preserved or described by the ancients, show an ass gnawing at the Ocnus rope and swallowing it. This agreement alone proves that the choice of the animal cannot have been guided by chance or by the caprice of the artist. Still more would the religious significance of the whole scene and its acceptance in the Lesche at Delphi oppose such an assumption. If we nevertheless wished to recognize in the ass a free invention of Polygnotus, retained by all his successors, even this could not have been without occasion. Wherein might such an occasion have lain? Here some relations do indeed offer themselves, which lack not truth, but depth of conception. To the artistic activity of human hands there would then be opposed the crude impulse to destruction of bestial nature in its most repellent form, and the myth of those Diomedean horses, whose teeth crush human bones, might seem to have been transferred into the artistic representation. But why then prefer the ass to the horse furnished by so familiar a tradition? For this too some points of connection could be found. Did not the ass stand so high in the use and esteem of the oldest generations that he is present in pictorial representations of the first formation of man,1) and is counted, as res mancipi, among the most necessary agricultural basic capital? Or should the artist have been guided by the thought of contempt for the animal? Proverbial expressions such as ὄνος ἐν πιθήκοις, to designate the ugliest among the ugly, ὄνος πρὸς λύραν or πρὸς αὐλόν as an expression of crude disposition, and further comparisons such as inepta et asinina cogitatio (Plut. Symp. 9, 5) and many similar ones2) are surely sufficient proof that mockery and scorn have at all times repaid that unhappy animal’s heavy services badly. All the attempts at explanation indicated, far from solving the riddle, only bring the need for a deeper conception closer. To satisfy this it is necessary to choose a comprehensive standpoint, and with the use of the whole material at our disposal to determine the religious significance that antiquity attached to the ass. Once this is done, it will also become possible, finally, to determine the significance of the female sex, which is expressly attributed to the gnawing animal and first occasioned its relation to the spendthrift wife. 14. The phallic nature of the ass is emphasized by the most various testimonies in such a way that the animal’s relation to the idea of natural generation cannot be mistaken. Lactant. div. instit. 1, 21 tells of the certamen de obscœni magnitudine, in which Priapus is defeated by the ass. e: the moist depths of the earth dwells the phallic god, withdrawn from the eyes of mortals. But the reed bed shooting up out of the ground bears witness to his existence and his force. In this conception we find confirmed the relation of the ass to the wild hetaeric swamp generation, as it was emphasized earlier. If in other parts of the myth Midas enters into the closest relation with agriculture and with the laborata Ceres,1) yet his shape as an ass is brought precisely and exclusively into connection with the free swamp vegetation. To the swamp belongs the reed pipe, to which he gives the preference; to the swamp that thicket of reeds shooting up, which conceals the animal form of his ears. In the swamp religion, furthermore, is rooted the comparison of the reed bed with the equally spontaneous growth of the hair of the human head;2) in it, the idea of the calami loquentes, which proclaim in the soft whispering of the wind the secrets of that supreme natural force from which they have sprung.3) To this mightiest yet deepest stage of tellurian life corresponds that trait of the myth which traces back to Midas the invention of white and black lead.4) If the relation of lead to tomb and death, probably a consequence of the corpse-like color of that metal, emerges from individual tomb finds,5) then the change of color between white and black is an image of the great natural force which, like Autolycus and Mercury, turns everything bright back into darkness, and which in the luxuriance of swamp life sets before our eyes this constant transition of color with the terrifying significance of an inescapable material law. Hence Lityerses, the bastard son of Midas, was held to be a greedy, insatiable glutton, as he is portrayed by the poet Sositheus in Athenaeus 10, p. 415. Three times three ὄνους κανθηλίους he devours daily. The myth therefore conceived him himself as a κάνθων, like Erysichthon, whose voracity is emphasized by Aelian, V. H. 1, 27. As a spurius, Λιτυέρσης corresponds to wild swamp mating. His very name reveals him as the rope-plaiting man of the swamp. e: ἔρσα, whence ἔρσις, the Latin sero, designates joining, plaiting together, every kind of nectere; λιτός, on the other hand, as the opposite of δαίδαλος, ποικίλος, the simple, artless work, such as we emphasized above in the plaiting of crude ropes as against the rich and fine work of weaving. Through these manifold relations to swamp and swamp generation the fable of Midas acquires a special significance for the two components of the depiction of Ocnus.1) For determining the meaning, above all, that the ancient nature religion attached to the ass, it is altogether decisive. Everywhere the animal appears as a representation of the primal generative force of tellurian matter. 15. Hence the ass now enters into connection with a whole series of equivalent divine figures. Above all with Priapus, the pene destricto deus, obscœna nimium quoque parte paratus (Ovid. F. 1. 437.), the ruber hortorum decus et tutela (Ovid. F. 1, 400. 415.), the god of the moist, luxuriantly fertile gardens (Catull. C. 115), before whom Lotis flees into the swamps,2) to whom Lampsacus offers the sacrifice of an ass (Ovid. F. 6, 345. Lactant. inst. 1. 21.), just as the Tyrrhenian Tages sets up the skull of an ass on the boundary post of the estate with the significance of a protecting terminus. (Columella de cultu hortor. X, 344.) But then with Silenus, whose inextincta libido was not diminished by old age. Ovid. F. 1, 413. Bent beneath the weight of the heavy body, the animal strides along. Ovid. F. 1, 439. With its rider it shares the same divine nature. The most luxuriant lust of generation binds the two together. Silenus himself wears ass’s ears. He thereby assumes the nature of Midas, as, according to Tertullian, de anima c. 2, he derives his animal form from the Phrygian king and is placed in the closest connection with him.3) Silenus is joined by his foster child Dionysus. To this lord of all flowing, swelling generation the constellation οἱ ὄνοι is traced back. e: his way to the Dodonaean Zeus-Achelous, arrives at its bank.1) A second myth ascribes to the ass yet another service to the god. On asses ride Liber, Vulcan, the Sileni and Satyrs into battle against the audacious, heaven-storming race of the Giants.2) The sound of their braying breaks all resistance. The braying of the animal, to which the force of victory is here ascribed, stands, according to the Egyptian view, on a line with the sound of the trumpet. Plut. Is. et Os. 29. This, however, we have already recognized above in its relation to the generative natural force of the chthonian waters. So in that second turn of the myth, too, the idea of the phallic force of the divine animal has found its expression. Vulcan, whose physical kinship with Dionysus emerges so often precisely on monuments as well, appears on vases, as on a very remarkable one in the Vienna Cabinet, in the company of the phallic animal, and of such appearances in which that μέγα τοῦ ὄνου σύμβολον is quite deliberately emphasized. It is only a single confirmation of the general connection when the ass is now brought into relation preferentially with figs,3) wine, and viticulture. In the sweet liquid the generative force of Dionysus emerges in its highest fullness and power; indeed, in the lascivious sensuality of the ass the lust of generation aroused by the gift of Bacchus seemed to have found its wholly corresponding expression. That this connection was resolved into some outward mythical relations, and that particular services to the art of pruning the vine were conceded to the ass, accords entirely with the procedure of the ancient peoples, which sought to make up for the lack of deeper understanding by such wonder stories. One such legend is reported especially of Nauplia. It attached itself to the image of the ass, which one saw there hewn out of a rock face, and which, as I scarcely doubt, derived from Phoenician antiquity.4) It recurs, however, also in the following report of Hyginus, f. 274. Antiqui autem nostri in lectis tricliniaribus in fulcris capita asellorum vite adligata habuerunt, significantes suavitatem (adde: vini) invenisse. The adornment of the couch intended for the meal with the head of the ass places this animal in a causal relation to the fullness of the table, which is regarded as its gift. That in this no thought was given to an Emeric David, Vulcain p. 42. Voss. de or. id. 2, 3; 3, 75. Cilicia laughed himself to death when he saw an ass eating figs. The Bacchic relation of the fig tree is well known, since the great phalli had to be made of fig wood.

e: exclusive relation to wine or to the fruits of Bacchus is evident from Juvenal 11, 96, whose description does not emphasize such a connection. Ancient Rome gave the ass an equally definite relation to the Demetrian yield of the harvest and to Vesta, the primal mother, from whom all the abundance and all the happiness of the hearth proceeds. On a Pompeian wall painting, which we mentioned earlier, the ass is represented beside the goddess.1) At her festival wreathed asses walked at the head of the procession. Rings of bread adorned their necks.2) The animal appears here as the very fecundator of Vesta, as the male causality of the blessing of the harvest. It stands at the side of the mother goddess as daimon, as Virbius does beside Diana: a comparison whose exact aptness will emerge still more definitely in the consideration of Diana and of the ass connected with her as well. The cult of the Vestals is described to us as a phallus cult,3) whereby the significance of the ass receives its determination. When Lydus cites the services of the animal in the mill, and Ovid the rescue of Vesta from the assault of the lustful Priapus through the untimely braying of the ass of Silenus, as the ground of the animal’s significance in the cult of Vesta, these are turns designed to justify, after the fact, the transmitted and established connection by a definite external occasion, such as popular belief offered almost alone to the mythographers. 16. If we inquire into further connections of the ass, the Hyperborean Apollo and the Thracian Artemis present themselves to our attention. According to Pausan. 3, 16, the Spartans find Ἀστράβακος and Ἀλώπεκος, the sons of Ἴρβος, the image of the Taurian Artemis Orthia, who, like the Samian Hera, is called Λυγοδέσμα, and is therefore a true fascelis. In this the idea of a phallus wound about with willow branches is as little to be mistaken as in the proper names of the children the designations ass and fox; and in Ἴρβος the Aricine Virbius (from vir, through the prefixing of the Aeolic digamma to the stem Ir, like oiorpata), whose meaning as a name recurs in Ἀμφισθένης, Ἀμφικλῆς, Ἅγις, his forebears.4) Thus the ass is also for Thrace secured as a divine ἡμέρᾳ ἑόρταζον οἱ ἀρτοποιοί, διὰ τοὺς ἀρχαίους τὸν ἄρτον ἐν τοῖς ἱεροῖς τῆς Ἑστίας κατασκευάζειν· ὄνοι δὲ ἐστεφανωμένοι ἡγοῦντο τῆς πομπῆς, διὰ τὸ τούτοις ἀλεῖσθαι τὸν σῖτον. — Ovid. Phrygia and Thrace appear here united in the cult of the ass as the highest representation of natural force, in such a way that the chthonian stage of religion, too, emerges clearly for both countries. The Thracian Orthia is joined by the Hyperborean Apollo. The hecatombs of asses offered to this god have found manifold mention among the ancients. They are recalled by Pindar, Pyth. 10, 30 f. Scholion on Pyth. 10, 49, p. 412. Boeckh. Eustath. on Il. 1, 36. Callimachus in Clemens in protrept. p. 8, and in the scholiast on Pindar Pyth. 10, 49 (Bentley, fr. 137. 138 in Spanheim on Callimach., p. 383), Antoninus Liber. c. 20, who drew on Boeus, de avium ortu, and Simmias Rhodius, in Apolline. To this is joined the myth of the three-eyed leader of the colony of those Dorians who crossed over by ship to the Peloponnese. Pausan. 5, 3, 5. When Cresphontes saw Oxylus driving up a one-eyed mule, he recognized the fulfillment of the oracle given to him. To the same Apolline connection may be added the votive offering of the Corinthian Ambraciots at Delphi. The defeat of the Molossians was ascribed to the braying of an ass, and therefore a bronze ass was dedicated to the Pythian god. — Athenaeus 10, p. 456. 457, reports on a remarkable image in the temple of Apollo at Carthaea on the island of Cos, and also communicates to us Simonides’s epigram relating to it. The Trojan legend, which Stesichorus mentions in Athenaeus op. cit. and Eustath. p. 1323, 56, made the son of Panopeus the water carrier of the Atridae, and he was so represented in that image. As in this a plain relation makes itself known to the water significance of the horse, whose name is borne by Epeus, the builder of the Ilian horse, so on the other hand the designation of the water-carrying Apolline ass as Epeus, as it is found in Simonides’s epigram, fits exactly with similar connections of this animal with rivers and springs, such as we already found above and shall see confirmed repeatedly later. — But Apollo Κιλλαῖος in particular recalls the connection of this god with the veneration of the ass. Pollux 7, 56: Κίλλον τὸν ὄνον οἱ Δωριεῖς καὶ Κιλλακτῆρα τὸν ὀνηλάτην.1) The designation is without doubt from the mobility of the ears [PDF 393] — 381 — derived, as the wagtail, because of a similar property, is called not only σεισοπυγίς but, according to Hesychius, also Κίλλουρος. As Κιλλαῖος Apollo is venerated preferentially at Κίλλα, Χρύσα, and Τένεδος. At Colonae the Aeolians founded a sanctuary of the same god. Strabo, who (13, p. 612. 613) instructs us most exactly about all this, attests for the same region also a Κιλλαῖον ὄρος,1) the Κιλλαῖος ποταμός that rises on the Trojan Ida, and the Κίλλου μνῆμα connected with the sanctuary of the Cillaean Apollo. In this connection with the ass Apollo appears as the phallic god of tellurian generation, hence beside the Thracian Orthia as Orthos, or Ὀρθάνης (Strabo, 13, 587). He is that Πριαπαῖος Ἀπόλλων mentioned by Tzetzes on Lycophron 29, who now attaches himself, locally as well, to the ass cult of fertile Lampsacus. In the lewd wantonness of the animal the god takes his delight. This is the meaning of the Pindaric expression: γελᾷ θ᾽ ὁρῶν ὕβριν ὀρθᾶν κνωδάλων, which must be understood wholly of the sensual appearance. When Herodotus 4, 33 describes the gift of the Hyperborean Perphereës as ἱρὰ ἐνδεδυμένα ἐν πυρῶν καλάμῃ,2) I can understand by this only a phallic sign of the god hidden in a bundle of wheat; and what the historian adduces for comparison concerning the similar offerings that the Thracian and Paeonian women present to the royal Artemis confirms my assumption, which is not in the least invalidated by vaguer descriptions either, such as that of Callimachus in Delum 283–285.3) For Herodotus’s Ἄρτεμις βασιληίη is evidently identical in meaning with that Orthia who, like Vesta, had the phallus cult. However that may be, the bundle of wheat, no less than the χρυσοῦν θέρος and the Κίλλα ζαθέη, as well as the hair offering of the Delian youths and maidens, makes the god’s relation to the yield of the earth, whose generative causality he is regarded as being, perfectly plain.4) In this nature he now joins the phallic Dionysus no less than Priapus, as he agrees with both in the sanctity of the ass, and even has the Bacchic Silenus for his father.5) In this nature also he enters into that close relation to the generative water of the earth which emerges quite definitely in the sanctity of the Tenedian crabs, in the plunge of the Hyperborean old men into the sea, in the Asia Minor Strabo 380. 393. οὐδένων. 43, 4. — Herod. 4, 34.

To this significance of the animal among the Semitic tribes there attach themselves, on the one hand, the ass hewn out in the rock face at Nauplia, which I already earlier traced back to the Phoenicians, and, on the other, the legend of the ass worship of the Jews.3) For this, however one may otherwise judge it, could not have been invented without a corresponding religious significance of the animal. In the accounts relating to it the connection of the ass with springs and waters emerges once more. In Plutarch’s account, however, the lewdness of the animal is especially stressed. “It seems to me,” says Lamprias, “that the Jews abstain from the hare on account of its likeness to the ass, which is of all animals the one most venerated by them. In size and swiftness, to be sure, the hare has nothing at all in common with the ass; but the color, the ears, the gleam of the eyes, and the lewdness make the two extraordinarily like each other, so that no other small animal has so complete a likeness of form to a large one.” On account of its generative drive and its great fertility the hare has entered into a very close relation to Dionysus, to which so many vase paintings bear witness. For this very reason it has also received its name λάγως from the stem la (consonantized like lacus, λάκκος, Lacinia, lac). In this it agrees entirely with the Priapus nature of the ass, which is called asinus from the stem Ar. For the religious significance of the ass in the land of the Nile its connection with Typhon is wholly decisive. It is repeatedly emphasized by Plutarch in his work on Isis and Osiris.4) Typhon, however, is in his original Germanic mythology. Mannhardt, Germanische Mythen, p. 267. 411 f. de aurei asini capite in Hierosolymi templi adyto. quite decidedly a symbol of Typhon-Seth, who is represented at Karnak ass-headed and bound, and punished by Horus. e: primal significance also a representation of the force of natural generation, and indeed in an entirely Poseidonian conception, so that in this connection too the ass remains wholly true to its phallic Priapus significance. Despite the complete transformation to which the god and his animal fell victim as a consequence of the victorious development of the Osiris cult, the phallic nature of the god, who belongs to an earlier and deeper religious system, is nonetheless still perfectly recognizable. As the physical foundation of Typhon there appears the sea, especially sea salt, whose generative significance has already been established on an earlier occasion through the testimonies of the ancients. Likewise there are assigned to him the depth of the swamps, the hippopotamus, the full moon, the pig. His divine symbol is the phallus; with his ass, on which he too rides out to battle,1) bread cakes are marked.2) So Typhon shares with Osiris the same physical foundation, as the Nephthys joined to him wholly corresponds to the mother Isis (c. 63). We have side by side two pairs of gods equivalent in their foundation: a phenomenon that stands entirely firm, even if the reasons that produced it are not easily determined, and may be sought equally in a progress of religious development and, in the opinion of Jablonski and Bunsen, in an opposition between the parts of the country, Lower and Upper Egypt, which were given over to different foreign influences. Whatever one may think of this, the end of the struggle that developed between the two religions is unmistakable. The two systems attained to fusion. A unified cult, in which now the whole land appears united, took shape. In this Typhon shows all those peculiarities that mark such gods thrust from the throne by victorious later formations. He is preserved as a representation of the evil demonic principle (c. 30. δαιμονικὴ δύναμις) and lends it an expression the gloomier, the more powerfully the luminous side of the life of nature had earlier emerged in him. Now everything that originally belonged to the latter passes over into the opposite significance. The sea, originally conceived as the all-begetting primal father, is now grasped from the side of its destructive nature, hostile to all growth, and abhorred as unclean. Its salt waves are Typhon’s foam of rage, as they are conceived by the Pythagoreans as a tear and that when he had escaped he begot the sons Hierosolymus and Judaeus, evidently draws the Jewish stories over into our legend.” However critical this remark of Plutarch’s may be, the legend underlying it nonetheless deserves attention. It shows how Egypt and Israel met in the significance of the ass, and in what light one conceived the connection of the two lands, which is so often attested also by the monuments.

e: of Kronos overthrown by Zeus. All evil influences of nature, the parching winds and the scorching heat of the sun, are sent over the land by Typhon. To the beneficent Osiris he opposes himself everywhere as a hindrance in his path. Rage and frenzy distinguish him. However often he is overcome, so often he tears himself loose again and begins the struggle anew. All harmful herbs and animals, as well as all destructive phenomena (c. 33. 32. 44 and often), are acts and effects of Typhon. Destruction is his principle, gloomy Tartarus his dwelling (c. 57), sterility the consequence of his union with Nephthys (c. 12. 44. 59. 38). He is the destroyer and annihilator of the holy doctrine which the goddess Isis gathers and hands down to the initiated (c. 2). Into the same nature all attributes necessarily pass over. The mighty phallus is made harmless by the victory of Horus. The red color, originally the expression of the most highly potentiated natural generation, as Priapus rubicundus and ver rubens (Virgil. G. 2, 219. Arnob. 6, 10.) show us, now counts as an attribute of the destructive force that proceeds from the glowing sun, hence as hateful and as a property of the demonic power hostile to man.1) The ass itself exchanges its priapic significance for that of a Typhonically destructive animal. The more emphatically the former originally emerged, the more glaringly the latter now appears. No animal has so completely embodied the demonic character of the god as that in which the earlier age saw the fullness of the force of natural generation most clearly represented. If animal nature is now regarded in general as demonic,2) and therefore every species of animal is brought into connection with Typhon, then in the ass in particular the red color, the stupidity, the lewdness, and all the bizarreness of its nature3) are emphasized, in order to justify the new significance. With bound feet it is represented on the bread cakes. The hurling from the rock (c. 30), originally an offering pleasing to the god, now appears as an act of vengeance and abhorrence; the braying, formerly an expression of generative force like the sound of the trumpet, as demonic roaring.4) The epithet Σήθ (c. 41), which according to the concordant explanation of Jablonski, Silvestre de Sacy, and Birch (Gallery 1, p. 48) signifies the ass’s foal (Coptic: βούριχος, burro, borricho, bourrique, are derived. e: The phenomenon that the land of the Nile presents to us contains an instruction important for the other religions as well. As in Egypt, so also among the other peoples the ass belongs to earlier stages of religion. Later, more developed systems have pushed it into the background and brought about a transformation similar to the Egyptian. This phenomenon emerges most clearly in the myth of Midas. If on the one hand the Priapus significance of the animal is wholly unmistakable here, and the relation to the generative natural force is retained in characteristic features, yet on the other hand the contempt into which the animal has fallen is emphasized no less definitely. If, according to Lycophron’s account, Midas of his own free will put on the ass’s ears for his Thracian campaign, the Phrygian legend traces the animal form of the king back to the punishing vengeance of Apollo. It is the stupidity of the ass that is emphasized here, as in Egypt. In contrast to the higher Apollonian divine nature, that tellurism which found its expression in the ass falls prey to the contempt that marks vanquished cults. Midas is ashamed of his animal form, as the reed pipe beside the Apollonian cithara can no longer maintain its old dignity. Above the swamp cult a purer religion rises; the ass, which belongs to the former, assumes a demonic nature in the face of the new god. The same phenomenon is shown by the Apollonian cult itself. With that stage of spiritualization to which the son of Latona rises in Hellas, the phallic nature of the ass is no longer compatible. It disappears here entirely, and proclaims its former existence only in a few slight traces. More distinct and more numerous are these in Western Asia, where under the influence of luxuriant nature and of historical influences from the interior of the continent Apollo retained to the last a much more material character. Only among the distant Hyperboreans, the race of primeval Titans, as they are expressly called,1) does the myth allow the [PDF 399] — 387 — ass significance persist in its entire primitiveness. Only the phallic Apollo of the Hyperboreans (Hyperboreus, Serv. Aen. 4, 146. Aelian, V. H. 2, 26) rejoices in the hecatomb of asses, which at Babylon he forbids to Clinis and punishes in his children. At Cumae the ass is connected with adultery, and regarded as preeminently demonic, as Suidas s.v. ὄνος εἰς Κυμαίους proves. In Elis a curse is laid on the mating of the ass with the mare.1) Even in the phallic cult of Dionysus the animal has sunk to an attribute, and is placed in connection with the primeval age of the battle of the Giants. Its braying spreads terror and thwarts the lustful enterprise of Priapus. With special emphasis this demonic conception emerges in the legend of the golden ass’s head in the temple at Jerusalem, and again in the transfer of the ass’s form to Christ.2) If the former attaches to the ancient ass veneration of the Phoenician tribes, the latter is an expression of the pagan way of viewing, to which its conqueror had to appear in the light of an evil demon. In the conferring of the ass’s head is revealed the whole transformation to which the priapic animal had fallen victim in the course of time. Formerly a representation of the creative natural force, it now appeared quite generally as the embodiment of the evil principle, and as bearer of the Typhonian nature in all domains of life. Of this conception the ass’s leg of Empusa3) also bears witness. She is called accordingly ὀνοσκελίς and ὀνόκωλος or ὀνοκώλη.4) With ass’s ears, tail, and foot she is depicted on a gem in Gorlaeus, Dactyl. T. 2. no. 41. In Aristophanes, Ranæ 294, she appears to Dionysus, who is visiting the underworld, and to Xanthus years ago. Tertull. in Apologet. c. 16. That the transfer of the ass’s form to Empusa did not arise from wholly groundless poetic caprice, and therefore may not be regarded as the worthless embellishment of a fantastic ghostly apparition, is for him who has followed the foregoing exposition established without further proof. As Empusa the ass appears wholly in that demonic significance which it bears in itself as a Typhonian animal. As the latter is banished to Tartarus, so Onoscelis too has the gloomy depths of the underworld as her dwelling. All the terrors that Hades inflicts on the race of the living have attained in her a spectral development. But beneath such demonic significance there lies here too an originally wholly opposite one. The connection of the ass with Hecate is probably a very ancient one. That Ionic exclamation Νὴ τὸν Ποσειδῶ καὶ Βολίτινον might later have been used by iambic poets as a mocking conjunction of the native god with the filthy and despised dung of animals; by its origin, however, it rests on a wholly serious idea, namely on the connection of Neptune and Apollo, who in their tellurian significance build the walls of Troy and are called the Ilian Penates.1) As Βολίτινος Apollo is the priapic Deus Stercutus, equivalent to the Elean Augeas. In the βολίτινον σκέλος of Hecate the same significance lies. The fecundating force of the earth is preferentially attached to the foot and the leg. To the proofs already communicated above may be added the legend of the Egyptian Bubastis.2) To this conception the idea of a leg of animal dung attaches itself quite naturally. What originally had its serious meaning, however, appears in the end as an expression of mockery and as a heightening of the spectral hideousness of an Empusa. The same transformation of meaning which debased the ass to a demon seized also the attribute of the ass’s leg. The kinship of the animal with fecundating dung lies in the phallic nature of both. To find ass and dung combined in the manner indicated can astonish neither in Apollo nor in Hecate. For both bear within them the whole fullness of natural force. Just as intelligible, however, is it that those two attributes later were preserved only in a wholly demonic significance, as was the case with Hecate, or else vanished entirely, even sank to the expression of a crude mockery, as occurred with Apollo. 19. We have now arrived, in the pursuit of the religious significance of the ass, at that point where the θήλεια ὄνος, who confronts the plaiting Ocnus as the representation of the destructive principle, presents herself of her own accord to consideration. One point is now fully secured. The choice of the ass to represent the evil principle rests neither on free invention, nor 241; 3, 119. ἐνεχάραξεν. One may think of the shoe of Perseus and of Jason, which remains stuck in the river mud. Deut. 25, 9; Plut. Qu. gr. 12. It attaches itself rather to the religious significance of the animal, and with Ocnus reaches back into those earliest times out of whose religious conception the sanctity of the ass proceeded. For Egypt in particular, the role of the ass in the Ocnus paintings shows so perfect an agreement with the Typhonian significance that the land of the Nile assigns to it that the assumption of a Libyan origin of the whole receives confirmation. The distribution of human and animal form between the two sides of the symbol repeats that Egyptian conception which already as such brings animal nature into connection with the evil principle of Typhon, and which, according to Plutarch’s remark, of the divine pair Isis-Osiris presents only the female potency in animal form, never the male. This phenomenon shows that between the dissolving principle and femininity there exists an inner connection, which has found its pictorial representation in the θήλεια ὄνος. This is confirmed by the fact that Typhon, the evil ass Seth, whose phallus is mentioned (Plut. Is. 55), appears on the monuments under the name Tipo as a female being, whom Wilkinson (4, p. 418) places beside the male Typhon as an independent evil being conceived as female.1) We now stand, then, before that peculiarity of the Ocnus paintings whose consideration we earlier postponed and reserved for this place. Its elucidation is most closely connected with the views of the ancients on nature and on the difference of the two sexual potencies. Since I have devoted greater care to this point in my work on mother right, only that shall be adduced here which has immediate application to the purpose at hand. Aristotle reproduces the general idea of antiquity when in various places in his works, most significantly in the Metaphysics 5, 28 (with Schwegler’s parallel passages, vol. 3, p. 239), he presents the male generative principle as the form-giving, the female receptive principle as the material, the former as εἶδος, the latter as ὕλη.2) It is in complete accord with this when the activity of man is regarded as an incorporeal ἐγείρειν, maternity on the other hand as χώρα καὶ δεξαμένη γενέσεως, as τόπος and locus, while figuratively the union of the two is conceived in the form of a vertical line falling upon the horizontal, and is therefore correspondingly posed of man, dog, and lion. Descript. de l’Egypte. 2, 277. dant one in Euripides, Orest. 539–549. The deed of Orestes led to the question, who is nearer to the child, father or mother? I have discussed the significance of this conception in my Mutterrecht, p. 44 f.

e: represented by the figure of the cross. Only the ὕλη offers locality and space for the reception and development of birth; to the εἶδος it is wholly foreign. According to this conception the wholly material spiritual tendency of the earliest age holds exclusively to the maternal origin of birth. The awakening, form-giving principle finds no consideration. Man is placed on a line with the rest of tellurian creation. The same law governs everything, that of the material maternal womb. In relation to it man takes no other position than that of the sower who scatters the seed and then disappears. If this relation governs the origination of life, it attains still higher significance in its destruction. With death the male potency stands in no connection. Destruction is the negation of the εἶδος, the dissolution anew of the given form. Woman, on the other hand, reveals precisely then the nature of the ὕλη to which she belongs. As for generation coming into being, so for dead generation too she serves as χώρα, as locus and τόπος. All birth sinks back again into the maternal womb out of which it once, awakened by the deed of man, stepped forth into the realm of light. Indeed the ancients recognize precisely in the taking back of the dead the highest expression of maternal love, which keeps faith with its offspring at the moment when it stands forsaken by all others.1) And so intimate does this relation appear that only woman mourns, man himself puts on women’s clothing,2) and the dead in their reunion with the earth mother are called Demetrians after Demeter, Manes after Mana Geneta, and Dani after Δᾶ.3) The truth of all these relations emerges still more clearly in the consideration of the lower creation, which sprouts up without the contribution of man, ultro et injussa. Invisible here is the male potency, a Jupiter arcanus, a true Androgeos. Unnoticed by the human eye, it performs in the depth of matter the work of the awakening of life. Noticeable is only the maternal matter, its connection with the reed in birth and in destruction. Thus here passage that one will read with great pleasure. Varro L. L. 5, p. 69 Spengel: peperit et resumit denuo. Aeschyl. Coëph. 115 f. Cicero, sen. 20, 72. The same correspondence of giving birth and taking back emerges in the rule that on Delos no one may give birth, but also no one may be buried. Euripid. suppl. 532–537. Virg. G. 3, 7. Serv. e: ὕλη emerges in exclusive validity. Here, however, the significance of woman in relation to death becomes all the more predominant, the more mightily in the swamp the creative force performs its work, the more luxuriant the generation, the swifter the passage from death to life. If we take all these aspects of the female nature into common consideration, three inwardly connected relations of it to the dissolving principle result. Standing as ὕλη over against the paternal εἶδος, the mother forms the representation of purely material nature, stripped of every form, such as alone remains after the dissolution of life. As χώρα καὶ δεξαμένη she offers the locality out of which the dead man emerged at birth, and into which he returns at death. Filled with love, she hides the forsaken one in the darkness of the same womb, quasi sinu et gremio matris, in which she once enfolded protectingly the life that was becoming. As Aphroditean swamp mother, finally, she now becomes Libitina or Epitymbia, the representation of the life that rapidly consumes itself through its own fullness, and of that Ananke-Adrasteia who, according to the Orphic conception, as supreme, all-ruling law of death pervades the whole of matter. Thus the idea of destruction lies wholly on the side of the female ὕλη, as that of becoming combines with the male εἶδος. The opposition of the active principle of movement to the female principle of rest appears completed in death. We see how this way of viewing absolutely required a θήλεια ὄνος and a female Typho, and recognize the inner connection that binds the she-ass most closely with the egg-shaped mothers of death on the Lycian Harpy monument, with the interment of the Egyptian king’s daughter in the body of the specially made cow,1) with the Gorgonian Minerva of sterile, deathly nature, with the idea of great tomb mothers, and with the Demetrian naming of the deceased. Everywhere woman appears as bearer of the law of death, and in this identification at once as a loving and as a gloomily threatening power, full of the highest affection, but also of the highest seriousness, like the maternally formed Harpies and the Egyptian-Phoenician sphinx, which bears in itself the law of all material life.2) 20. The elucidation of the individual components of the Campana Ocnus painting is now completed. The opposed activity of the rope-plaiting old man and the gnawing she-ass is the representation of a symbol of nature whose content can now no longer be enigmatic. What heightens its significance lies in this, that not some single aspect of tellurian life was grasped and embodied symbolically, but that rather the fundamental law that governs all life of nature and prevails over the whole visible creation has received its simple and perfectly intelligible expression. The life of the earth appears here in its eternal transformation, comparable to a stream that bursts restlessly from its source, has movement as its innermost principle, and by every step is led onward toward the ocean in which it is to vanish. The transience of all sublunary existence is the highest idea that confronts us. It is that flux of things that caused Heraclitus to utter the saying that the phenomenal world is like a water into which one cannot set the foot twice in such a way that it be still the same; but that led the physicists to the assertion that no existence at all can be ascribed to it, and nothing definite can be said, since it possesses no reality. Firm and unchangeable are only the two poles between which life moves to and fro in an eternal cycle. If the rope is at no moment wholly the same, Ocnus and the she-ass, by contrast, remain through all aeons wholly alike. In generating, the former is as indefatigable as the latter in devouring. Plut. Cons. ad Appoll. in Hutt. 7, 322. 339. “Others bloomed once, now we, soon others again.” Both poles meet in every organism, which at every moment both lives and dies, both diminishes and grows. They themselves lie hidden in the appearance of individual life, as the capita loramentorum conceal themselves in the insoluble Gordian knot.1) With double weight this opposition of the transient and the abiding emerges on the negative side, that of disappearance. The movement of life finds its goal in the repose of death. In life the absence of every sameness, in death the abolition of every change. e: of such frail and perishable material, while on the tombs of the dead they lavished such extraordinary care and art, pointed out that the former serve only a short time and are destined as a temporary lodging for the wanderers, who at last reach in the tomb the goal of their journey.1) What is here so emphatically stressed for times of settled habitation holds a truth still more striking for peoples of a nomadic way of life. For them the tomb is the only fixed abode, life eternal movement, death rest. With good reason the Scythians answered the Persian king who demanded their submission: their wandering life meant that they would nowhere make a stand; the living had no fixed seats, only the dead. Should it occur to the king to approach these, then the army of the Scythians would already stand ready for battle and for the protection of the tombs. Herod. 4, 127. The same idea emerges movingly in the custom of erecting for the dead their æterna domus along the highways. It may itself stem from the times of nomadic life, as indeed the shepherds of the Tuscan Maremma to this day prepare the grave by the wayside for their traveling companions and mark the place of final rest by a heap of earth and stones. Thus the oldest cities may have grown up around burial places, just as later the streets of tombs formed the approach to the cities. The farther we ascend into those primeval times to which the artless Ocnus symbol belongs, the greater appears the agreement of the custom of life with that natural law which raises movement and eternal passing away to the principle of visible creation, and ascribes firmness, rest, and eternal duration to death alone. How well the ancients succeeded in giving reality to this idea in the layout of their tombs is shown by the continued existence of their necropolises, to which today we owe almost alone our knowledge of ancient life, which show it to us from its fairest side, and which will still arouse the loving sympathy of the most distant generations when the cheerless sobriety of Christian burial places has long since won no heart. The eternity that antiquity knew how to give to death sets the idea of transience, as it emerges so overwhelmingly from the Ocnus symbol, in still sharper relief. The whole effort seems directed at giving to that cry of anguish: ματαιότης τῶν ματαιοτήτων καὶ πάντα ματαιότης a most melancholy expression, and at proclaiming, in the place of the death that annihilates what is dearest, that lesson that too great an attachment is not fitting for man. Φεῦ φεῦ· βροτοῖς ἔρωτες ὡς κακὸν μέγα.2) [PDF 407] — 395 — 21. And yet this is not the last idea that called forth the admission of the Ocnus painting into the tombs of the ancients. Another, far higher, is joined with it. An antithesis rises before the soul that belongs to a wholly new order of ideas and contains wholly new considerations. It is the last part of my task to bring these to consciousness. In the account so far, only the original content of the Ocnus symbol has found elucidation. Its admission into the world of the tombs and the connection in which it appears here remained wholly out of consideration. This, however, has given the original religious idea a wholly new, unexpected turn. Ocnus appears in the ranks of the great penitents of Hades. Ixion, Tantalus, the Danaids are his companions. The terrors of the underworld surround him. He himself appears as their victim. Toil and torment that never end make up his lot and that of his companions. The sole thought that the sight of the picture arouses is punishment and penance on the bank of the groaning underground river of eternal suffering. To the original meaning, which we elucidated above, every such idea remains foreign. Of penance and torment no mention, nothing of the terrors of the underworld, no deed that might justify them. In the old man’s unwearied diligence there emerged rather a disposition kindly toward mortals and the nature of the life-generating, life-preserving Agathodaimon; indeed, in contrast to the Typhonian she-ass, the old man appeared as the embodiment of the good principle, which eternally disputes the victory with the demonic, annihilating one. A veritable abyss seems to separate the Acanthian rope plaiter from the penitent Ocnus of the Roman tombs. Far from failing to recognize this difference, we must rather establish it in all its sharpness. We stand before a phenomenon that is established as a mythological fact and that finds a wholly corresponding analogue in the development of the perforated vessel of the Danaids. The vessel of the Danaids, too, is a symbol of nature, which from the outset wholly lacks any relation to the underworld and to the idea of never-ending punishment. Native to the land of the Nile, and, like the Ocnus rope, still in Diodorus’s time the object of an actual cult act there, it symbolizes the constant fecundation of the great maternal womb of the earth, which so takes in the penetrating moisture that it vanishes fecundatingly within it, like the overflowing floods of the Nile in the black soil, like the waters in the Argive mount Pontinus.1) In the sieve of the Vestal, as in the act of Iphimedeia, αὐτὸ καταδέχεται. e: who walks daily to the seashore and pours Poseidon’s wave, yearning for the embrace of the beloved god, into her bosom, the same idea has put on another symbolic expression, as it were another garment.1) But beside the original natural meaning there now stands a second, an ethical one. The perforated vessel becomes the center of a myth wholly dominated by the idea of eternal punishment, and made to serve for an impressive depiction of the terrors of the underworld and of judgment in the beyond. In this turn of conception rope and vessel meet. Their fate is the same, and their correspondence all the more noteworthy because both have their home in Egypt, are still connected there in later times by local proximity, and preserve their kinship even in the funerary scenes. Beside the similarity in principle, there shows itself, on the other hand, a remarkable difference. With the perforated vessel the myth of the Danaids enters into connection, whereas every similar relation has remained foreign to the Ocnus rope. Through that coming together of symbol and myth in the vessel of the Danaids, the fact of a definite crime is laid at the foundation of the punishment, and the torment after death is thus justified by the bloody deed done in life: a supplement that is wholly lacking in the case of Ocnus. In the Danaid myth it now becomes possible for us to observe the course that the simple natural symbol followed in its transformation into the image of eternal punishment. The story of the Danaids falls into two halves. The one comprises the great drama of their struggle against the forced union with the sons of Aegyptus, which ends on the shore of Inachus with the bloody murder of the wedding night; the other, the judgment of punishment to which the maidens fall victim in the realm of the dead. The two components bear a wholly different character. The struggle and bloody deed of the Danaids belong to history, as indeed the fathers Danaus and Aegyptus are listed in the excerpts of the royal lists and exactly fixed as to time and descent.2) No less is the nature of the struggle that divided the two related lines wholly clear, and in full accord with the gynecocratic φυομένων.
