e: Amazonian nature of the daughters of Danaus. According to all versions of the legend, the right lies on the side of the fleeing maidens, who seek to escape the impiety, hateful to the gods, of their violent cousins. According to the principle of gynecocracy, the last and highest decision was theirs, theirs the dominion over themselves and over the man. When Hypermnestra spared her bridegroom, she thereby made herself guilty of a crime against her sex. With good reason she was brought to trial by her bloody sisters. For to uphold the right of woman against the violent cousins, and to atone for its breach in their blood, that was not only their right but their highest duty. From the standpoint of gynecocracy, which is established for the Nile valley, no one was blameworthy but the sparing Hypermnestra, who preferred to serve her heart rather than her right. The idea of punishment could not belong to this standpoint. To conceive the deed of the maidens in the light of crime required the destruction of the law and of the whole mode of conception of the oldest time. Only when this had been completed did abhorrence strike the wicked blood-deed of the husband-murdering women. Only now did Hypermnestra alone appear free of guilt, all the others monsters dripping with murder. The imposition of eternal penance in the realm of darkness thus rests on presuppositions that were fulfilled only in the course of time, and so the second mythic half of the story cannot be held to be as original as the historical event that underlies it. But the conception, too, of the nature of the punishment to which the Danaids fall victim is anything but arbitrary. On the contrary, there shows itself between it and the deed itself the most perfect agreement, and a correspondence that keeps the two halves of the whole story in harmony. In following the command of Amazonian gynecocracy, the Danaids broke the Aphroditean law that imposes on woman surrender and love of motherhood. Hypermnestra alone remained obedient to it, and therefore the goddess takes over her defense. In the splendid fragment of the Aeschylean Danaids (Herrmann Vol. 1, p. 320; compare Euripid. Hippol. 445–452; 1257–1271) that has been preserved for us in Athenaeus, Aphrodite stresses material union and generative embrace as her highest law and that of woman, and thereby gives most clearly to understand wherein she finds the guilt of the bloody sisters. This very natural law that was broken, however, has its representation in the perforated vessel, which again and again takes in the generative moisture; and so the myth, in assigning to the transgressors the work of drawing water, follows the principle that crime and punishment must correspond to each other. Bloody, man-hating Amazons [PDF 410] — 398 — now perform eternally the work that is the symbolic representation in nature of that sexual mingling which they impiously thrust from them. The cult act of Egypt, in connection with the memory of the Danaids’ misdeed, becomes the image of eternal punishment and never-ending torment. What was originally the expression of all the blessing of nature now appears turned into a curse. The perforated vessel, surrounded by the Danaids, becomes the instrument of never-ending torture in the dark spaces of the underworld; the idea of beneficent, ever-repeating fecundation is transformed into that insidious frustration of every effort. But with this transformation of the natural symbol into the expression of eternal punishment the development has not yet arrived at its final goal. The penance of the Danaids takes on a further meaning. It enters into connection with the mysteries, and now becomes the image of the tormenting lot that awaits all the uninitiated after death. The eternal damnation of the uninitiated is the last idea into which the labor at the perforated vessel is developed. The relation to the husband-murder of the maidens is given up. No single definite crime is set forth as the cause of the eternal torment. The vain, never-ending labor of the Danaids now appears as the lot of the uninitiated; the daughters of Danaus are the representatives of the uninitiated. This last development of the natural symbol gains still greater significance from the fact that it depicts the cheerless future of those who live and die without having received initiation in the image of the very maidens to whom the Greek people, according to Herodotus 2, 171, ties the first introduction of the Egyptian mysteries into Pelasgian Argolis. The daughters of Danaus, bearers and teachers of the holiest Cerealian initiations, now appear as the representatives of uninitiated, profane life. Above their image one read in the Lesche at Delphi the words τῶν οὐ μεμνημένων.1) In no myth do the most decisive contrasts lie so close beside one another as in theirs. Curse and blessing are joined. As both are recognized in the perforated vessel, so also in the water-drawing maidens. e: the mysteries he chooses as his portion the better hopes that they offer; for ill, if by scorning them he surrenders himself wholly to matter and to the law of matter, to passing away and to the eternal change of the sublunary world of becoming. The life of such a man is vain toil and sheer delusion, like drawing water into a perforated vessel; his future never-ending torment, such as the Danaids suffer. The initiate, by contrast, does not fall prey to the sad lot of a purely material life; his existence is not lost and not in vain, no drawing of water into a running sieve; for him death is the fulfillment of better hopes, the νέος θάνατος, the beginning of those nova salutis curricula that lead him across the boundaries of the material world of becoming into the immaterial, timeless world of being. Τέλος and τελετή coincide for him.1) The end of bodily life becomes the fulfillment of the hope that initiation gave. Out of the destruction of matter he presses through to communion with his god, as from the darkness of the egg the bird flies off on light wings toward the light. ἦμαρ γὰρ τόδε θανοῦσαν εἶδε καὶ βλέπουσαν παῖδα σήν.2) The relation of the Danaid vessel and its torment to the life of the uninitiated is turned by Socrates in the Gorgias, p. 493, to the following account: “Life is, even as you describe it, Callicles, nonetheless wearisome. I at least would not be surprised if Euripides3) were right where he says: come to knowledge (of the fate allotted to it), and then there takes place in it the change that those undergo who are initiated into the great mysteries. Hence it comes that the words τελευτᾶν and τελεῖσθαι, like the thing itself, are very similar to one another. The first thing that falls to our lot in this life is a wearisome and troublesome roaming about, a restless running through dark and dreadful ways. Even when we believe we have reached the end, all kinds of terrors still await us, anguish, trembling, sweat of death, and senseless stupor. But at last a wondrous light suddenly shimmers toward us. We now enter the most charming fields, where cheerful songs and dances reign everywhere, where eye and ear are enraptured by the holiest, most sublime objects. Here the perfected one, the initiate, freed from all bonds, wanders about in full freedom, celebrates the holy mysteries crowned with wreaths, enjoys the company of pious and just men, and looks down with pity on the uninitiated and unclean throng of those who still here on earth drive anxiously about in mire and mist, and, partly from fear of death, partly from distrust of the blessedness of the other world, persist in their wretched condition.” Plut. Dieß ist nun allerdings ziemlih wunderlich, es macht aber doH deutlich, was ich dich gerne, wenn ich es irgend zeigen könnte, überreden möchte zu wechseln, und anstatt des unersättlichen und ungebundenen Lebens das besonnene, und mit dem jedesmal Vorhandenen sich begnügende zu wählen.“ Daß hier das Leben der Eingeweihten und Profanen sich entgegengestellt wird, ist hinlänglich klar. e: Who knows whether our life is not only a death, and being dead, by contrast, life? and whether we are perhaps in truth dead. What I have also heard before from one of the wise, that we are now dead, and our bodies are only our tombs, but that the part of the soul in which the desires are is a constant inclining and repelling upward and downward, which a distinguished man who composes symbols, a Sicilian perhaps or an Italian, playing on the word, called a jar, because of its filling and its wanting to hold, and the unrestrained he called the shut out; and in these shut out ones the part of the soul where the desires are, precisely because of its unboundedness and lack of hold, could not close, like a leaky jar, to which he compared it on account of its insatiability. And in complete opposition to you, Callicles, this man shows that in the world of shades, by which he meant the world of spirits, those shut out ones would be the most wretched, and would carry water into the leaky jar with an equally leaky sieve. By the sieve, however, he understood, as he said who told it to me, the soul, and the soul of the unrestrained he compared to a sieve, because it is leaky and can hold nothing fast, from uncertainty and forgetfulness. This is, to be sure, rather strange, but it makes clear what I should like, if I could show it in any way, to persuade you to change: and instead of the insatiable and unbridled life, to choose the temperate one that contents itself with whatever is at hand.” That the life of the initiated and that of the profane are here set against each other is sufficiently clear. In this connection the leaky jar takes shape as the image of the soul of the profane, the world of shades to which it belongs as the realm of spirits, the whole symbol as a recommendation of that sanctification which was also impressed upon the mystae, as the highest commandment, by the call: ne intret nisi qui se innocentem noverit.1) Although Plato, then, calls the image of the leaky jar a strange one, which will hardly convince Callicles, one nevertheless recognizes that it did not originate in Socrates’ own invention but was offered to him by the mysteries,2) and thus linked up with familiar conceptions. Thereby it loses its strangeness, and the supporting word plays (ἀνόητος-ἀμύητος; πείθω, πιθανός-πίθος; ᾅδης-ἀειδής; σῶμα-σῆμα) lose everything offensive that would weigh upon them if the sole occasion of the comparison employed lay in them.

o: Wir haben uns bemüht, für das durchlöherte Faß die ganze Jdeenreihe darzulegen , welche das Natursymbol zum Träger der höchsten Mysterien-Jdeen emporhob. - Dem gleichen Gang der Entwicklung fiel auH das Seil der Panegyris von Acanthus anheim. Gleich den Danaiden wird Ocnus in die Unterwelt verwiesen. Gleich ihner nimmt er die Natur eines großen Büßers an. Hicr wie dort wird der Ausdr«.> des Seegens zum AusdruF des Fluchs, und wie für die Danaiden jeder Gedanke an ein besonderes Verbrechen verschwindet, so knüpft sich auH Ocnus Strafe und Pein an keine einzelne Unthat an. Neben den wasserschöpfenden Mädchen wird der seilflehtende Greis zur Darstellung des hoffnungslosen Lebens und der ebenso hoffnungslosen Zukunft derer, welche die Wohlthat der Mysterien von siH stoßen, und dem stofflichen Dasein allein anheimfallen. Das ist der höchste und lezte Gedanke, zu dem das Symbol des seilflehtenden Greises erhoben wurde, das auch derjenige, welcher seine Aufnahme in die Gräberwelt leitete, und dem Beschauer aus seinem Bilde entgegentrat. Nur der Mysteriengedanke bietet für die Stätte des Todes einen vollkommen befriedigenden Sinn. Für sich allein hat der Jnhalt des Natursymbols nur Trauer über den unabwendbaren Untergang aller Erdzeugung im Gefolge. Durch ihn wird der Schreckken des Todes noH erhöht, noh dichter die Finsterniß des Grabes, die nun kein Lichtstrahl besserer Hoffnung erhellt. Kann der Beschauer in dieser Jdee keine Ruhe finden, so wird ihn der Gedanke an eine mit dem Tode beginnende Ewigkeit voller Leiden und Pein noch mehr abschrefen. Wer in dem Campana'shen Grabe door jene Aedicula und die in ihr geborgenen Aschen-Urnen tritt, und dann auf dem Friese die Darstellung unterweltlicher Szenen, und alle Shrecken erblickt, mit welhen die Vorstellung des Alterthums den Ort des Gerichts ausstattet, der wird nothwendig zur Frage geführt, was denn wohl diejenigen, die hier die Asche geliebter Todten beiseßten, zur Wahl der trostlosesten aller Darstellungen vermocht haben mag. e: 22. We have endeavored to set forth, for the perforated vessel, the whole series of ideas that raised the natural symbol to be the bearer of the highest mystery ideas. The rope of the Panegyris of Acanthus fell victim to the same course of development. Like the Danaids, Ocnus is banished to the underworld. Like them, he takes on the nature of a great penitent. Here as there the expression of blessing becomes the expression of the curse, and as for the Danaids every thought of a particular crime vanishes, so too Ocnus’s punishment and torment attach to no single misdeed. Beside the water-drawing maidens the rope-plaiting old man becomes the representation of the hopeless life, and of the equally hopeless future, of those who thrust from them the benefit of the mysteries and fall prey to material existence alone. That is the highest and last idea to which the symbol of the rope-plaiting old man was raised, an idea that was also that of him who guided its admission into the world of the tombs, and that confronted the beholder out of its picture. Only the mystery idea offers a wholly satisfying meaning for the place of death. By itself the content of the natural symbol brings in its train only sorrow over the inescapable destruction of all earthly generation. Through it the terror of death is increased still more, the darkness of the tomb made denser still, which now no ray of better hope illumines. If the beholder can find no peace in this idea, the thought of an eternity of suffering and torment beginning with death will deter him still more. Whoever in the Campana tomb steps before that aedicula and the ash urns sheltered in it, and then sees on the frieze the representation of underworld scenes, and all the terrors with which the conception of antiquity furnishes the place of judgment, will necessarily be led to ask what can have induced those who deposited here the ashes of beloved dead to choose the most cheerless of all representations. Is the hell full of horror and terror that is here set before the eye to receive the departed as well? Is he to suffer eternal torment with the blood-dripping Danaids, to find with Ocnus neither peace nor rest? Is that the lot of which the children think when they visit the paternal burial place, whose dreadfulness is to be set vividly before their eyes at the annual sacrifice that love brings? But in that no human soul could at any time find its rest. That idea must be given a higher resolution. The terror of the underworld demands reconciliation, despair calming, discord a dissolving harmony. Where this lies, we have 26

e: already said. It is that higher mystery idea to which the representation of the underworld torments and terrors is subordinated. There is a deliverance from the hands of those dark powers who terrify mortals with never-ending pain. He who through the initiation of the mysteries chooses the god as his guide1) has won the victory over them not only on the stormy sea but also in death, like Heracles over the hound of Hades, Oedipus over the Sphinx, Orpheus over the Sirens, against whose death-bringing song he sings the saving song of his higher wisdom. Not what the dead man awaits, but what he has overcome, is what the Campana frieze shows. Τῶν μὴ μεμνημένων, that is the consoling explanation that must be read above Ocnus and above the heads of the Danaids. What is expressed in words in the Lesche at Delphi, the picture of the pediment represents in the tomb at the Porta Latina.2) Achilles, instructed by the wise Chiron in lyre playing, forms the higher member of that antithesis which, above the night side of the human lot, opens the view into the realm of light. With pleasure the eye rises from the penitents of the dark depth to the wise centaur and his pupil listening with satisfaction, to rest, after the sight of the terrors, on the picture of the hero who has pressed through to the enjoyment of the highest eternal bliss. If in the lyre the reference to Orpheus, the founder of all higher mystery wisdom, is not to be mistaken, as in the world of the tombs initiation received is often symbolically indicated by it alone, then Achilles’ attentive devotion to the instructing word of the wise teacher corresponds wholly to that principle of initiation already stressed above, which demands of the initiates a purely passive receptivity (παθεῖν), no examining and investigating activity of the spirit (μαθεῖν), and which recognizes in the childlike subordination of the one to be received under the higher wisdom of the mystagogue, raised to spiritual father through the conferring p. 408. e: of initiation,1) the first and indispensable condition of an initiation that brings blessing. (Above, p. 211, note 1.) No representation could bring this mystery idea before the soul with equal vividness and truth as that of the wise centaur and the seven-year-old Ligyron entrusted to him, to whom the artist knew how to lend the most eloquent expression of attentive devotion to the teacher’s instructing word. No representation, further, corresponds so exactly to that other fundamental idea of the mysteries, that immortality is bestowed not on matter but only on spirit. In vain did the mother strive to equip her offspring with that imperishability which she herself enjoys. She is unable to shield the bloom of the body against the inescapable lot of death. But by entrusting the boy to Chiron’s teaching (cf. Eurip. Suppl. 914–919) she attains on a higher plane what on the lower stage of material life is not possible even for the immortal mother. Instructed in all that benefits the heart by the holiest of men, the Philyrid, and above all enjoined always to be of simple custom,2) the son of Peleus overcomes the bitter lot of death that is allotted to him like the humblest product of perishable creation. If the mother, with the whole chorus of the Nereids, mourns the splendid youth’s early destruction, if the mothers all3) weep in him the most poignant expression of that inescapable transience to which everything falls victim that their womb bears, yet in Achilles’ fate it is set before their eyes that spiritual excellence, heedless of bodily perishability, is able to win eternal fame. Led by Chiron already as a boy to everything great, Thetis’s son acquires through the glory of his works that immortality which the anxious mother could not give to his body. On Leuke, united in eternal bliss with the fairest of women — he, the greatest of heroes — Achilles comes to share in all that he sought in vain on earth and could not win lastingly. “Blessed as ever a man was, I should have become, had I won your hand, daughter of Agamemnon.”4) This he owes to Chiron’s teaching, Apollon. 4, 812; 1, 558 with the Schol. e: which implanted in his soul what Thetis had falsely regarded as an inheritance of matter. Achilles sets before our eyes both sides of human existence in their most shattering contrast. To the excellent as to the most cowardly the same lot of death is allotted. Indeed, it snatches the noble away with double greed, as though Hades looked more covetously to the possession of the good than of the bad. But over spiritual sublimity death has no power. “For brave men are not hateful to the gods, and only the lot of the ignoble is endless woe.”1) Never-ending bliss of a higher, blessed existence is allotted to virtue after the destruction of the body. Thus Achilles is man’s consolation and model at once. He resolves the mother’s grief over the annihilation of matter into joy over the spirit that, through the excellence of its striving, has pressed through to the enjoyment of eternal bliss.2) If Peleus, the swamp man, begot the boy with Thetis, the mother of moist matter, as perishable as rushes and frogs, those Peleids of the muddy shallows,3) then Chiron, his spiritual father, has prepared for him the way to Apollonian luminous nature, in which he, risen out of the material world of becoming, associates himself with the timeless world of being.4) For Achilles shares in Apollonian nature. In Apollo’s Delphic sanctuary he has found admission. There he rests, united with the god,5) to whose luminous nature he aspired in life, and his descendant too presides protectingly over the holy place.6) Chiron’s wisdom is Apollo’s gift, his lyre Apollo’s instrument, whose soothing, beautiful harmony has carried off the victory over the shrill tones of the tellurian reed pipe.7) In this eternally serene, Apollonian luminous nature Bacchus’s related yet more material Creuzer, Commentt. Jegt ist die Bedeutung der Darstellung im Giebelfelde des römishen Grabes, und ihr Verhältniß zu jener auf dem tieferliegenden Friese in der ganzen Fülle und Shönheit dargestellt. Ergreifend erscheint der Gegensaß durch seine Einfachheit und Tiefe. Unten des Acheron schilferfüllter dunkler Abgrund , oben des Lichtreichs ewige Klarheit. Dort der Gedanke von Tod und Untergang, hier der des Lebens. Dort Buße und Pein, hier die Aussiht auf den Lohn eines seeligen Daseins. Unten zweloses Leben und vergeblihe Mühe, oben höheres Streben mit der Aussicht auf den schönsten Lohn. Unten der Tellurismus mit all seinen Schreken, oben apollinische Lichthöhe mit all ihrer beruhigenden Klarheit. Was des Tartarus Schrecken überwindet, stellt Chirons apollinische Cithara dar. Haben wir dort der ungeweihten, rein stofflichem Leben hingegebenen Menschen hoffnungslose Zukunft erblickt, so lehrt der weiser Lehre horhende Achill, was den Tod mit bessern Hoffnungen zu umgeben und der tellurischen Gewalten finstere Macht zu brechen vermag. Den Büßern tritt Chiron als die höhere Lösung gegensäßlich zur Seite, wie in dem Pamfilishen Grabe Niobe's Schmerz mit Prometheus Errettung in Parallele geseßt wird. ') Der Duldenden Schmetzenstöne haben in den harmonischen Klängen der himmlischen Lyra ihre Auflösung gefunden. Jn der Darstellung des Hades und seiner Qualen erkennen wir nun die Absicht, die Wohlthat der Weihen nachdrücklich vor Augen zu steslen, und die so of wiederholte Lehre der Alten von ihrem Seegen bildlich zu vergegenwärtigen. Der Anblick so vieler hoffnungslos Büßender soll die Wahl des höhern Lebens, wie es die Mysterien verlangen, als das bessere Theil empfehlen. Jn dieser Absicht wurden die Qualen des Tartarus von den Alten nicht seltener dargestellt, als in dem heutigen Jtalien die Feuerpein der Verdammten. *)
e: being has also climbed to its highest stage of purity, as in the wise Chiron the Dionysian centaur puts on perfected Apollonian luminous nature. Now the meaning of the representation in the pediment of the Roman tomb, and its relation to that on the lower-lying frieze, is presented in all its fullness and beauty. The antithesis appears moving through its simplicity and depth. Below, the dark abyss of Acheron filled with reeds; above, the eternal clarity of the realm of light. There the idea of death and destruction, here that of life. There penance and torment, here the prospect of the reward of a blessed existence. Below, purposeless life and vain toil; above, higher striving with the prospect of the fairest reward. Below, tellurism with all its terrors; above, the Apollonian height of light with all its calming clarity. What overcomes the terrors of Tartarus is represented by Chiron’s Apollonian cithara. If we beheld there the hopeless future of uninitiated human beings given over to a purely material life, then Achilles, listening to the instruction of the wise teacher, shows what is able to surround death with better hopes and to break the dark power of the tellurian forces. Chiron stands beside the penitents as the higher resolution, in contrast to them, just as in the Pamphili tomb Niobe’s grief is set in parallel with the deliverance of Prometheus.1) The tones of anguish of those who suffer have found their resolution in the harmonious sounds of the heavenly lyre. In the representation of Hades and its torments we recognize, then, the intention of setting the benefit of the initiations emphatically before the eyes, and of making visible in a picture the so often repeated doctrine of the ancients about their blessing. The sight of so many hopelessly penitent souls is meant to recommend the choice of the higher life, as the mysteries demand it, as the better portion. With this intention the torments of Tartarus were depicted by the ancients no less frequently than the fire-torment of the damned is in Italy today.2) duced in O. Jahn, no. 3, 6. See Brunn, Rhein. Mus. New Series, p. 345 f. c. Aristog. 52, p. 786. Ovid. M. 4, 448. For the proper understanding of such scenes, what Plutarch says in the beautiful letter of consolation to his wife on the death of her child 10 (Hutt. 10, p. 397) is very important: “As to that opinion which some seek to spread everywhere, that for the departed there is nowhere any longer any evil or hardship, I know for certain that neither the ancient doctrine of our fathers nor the holy practices in the Bacchic mysteries, which are known to us both as initiates, will permit you to accept it as true.” Stobæus 3, 90 Meineke.

Achill hat ganz die Prometheus-Natur. Er trug bei den Alten auch selbst diesen Namen. s) Und er ist Prometheus nicht nur seiner physischen Grundlage nachH, nicht nur als Träger der vereinigten Feuer- und Wasserkraft , in welcher er als leuchtender Blikstrahl den feuchten Aether zertheilt, zu Erzarbeit und zu der euböischen Chalcis in die nächste Beziehung tritt, und in dem cretishen Namen Pemptus den idäischen Dactylen-Corybanten sich anreiht zs) er ist es auch in geistiger Beziehung, als der kühne Träger des geistigen Funkens, welhen er durch alle Kämpfe des Lebens hindurh zu erhalten weiß, und den er durch sein unermüdetes Ringen und Dulden zulezt zum Siege führt. Dadurch ist er gleich Heracles zum geistigen Erlöser des Menschengeschlehtes geworden und höher gestiegen als Chiron selbst, der von dem vergifteten Pfeile am Fuße getroffen, an Heracles Statt, wie Menoikeus für die Kadmeer- Erehthiden , dem siegreih überwundenen Tellurismus als letztes großes Opfer fällt. Au über den Vater Peleus hat er sich erhoben.
e: Tales of terror avail To exalt the glory of the heavenly ones; forgetting them, you Slay your husband, co-begetter of noble children.1) Not without struggle is the palm granted to man. Initiation alone does not lead him to participation in the changeless existence of the heavenly ones. Should the thief Pataecion be dearer to the immortals because he was initiated than Epaminondas, the uninitiated?2) Achilles shows in what way this question was answered by the ancients. Only through the excellence of his life does he press through to that bliss which is prepared for him on the sea-washed, shining lunar island in eternal spring. For since it had been prophesied to the son of Peleus that if he slew Hector he would die, but if not, would reach old age at the hearth of his home, he chose the former, and preferred not only to avenge Patroclus but to die after the dying man.3) Chiron’s teachings are the commandments that everyone must fulfill, Achilles’ example that which everyone must imitate. Promethean suffering must be steadfastly endured if the much-tried man is at last to find admission with Heracles into the company of the immortals. “Great, and by no means slight, is the struggle whether one becomes good or bad; all guilt is the chooser’s, god himself guiltless.”4) Achilles has wholly the Promethean nature. Among the ancients he even bore this name itself.5) And he is Prometheus not only according to his physical foundation, not only as the bearer of the united force of fire and water, in which, as a shining lightning flash, he cleaves the moist aether, enters into the closest relation to bronzework and to Euboean Chalcis, and in the Cretan name Pemptus ranges himself with the Idaean Dactyl-Corybantes;6) he is so also in the spiritual relation, as the bold bearer of the spiritual spark, which he knows how to preserve through all the struggles of life, and which through his untiring wrestling and enduring he at last leads to victory. Thereby he has become, like Heracles, the spiritual redeemer of the human race and has risen higher than Chiron himself, who, struck on the foot by the poisoned arrow, falls in Heracles’ stead, as Menoeceus for the Cadmean-Erechthid line, as the last great sacrifice to the victoriously overcome tellurism. Over his father Peleus, too, he has raised himself. Ἄσπετος, Hesych. s. v. Pyrisoos: Muralt no. 8, p. 32.

Thus an ascent from matter to the immaterial, from the φύσις ἐν γενέσει (10, 3) to the world of immaterial being, which 5, 18 at the end is compared to a ladder. Jamblich 8, 5 brings it out with particular [PDF 420] — 408 — ever greater perfection of the created, the creative principle too comes to revelation in ever-growing beauty. Like that stepped pyramid joined to so many funerary monuments, the religious development of our race builds itself up on the broad base of the purely material conception in such a way that, in gradual elevation out of matter, it strives ever more heavenward. Tellurism with its materiality yields to the higher solar principle, the chthonian conception of force to the recognition of its uranian nature. Above the Poseidonian-Plutonian rises the Apollonian principle of light. Over against this, the former appears not only as a more impure and lower stage of divinity; it also often takes on the meaning of a demonic power hostile to man, which can be turned again to blessing for the mortal only through its subordination under the new, higher law of light. Thus the bloody law of the Erinyes has yielded to Apollo’s atoning divinity and in the end been reconciled. Tellurism with all its dark violence has bowed before the higher heavenly law of light of the Pythian, and subordinated its older claims to those of the new god. In a similar position Ocnus, too, and the Danaids, and everything that belongs to the tellurism of the draconteum genus, fall back. If all these figures banish the generative force of nature into the dark depths of the moist matter of the earth, then above them Apollo rises in the purer incorporeality of heavenly light. Over against him those appear as conquered powers, whose Delphic connection is destined to glorify the power and glory of the victorious god. To Apollo are traced back Oedipus and the destruction of the Sphinx completed through him, and likewise the overcoming of the dark, hopeless existence of the dragon seed. Through him Orestes escapes the pursuit of the Erinyes, and the law of fatherhood is led to victory over the bloody one of the maternal earth law. To his sanctuary, as to that of the Gaditan Heracles, woman may not approach. With his principle of light the predominance of maternal matter is incompatible. If the Danaids nevertheless find admission into the Delphic Lesche, they are meant here to set off still more brilliantly the benefit of the Apollonian nature, which brought destruction to that dark time of hopeless tellurism. The same idea is joined with all those pictures which Polygnotus emphasis that the Egyptian religion indeed has a physical foundation, but that it was the effort of the priests to lead from it to the immaterial divinity, as fire always flames upward toward heaven. 5, 11, 12. p. 214–216. The contrast of heavenly being and of tellurian becoming, caught in constant flux, is developed very beautifully 10, 5, p. 291, the ψυχῆς κάθαρσις as the last goal of religion 10, 7, p. 293.

e: transferred from the Greek world of Hades into the Delphic hall. Above them the beneficent, purer nature of the Pythian god shines forth all the brighter. Ocnus and the she-ass take up over against him the same position that is assigned to them in the Roman tomb by their subordination to Chiron’s lyre playing. The sight of them shows the victorious power of the Pythian, who rescued the human race from the cheerlessness of earlier views, such as the Sphinx represents and Silenus laments, and raised its gaze from the figures of suffering in subterranean spaces to the calm clarity of his eternally youthful, changeless heavenly being.1) In connection with Ocnus the ass, too, now appears as an animal hateful to the god of light and banished to Hades. Formerly the joy and delight of the Hyperborean, it is now little agreeable to the purer nature to which the Delphian has risen. Belonging wholly to the phallic nature of tellurian matter and bearing within it its unregulated sensual lust, the ass now represents the nature of impure matter, hostile to Apollonian purity. It is the negation of everything that initiation gives and demands of man. With this significance it forms the center of the mystery tale presented by Apuleius. It appears here as the embodiment of the purely sensual life, of all the errors and sufferings into which that life leads. With the reception of the initiations the animal form vanishes. Risen from the chrysalis of matter, man recognizes his beauty and the conditions of an untroubled happiness. To the nature of the ass the initiations form so deep a contrast that the proverb Asinus mysteria vehens can represent, in this sense too, the incompatibility of the two things.2) 24. If we have thus recognized in the picture of the Delphic Lesche the same idea that dominates the contrast of the penitent Ocnus and the Apollonian Achilles on the aedicula of the Roman tomb, then it will now be an easy task to appreciate, in its occasion and significance, the particular turn that the artist of the Pamphili columbarium gave to the representation of Ocnus. In the departure from the other representations, as writers and monuments alike show them to us, lies the particular interest of the painting communicated on our Plate 2. e: that it lends the old man. Given up here is that labor of rope plaiting which we found to be the most essential feature of the Ocnus representation. The deep rest to which the old man abandons himself brings out quite deliberately the contrast with the traditional conception. It has received in the reclining posture of the animal a no less conscious continuation. Vanished from the surroundings are all those penitents of the underworld who lead the beholder into the terrors of Hades. As Ocnus himself by his inactivity excludes every thought of torment and punishment, so too the landscape, in whose midst he has settled down, breathes only rest and peace. The stillness of the evening seems to have lured the old man out before his farmstead. Here he rests from the labor of the day, and grants the animal, which shared his rural toils, the play with the rope. Thus the Delphic model is wholly given up, and everything deliberately turned to its opposite. What idea could have determined the painter to this procedure? It would be impossible to find any explanation or justification for it if we were to take our departure from the natural-symbolic meaning of the Ocnus picture. For this, the act of rope plaiting is so indispensable that rather everything else could be given up, if only it found its expression. Thereby we are compelled to betake ourselves to an entirely different field of explanation, and to bear in mind the meaning that Ocnus assumed in relation to the mysteries. Now everything receives a satisfying solution. The idea of the Pamphili picture appears in all its beauty. By the simplest means a turn of ideas is brought forth such as would be unattainable for written expression in equal brevity and concise clarity. Out of the penitent Ocnus the liberated Ocnus has come. Where the idea of punishment and eternal torment reigned, rest steps forth, and an equally eternal peace. If the former is the lot of the uninitiated, the latter forms the hope of the initiated. Both parts of the great contrast lie here united in one representation, whereas the picture of the Campana tomb brings them to representation separately. The resting Ocnus arouses at one stroke two ideas: that of the lot of the uninitiated, and that of the liberation which initiation brings. The curse of profane life and the blessing of the life consecrated to god is the double language of a single pictorial expression. In this turn the identification of the deceased with the image of Ocnus has its occasion and its justification. The bearded old man shows us the initiate himself. The figure has the same double reference as the whole representation. It calls before the soul at once the mythological Ocnus and the owner, nameless to us, of that farmstead which he left in dying, and sets before the eyes, for the former, the final liberation from his torment, for the latter the [PDF 423] — 411 — beginning of eternal rest, for both the victorious force of the higher mystery powers that overcome the terrors of death. That is the last form that the natural symbol of the rope-plaiting old man has assumed. From a representation of tellurian life, and of the law that governs it, it has at last become the symbol of the highest stage of human existence. At first wholly restricted to the material cycle, it now leads the gaze beyond its limits into the realm of the life that begins with bodily destruction. At first the expression of the world of becoming, it is now the image of the world of being. At first akin to the idea of transience, it now shows the hope of a changeless future, which may calmly and indifferently leave the coarse tissue of the body to the gnawing she-ass. With religion itself Ocnus has risen from the dark swamp depths into the heights of light. He designates the lowest and the highest that the earth offers, the whole weakness and the whole greatness of the perishable creature, man’s subjection to the law of death and his sublimity above it. The higher existence prevails. Two worlds stand side by side, a sensual and a supersensible. Foolish it would be, as Aristotle expresses it in the Metaphysics, to sacrifice the latter to the former. For all is affliction on earth And we find no rest from our sufferings. Whatever is sweeter than this life, that conceals Enveloping night from the gaze of mortals. We love only this with such ardent longing, Because here on earth it shines upon us, And the other no one ever explored.1) If in this way the two poles between which the riddle of all earthly existence moves come into immediate contact, then the distances in time and space too seem wholly removed. The Ocnus symbol, native to the land of the Nile, returns at Delphi and in Roman tombs, and while its origin is shrouded in the darkness of primeval states, it accompanies the ancient peoples down to those times to which, on the lonely high seas, the destruction of the great Pan was proclaimed,2) and above the hut the new star appeared. subject because the Echinades, those swamp islands of Alcmaeon, the Egyptian Thamus, and the reference to Pan, the son of Penelope, contain a clear pointer to the lowest stage of materiality and to the old tellurism with its dark side of death. Tiberius had the event investigated. It falls, then, in the time when the new light appeared, and attests in any case how deeply the conviction of the decay of the old religion, and of the beginning of a new age of the world, was rooted.

o: Das ist es, was der antiken Gräberwelt eine so hohe Bedeutung leiht und ihre Betrachtung nach allen Seiten hin so fruchtbringend macht, daß in ihr die innere Einheit der alten Gedankenwelt schlagender und greifbarer als ander8wo hervortritt, und eilende Jahrhunderte ihre umgestaltende Macht niht durchzuführen vermögen. Unwandelbar wie der Tod ist die Grabeswelt. An ihr geht jede Neuerung spurlos vorüber. Die ältesten Symbole und Anschauungen der Menschheit finden hier ihre lezte aber sichere Zufluchtsöstätte. Eine Fülle geistiger Shäte liegt in den Nefropolen verborgen. Die Erde bietet wieder, was sie vor Tausenden von Jahren empfieng. Noch ist das Meiste unverständlih, das Studium der alten Gräberwelt überhaupt kaum in den Kreis unserer Forschung eingeführt. Wenn die vorliegenden Versuche auchg nur eine Ahnung von ihrer Wichtigkeit und Bedeutung zu erwecken vermochten, so werden Überraschende Erfolge nicht lange mehr auf sich warten lassen, die Grabfunde unsers Jahrhunderts in ihrem wahren Werth erkannt werden, und Sigalion wie der stumme Crösussohn endlich seine Sprache finden,
e: That is what lends the ancient world of the tombs so high a significance and makes its contemplation so fruitful on every side: that in it the inner unity of the ancient world of thought emerges more strikingly and tangibly than elsewhere, and hastening centuries are unable to carry through their transforming power. Unchanging as death is the world of the tomb. Every innovation passes it by without a trace. The oldest symbols and conceptions of mankind find here their last but secure place of refuge. A wealth of spiritual treasures lies hidden in the necropolises. The earth gives back what it received thousands of years ago. Most of it is still unintelligible; the study of the ancient world of the tombs has hardly been introduced at all into the circle of our research. If the present attempts have been able to awaken even only an intimation of its importance and significance, then surprising successes will not be long in coming, the tomb finds of our century will be recognized in their true value, and Sigalion, like the mute son of Croesus, will at last find his speech.

e: The recently published catalogue of the Museo Campana furnishes some important contributions to the points discussed especially in our first treatise. A belated mention of them forms the main content of this Appendix. The color combination of white and black, like that of white and purple-red, whose meaning and relation to the Bacchic divine nature we have explained, appears on a larger number of funerary vases of decidedly Dionysian relation. I call attention to a few. Classe I, serie quarta, vassellame dipinto, n. 335 shows as its main scene Bacchus and a satyr. Tutto il fondo è coronato di tralci di vite con grappoli. Nel collo è un frigio di edera con corimbi e nell’ orlo sono alternati i colori nero e giallo. — No. 391: Il collo ha un frigio di edera e la parte superiore di esso è ornata di dadi alternati gialli e neri. Cf. further 396, 400. — Classe I, serie 9, 10. Sala G. 55. — No. 302 of the same section shows, beside the Bacchic eyes, a wreath of alternating white and black color. Cf. besides Noël des Vergers on the recently discovered tomb paintings of Vulci, Bulletino 1857, p. 117. — White and purple-red are shown by the following monuments: No. 407: Piccoli globi di color purpureo e bianco. — Cl. I, ser. 9, Sala H, 273: corona formata di una larga tenia a color bianco e purpureo. Particular attention is deserved by the terracottas described in Classe VI pitture etrusche grecche e romane, which adorned the walls of a Caeretan tomb and in many details recall Asiatic customs, usages, and practices. Many will be grateful to me if I communicate here, in its whole extent, the description of at least one of the numerous pictures. La prima d’esse dipinture, secondo l’ordine in che trovansi collocate, rappresenta un uomo barbato coi capelli sparsi e coperto di corta tunica, assiso sopra una sedia plicatile, tenendo nella sinistra mano uno scettro. Innanzi a lui vedesi elevato un alto imbasamento formato di grandi massi e diviso in due piani, in cima a cui sta una Dea colle braccia aperte, con bianca sottoveste e manto purpureo, l’una e l’altro molto aderenti alla persona per via d’una cintura che la cinge ai fianchi. Il capo è coperto da tiara [PDF 426] — 414 — assira, i capelli sono disciolti; ed ai piedi dell’ara o suggesto di tale divinità è dipinto un serpente. Nei lembi della veste dell’uomo scorgonsi ornamenti vari son le tinte del vestiario e degli accessori; ma le carni sono dipinte di un rosso tendente al fosco. Sotto la linea poi della parte figurata di questo quadro è rappresentata una grande scacchiera distinta dai colori bianco e rosso, mentre nella parte superiore ricorre un meandro a guisa d’una greca. I quali accessori, cioè di cotali scachiere ovvero di lunghe liste o zone avvicendate di bianco e di rosso, appariscono anche nell’imbasamento degli altri quadri, coronati presso che tutti da una grande cornice a rilievo, le cui membrature sono dipinte con ornati, in cui si alternano i colori bianco, rosso, nero ed azzurro. The same change of color is also transferred to the egg ornament. Classe I, serie 9, Sala G. No. 70, shows a mantle figure provided with a burning torch and cymbals; the female figure carries a mirror and a casket. Al esterno mezzi ovoli alternati di color bianco e purpureo. Cf. further no. 340, 356, 420, 445. Sala J. 204. Sala L. 1, 3, 6, 8, 15, 17, 18, 19. — The combination of purple and white emerges with particular significance in the Persian royal regalia, Curtius, 3, 8. The further testimonies are collected by Brissonius, de regio Persarum principatu s. v. Tiara and Kandys. Thereby we are led back to the time of the oldest Assyrian monarchy. Cf. Herod. 1, 98. — Besides the color combinations named, that of black and purple-red is also found not infrequently. Classe I, ser. 3, Vasi Etruschi 145: Il corpo è ornato di scanalature ad arco rilevate e dipinte nel fondo a color nero e purpureo. — Ser. 9, Sala G. 353: Corona di edera a color nero e purpureo. In this opposition purple-red takes on the significance of life and divinity, as black belongs to death and to the idea of transience. Lucian, veræ hist. 3, 12. For the combination of white and purple-red a new conception results from this. It shows in its two components the idea of apotheosis, and is thereby preeminently suited to indicate the divine nature with which Asia clothed its kings. The antithesis then lies in the degree of purity of the two colors. If red bears the materiality of the sun as a generative natural potency, then in the white color the principle of light appears in its highest purity and complete immateriality. We can call the former the Dionysian, the latter the Apollonian stage of the luminous nature. Nothing stands in the way of attributing the same meaning to the red-and-white double color of the Bacchic egg. The antithesis of a higher and a lower stage of being, which we emphasized above, p. 294 f., as the fundamental meaning of that color combination, remains in this conception too wholly [PDF 427] — 415 — preserved. Beside black, red appears as the higher, beside white as the lower side of existence and of force. — Unquestionable depictions of eggs are not communicated in the Museo Campana. Nevertheless, on closer examination nos. 43, 86 of Classe I, ser. 9. Sala K. may prove to be such. No less Sala L, 46. Anfora. In the midst of this scene the egg of the Bacchic mysteries alone is conceivable. On the Egyptian egg see further Parthey on Plut. Is. et Os. 32, p. 224. Above, p. 128. — Finally the significant and especially frequent emergence of the number five deserves attention. Thus we meet five warriors, five dancing figures, five horses’ heads, five Ionic columns, five winged sphinxes, five flowers, and objects of various kinds too are combined with one another in the number five. For the application of the Pentas, moreover, Alexandria quinquevertex is significant. The city of the united cult of Sarapis and Isis (Arr. 3, 1.) is the city of five hills, as Rome is septemplex. Above, p. 281. Jul. Val. Res gestæ Al. M. 1, 18. 29. To the five hills correspond the first five letters of the alphabet, which bear the walls of the newly founded city and its five quarters (Philo in Flaccum ed. Mangey T. 2, p. 525), and to which later writers gave the interpretation: Ἀλέξανδρος Βασιλεὺς Γένος Διὸς Ἐποίησεν (Ἔκτισεν). Here we have again the E of Delphi as the highest number, and this agrees with the Pythian oracle, which calls the god of Sinope Apollo- Father. Tacit. Ann. 4, 83. 84. It is the Hyperborean god in whose stations the Pontus city is also listed. His phallic nature is matched by the Dionysian Pentas, not by the perfect seven of uranian-spiritual nature. — With the number five Alexander’s ἑτεροφθαλμία, corresponding to the ἑτερημερία of the Dioscuri, whom Alexander also especially venerated (Itinerar Al. 90), stands in connection. Pseudo-Callisth. 1, 13 with Müller’s n. 10. Tzetz. hist. 11, p. 268. — At Alexandria the serpent cult occupies a prominent place. Jul. Valerius or his source, which bears on its brow the mysterious name of Callisthenes, famous for his learning no less than for his unhappy death, contains on this a statement which casts new light on the feeding of serpents discussed above, pp. 131, 140. On the myrtle wreath in the mysteries Tzetzes on Cass. v. 1328, p. 1006 Müller. — Wieseler treats the Delphic omphalos in the Ann. dell’ Instit. 1857, p. 160–180. This essay gives me occasion for some remarks. The omphalos is referred in it to Hestia and called the symbol of this deity. Two concessions lie in this. First, the Delphic omphalos is detached from Apollo, and moreover the female connection with the material primal motherhood is substituted for the male bond with the θεὸς πατρῷος. These two propositions agree completely with the conception carried out above, pp. 106–108. The divergence of our views begins only with the further question, in what personification we are to conceive that motherhood? W. decides for Hestia, the above consideration for Themis- Gaea; to the latter opinion I still hold fast. It is supported by various circumstances already indicated by Ulrichs, Reisen und Forschungen in Griechenland, pp. 78, 93. Orestes’ atonement at the omphalos, over which the blood of the piglet runs off, shows that the latter belongs to the earth, for through the matricide the earth is violated, hence the atonement and consequently the omphalus can apply only to the earth. Further, it is said in Euripides, Ion 5, Plato, Republic 4, 5, that, seated on the omphalos, Apollo proclaims his oracles; since now, according to Aeschylus’s Eumenides, the oracle passed from Themis-Gaea to the male god, the conclusion is inescapable that the Apollonian omphalos must originally have belonged to the great mother Themis-Gaea, and not to Hestia. Third, the expression Γῆς ὀμφαλός is entirely constant, as the passages in Ulrichs, p. 93, n. 61 show, Ἑστίας ὀμφαλός without example, although Hestia’s connection with Delphi cannot be denied, but is rather as firmly established for the Pythian sanctuary as for any other whatever. Hymn. Hom. in Vest. et Mercur. 1. 3. Γῆς ὀμφαλός is, to be sure, finally used as a designation of the center of the earth. But this meaning presupposes an older one, from which it was derived. In the original sense Γῆς ὀμφαλός designated the cult image of Mother Earth. From this the idea of the center of the earth develops in the following way. In motherhood lies the generative significance. The female κτείς belongs in this sense to the symbols of the Themis mysteries. But the generative forms the center, and takes this place locally as well. Varro. L. L. 7, p. 303 Spengel: Neque hic locus est terrarum medius, neque noster umbilicus est hominis medius. Itaque pingitur qui vocatur ἡ χθὼν Πυθαγόρα, ut media cœli ac terræ linea ducatur infra umbilicum per id quo discernitur, homo mas an femina sit, ubi ortus humanus similis ut in mundo; ubi enim omnia nascuntur in medio, quod terra mundi [PDF 431] — 419 — media. For the same reason the mundus lies in the center of a newly founded city. It is therefore the maternal κτείς that lends the omphalos the significance of the center of the earth. In consequence of this the Aphroditean omphalos at Paphos too becomes the center of the earth. Hesych. Γῆς ὀμφαλός. Cf. Tacit. H. 2, 3. Serv. Aen. 1, 724. Themis-Gaea as well as Aphrodite have the earth as their material foundation. Their κτείς appears accordingly as the center of the whole surface of the earth, and hence the omphalos erected to the γυναικεῖον μόριον appears as μεσόμφαλος γῆς. In the face of these phenomena the connection of the Delphic omphalos with Themis-Gaea, the original oracle mother, can admit of no doubt. But the egg form too, which is so wholly certain on the Ruvo vase painting, now appears fully justified. To the birth-giving μόριον γυναικεῖον nothing corresponds so perfectly as the egg, which can be designated not only as uterus expositus, but lets birth issue from itself just as the tellurian organisms spring from the womb of the earth. Since now the maternal womb of the earth not only cherishes birth and sends it to the light, but finally takes it back again into itself, and through the cooperation of both activities keeps generation eternally young, the egg must unite in itself the same double significance of giving and taking, of life and death. In fact the Delphic stone is regarded as the burial place of the dragon Pytho. The omphalos itself is held to be his μνῆμα, as Pythonos βουνός or tumulus. Hesych. Τοξίου βουνός. Varro L. L. 7, p. 303. Sp. Alexandria too, the urbs quinquevertex, has its Draconis sepulcrum or heroon, to which the omphalos form may be ascribed all the more surely since Zeus Ammonius, the Alexander-father, possessed an omphalos especially venerated by the matrons. Curtius 4, 31. Strabo 6, 1, 1. In the connection of the dragon Pytho with the omphalos there shows itself again that union of serpent and egg which we have demonstrated in a larger number of cases. To the examples named on p. 131 ff. others may still be added. An Etruscan tomb relief in Raoul-Rochette, monum. inédits pl. 26, fig. 2 shows, set up on the altar, the egg girdled by the serpent, in the same form in which we found it on the coin in Lajard, culte de Vénus pl. 14. H, 11. The sacrifice of Iphigenia, which forms the subject of the whole representation, leaves no doubt that the serpent egg was here conceived in the same relation to Artemis as the Delphic one to Themis-Gaea, others to a Cerealian Fortuna and to Hygieia. Set up in a sacred shrine the ovum anguinum appears again on a second Etruscan ash chest in Gori, Mus. Etrusc. 1, tav. 170. Müller, Archeol. § 361, 5, to which Wieseler, p. 167 adds as a third example a sarcophagus in [PDF 432] — 420 — Wicar, tableaux statues etc. de la gallerie de Florence et du palais Pitti T. 4, pl. 11. On the walls of Pompeian houses Mercury is joined with the serpent-entwined half-egg. Avellino, bulletino Napoletano, serie antica 1, p. 11. On others we see it surrounded by the two Lares, as at Delphi by the two eagles (Museo Borbon. T. 9, tav. 20), on the denarii of the gens Eppia and Rubria by a double herm. Eckhel, Doctr. T. 5, p. 296. Wieseler, p. 168. It is the dualism of force according to its creative and its destructive, its light and its night side that occasions and governs the connection of these double figures with the maternal omphalos. Thus Leda’s sons issue from the mother egg in the number two, as two dragons too appear as serpent guardians. In face of this fundamental idea the personal identification of the mother goddess to whom the serpent-girdled omphalos of the Pompeian wall paintings cited belongs is of only secondary importance. Besides Vesta, other rival claimants can be thought of (above, p. 149), if we do not prefer to attribute to the symbol an independent validity. If the maternal relation of the Delphic omphalos is indisputable, its elevation to Apollonian significance must not on that account be denied. In the transfer of the oracle from Themis-Gaea to the paternal god there is revealed the progress from the principate of the maternal-material principle to that of the male principle of light. The former appears as a surmounted stage of religion, which finds recognition only in a subordinate position. Above the tellurism of the omphalos there now rises up the founder of a higher law, the power of light Apollo. His power derives from the highest Zeus (Aen. 3, 251. Serv. Aen. 1, 24. Aesch. Eum. 19. Soph. Oed. R. 151), not from the primal mother Themis, although he too in body sprang from woman and is significantly reminded of this his maternal origin by the Erinyes in Aeschylus. Hence the omphalos appears at times beneath the feet of the god. Müller, Archeol. § 361. 5. But in union with Apollo it now itself passes over into Apollonian nature. The mark of the primal mother Earth becomes the attribute of the male god, like the Ammonian omphalos of Zeus. The originally maternal relation of the Delphic cult stone is not the only one. If Wieseler presents it in the light of such exclusiveness, he is no less in error than those who, over the paternal connection with Apollo and Zeus, leave the maternal one with the earth out of consideration. Only by virtue of its Apollonian nature can the omphalos grant the matricide Orestes protection against the pursuit of the Erinyes. The female connection of the egg recedes here wholly into the background. Lifted out of the law of the earth, it is now clothed with Apollonian luminous nature, the eagle pair [PDF 433] — 421 — itself receives a higher Jovian relation. Schol. Pind. Pyth. 4, 6. Schol. Soph. Oed. R. 475. Schol. Eurip. Or. 330. Schol. Luc. Saltat. 38. In this elevation the omphalos is no longer the material primal egg that gives birth to all births into the world of becoming, but that which mediates the passage out of this into that of being. It cannot be mistaken that on the two Etruscan tomb reliefs this latter higher relation has been attributed to the serpent-entwined egg. Iphigenia’s sacrifice, as a sarcophagus picture, can have no other meaning than to serve as pictorial expression for those higher mystery hopes which open to the initiate after death the prospect of nova salutis curricula. One day sees the maiden die and gaze out toward the light. Mourned as lost by her mother, she has yet, saved, penetrated to a higher union. Death itself mediates birth into a more divine existence. What we call life is death, what we call dying is life. The same idea lies in the egg, which just thereby enters into the closest union with the sacrifice of Agamemnon’s daughter. Symbol and myth join and illumine each other. The archaeological explanation has been content, with the sarcophagus picture just discussed as well, to establish the subject of the representation itself, and to assign to all details the right relation to the whole. The sepulchral meaning has been left wholly out of the question, and the archaeological task therefore only half solved. In that the monuments were detached from their original destination, the funerary significance receded wholly into the background. Art archaeology has thereby deprived itself of the best fruits of its labor. A field still little trodden opens before research. The difficulty of the task must not deter us. The goal is set, the prize worth every effort.

e: Summary of Contents. First Treatise. pp. 1–297. The Three Mystery Eggs. § 1. pp. 1–27. Description of the tomb painting on pl. 3. — The eggs and their double color. — Examples of the same combination on monuments and in authors. — Its significance. — The two-colored egg and the wreath in the Bacchic mysteries. § 2. pp. 27–38. The egg as a sign of Bacchic initiation on funerary monuments. Consideration of the individual monuments, in particular of a still unpublished marble fragment from Munich, of a tomb candelabrum of the Karlsruhe Museum, of a Vulcian balsamarium. § 3. pp. 38–48. Consideration of the sarcophagus of Santa Chiara. — Significance of the egg in the myth of Protesilaus and Laodamia. § 4. pp. 48–64. Enumeration of the egg finds in ancient tombs. — Eggs of burnt clay. — Determination of the significance of the terracotta and of its relation to the physical foundation of the Bacchic divine nature. — Consideration of bronze in its relation to Dionysus, Achilles, and as tomb material. § 5 and 6. pp. 64–75. Dionysian women’s life. — Its significance in funerary scenes. — In particular veils, monile, cloak clasps. § 7. pp. 75–85. Significance of the moon. — Its relation to the Bacchic egg, to the mother goddesses, and to woman in general. § 8. pp. 85–114. Significance of the lamp on the Pamphili tomb painting. — Its relation to the nocturnal festivals of Dionysus and to the moon. — Oil and salt in their cultic significance. — Consideration of the individual monuments and myths in which the lamp emerges significantly, in particular the fable of Psyche. — Fire and light in the various stages of their purity. — Mystery significance. — Connection of the egg with the principle of light. — Omphalos and phoenix egg. — Progress from materiality to immateriality, the principle of human and of religious development. § 9. pp. 114–122. The moon in its relation to death, especially in the world of the tombs. — The union of becoming and passing away in the moon and in the lunar sphere. The heavenly earth as a link between two worlds in the mysteries and the tombs. — Lunar animals, especially the ape in its sepulchral meaning.

e: Ocnus the Rope Plaiter. § 1. pp. 301–307. Compilation of the monuments and testimonies. § 2. pp. 307–315. Determination of the significance of plaiting and weaving, of spun threads and of the rope. § 3. pp. 315–318. Significance of swamp plants in the ancient nature religion; the ultronea creatio and its sanctity. § 4. pp. 318–325. Continuation of the consideration of swamps and swamp plants with particular reference to Egypt, the homeland of the Ocnus symbol. § 5. pp. 325–328. Continuation of the consideration of swamps and swamp plants. — Their equation with human hair and the relation of both to hetaeric sexual mingling. § 6. pp. 328–341. Continuation of the consideration of swamps and swamp plants. — Demonstration of their sanctity in myths, in cult practices, and in connection with individual deities. — Application of these views to the rope of Ocnus. § 7. pp. 341–347. The Mantuan Ocnus. — Proof of the identity of his divine nature with that of the rope plaiter. — Consideration of the name Vianor and of its relation to the sanctity of the swamps. § 8. pp. 347–349. Historical connection of Boeotia with Mantua; the Cadmeans in the north of Italy. § 9. pp. 349–354. Ocnus-Aucnus. — Etymology and meaning of the word. — Various transformations and turns of the meaning according to their inner connection. § 10. pp. 354–361. The augural significance of the king heron Ocnus. — Connection of the same with that of the rope plaiter. — Religious significance of swamp birds, in particular of herons and storks. — Their names as names of peoples, in particular Pelasgians, Tyrrhenians, Rutulians, Ardeates. § 11. pp. 361–370. Continuation of the consideration of individual features of the Ocnus pictures. — The old age of the rope plaiter. — Significance and connection of the same with the fundamental idea of the Ocnus symbol. § 12. pp. 370–373. Transition to the consideration of the second main part [PDF 438] — 426 — of the Ocnus representation, the gnawing she-ass. — Antithesis of the creative and the dissolving principle. Significance of the visible end of the rope. § 13. pp. 373–374. The significance of the ass. § 14. pp. 374–377. Continued. — The phallic significance of the animal. § 15. pp. 377–379. Continued. — Connection of the ass with Priapus, Silenus, Dionysus, Vulcan, Midas, Vesta. § 16. pp. 379–382. Continued. — Connection of the ass with Apollo Hyperboreus and with Artemis. — The ass among Scythians, Carmanians, Indians. § 17. pp. 382–386. Continued. — The religious significance of the ass among Phoenicians, Jews, Assyrians, Egyptians. — Its Typhonian-evil nature. § 18. pp. 386–389. Continued. — The Typhonian significance of the ass demonstrated in a series of mythological formations. § 19. pp. 389–392. Application of the view obtained to the Ocnus symbol. — Significance of the female sex of the gnawing she-ass. § 20. pp. 392–394. Antithesis of the plaiting and the devouring principle. — The eternal flux of the phenomenal world brought forth by the united labor of both. § 21. pp. 395–400. Admission of the Ocnus symbol into the tombs. — Sepulchral meaning of the same. — Ocnus as penitent of the underworld. — His connection with the Danaids. — Elucidation of the myth of the Danaids and of the mystery idea contained in it. § 22. pp. 401–407. Antithesis of the scene of the tomb frieze with that of the pediment of the aedicula, of Ocnus doing penance in the underworld with the boy Achilles instructed by Chiron in lyre playing, of uninitiated with initiated life. Sepulchral meaning of Achilles. § 23. pp. 407–409. Further development of this antithesis. — The subjugation of tellurism by the Apollonian luminous nature. § 24. pp. 409–412. The resting Ocnus of the Pamphili tomb. — Antithesis of the penitent and the liberated old man. — Juxtaposition of the original physical significance and the highest spiritualization of the Ocnus symbol. Addenda. Emphasis on some funerary vessels described in the Museo Campana. — On the Delphic omphalos. — The egg in connection with the sacrifice of Iphigenia.
